topics.title: Combat Robot Design Archetypes
topics.scope_note: The complete taxonomy of combat robot design archetypes, biased toward 1 lb antweight and plastic antweight: how each works, what it counters, what counters it, realistic weight budgets, and the jargon around them.

topics.title: Batteries & Power: Selection, Budgeting and Electrical Safety for Antweights
topics.scope_note: Covers LiPo/LiHV/Li-ion/LiFePO4/NiMH battery chemistry, cell-count and capacity selection, C-rating reality, voltage sag, power budgeting, charging practice, and electrical/mounting safety for 1 lb antweight and plastic antweight combat robots.

topics.title: Design Math: The 1 lb Antweight Engineering Toolkit
topics.scope_note: The complete engineering-math reference for designing a 1 lb (454 g) antweight combat robot: rotational dynamics and weapon inertia, gyroscopic effects, drivetrain and traction, electrical motor/battery sizing, structural impact and armor, weight/CG budgeting, and weapon bite geometry. Every formula carries a fully-worked numeric example using realistic antweight-scale values so an LLM (or a builder) can plug in their own numbers and compute a real answer.

topics.title: Drive Motors & Drivetrain Sizing
topics.scope_note: Drive motors, gearboxes, wheels, hubs, and drivetrain sizing for 1 lb antweight and plastic antweight combat robots, covering FingerTech, Repeat Robotics, N-series, Pololu, and brushless options plus the physics formulas used to size a drivetrain.

topics.title: Plastic Antweight (1 lb All-Plastic) Combat Robots
topics.scope_note: Complete reference for the 1 lb / 454 g all-plastic antweight combat robot class: exact ruleset wording and org-to-org variation on allowed/banned materials and metal exemptions, why the class exists, the dominant weapon/drive archetypes and why the plastic-only rule reshapes the meta, concrete build specs with per-part weight budgets, 3D printing material/settings/design-pattern practice, and where the community shares open-source designs.

topics.title: Competition Strategy, Driving and the Antweight Meta
topics.scope_note: Matchup analysis across the antweight archetypes, driving skill, event and tournament strategy, and why the modern 1 lb meta looks the way it does.

topics.title: Weapon Motors: Selection & Sizing for Antweights
topics.scope_note: How to pick and size a spinning-weapon motor for 1 lb antweight and plastic antweight combat robots, using the FPV-drone brushless motor size ladder (11xx-28xx). Covers KV selection, motor constants, drivetrain layout (direct/belt/gear), spin-up time, thermal and mechanical failure modes, mounting, and worked numeric examples.

topics.title: Weight Classes, Rulesets & Safety Regulations
topics.scope_note: Covers the full combat-robotics weight class ladder (fairyweight through heavyweight), the major rulesets that govern competitions (SPARC, NHRL, RoboGames, BattleBots, AWS/UK, European/Australian variants), weight bonuses for walkers and multibots, banned weapons and materials, safety and inspection requirements, and match/judging rules. Every judgement is biased toward 1 lb antweight and plastic antweight, the classes most builders start in.

entities.name: Vertical Disc Spinner
entities.summary: A toothed disc spinning on a horizontal axis at the front of the robot, throwing opponents upward. The dominant competitive antweight archetype.
pros: Vertical hits convert into lift, which removes the opponent's traction and often self-rights you
Impact forces load the weapon bearings axially in a direction the chassis can brace against
Gyroscopic forces are largely harmless and can even aid self-righting
Works when inverted if the weapon clears both ways
cons: Gyroscopic precession makes the robot resist turning and 'gyro dance' across the floor
Vulnerable to being wedged under before the weapon engages
Needs meaningful ground clearance control, or the disc hits the floor
entities.notes: The vertical disc is the default competitive answer at 1 lb because its damage vector (upward) is the one a 454 g robot cannot brace against. A 1 lb bot weighs little enough that even a modest vertical hit lifts it clear of the floor, ending its ability to drive or defend for a second or more. Modern builds pair the disc with a front wedge so the archetype also wins the ground game it would otherwise lose to a dedicated wedge.

extra.typical_weapon_motor: 2205-2306 brushless outrunner, 1800-2600KV on 3S-4S
extra.typical_drive: Two brushed 16mm/N20 gearmotors, or brushless drive pods

entities.name: Vertical Bar Spinner
entities.summary: A long bar spinning on a horizontal axis. Nearly all the stored energy sits in the two tips, giving very high energy for the mass.
pros: Mass concentrated at the tips maximises moment of inertia per gram
A long bar reaches past an opponent's wedge better than a small disc
Simple to make: bar stock, two teeth, a hub
cons: Long bar means a long spin-up and large gyroscopic effects
A bent bar after a hard hit becomes an unbalanced bar, which destroys bearings
Harder to armour the weapon arc than a compact disc
entities.notes: Bar versus disc at the same mass is a trade of energy against spin-up and robustness. A bar of length L about its centre has I = mL^2/12, so doubling length quadruples inertia at constant mass. That is free energy on paper, and a longer spin-up plus a bigger gyro problem in practice.

extra.typical_weapon_motor: 2205-2306 brushless outrunner, 1600-2300KV on 3S-4S
extra.typical_drive: Two brushed 16mm gearmotors or brushless pods

entities.name: Horizontal Bar Spinner
entities.summary: A bar spinning on a vertical axis, sweeping a circle far wider than the robot. Hits from any direction in the horizontal plane.
pros: Enormous reach — it threatens well outside the robot's footprint
Attacks the whole horizontal plane, so approach angle matters less
Devastating against other spinners' exposed weapons and against wheels
cons: Every hit throws the robot backwards as hard as the opponent — self-inflicted chaos
Loses to a low wedge that gets under before the bar can bite
Needs a lot of floor clearance discipline; scraping the floor kills energy
entities.notes: Horizontals have fallen out of top-level antweight favour because a wedge beats them reliably: the bar passes harmlessly over a well-built wedge while the wedge drives under. They remain excellent against other spinners and against anything with exposed wheels, and they are still the archetype most likely to end a match in one hit.

extra.typical_weapon_motor: 2205-2812 brushless outrunner, 1400-2200KV on 3S-4S
extra.typical_drive: Two brushed gearmotors, often with extra ground clearance control

entities.name: Undercutter
entities.summary: A horizontal bar sweeping very low to the floor, striking beneath an opponent's armour line at wheels and ground clearance.
pros: Defeats the wedge that beats an ordinary horizontal — it goes under the wedge's edge
Attacks wheels and drive pods, which are the least armoured parts of most robots
Very hard for a low flat robot to present a safe face to
cons: Extremely sensitive to floor contact; a few millimetres of ride-height error destroys the weapon
Arena floor seams and dents are a real hazard
Difficult to build with adequate ground clearance in 1 lb
entities.notes: The undercutter is the specific counter to the wedge-heavy antweight meta. Because it runs below the wedge's leading edge, the wedge's shape no longer protects it. The cost is precision: the weapon must run a few millimetres off the floor and stay there after impacts.

extra.typical_weapon_motor: 2205-2306 brushless outrunner, 1400-2000KV on 3S-4S
extra.typical_drive: Two brushed gearmotors with protected wheels

entities.name: Drum Spinner
entities.summary: A wide toothed cylinder spinning on a horizontal axis low at the front. Combines a vertical spinner's damage vector with exceptional bite.
pros: Best bite of any spinner: the large diameter and low mounting scoop under an opponent's edge
Wide face means you rarely miss laterally
Compact and rigid — the drum is its own structural member
Low gyroscopic effect compared to a large disc at the same energy
cons: Lower moment of inertia per gram than a bar, so less stored energy for the mass
Machining or printing a true, balanced drum is harder than cutting a disc
Dead-shaft drum construction is fiddly at 1 lb scale
entities.notes: Drums are arguably the best all-round antweight weapon: they hit upward like a vertical spinner but engage far more reliably because the drum body itself acts as a wedge that pulls the opponent in. The tradeoff is energy density — a drum's mass sits at a smaller radius than a bar's tips.

extra.typical_weapon_motor: 2205-2812 brushless outrunner, 1600-2400KV on 3S-4S
extra.typical_drive: Two brushed 16mm gearmotors or brushless pods

entities.name: Beater Bar
entities.summary: A simple bar spinning on a horizontal axis at the front — a drum's geometry without a drum's fabrication cost.
pros: Cheapest real weapon to build — bar stock, a hub and a motor
Good bite from the low horizontal-axis mounting
Forgiving: a beater bar that takes a hit usually still works
cons: Much lower energy than a proper drum or disc of the same mass
Little reach; you must close the distance to use it
Easy to bend
entities.notes: The beater bar is the standard first weapon for a new antweight or plastic ant builder. It teaches spinner driving, bite and spin-up management without the cost or the balancing precision of a disc, and it is genuinely competitive at club level.

extra.typical_weapon_motor: 1806-2205 brushless outrunner, 2000-2800KV on 2S-3S
extra.typical_drive: Two brushed N20 or 16mm gearmotors

entities.name: Eggbeater
entities.summary: An open cage weapon spinning on a horizontal axis — light for its diameter, and an excellent self-righter.
pros: Large diameter for little mass, so it reaches over wedges
The cage shape makes self-righting almost automatic
Open structure sheds debris rather than jamming
cons: Lower energy density than a solid disc of the same mass
The cage deforms on hard hits and is awkward to true up again
More drag than a solid weapon
entities.notes: Eggbeaters trade raw energy for geometry. The wide, tall cage engages opponents a low disc would pass under, and the same shape lets the robot roll itself back over. In plastic ant they are attractive because a printed cage is light and cheap to replace.

extra.typical_weapon_motor: 2205-2306 brushless outrunner, 1800-2400KV on 3S
extra.typical_drive: Two brushed gearmotors

entities.name: Full-Body Shell Spinner
entities.summary: The robot's entire outer shell rotates on a vertical axis, so every approach angle meets the weapon.
pros: No safe angle of approach — the whole robot is the weapon
Huge moment of inertia because all the mass sits at maximum radius
The shell doubles as the armour
cons: Very hard to build in 1 lb: the support ring, bearings and drive must all fit inside
Any imbalance is catastrophic because the weapon is the whole robot
Self-righting is difficult, and the shell can ground out
entities.notes: Shell spinners are the highest-energy archetype per gram because every gram sits at the maximum possible radius. At 1 lb the engineering is genuinely hard — you need a large-diameter bearing race, a drive system that fits inside it, and near-perfect balance — which is why they are rarer at antweight than at beetleweight and above.

extra.typical_weapon_motor: 2812-2814 brushless outrunner, 1000-1800KV on 3S-4S
extra.typical_drive: Two brushed gearmotors inside the shell, or hub drive

entities.name: Full-Body Ring Spinner
entities.summary: A variant of the shell spinner where a ring rotates around a chassis that stays upright, usually on a vertical axis.
pros: All the shell spinner's omnidirectional threat
The open centre makes internal access far easier than a closed shell
Ring geometry gives maximum inertia for the material used
cons: The ring must be supported at several points or it deflects and jams
Bearing and guide-roller wear is constant
Complex to make accurately at 1 lb
entities.notes: The ring spinner solves the shell spinner's maintenance problem — you can reach the electronics without removing the weapon — at the cost of needing a ring that stays round under load. Guide rollers rather than a single bearing are the usual answer.

extra.typical_weapon_motor: 2812 brushless outrunner, 1000-1800KV on 4S
extra.typical_drive: Two brushed gearmotors within the ring

entities.name: Melty Brain
entities.summary: The entire robot spins continuously and translates by pulsing its drive in sync with rotation, using an accelerometer to know which way is forward.
pros: No weapon motor needed — the drivetrain is the weapon
Omnidirectional threat like a shell spinner, with far simpler mechanics
Weapon energy and mobility come from the same system
cons: Requires custom firmware and an accelerometer; this is a software project as much as a mechanical one
Translation is slow and imprecise compared to normal driving
Loses all weapon energy the moment it needs to manoeuvre
Hard to drive and hard for judges to score
entities.notes: Melty brain — also called translational drift — is the most software-dependent archetype in combat robotics. The controller reads centripetal acceleration to estimate heading, then pulses each drive motor once per revolution so net thrust points in the commanded direction. It is a brilliant solution to getting spinner energy without a weapon motor, and a difficult one to make reliable.

extra.typical_weapon_motor: No separate weapon motor — the drive spins the robot
extra.typical_drive: Two brushed or brushless motors run continuously

entities.name: Overhead Saw
entities.summary: A spinning blade on a pivoting arm that comes down onto the top of an opponent.
pros: Attacks the top surface, which is usually the thinnest armour
Visually dramatic and scores well on aggression
Can be used to hold an opponent down
cons: Needs both a weapon motor and an arm actuator inside 454 g
Very little energy actually transfers — saws cut, and combat armour resists cutting
The arm is a structural weak point
entities.notes: Saws look spectacular and rarely win. In 1 lb the weight spent on an arm mechanism plus a blade motor buys less damage than the same grams in a disc. They persist because they are fun and because a saw that pins an opponent scores control points.

extra.typical_weapon_motor: 1806-2205 brushless outrunner, 2000-3000KV on 3S
extra.typical_drive: Two brushed gearmotors

entities.name: Flywheel Spinner
entities.summary: A thick, small-diameter disc chosen for mass concentration rather than reach — high energy in a compact package.
pros: Compact and easy to armour around
Rigid — a thick disc resists bending far better than a bar
Shorter spin-up than a long bar of equal energy
cons: Little reach; you must get close
Mass at small radius means you need high rpm for the same energy
entities.notes: A flywheel trades radius for thickness. Because energy scales with I and I scales with r^2, a small disc must spin much faster for the same energy — which puts the demand on the motor and the bearings rather than on the structure.

extra.typical_weapon_motor: 2205-2306 brushless outrunner, 1600-2200KV on 4S
extra.typical_drive: Two brushed gearmotors

entities.name: Wedge
entities.summary: A low inclined plane whose job is to get beneath an opponent and take away their traction. The foundation of control robotics.
pros: No weapon motor means the entire weight budget goes to drive and armour
Beats every archetype whose weapon cannot reach below its own edge
Extremely reliable — there is almost nothing to break
Cheapest competitive robot to build
cons: Cannot generate damage, so it must win on control and judges' decisions
Loses to anything that attacks below the wedge line
A wedge that gets high-sided is helpless
entities.notes: A wedge wins by making the opponent's weapon irrelevant. Ground clearance and edge quality matter more than anything else: the leading edge must be thin, hard, flat against the floor, and backed so it does not curl. A wedge that lifts even two millimetres off the floor stops being a wedge.

extra.typical_weapon_motor: None — the wedge is passive
extra.typical_drive: Four-wheel drive or two powerful brushed gearmotors

entities.name: Wedge + Vertical Spinner Hybrid
entities.summary: A vertical spinner with wedge-shaped forks flanking the weapon, so the robot wins the ground game and still carries damage.
pros: Removes the vertical spinner's single biggest weakness — losing the wedge war
The forks feed opponents into the weapon rather than letting them ride over
Dominant in the modern antweight meta
cons: Packaging is tight: forks, weapon and drive all compete for the front of the robot
The forks must not foul the weapon arc
Heavier than a pure spinner, so weapon energy is slightly reduced
entities.notes: This is the defining configuration of modern competitive antweight. A bare vertical spinner loses to a wedge; a bare wedge loses to anything that can out-control it. Bolting low hinged forks either side of a vertical weapon means the robot wins the initial engagement and then applies damage. Almost every top 1 lb design converges on some version of this.

extra.typical_weapon_motor: 2205-2306 brushless outrunner, 1800-2400KV on 3S-4S
extra.typical_drive: Two brushed 16mm gearmotors or brushless pods

entities.name: Forkbot
entities.summary: A control robot with thin hinged forks that ride on the floor, sliding under an opponent before they can get under you.
pros: Hinged forks self-level to the floor, beating fixed wedges on uneven arenas
Cheap, light and easy to replace between matches
Forks can be made sacrificial so damage costs nothing
cons: Forks bend, and a bent fork is worse than no fork
No damage output at all
Can be defeated by an opponent with even lower clearance
entities.notes: Forks beat fixed wedges because they float. A rigid wedge is only as good as the flattest part of the arena; hinged forks follow the floor and stay in contact. Make them from spring steel or hardened stock and expect to straighten them between matches.

extra.typical_weapon_motor: None — forks are passive
extra.typical_drive: Four-wheel drive or two high-torque brushed gearmotors

entities.name: Control Bot
entities.summary: A weaponless robot built entirely around drivetrain and armour, winning on pushing, pinning, ring-outs and judges' decisions.
pros: Every gram not spent on a weapon goes into being unkillable
Reliability wins tournaments — a bot that finishes every match accumulates decisions
Ideal first build: teaches driving, which matters more than weapons at this level
cons: Must win on judges' scores, which is never guaranteed
Against a damaging opponent you have to be perfect for three minutes
entities.notes: The control bot is the most underrated archetype for new builders. At 1 lb, more matches are lost to broken robots than to out-designed ones, and a robot that reliably drives for three minutes beats a fragile spinner more often than beginners expect.

extra.typical_weapon_motor: None
extra.typical_drive: Four-wheel drive, high torque, maximum traction

entities.name: Invertible Brick
entities.summary: A symmetric armoured box that drives identically either way up, built to survive rather than to damage.
pros: Being flipped costs nothing — no self-righting mechanism needed
Extremely simple and hard to disable
The saved srimech weight goes into armour
cons: No damage output
Wheels must protrude both ways, which exposes them to undercutters
entities.notes: Invertibility is the cheapest possible self-righting mechanism: build the robot so being upside down does not matter. At antweight this is nearly always the right call, because a dedicated srimech costs grams a 454 g robot cannot spare.

extra.typical_weapon_motor: None
extra.typical_drive: Four-wheel drive with wheels protruding top and bottom

entities.name: Lifter
entities.summary: A powered arm that pivots upward to lift an opponent's front off the floor, removing their traction and control.
pros: Controls opponents without needing to damage them
Slow, controllable lift is better for carrying an opponent than a flipper's single throw
Can hold an opponent up for the whole match, which scores heavily on control
cons: The arm is a lever that transmits impact straight into its pivot
Needs a wedge-quality edge to get under in the first place
Slow — a spinner will hit you during the lift
entities.notes: A lifter is a wedge with a follow-through. The hard part is not the lifting, it is the getting under: a lifter whose leading edge is not as good as a dedicated wedge's never gets to use its arm.

extra.typical_weapon_motor: Geared brushed motor or a modified servo driving the arm
extra.typical_drive: Two to four brushed gearmotors

entities.name: Linear Actuator Lifter
entities.summary: A lifter driven by a leadscrew or linear actuator rather than a rotating arm, giving high force at low speed.
pros: Very high force for the power consumed
Holds position without drawing current, so you can pin indefinitely
Compact compared to a long arm
cons: Slow — seconds per stroke
Leadscrews jam when bent or contaminated
Complex to build at 1 lb
entities.notes: Linear actuators give a 1 lb robot genuine crushing or lifting force because a screw multiplies torque enormously. The price is speed: an actuator that can lift a robot takes a second or more to do it, which is a long time in a match.

extra.typical_weapon_motor: Small leadscrew actuator or geared motor with a screw drive
extra.typical_drive: Two to four brushed gearmotors

entities.name: Spring Flipper
entities.summary: An arm that releases stored spring energy in a single stroke to throw an opponent into the air.
pros: A successful flip can end a match instantly against a non-invertible robot
Beats vertical spinners by attacking them from underneath, where they cannot respond
No compressed gas system needed, so it is legal everywhere
cons: One shot, then a slow re-cock
Useless against an invertible opponent
The cocking mechanism is complex and a common failure point
entities.notes: Spring flippers are the practical flipper for 1 lb, because pneumatics do not scale down well. The design problem is the latch: it must hold the full spring force, release cleanly on command, and survive being hit. Most antweight flipper failures are latch failures.

extra.typical_weapon_motor: Spring or elastic store, cocked by a geared motor or servo
extra.typical_drive: Two to four brushed gearmotors

entities.name: Electric Flipper
entities.summary: A flipper driven directly by a high-torque motor or a released flywheel rather than a gas or spring store.
pros: Repeatable — no gas to run out of and no re-cock cycle in the flywheel variant
Simpler plumbing than pneumatics and legal under every ruleset
Doubles as a self-righting mechanism
cons: Much less instantaneous power than a spring or gas system
Draws heavily on the same battery as the drive
Gearbox takes the full shock of every flip
entities.notes: Electric flippers trade peak power for repeatability. At 1 lb the usual approach is a motor with a very large reduction driving a short, stiff arm — enough to upend an opponent even if it will not throw them across the arena.

extra.typical_weapon_motor: High-torque geared brushed motor, or a spun-up flywheel released into the arm
extra.typical_drive: Two to four brushed gearmotors

entities.name: Pneumatic Flipper
entities.summary: A flipper driven by compressed gas. Common at larger weights and rare at antweight, where the system's mass does not fit the budget.
pros: Enormous instantaneous power — the most violent flip available
Fast reset compared to a mechanically cocked spring
cons: Cylinder, regulator and valve rarely fit inside 454 g
Pressure systems attract extra safety scrutiny and are banned or restricted at some events
Leaks end your day
entities.notes: Pneumatics are essentially a larger-class archetype. They are documented here because antweight builders copy the geometry downward using springs — the arm, pivot and latch design carry over even though the power source does not. Check your event's rules before building any pressurised system.

extra.typical_weapon_motor: CO2 or HPA cylinder, regulator, valve and ram
extra.typical_drive: Two to four brushed gearmotors

entities.name: Grabber / Clamper
entities.summary: Two jaws that close on an opponent so the driver can carry them to a wall, a hazard or the pit.
pros: Completely neutralises a spinner once clamped — the weapon cannot reach you
Total control: you decide where the opponent goes
Scores extremely well on control with judges
cons: You must survive the approach against a live weapon to clamp at all
Useless if the grab fails, and grabs fail often
Mechanically the most complex archetype to build in 1 lb
entities.notes: The grabber is the theoretical counter to every spinner and the hardest archetype to execute. Once you have hold of a spinner it is finished, but closing the distance to a weapon at full speed with jaws open is exactly the scenario spinners are built for.

extra.typical_weapon_motor: Geared brushed motor or linear actuator driving the jaws
extra.typical_drive: Two to four brushed gearmotors, high torque

entities.name: Crusher
entities.summary: A hardened beak or spike driven by a very high-force, low-speed actuator to punch through an opponent's armour.
pros: Does damage no spinner can do — it pierces rather than dents
Holding an opponent pierced is total control
Immune to the energy-transfer problem that limits spinners
cons: Extremely slow; you must already have the opponent held still
Hard to generate meaningful force in 454 g
Very complex for the result
entities.notes: Crushers scale badly downward. The force needed to pierce even thin armour requires gearing that makes the mechanism slow and heavy, and a 1 lb robot has neither the weight budget nor the traction to hold an opponent still while it works. They appear at antweight mainly as novelty or demonstration builds.

extra.typical_weapon_motor: Leadscrew actuator or heavily geared brushed motor
extra.typical_drive: Two to four brushed gearmotors

entities.name: Hammer / Axe
entities.summary: A weighted head swung through an arc to concentrate its energy into a single point of impact.
pros: Concentrated point impact can punch through thin top armour
Doubles as a self-righting mechanism
Scores well on aggression and looks dramatic
cons: Very low total energy compared to a spinner — the arm only accelerates over a short arc
Must be almost touching the opponent to land a hit
The arm and its pivot take the full reaction force
entities.notes: Hammers suffer from a simple energy problem: a spinner accumulates energy over seconds of spin-up, while a hammer only has the arc of its swing. At 1 lb the head mass you can afford is small enough that the result is rarely decisive. They remain popular because they self-right, look good, and are satisfying to drive.

extra.typical_weapon_motor: High-torque geared motor, or a spring/gas store released into the arm
extra.typical_drive: Two to four brushed gearmotors

entities.name: Hammer Saw
entities.summary: A hammer whose head is a powered spinning blade, combining an overhead strike with a cutting weapon.
pros: Keeps working after the swing lands — it grinds as well as strikes
Two threats from one mechanism
cons: Two actuators plus a blade inside 454 g is a severe packaging problem
Wiring to a moving arm is a reliability liability
Neither function is as good as a dedicated version of it
entities.notes: The hammer saw is a larger-class idea that rarely survives the 1 lb weight budget. Documented for completeness; if you want an overhead threat at antweight, a plain hammer is lighter and a vertical spinner does more damage.

extra.typical_weapon_motor: Small brushless outrunner on the head plus an arm actuator
extra.typical_drive: Two to four brushed gearmotors

entities.name: Thwackbot
entities.summary: A robot that spins on its own axis so a rigid tail sweeps around and strikes — no weapon motor required.
pros: No weapon motor, no weapon ESC, no weapon battery draw
Very simple and very robust
Tail doubles as protection and as a self-righting lever
cons: Cannot attack and manoeuvre at the same time — spinning means not driving
Energy is limited by drivetrain torque and traction
Judges often score it poorly on aggression because it looks passive between swings
entities.notes: The thwackbot is the cheapest way to have a weapon. Its fundamental limitation is that its weapon and its mobility are the same system: while it is spinning up to strike, it is not going anywhere, and a competent opponent simply drives away or gets underneath.

extra.typical_weapon_motor: None — the drivetrain swings the tail
extra.typical_drive: Two powerful brushed gearmotors with good traction

entities.name: Overhead Thwack
entities.summary: A thwackbot whose tail swings in a vertical plane, striking downward rather than sweeping horizontally.
pros: Strikes the top armour without needing a weapon motor
Self-rights naturally
Simple and hard to break
cons: Requires sharp drivetrain reversals to build momentum
Inconsistent — the arm does not always come over cleanly
Low energy
entities.notes: An overhead thwack uses drivetrain reversal to throw a pivoting arm over the top of the robot. It is a clever way to get an overhead strike for almost no weight, and it is unreliable enough that it is best treated as a secondary threat on a control bot.

extra.typical_weapon_motor: None — momentum from the drivetrain flips the arm over
extra.typical_drive: Two high-torque brushed gearmotors

entities.name: Rammer
entities.summary: A reinforced nose and a powerful drivetrain — damage comes from the whole robot's momentum.
pros: Simple and durable
All the weight goes into drive and structure
Can genuinely damage lightly built opponents
cons: A 454 g robot carries very little momentum — ramming damage is modest
Loses the wedge war to anything with a proper edge
Every impact is taken by your own structure too
entities.notes: Ramming works better in heavier classes where kinetic energy scales with mass. At 1 lb the energy in a full-speed ram is small next to even a modest spinner. Ram robots at antweight are better understood as control bots with a hard front.

extra.typical_weapon_motor: None
extra.typical_drive: Four-wheel drive, geared for acceleration

entities.name: Multibot / Swarm
entities.summary: The class weight limit divided between two or more robots that fight as a team.
pros: Two robots can pincer an opponent from both sides at once
Losing one robot does not necessarily lose the match
Forces the opponent to split attention
cons: Each robot is tiny and individually fragile
Usually both must be immobilised to lose, but check your ruleset — some require only one
Driving two robots on one transmitter is genuinely hard
entities.notes: Multibots split 454 g into pieces that are each easy to destroy, in exchange for numbers and positioning. Rules vary sharply on what counts as a knockout, so read the specific event's ruleset before committing to the strategy.

extra.typical_weapon_motor: Usually one armed robot and one wedge, or two wedges
extra.typical_drive: Two small brushed gearmotors per robot

entities.name: Walker
entities.summary: Legged locomotion instead of wheels, which most rulesets reward with a large weight bonus.
pros: A true walker bonus can double the weight limit, which is an enormous advantage
Immune to having its wheels attacked
Novel and popular with crowds and judges
cons: Walking mechanisms are slow, complex and fragile
Qualifying as a 'true walker' is strictly judged — no wheels or cams touching the ground
The mechanism eats much of the bonus it earns
entities.notes: Weight bonuses for genuine legged locomotion are substantial — commonly up to double the class limit for a true walker, with a smaller bonus for shufflers. The catch is that qualifying is strict and the mechanism is heavy, so the bonus is less free than it looks. Confirm the exact bonus with your event before designing around it.

extra.typical_weapon_motor: Varies — the bonus weight usually funds a real weapon
extra.typical_drive: Linkage-driven legs powered by brushed gearmotors

entities.name: Shuffler
entities.summary: A robot using cams or eccentric linkages to shuffle along, qualifying for a partial non-wheeled weight bonus at many events.
pros: Earns a weight bonus at most events without a full walking linkage
Simpler than a true walker
cons: Smaller bonus than a true walker
Slow and imprecise to drive
Some rulesets classify shufflers as wheeled and give no bonus at all
entities.notes: Shufflers sit between wheels and true walkers. Because classification varies by organisation, the bonus is the first thing to confirm — a shuffler judged to be wheeled is simply a slow robot with no compensation.

extra.typical_weapon_motor: Varies — bonus weight typically funds a spinner
extra.typical_drive: Cam or crank-driven feet

entities.name: Tracked Robot
entities.summary: Tracks instead of wheels, for maximum ground contact and a very low, stable platform.
pros: Large contact patch gives excellent pushing traction
Naturally low and stable
Tracks can absorb hits that would break a wheel
cons: Thrown tracks are a very common and match-ending failure
Heavy for the traction gained
Steering scrubs and wastes power
entities.notes: Tracks look ideal for a pushing robot and usually disappoint at 1 lb. A thrown track is an instant loss, and at antweight scale it is hard to build a tensioner robust enough to prevent it. Most builders who try tracks return to wheels.

extra.typical_weapon_motor: Usually none, or a small lifter
extra.typical_drive: Two brushed gearmotors driving track loops

entities.name: Passive Spike / Static Weapon
entities.summary: Fixed spikes, blades or horns with no moving parts, relying on the robot's own motion to do damage.
pros: Weighs almost nothing and cannot fail
Can catch and disrupt an opposing spinner's weapon
Legal everywhere and needs no extra electronics
cons: Almost no damage potential on its own
Can snag on the arena or on your own opponent awkwardly
entities.notes: Static weapons are best understood as an accessory rather than an archetype: a spike on a control bot occasionally turns a push into a puncture, and costs nothing to carry.

extra.typical_weapon_motor: None
extra.typical_drive: Two to four brushed gearmotors

entities.name: Defensive / Armour-Only Bot
entities.summary: A robot built purely to survive, betting that the opponent breaks itself or runs out of time.
pros: Spinners frequently destroy themselves on heavy armour
Simple, cheap and very hard to knock out
An excellent way to learn what actually survives
cons: Wins almost nothing on aggression or damage, so decisions go against you
Boring to drive and to watch
entities.notes: A pure armour bot exploits the fact that a spinner's energy has to go somewhere. Against a hard, compliant, well-braced target, much of it goes back into the spinner. It rarely wins tournaments but it is an instructive build and a genuine counter to fragile high-energy opponents.

extra.typical_weapon_motor: None
extra.typical_drive: Two to four brushed gearmotors, protected

entities.name: Bite
entities.summary: How deeply a spinning weapon's tooth/edge engages an opponent's armor per revolution before sliding off -- determined by weapon RPM relative to the combined driving speed of both robots, not by tip speed or KE alone. Lower weapon RPM (for the same tip speed, i.e. bigger diameter/lower KV) generally gives more bite because the tooth has more time to dig in per revolution.
entities.notes: Bite depth is set by how far the robots close in the time between tooth arrivals. With a weapon at N rpm and t teeth, impacts arrive at N/60*t per second, so maximum bite = closing speed / that rate. Fewer teeth and lower rpm mean deeper bite. This is why a hard-hitting spinner often runs one or two teeth rather than six: a six-tooth weapon at 20,000 rpm presents a tooth every 0.5 ms, giving a bite measured in microns — it polishes the opponent instead of cutting them.

entities.name: Tooth Count
entities.summary: The number of impacting features on a spinning weapon; trades bite depth against hit frequency and balance.
entities.notes: One tooth gives maximum bite but an inherently unbalanced weapon unless counterweighted. Two teeth balance naturally and halve the bite. Three or more are used mainly where the weapon is expected to grind rather than bite. Most competitive antweight discs run one or two effective teeth.

entities.name: Gyro Dance
entities.summary: The wobbling, walking motion a robot with a spinning weapon makes when it turns, caused by gyroscopic precession.
entities.notes: A spinning weapon resists any change to its axis of rotation. When the robot turns, that resistance appears as a torque about a perpendicular axis, which lifts one side of the robot. The robot lands, turns again, lifts again, and appears to dance across the floor. Precession torque = I * omega_weapon * omega_turn, so it grows with weapon inertia, weapon speed and how sharply you turn. Mitigate it by turning more gently, lowering weapon inertia, widening the wheelbase, or lowering the centre of gravity.

entities.name: Gyroscopic Precession
entities.summary: The tendency of a spinning object's rotation axis to react to an applied torque by tilting perpendicular to both the spin axis and the applied torque, rather than in the direction naively expected. In vertical spinners, turning the chassis while the weapon is spinning applies exactly this kind of torque, producing an unwanted tipping reaction.
entities.notes: For a weapon of inertia I spinning at omega_w, turning the robot at omega_t produces a precession torque of I * omega_w * omega_t about the third axis. For a vertical spinner this lifts a wheel; for a horizontal spinner it tries to pitch the robot nose-up or nose-down. It is not a loss mechanism — no energy is consumed — but it strongly affects handling.

entities.name: Tip Speed
entities.summary: The linear speed of the outermost point of a rotating weapon, calculated as RPM x diameter x 0.00436 to get feet/second (the formula SPARC uses for its slow-spinner and open-air-combat speed limits); a key design variable because plastic weapons have a much lower survivable tip speed than metal ones before they self-destruct.
entities.notes: Tip speed = omega * r, where omega = rpm * 2*pi/60. Competitive antweight weapons generally run somewhere in the region of 70-110 m/s. Higher is not automatically better: past a point, extra tip speed reduces bite and increases the share of energy that goes into noise, sparks and your own robot rather than the opponent.

entities.name: Spin-Up Time
entities.summary: How long a weapon takes to reach its operating speed from rest (or from a partial-speed dip after a hit), set by the available average motor torque and the weapon's total moment of inertia. A liability when too long, since the weapon is weak while re-spinning.
entities.notes: Spin-up time scales with weapon inertia and inversely with motor torque. A weapon that takes more than about three seconds is a liability: opponents will box-rush you at the start of the match and attack during every recovery. Reducing weapon mass or moving mass inward shortens spin-up at the cost of stored energy.

entities.name: Wedge War
entities.summary: The opening contest between two robots each trying to get underneath the other.
entities.notes: Won by ground clearance, edge quality, approach angle and drivetrain power — roughly in that order. A wedge with a genuinely flat, sharp, floor-contacting edge beats a thicker or slightly raised one almost regardless of the rest of the robot. Hinged forks usually beat rigid wedges because they follow an imperfect floor.

entities.name: High-Siding
entities.summary: Ending up balanced on an edge, a wedge or the arena wall with the wheels unable to reach the floor.
entities.notes: A high-sided robot is immobilised without being damaged, and is usually counted out. Wide wheels that protrude beyond the chassis, a low centre of gravity, and a body shape that cannot rest stably on an edge all reduce the risk.

entities.name: Tapout
entities.summary: Conceding a match before the count, usually to protect a robot that is about to be destroyed.
entities.notes: Tapping out is a legitimate tournament strategy: a robot that survives to fight the next round is worth more than one extra minute of a lost match. Most rulesets require the team to signal clearly to the referee.

entities.name: Pushout
entities.summary: Forcing an opponent out of the arena, where the ruleset permits it, for an immediate win.
entities.notes: Not every arena has a pushout rule or a low wall. Where one exists, control robots gain enormously: a wedge that cannot damage anything can still win in seconds. Check the arena and the ruleset before relying on it.

entities.name: Box Rush
entities.summary: Charging the opponent the instant the match starts, before their weapon reaches speed.
entities.notes: The standard counter to any spinner with a long spin-up. To defend it, spin up before the count where rules allow, start at an angle rather than square on, and build a robot whose front is safe to be hit at any weapon speed. Driving away from a box rush usually works better than trying to meet it head-on.

entities.name: Self-Righting
entities.summary: Getting back onto your wheels after being flipped.
entities.notes: Three approaches: be invertible so it does not matter, use the weapon's reaction torque to flip yourself, or carry a dedicated mechanism. At 1 lb, invertibility is almost always the right answer because a srimech costs grams the weight budget cannot spare.

entities.name: Srimech
entities.summary: Self-righting mechanism — a dedicated device whose only job is to turn the robot back over.
entities.notes: Common forms are a pivoting arm, a gas or spring ram, or the weapon itself used as a lever. In antweight a srimech is a luxury: most builders make the robot invertible instead and spend the weight on armour or weapon.

entities.name: Invertibility
entities.summary: Being able to drive and fight equally well either way up.
entities.notes: Achieved with wheels that protrude above and below the chassis, a symmetric weapon arc, and a transmitter invert switch that reverses steering when upside down. It is the cheapest form of self-righting and the default choice at antweight.

entities.name: Ground Game
entities.summary: The contest for who gets underneath whom — the part of a match that decides whether weapons ever matter.
entities.notes: A robot that wins the ground game controls the engagement: it chooses when contact happens and at what angle. This is why the modern antweight meta bolts wedges onto spinners rather than choosing between them.

entities.name: Ground Clearance
entities.summary: The gap between the bottom of the robot and the floor.
entities.notes: Less is better for wedges and for not being wedged, but too little means scraping, snagging on arena seams, and losing drive on uneven floors. Wedge edges want to be effectively zero; the rest of the chassis usually wants 1-3 mm at antweight.

entities.name: Weight Budget
entities.summary: The practice of planning, before printing or buying anything, how the full 454g allowance will be split between armor/structure, weapon, drive, electronics and fasteners — critical in plastic ants because printed structure typically consumes over half the total weight, far more than in a metal antweight of the same class.
entities.notes: At antweight the limit is 454 g and every gram is contested. A typical competitive vertical spinner runs roughly 30-35% weapon, 18-22% drive, 22-26% armour and chassis, 10-14% electronics and 7-9% battery. Control robots move the weapon share into drive and armour. Always leave 3-5% slack — robots come in heavier than the CAD says.

entities.name: Dead Shaft
entities.summary: A weapon-mounting scheme where the shaft itself does not rotate -- it is bolted rigidly to the frame -- while the weapon blade/hub and its pulley (bolted together) spin freely around the fixed shaft on bearings pressed into the hub.
entities.notes: Advantages: no need to machine a keyed rotating shaft, easier to swap a weapon belt in the pits since the hub simply lifts off the fixed shaft, and impact loads are reacted directly into the frame rather than through motor bearings. Disadvantage: the dead shaft's mounting screws must be re-torqued carefully every time it's removed, since a loose dead shaft binds and generates heat in the hub bearings.

entities.name: Live Shaft
entities.summary: A weapon mounting where the shaft rotates with the weapon, usually driven directly by the motor.
entities.notes: Simpler and lighter than dead-shaft, and much weaker in bending if supported at only one end. Acceptable for small discs mounted straight onto a motor; risky for anything long or heavy.

entities.name: Wedgelet
entities.summary: A small hinged wedge or fork mounted at the front corners of a robot, usually flanking a weapon.
entities.notes: Wedgelets float on the floor independently of the chassis, so they keep contact over an imperfect arena. They are the mechanism by which a modern vertical spinner also wins the wedge war.

entities.name: Tattu 300mAh 2S 45C LiPo
entities.summary: A very common micro LiPo pack used in antweights and micro FPV, sized to fit inside the tightest 1 lb chassis while still driving a small brushless weapon and a pair of brushed drive motors.
pros: Widely stocked by FPV/combat vendors
Good size-to-power ratio for micro antweights
Burst rating (90C) covers weapon spin-up spikes
cons: 45C continuous is optimistic on paper; real sustained current is lower
300mAh is tight for a 3-minute match with a hungry spinner
entities.notes: Tattu (made by Grepow) is one of the most common battery brands cross-used from FPV drones into antweight combat because the physical sizes and JST/PH-style connectors already match what small combat electronics expect. This exact SKU is also sold in a 75C LiHV version (see battery-tattu-300mah-2s-75c-hv).

entities.name: Tattu 300mAh 2S 75C LiHV
entities.summary: LiHV version of Tattu's popular 300mAh micro pack, charged to 4.35V/cell (7.6V nominal, 8.7V full) instead of the standard 4.2V/cell, giving roughly 4-8% more usable energy in the same size and weight.
pros: More energy and higher rate in the same physical size as standard LiPo
Higher continuous voltage under load helps weapon RPM hold up
cons: Needs an LiHV-capable (4.35V/cell) charger profile or it will be undercharged
Slightly shorter cycle life than standard LiPo at the same charge/discharge rate
Must not be charged on a standard 4.20V/cell LiPo-only charger setting
entities.notes: Weight is an estimate consistent with the standard-LiPo sibling SKU; exact published weight for the HV variant was not independently confirmed.

entities.name: GNB LiHV 2S 300mAh 60C
entities.summary: Gaoneng (GNB) LiHV micro pack sold specifically as an antweight combat battery by hobby retailers; charges to 4.35V/cell for extra punch in the same 2S micro-pack footprint.
pros: Marketed directly to the combat robotics niche, not just FPV
LiHV chemistry gives more usable capacity per gram than standard LiPo
cons: Weight not published by the retailer; must be weighed on arrival for tight builds
entities.notes: Sold by Robot Smashing League specifically as an antweight part, which is unusual — most LiHV packs this size are marketed to micro FPV pilots and only cross over into combat use informally.

entities.name: GNB LiHV 4S 350mAh 70C
entities.summary: A 4S LiHV micro pack from Gaoneng, appropriate for higher-voltage antweight or light plastic-antweight drivetrains and higher-KV weapon setups that want 4S punch without the weight of a full-size 4S standard LiPo.
pros: 4S voltage in a small, light package thanks to LiHV energy density
XT30 connector handles the higher current of a 4S weapon setup better than JST
cons: 4S at 350mAh is a narrow-margin pack for a hard-hitting spinner; sized more for control bots or lighter weapons

entities.name: GNB 1S 450mAh 4.35V HV
entities.summary: Single-cell LiHV pack, too low-voltage to run most antweight drivetrains alone but a real-world example of the small HV cells sometimes used to power an isolated receiver, telemetry, or a low-voltage weapon controller board in a combat robot's electronics bay.
entities.notes: 1S packs are not used as the main pack in antweights (too low voltage for typical brushed/brushless drive), but the same category of small 1S/2S HV or LiFe cell is what builders reach for when isolating receiver power from a sagging main weapon battery.

entities.name: CNHL MiniStar 3S 450mAh 70C
entities.summary: A compact 3S 450mAh pack from CNHL (China Hobby Line) with an XT30 connector — a very typical capacity/voltage combination for an antweight or light plastic-antweight running a mid-KV brushless spinner plus two brushed drive motors.
pros: 450mAh/3S is a sweet-spot size for antweight spinners
XT30 rated comfortably above realistic antweight draw
cons: Weight not published; CNHL's small-format packs typically run 30-40g in this capacity/cell class based on comparable packs

entities.name: CNHL LiHV MiniStar 3S 450mAh 70C
entities.summary: LiHV sibling of the CNHL MiniStar 3S 450mAh pack, charged to 4.35V/cell (11.4V nominal vs 11.1V standard) for extra energy in the same physical package — a direct example of the real-world capacity gain LiHV offers antweight builders.
entities.notes: Same 450mAh capacity rating as the standard-LiPo MiniStar, but because it runs a higher voltage curve throughout the discharge, it delivers more actual watt-hours — direct evidence for the LiHV energy-density claim rather than a marketing rating.

entities.name: Palm Power 2S 300mAh 65C (Gen2)
entities.summary: House-brand antweight LiPo sold directly by Palm Beach Bots, a US combat robotics vendor, with a JST connector and a separate balance lead — a pack designed and sold specifically for the antweight community rather than repurposed from FPV.
pros: Sold explicitly for combat robots, so sizing/leads already match common antweight ESCs
65C is a middle-of-the-road, reasonably credible discharge rating for this size

entities.name: Palm Power 3S 450mAh 45C (Gen2)
aliases: Palm Beach Bots Palm Power 3S 450mAh XT30
entities.summary: 3S 450mAh combat-specific pack from Palm Beach Bots with an XT30 connector, a common upgrade path from a 2S 300mAh pack once a builder moves to a higher-voltage brushless weapon.
pros: Priced and packaged for the antweight market specifically
XT30 suits the higher current of a 3S weapon setup

entities.name: FingerTech Galaxy 2S LiPoly Pack
entities.summary: FingerTech Robotics' house line of small LiPo packs sold in multiple capacities for antweight and beetleweight kits such as the Viper V3; a long-running, combat-specific option predating the recent wave of Chinese FPV-brand crossover packs.
entities.notes: FingerTech sells the Galaxy line in a range of mAh sizes rather than one fixed SKU; exact capacity/weight/price depend on which size is ordered, so specific numeric specs are intentionally left out here rather than guessed. Commonly bundled with FingerTech's own kits (e.g. Viper V3).

entities.name: Gens Ace 2S 300mAh 45C (typical)
entities.summary: Gens Ace is Tattu's sister brand under the same parent manufacturer (Grepow group) and sells directly comparable micro 2S/3S packs; a 300mAh 2S 45C pack in this line is a realistic, commonly-seen antweight-size option.
entities.notes: Gens Ace and Tattu packs of the same capacity/C-rating/cell-count are frequently near-identical in weight and dimensions since both brands are produced by the same manufacturer; the weight given here is carried over from the equivalent Tattu SKU and should be treated as an estimate, not a confirmed Gens Ace datasheet figure.

entities.name: Lumenier 2S 300mAh (micro FPV crossover)
entities.summary: Lumenier is primarily an FPV racing-drone battery brand; its micro 1S-2S packs are occasionally repurposed by antweight builders for the same reason Tattu/CNHL micro packs are — the size class overlaps almost exactly with what a 1 lb combat robot needs.
entities.notes: Not a combat-specific product line; included here because it is a real, commonly cross-shopped brand in this size class. Exact weight, price, and C-rating for a current Lumenier 300mAh 2S SKU were not independently verified, so no numeric C-rating or weight is claimed.

entities.name: RDQ Series 3S 450mAh (small format)
entities.summary: RaceDayQuads' in-house RDQ Series battery line spans micro FPV sizes up through 6S packs; a small 3S 450mAh option in this line is representative of the budget/value house-brand packs antweight builders sometimes substitute for name-brand Tattu/CNHL cells.
entities.notes: RDQ Series is confirmed to sell small-format packs (e.g. 2200mAh 3S for whoop-class FPV), but a verified 450mAh SKU with published weight/price/C-rating was not located; treat capacity/voltage as representative rather than confirmed catalog numbers.

entities.name: Turnigy Nano-Tech 2S 300mAh
entities.summary: Turnigy's Nano-Tech line is a long-standing budget/value LiPo option sold through HobbyKing and resellers; still referenced as an entry-level combat robot battery choice, though less common today than dedicated combat-market brands.
entities.notes: Included as a well-known budget-brand reference point. Current-generation weight/price/C-rating for this exact SKU were not independently verified in this pass.

entities.name: Molicel INR18650-P28A (Li-ion, context)
entities.summary: A high-drain 18650 cylindrical Li-ion cell, used here as the reference point for Li-ion in combat robotics: much higher capacity-per-cell and better cycle life than a LiPo pouch cell, but lower cell voltage (3.6-3.7V nominal vs 3.7V LiPo, similar) and a hard steel/nickel can that adds weight relative to energy density, plus a lower safe continuous discharge current per gram than a hot LiPo pouch.
pros: Very high energy density per dollar and excellent cycle life vs LiPo
Rigid metal can survives rough handling better than a pouch cell
Popular and well-proven in flashlights, vapes, and e-bikes so cells are cheap and easy to source
cons: A single 18650 weighs ~48g for 2800mAh — far too heavy per Wh for a 1 lb robot once you need series cells for voltage
35A max discharge on one cell is high in absolute terms but low relative to the weight, and nowhere near what a spinner needs at 3S-4S-equivalent voltage from series 18650s
Round cells are hard to package efficiently in a flat antweight chassis
entities.notes: 18650/21700 Li-ion (Molicel, Samsung, LG, Sony/Murata) is essentially never used as the main weapon+drive pack in a competitive 1 lb antweight because the form factor and weight-per-amp are wrong for the class; it shows up mostly as context, in bigger weight classes (beetleweight and up) or in stationary test rigs, not on 1 lb bots.

entities.name: 2S LiFePO4 Receiver/Backup Pack
entities.summary: A small 2-cell LiFePO4 ("LiFe") pack at 6.6V nominal (3.3V/cell), the classic RC receiver-pack chemistry: much flatter discharge curve and far more abuse-tolerant than LiPo, occasionally used by antweight builders to power an isolated receiver or weapon-control board so it never browns out even if the main LiPo sags hard under weapon load.
entities.notes: LiFePO4 has lower energy density than LiPo (roughly 90-110 Wh/kg vs 150-200+ Wh/kg for LiPo) so it is not competitive as a main antweight power source, but its flat voltage curve and much lower fire risk make it a sensible choice specifically for a dedicated, isolated receiver/electronics rail. Capacity/weight given are representative of small RC LiFe RX packs, not a single named product.

entities.name: NiMH Stick Pack (legacy antweight power)
entities.summary: Nickel-metal-hydride packs were the default antweight power source in the earliest days of the class (roughly the 1990s through mid-2000s, before LiPo became affordable and reliable), typically a 6-cell 7.2V stick pack. Almost entirely obsolete today because LiPo offers 2-3x the energy density and can supply far higher current for its weight.
pros: Very tolerant of abuse and overdischarge compared to LiPo
No fire risk from puncture the way LiPo has
Simple to charge with a basic NiMH charger
cons: Roughly 1/3 the energy density of LiPo by weight, a major handicap at 1 lb
Cannot sustain the burst current a modern brushless spinner setup needs without severe sag
Self-discharges faster in storage than LiPo
entities.notes: Included for historical/legacy context per the research brief. A new antweight build today has essentially no reason to choose NiMH over LiPo or LiHV; it survives mostly in old kit documentation and vintage-rules exhibition classes.

entities.name: ISDT 608AC Balance Charger
entities.summary: Compact 8A/200W AC/DC balance charger for 1-6S LiPo, LiHV, Li-ion, LiFe, NiMH and Pb packs with a detachable power supply and an XT60 charge port — a common choice among antweight builders for its small size and multi-chemistry support.
pros: Supports LiPo, LiHV, Li-ion, LiFe and NiMH from one charger
Small and light enough to bring in a pit box

entities.name: HOTA D6 Pro Charger
entities.summary: A well-regarded 200W AC hobby balance charger for 1-6S packs with up to 1.6A per-cell balance current, popular in FPV and increasingly seen in antweight pits for its accuracy and fast balancing on small packs.
pros: High balance current (1.6A/cell) means fast, accurate balancing even on tiny antweight packs
Well regarded for measurement accuracy on small-capacity cells

entities.name: SkyRC T1000 Charger
entities.summary: A 1-6S LiPo/LiHV balance charger and discharger from SkyRC, one of the long-established hobby charger brands; used by antweight builders both to charge match packs and to discharge them to storage voltage after an event.
pros: Charge and discharge in one unit, useful for setting storage voltage after events

entities.name: JST-PH 2.0mm Connector
entities.summary: A small 2.0mm-pitch connector rated for only a few amps continuous, standard on 1S-2S micro LiPo/LiHV packs; used throughout antweight electronics for battery main leads on the smallest packs and almost universally for balance leads on any pack size.
entities.notes: Because JST-PH is only rated for a few amps, it is a real bottleneck if used as the main power connector on anything but the smallest antweight drive+weapon combos; many builders re-terminate small packs to XT30 once total system draw regularly exceeds a few amps continuous.

entities.name: XT30 Connector
entities.summary: A compact bullet-style connector rated for roughly 15-30A continuous depending on source and wire gauge, the standard 'step up' connector from tiny JST leads once an antweight's 3S or 4S pack needs to support real weapon current.
entities.notes: XT30 is used on most of the CNHL and GNB antweight-size packs referenced in this file; it is a reasonable middle ground for antweight current levels — small enough to fit the chassis, rated well above realistic sustained antweight draw (see the power-budget chunk), while leaving XT60/XT90 for larger weight classes.

entities.name: C Rating
entities.summary: A LiPo battery's discharge capability expressed as a multiple of its own capacity per hour -- a 300 mAh pack rated 60C can (by the label) sustain 60 x 0.3 A = 18 A continuously. Real sustained performance is often lower than the printed rating suggests.
entities.notes: Real-world LiPo packs commonly deliver less than their printed C-rating in sustained use; loaded voltage under real test conditions is a better indicator than the label alone.

entities.name: Voltage Sag
entities.summary: The temporary drop in a battery's output voltage under load, caused by the pack's internal resistance; the higher the current draw and the higher the internal resistance, the larger the sag, and severe sag can drop system voltage below what the ESC or receiver needs to keep operating.

entities.name: LiHV (High-Voltage LiPo)
entities.summary: A LiPo cell chemistry variant built to be charged safely to 4.35V per cell instead of the standard 4.20V, giving roughly 5-10% more stored energy in the same physical cell at the cost of slightly reduced cycle life and the requirement for an LiHV-aware charger.

entities.name: Balance Charging
entities.summary: Charging method that monitors and tops off each individual cell in a multi-cell pack through its balance lead, so no single cell is overcharged or left behind, which is what keeps a multi-cell LiPo/LiHV pack safe and its cells even over many cycles.

entities.name: Storage Voltage
entities.summary: The recommended per-cell voltage (about 3.8V/cell, roughly 3.7-3.85V) at which a LiPo/LiHV pack should be kept for any period longer than a few days, chosen to minimize chemical stress on the cell compared to storing it fully charged or fully depleted.

entities.name: Brownout
entities.summary: A drop in supply voltage severe enough to cause a receiver, flight/weapon controller, or ESC to reset or behave erratically without fully losing power; in a 1 lb combat robot this is most often triggered by weapon-motor spin-up current sagging the shared main battery voltage below the electronics' minimum operating threshold.

entities.name: Internal Resistance
entities.summary: The effective resistance inside a battery pack (cell chemistry plus connections) that causes its terminal voltage to drop under load; internal resistance rises with cell age, cycle count, cold temperature and physical damage, which is why an older or damaged pack sags far more than a fresh one of the same rated C rating.

entities.name: Puffed Pack
entities.summary: A LiPo/LiHV pack whose pouch has visibly swollen from internal gas generation, a sign of degraded or damaged cell chemistry; a puffed pack should be retired immediately, never charged or discharged normally, and disposed of separately from healthy batteries.

entities.name: Pack Energy (Watt-hours)
entities.summary: Converts a pack's mAh capacity and nominal voltage into total stored energy in watt-hours, the unit that lets you compare packs of different cell counts and capacities on equal footing.

variables.Energy_Wh: total stored energy in the pack, watt-hours
variables.Voltage_nominal_V: nominal pack voltage (3.7V/cell LiPo, 3.8V/cell LiHV, times cell count)

extra.worked_example: A Tattu 300mAh 2S pack: 7.4V nominal. Energy = (300/1000) * 7.4 = 2.22 Wh. A CNHL LiHV MiniStar 450mAh 3S pack at 11.4V nominal: (450/1000) * 11.4 = 5.13 Wh, versus the standard-LiPo 450mAh 3S sibling at 11.1V nominal: (450/1000) * 11.1 = 5.0 Wh — about 2.7% more usable energy from LiHV at the same mAh rating, and more once you account for LiHV's higher voltage across the whole discharge curve, not just at nominal.

entities.name: Continuous / Burst Current from Capacity and C Rating
entities.summary: The standard way manufacturers express a pack's maximum discharge current, and the calculation an antweight builder should run backward — from an estimated real current draw — to check whether a candidate pack's C rating is remotely credible.

variables.Max_Current_A: maximum current the pack is rated to supply, amps
variables.C_rating: manufacturer discharge rating (continuous, and separately burst if given)

extra.worked_example: A CNHL MiniStar 3S 450mAh 70C pack: (450/1000) * 70 = 31.5A claimed continuous. A realistic antweight rule of thumb (see chunk-c-rating-marketing-vs-reality) is to only trust roughly 40-60% of a budget/unknown pack's printed C rating for sustained draw, so a safer planning number for this pack is about 13-19A continuous, which is still comfortably above what a typical antweight drive+weapon combo pulls in steady state (see formula-power-budget-drive-weapon).

entities.name: Voltage Sag from Internal Resistance
entities.summary: Estimates how far pack voltage will drop under a given current draw using the pack's internal resistance, the direct cause-and-effect behind weapon-spin-up brownouts in small combat robots.

extra.expression: V_sag = I_draw * R_internal;  V_under_load = V_nominal - V_sag

variables.R_internal: pack internal resistance, ohms (a fresh small antweight LiPo pack is roughly 0.015-0.04 ohm per cell; multiply per cell for series count, and note resistance rises with age/damage/cold)
variables.V_under_load: actual voltage seen by the ESC/receiver while the load is applied
variables.V_nominal: pack's resting/nominal voltage before the load hit

extra.worked_example: A used 3S pack with internal resistance of 0.03 ohm/cell (0.09 ohm total for the 3S series stack) hit with a combined weapon-spinup-plus-drive spike of 25A: V_sag = 25 * 0.09 = 2.25V. Starting from 11.1V nominal, the pack momentarily sags to about 8.85V — potentially below the brownout threshold of a receiver or BEC that expects a stable 3S-range input, which is exactly the mechanism behind an RX reset at the moment the weapon motor spins up while the drive motors are also under load.

entities.name: Match Runtime from Average Current Draw
entities.summary: Estimates how long a pack will last in a match given an average (not peak) current draw across drive and weapon combined, used to size capacity against the standard 3-minute combat robotics match length.

variables.Runtime_min: estimated run time at the given average draw, minutes
variables.Capacity_mAh: usable pack capacity in mAh (using rated capacity is optimistic; treat only ~80% of rated capacity as safely usable before voltage drops too far)
variables.Average_Current_mA: average combined drive+weapon current draw over the match, milliamps

extra.worked_example: A 3S 450mAh pack (using 80% = 360mAh usable) against an estimated average combined draw of 6A (6000mA) for a moderately aggressive antweight spinner+drive combo: Runtime = (360/6000) * 60 = 3.6 minutes — enough margin over a standard 3-minute match, but not by much, which is why builders round capacity up 25-50% over the bare computed minimum (see chunk-power-budget-current-draw-estimate).

entities.name: Total System Current Draw (Drive + Weapon)
entities.summary: Builds a rough total current budget for an antweight by summing estimated drive-motor stall/running current and weapon-motor running current, the starting point for both C-rating and capacity sizing.

variables.I_drive_per_motor: current draw of one drive motor under typical pushing load (small antweight brushed gearmotors: roughly 1-3A typical, up to 5-8A stalled)
variables.I_weapon_running: brushless weapon motor current once at speed under normal cutting/spinning load (highly variable: roughly 3-10A typical for antweight-class brushless outrunners, spiking much higher at spin-up or when the weapon bites something)

extra.worked_example: Two small brushed drive motors at ~2A each typical running current, plus a brushless weapon motor drawing ~8A running: I_total = (2*2) + 8 = 12A typical combined draw, with momentary spikes during weapon spin-up and simultaneous hard driving easily reaching 20-25A+ for a second or two — which is the spike the pack's burst rating (not its continuous rating) needs to absorb without collapsing.

entities.name: Angular velocity from RPM
entities.summary: Converts a motor or weapon speed given in RPM (revolutions per minute) into angular velocity in radians per second, the unit every rotational-KE and torque formula on this page needs.

extra.worked_example: A vertical-spinner disc is spinning at 20,000 rpm. omega = 20000 * 2 * 3.14159 / 60 = 20000 * 6.28318 / 60 = 125,663.7 / 60 = 2094.4 rad/s.

entities.name: Moment of inertia — solid disc / cylinder about its central axis
entities.summary: MOI of a uniform solid disc (or short solid cylinder) spinning about the axis through its own center, perpendicular to its face. This is the base case for most vertical-spinner and drum weapon discs.

variables.r: outer radius of the disc, m

extra.worked_example: A single-tooth vertical-spinner disc has mass m = 0.060 kg (60 g) and radius r = 0.028 m (56 mm diameter). I = 0.5 * 0.060 * 0.028^2 = 0.5 * 0.060 * 0.000784 = 0.0000235 kg*m^2 (2.35e-5 kg*m^2).

entities.name: Moment of inertia — annulus (ring with a hole, e.g. a hub or drum wall)
entities.summary: MOI of a flat ring-shaped mass with both an outer and inner radius (a washer shape), such as a weapon disc with a large center bore, or a drum's cylindrical wall seen end-on.

extra.worked_example: A drum-spinner end plate has mass m = 0.025 kg (25 g), outer radius r_outer = 0.030 m, and a large center bore r_inner = 0.012 m for the motor shaft. I = 0.5 * 0.025 * (0.030^2 + 0.012^2) = 0.5 * 0.025 * (0.0009 + 0.000144) = 0.5 * 0.025 * 0.001044 = 0.00001305 kg*m^2 (1.305e-5 kg*m^2).

entities.name: Moment of inertia — thin ring / hoop (all mass at one radius)
entities.summary: MOI of a thin hoop or ring where essentially all the mass sits at a single radius, such as a steel reinforcement band shrunk onto the rim of a disc weapon.

extra.worked_example: A thin steel rim-reinforcement ring has mass m = 0.015 kg (15 g) at radius r = 0.030 m. I = 0.015 * 0.030^2 = 0.015 * 0.0009 = 0.0000135 kg*m^2 (1.35e-5 kg*m^2).

entities.name: Moment of inertia — slender rod about its own center (horizontal bar spinner)
entities.summary: MOI of a uniform straight bar rotating about an axis through its own midpoint, perpendicular to its length. This is the standard model for a horizontal (full-width) bar spinner weapon.

variables.m: total mass of the bar, kg
variables.L: total length of the bar (tip to tip), m

extra.worked_example: A horizontal bar-spinner blade has mass m = 0.090 kg (90 g) and total length L = 0.090 m (90 mm, so each tip is 45 mm from center). I = (1/12) * 0.090 * 0.090^2 = (1/12) * 0.090 * 0.0081 = (1/12) * 0.000729 = 0.00006075 kg*m^2 (6.075e-5 kg*m^2).

entities.name: Moment of inertia — slender rod about one end (hammer / axe / flail arm)
entities.summary: MOI of a uniform straight arm rotating about a pivot at one of its own ends, rather than its center — the correct model for a hammer, axe, or single-pivot flail arm.

variables.L: length of the arm from the pivot to its free tip, m

extra.worked_example: A hammer weapon's swinging arm has mass m = 0.050 kg (50 g) and length L = 0.080 m (80 mm) from the pivot to the striking head. I = (1/3) * 0.050 * 0.080^2 = (1/3) * 0.050 * 0.0064 = (1/3) * 0.00032 = 0.0001067 kg*m^2 (1.067e-4 kg*m^2).

entities.name: Moment of inertia — point mass at a radius
entities.summary: MOI of a small, compact mass treated as concentrated at a single point, a distance r from the rotation axis. Used for bolts, counterweights, or small hard-faced tips whose own size is negligible next to their distance from the axis.

variables.m: mass of the point-like object, kg
variables.r: distance from the rotation axis to the mass, m

extra.worked_example: A small steel balance-counterweight bolt has mass m = 0.005 kg (5 g) mounted at radius r = 0.040 m. I = 0.005 * 0.040^2 = 0.005 * 0.0016 = 0.000008 kg*m^2 (8.0e-6 kg*m^2).

entities.name: Moment of inertia — thin-walled cylinder / tube about its long axis
entities.summary: MOI of a thin cylindrical shell (a tube or drum's outer wall) spinning about its own central longitudinal axis. Mathematically identical in form to the thin-ring case (all wall mass sits at radius r regardless of the tube's length), and is the right model for a hollow drum-spinner shell or a shaft/hub.

variables.m: mass of the cylindrical shell/wall, kg
variables.r: radius of the cylindrical wall, m

extra.worked_example: A drum-spinner's hardened-steel outer shell (thin wall, ignoring the end plates) has mass m = 0.040 kg (40 g) and radius r = 0.020 m (20 mm). I = 0.040 * 0.020^2 = 0.040 * 0.0004 = 0.000016 kg*m^2 (1.6e-5 kg*m^2).

entities.name: Parallel axis theorem — combining a compound weapon's parts into one total MOI
entities.summary: The general rule for adding up the MOI of a multi-part weapon (a disc plus a bolted-on tooth, a hub plus inserts, etc.): each part's own MOI about its own center of mass, plus that part's mass times the square of how far its center of mass sits from the actual rotation axis. Summing this over every part gives the true total MOI used in every KE/tip-speed/spin-up calculation.

extra.expression: I_axis = I_cm + m * d^2 ; I_total = sum over all parts of (I_cm_part + m_part * d_part^2)

variables.I_axis: moment of inertia of one part about the actual rotation axis, kg*m^2
variables.I_cm: that part's own moment of inertia about a parallel axis through its own center of mass, kg*m^2
variables.d: perpendicular distance from the part's center of mass to the actual rotation axis, m

extra.worked_example: A compound vertical-spinner weapon = a solid disc (from formula-moi-solid-disc: I_disc = 2.35e-5 kg*m^2, already about the rotation axis since the disc is centered on it) plus one bolt-on steel tooth treated as a point mass m_tooth = 0.010 kg (10 g) whose own I_cm is negligible, bolted at d = 0.030 m from center. Tooth contribution = I_cm + m*d^2 = 0 + 0.010 * 0.030^2 = 0.010 * 0.0009 = 0.000009 kg*m^2 (9.0e-6 kg*m^2). I_total = 2.35e-5 + 9.0e-6 = 3.25e-5 kg*m^2 -- this compound-weapon total (3.25e-5 kg*m^2) is the number used in every rotational-KE, tip-speed and spin-up example elsewhere on this page.

entities.name: Rotational kinetic energy stored in a spinning weapon
entities.summary: The total kinetic energy stored in the weapon at a given spin speed -- the number combat robotics people mean when they say a weapon 'has X joules'.

variables.I: total weapon moment of inertia about its spin axis, kg*m^2

extra.worked_example: Using the compound weapon I_total = 3.25e-5 kg*m^2 spinning at omega = 2094.4 rad/s (20,000 rpm): KE = 0.5 * 3.25e-5 * 2094.4^2 = 0.5 * 3.25e-5 * 4,386,506 = 0.5 * 142.56 = 71.3 J stored.

entities.name: Tip speed of a spinning weapon
entities.summary: The linear (straight-line) speed of the outermost point of the weapon -- the speed at which the tooth or blade edge is actually moving through the air, which is what does the cutting/hitting.

variables.r_tip: radius from the spin axis to the outermost striking point (including any tooth extension), m

extra.worked_example: Same compound weapon, tooth tip extends out to r_tip = 0.032 m (32 mm) at omega = 2094.4 rad/s: v_tip = 2094.4 * 0.032 = 67.0 m/s. Converting: 67.0 m/s * 3.281 ft/m = 219.8 ft/s (~149.9 mph) -- a hard-hitting but achievable tip speed for a 1 lb vertical spinner.

entities.name: Effective (reduced) mass of a spinning weapon at its tooth
entities.summary: Converts a rotating weapon's inertia into an equivalent straight-line mass, as felt at one specific radius (usually the tooth/tip). This lets you treat a weapon hit like a simple linear collision: KE = 0.5 * m_eff * v_tip^2 gives the same energy as the rotational formula.

variables.m_eff: effective linear mass at the reference radius, kg
variables.I: total weapon moment of inertia about its spin axis, kg*m^2
variables.r_tip: radius from the spin axis to the reference point (usually the tooth tip), m

entities.name: Momentum transfer to the opponent on impact
entities.summary: Models a weapon strike as a partially-inelastic collision between the weapon's effective mass (at the tip) and the opponent's total mass, to estimate how fast the opponent gets thrown/launched. Coefficient of restitution e is empirical: roughly 0.2-0.3 for a mostly-absorbed/deforming hit, 0.4-0.5 for a stiffer, more elastic bounce-off hit.
entities.notes: Coefficient of restitution for robot-on-robot hits is not rigorously measured in the hobby; treat e as a tunable estimate, not a precise material constant.

variables.delta_v_opponent: velocity imparted to the opponent by the hit, m/s
variables.e: coefficient of restitution, dimensionless (0 = perfectly inelastic, 1 = perfectly elastic)
variables.m_eff: weapon's effective mass at the tip, kg (see formula-effective-mass-at-tooth)
variables.v_tip: weapon tip speed just before impact, m/s
variables.m_opponent: mass of the struck opponent robot, kg

extra.worked_example: m_eff = 0.03174 kg, v_tip = 67.0 m/s, hitting a full 1 lb opponent m_opponent = 0.454 kg, e = 0.4: delta_v = (1.4) * 0.03174 * 67.0 / (0.03174 + 0.454) = (1.4 * 2.127) / 0.4857 = 2.978 / 0.4857 = 6.13 m/s -- the opponent can be launched/kicked at roughly 6 m/s from a solid hit if it is free to move.

entities.name: Spin-up time from motor torque and weapon MOI
entities.summary: Estimates how long a weapon takes to reach operating speed from a standstill, using the average available motor torque over the acceleration and the weapon's total MOI. Long spin-up times are a real tactical liability (weapon is weak/inert while re-spinning after a hit).

variables.I: total weapon moment of inertia, kg*m^2
variables.delta_omega: change in angular velocity, rad/s (target minus starting, usually target minus 0)
variables.T_avg: average torque delivered by the motor over the spin-up range, N*m

extra.worked_example: I_total = 3.25e-5 kg*m^2, target omega = 2094.4 rad/s (20,000 rpm) from rest. Motor: Kv = 2750 rpm/V, V = 11.1 V (3S), stall current I_stall = 30 A. Kt (exact) = 9.5493 / 2750 = 0.003472 N*m/A. T_stall = Kt * I_stall = 0.003472 * 30 = 0.1042 N*m. No-load rpm = Kv * V = 2750 * 11.1 = 30,525 rpm (omega_nl = 3196 rad/s). Torque at the 20,000 rpm operating point (linear torque-speed curve): T(omega) = T_stall * (1 - omega/omega_nl) = 0.1042 * (1 - 2094.4/3196) = 0.1042 * 0.345 = 0.03595 N*m. T_avg (approx, midpoint of a linear torque curve) = (0.1042 + 0.03595) / 2 = 0.0701 N*m. t_spinup = 3.25e-5 * 2094.4 / 0.0701 = 0.06807 / 0.0701 = 0.97 s -- under one second, a good, fight-safe spin-up time.

entities.name: Energy actually delivered in one hit, vs total energy stored
entities.summary: A weapon rarely dumps its entire stored KE into a single hit -- the disc only slows down by however much the impact actually resists it, and keeps most of its spin for the next hit. This computes the energy actually delivered from the RPM drop observed/expected during a strike.

variables.E_hit: kinetic energy delivered to the target in one hit, J
variables.I: total weapon moment of inertia, kg*m^2
variables.omega_before: weapon angular velocity just before the hit, rad/s
variables.omega_after: weapon angular velocity just after the hit, rad/s

extra.worked_example: I = 3.25e-5 kg*m^2, weapon at 20,000 rpm before the hit (omega_before = 2094.4 rad/s) drops to 17,000 rpm after (omega_after = 1780.2 rad/s). E_hit = 0.5 * 3.25e-5 * (2094.4^2 - 1780.2^2) = 0.5 * 3.25e-5 * (4,386,506 - 3,169,112) = 0.5 * 3.25e-5 * 1,217,394 = 0.5 * 39.57 = 19.8 J delivered -- only about 28% of the 71.3 J total stored KE from formula-rotational-ke. The rest stays in the still-spinning weapon for the next hit, and the ~1s spin-up time formula shows how quickly the lost 3,000 rpm can be recovered mid-fight.

entities.name: Gyroscopic precession torque from turning while the weapon spins
entities.summary: When a chassis carrying a spinning weapon is itself rotated (yawed) by the drivetrain, gyroscopic precession produces a reaction torque trying to tip the chassis about a THIRD axis, perpendicular to both the weapon's spin axis and the turn axis. This is the physics behind vertical-spinner 'gyro dance'.

variables.I: weapon moment of inertia about its spin axis, kg*m^2
variables.omega_turn: chassis turning (yaw) angular velocity commanded by the drivetrain, rad/s
