extra.worked_example: I = 3.25e-5 kg*m^2, weapon at omega_weapon = 2094.4 rad/s (20,000 rpm), driver spins the chassis in place at omega_turn = 3.0 rad/s (~0.48 rev/s, a brisk turn-in-place). tau_precession = 3.25e-5 * 2094.4 * 3.0 = 3.25e-5 * 6283.2 = 0.2042 N*m.

entities.name: Tipping-moment threshold for a 1 lb chassis
entities.summary: A first-order estimate of how much overturning moment a lightweight chassis can resist before it starts to lift/rock about the edge of its wheel track, using just weight and half the track width. It ignores CG height (a more complete model also uses formula-cg-tipping-angle), but is a fast way to check a precession torque against a real robot.
entities.notes: A simplified planar moment-balance estimate; real tipping also depends on CG height and suspension compliance.

variables.M_tip: approximate moment needed to lift the chassis about one side's wheel line, N*m
variables.track_width: side-to-side distance between the drive wheels' contact patches, m

extra.worked_example: A 454 g (0.454 kg) antweight has W = 0.454 * 9.81 = 4.453 N, track_width = 0.090 m (90 mm). M_tip = 4.453 * (0.090/2) = 4.453 * 0.045 = 0.2004 N*m. Compare this to the 0.2042 N*m precession torque computed in formula-gyroscopic-precession-torque for the same robot: the precession torque slightly EXCEEDS the tipping threshold -- this robot would start to rock/tip if the driver spun it that fast while the weapon was at full speed. This is exactly the 'gyro dance' effect vertical-spinner drivers are warned about.

entities.name: Predicting the maximum safe turn rate before gyro-dance tipping
entities.summary: Rearranges the precession-torque and tipping-moment formulas to solve directly for the fastest a driver can yaw the chassis (at a given weapon speed) before the precession reaction exceeds the tipping threshold and the robot starts to rock.

variables.omega_turn_max: maximum safe chassis turning (yaw) rate before tipping, rad/s
variables.M_tip: tipping-moment threshold of the chassis, N*m (formula-tipping-moment-threshold)

extra.worked_example: M_tip = 0.2004 N*m, I = 3.25e-5 kg*m^2, omega_weapon = 2094.4 rad/s (20,000 rpm weapon speed): omega_turn_max = 0.2004 / (3.25e-5 * 2094.4) = 0.2004 / 0.06807 = 2.944 rad/s (~28.1 deg per 60ms tick, or about 169 deg/s, ~0.47 rev/s). A driver should keep in-place turns slower than this, or turn in a wide arc instead of spinning on the spot, whenever the weapon is at full speed.

entities.name: Top speed from motor RPM, gear ratio, and wheel diameter
entities.summary: Converts a drive motor's raw (ungeared) no-load RPM through the gearbox ratio and wheel size into the robot's theoretical top ground speed.

variables.rpm_motor: drive motor's own (ungeared) no-load RPM at the battery's nominal voltage
variables.gear_ratio: gearbox reduction, dimensionless (output turns once per this many motor turns)

extra.worked_example: Drive motor no-load rpm_motor = 11,000 rpm at 7.4V (2S), gear_ratio = 20:1, wheel diameter D_wheel = 0.032 m (32 mm). Output shaft speed = 11000/20 = 550 rpm. v_top = (550/60) * pi * 0.032 = 9.167 * 0.1005 = 0.921 m/s (~3.02 ft/s, ~2.06 mph) -- a typical, controllable antweight top speed.

entities.name: Acceleration from motor torque (torque-limited case)
entities.summary: Converts drive-motor output torque, through the gearbox and wheel radius, into a forward driving force, and from there into acceleration -- BEFORE checking whether the wheels can actually put that much force onto the arena floor (see formula-traction-limited-force, which usually governs instead for lightweight antweights).

extra.expression: F_drive = (T_motor * gear_ratio * eta) / r_wheel ; a = (F_drive * n_wheels) / m_robot

variables.F_drive: driving force delivered at one wheel's contact patch, N
variables.T_motor: motor output (shaft) torque before the gearbox, N*m
variables.eta: drivetrain mechanical efficiency, dimensionless (0-1; typical small spur gearbox ~0.75-0.85)
variables.n_wheels: number of independently driven wheels contributing force

extra.worked_example: T_motor = 0.010 N*m (10 mN*m), gear_ratio = 20, eta = 0.80, r_wheel = 0.016 m (32mm dia wheel), n_wheels = 2, m_robot = 0.454 kg. F_drive (per wheel) = (0.010 * 20 * 0.80) / 0.016 = 0.16 / 0.016 = 10.0 N. Total force = 10.0 * 2 = 20.0 N. a = 20.0 / 0.454 = 44.1 m/s^2 IF the wheels could grip that hard -- see formula-traction-limited-force for why they usually can't, and formula-wheel-slip-threshold for the real limit.

entities.name: Traction-limited pushing/driving force
entities.summary: The maximum forward (or pushing) force a robot's drive wheels can transmit to the floor before they simply spin in place, set by the robot's weight on the wheels and the wheel-to-floor friction coefficient -- NOT by how much torque the motors can produce. For a 454 g robot this is almost always the true limiting factor, well below what the drivetrain can output.

variables.mu: coefficient of friction between wheel and arena floor, dimensionless (foam/rubber on polycarbonate/Lexan: roughly 0.6-1.0)
variables.N: normal force pressing the drive wheels onto the floor, N (approximately the full robot weight if all wheels are driven)

extra.worked_example: A 0.454 kg antweight, all weight on driven wheels: N = 0.454 * 9.81 = 4.453 N. Using mu = 0.8 (grippy foam wheel on a typical arena floor): F_max = 0.8 * 4.453 = 3.56 N. Compare to the 20.0 N the drivetrain could produce in formula-acceleration-from-torque -- the wheels will spin/slip long before the motors run out of torque.

entities.name: Wheel-slip threshold and the resulting real acceleration
entities.summary: Compares the torque-limited drive force against the traction-limited force to determine which one actually governs, then computes the robot's real (traction-limited) acceleration -- the number that matters for a 1 lb robot, which is almost always far below the torque-limited number.

extra.expression: if F_drive > F_max: a_real = F_max / m_robot (traction-limited) ; else: a_real = F_drive_total / m_robot (torque-limited)

variables.F_drive: total force the drivetrain could deliver from torque alone, N

extra.worked_example: F_drive (total, both wheels) = 20.0 N, F_max = 3.56 N. Since 20.0 N > 3.56 N, the drivetrain is traction-limited: a_real = F_max / m_robot = 3.56 / 0.454 = 7.85 m/s^2 -- roughly 0.8g, reached almost instantly since there is huge spare motor torque behind it. This also means a lighter/higher-torque motor swap would do nothing for straight-line acceleration here; better wheels/tires (higher mu) would.

entities.name: Torque and traction required to climb an opponent's wedge
entities.summary: Two separate conditions must both hold to drive up onto an opponent's wedge at angle theta: (1) the drivetrain must supply enough torque at the wheel, and (2) the wheels must have enough traction against the now-tilted (and often slippery) wedge surface -- whichever is smaller sets the actual climbable angle.

extra.expression: F_needed = m_robot * g * sin(theta) ; T_needed_at_wheel = F_needed * r_wheel / eta ; traction_ok if mu * m_robot * g * cos(theta) >= F_needed

variables.F_needed: force needed up the slope to overcome gravity component, N (ignoring rolling resistance)
variables.T_needed_at_wheel: output torque needed at the wheel to supply F_needed, N*m

extra.worked_example: m_robot = 0.454 kg, theta = 15 deg (0.2618 rad), r_wheel = 0.016 m, eta = 0.80, mu = 0.8 (assume similar grip on the wedge surface). F_needed = 0.454 * 9.81 * sin(15deg) = 4.453 * 0.2588 = 1.152 N. T_needed_at_wheel = 1.152 * 0.016 / 0.80 = 0.01843 / 0.80 = 0.02304 N*m -- well inside the drivetrain's available 0.16 N*m per wheel from formula-acceleration-from-torque, so torque is not the bottleneck. Traction check: mu * m_robot * g * cos(theta) = 0.8 * 4.453 * cos(15deg) = 3.562 * 0.966 = 3.44 N, which is far more than the 1.152 N needed, so this 15 degree wedge is climbable. Solving tan(theta_max) = mu gives theta_max = atan(0.8) = 38.7 deg as the traction-limited steepest wedge this robot could climb at all (before its own weight component alone overcomes available friction), independent of motor torque.

entities.name: Mechanical power delivered at a given speed
entities.summary: Basic power = force x velocity relationship, used to check how much continuous power the drivetrain is actually asking of the battery/ESC at cruising speed versus during a hard push.

variables.F: force being delivered (driving or pushing force), N
variables.v: speed at which that force is being delivered, m/s

extra.worked_example: Cruising at top speed v_top = 0.921 m/s while only overcoming rolling resistance F_roll = 0.223 N (about 5% of weight): P = 0.223 * 0.921 = 0.205 W -- trivial power draw at cruise. Pushing hard at the traction limit F_max = 3.56 N while still moving at 0.921 m/s: P = 3.56 * 0.921 = 3.28 W -- the practical upper bound on continuous drivetrain mechanical power for this robot.

entities.name: Torque constant Kt from velocity constant Kv (exact form AND common hobby shorthand)
entities.summary: Kv (rpm per volt of back-EMF) and Kt (torque per amp) describe the same physical motor constant in different units. The EXACT, physically-derived relation is Kt[N*m/A] = 60 / (2*pi*Kv[rpm/V]) = 9.5493 / Kv. The widely-used HOBBY SHORTHAND Kt = 8.27 / Kv is NOT the same physical law -- it silently bakes in an assumed ~87% mechanical/electrical efficiency (8.27/9.5493 = 0.866), so it already includes a loss derating. Use the exact 9.5493 form for real torque/spin-up physics, and only use 8.27 if you specifically want a quick 'expected real-world output torque' guess and are not also applying a separate efficiency factor on top of it.
sources: domain knowledge (standard DC/BLDC motor-constant physics: Kt[N*m/A] = 60/(2*pi*Kv[rpm/V]))

variables.Kt_hobby_shorthand: hobby rule-of-thumb torque constant that already assumes ~87% efficiency, N*m/A
variables.Kv: motor velocity constant, rpm per volt

extra.worked_example: A small antweight weapon brushless motor is rated Kv = 2750 rpm/V. Kt_exact = 9.5493 / 2750 = 0.003472 N*m/A. Kt_hobby_shorthand = 8.27 / 2750 = 0.003007 N*m/A. The hobby value is 0.003007 / 0.003472 = 86.6% of the exact value, matching the ~87% efficiency it bakes in. All other worked examples on this page use the EXACT form (9.5493/Kv) for Kt.

entities.name: Stall torque from Kt and stall current
entities.summary: The maximum torque a motor can produce, occurring at zero RPM (locked rotor) when the full stall current flows.

variables.Kt: torque constant, N*m/A (use the exact 9.5493/Kv form)

extra.worked_example: Kt (exact) = 0.003472 N*m/A, I_stall = 30 A (typical small antweight weapon brushless motor at 3S). T_stall = 0.003472 * 30 = 0.1042 N*m (about 1.06 kgf*cm).

entities.name: Stall current from voltage and winding resistance
entities.summary: The current a motor draws when its rotor is locked (RPM = 0), limited only by the winding resistance since there is no back-EMF at zero speed. This is the highest current the motor (and its ESC) will ever be asked to pass.

variables.R: motor winding resistance (phase-to-phase or armature), ohm

extra.worked_example: A small brushed antweight drive motor has R = 1.2 ohm and is run at V = 7.4 V (2S): I_stall = 7.4 / 1.2 = 6.17 A.

entities.name: No-load RPM from Kv and voltage
entities.summary: The speed a motor spins at with no mechanical load and no current-draw losses -- an idealized upper bound. Real no-load speed under actual bearing/brush/air-drag friction is slightly lower than this.

extra.worked_example: Kv = 2750 rpm/V at V = 11.1 V (3S): rpm_no_load = 2750 * 11.1 = 30,525 rpm (omega_nl = 30525 * 2*pi/60 = 3196 rad/s). Actual free-spin speed will be a few percent lower once bearing drag and air resistance are subtracted.

entities.name: DC motor power curve and peak power at half stall speed
entities.summary: For an ideal DC (brushed or BLDC-as-DC-equivalent) motor, torque falls off linearly with speed from T_stall at 0 rpm to 0 at no-load rpm. Multiplying torque by speed gives a power curve that peaks exactly halfway between (at half the no-load speed and half the stall torque), which is the operating point a weapon or drivetrain wants to sit near for maximum mechanical power.

extra.expression: T(omega) = T_stall * (1 - omega/omega_no_load) ; P(omega) = T(omega) * omega ; P_max = T_stall * omega_no_load / 4 at omega = omega_no_load / 2

variables.T(omega): torque at angular velocity omega, N*m
variables.P(omega): mechanical power at that angular velocity, W
variables.P_max: peak mechanical power, W (occurs at omega_no_load/2)

extra.worked_example: T_stall = 0.1042 N*m, omega_no_load = 3196 rad/s. Peak power point: omega = 3196/2 = 1598 rad/s (15,262 rpm), T there = 0.1042/2 = 0.0521 N*m. P_max = T_stall * omega_no_load / 4 = 0.1042 * 3196 / 4 = 333.2 / 4 = 83.3 W. At the actual 20,000 rpm (2094.4 rad/s) operating point used elsewhere on this page (past the peak-power point, on the higher-speed/lower-torque side): T = 0.1042*(1-2094.4/3196) = 0.03595 N*m, P = 0.03595*2094.4 = 75.3 W -- slightly below the 83.3 W peak, consistent with running a bit faster than the ideal peak-power point.

entities.name: ESC current headroom / derating
entities.summary: An ESC's continuous-current rating should be sized well above the motor's realistic stall current, since brief stalls (weapon impacts, drivetrain jams against a wall) are normal in combat and are exactly when full stall current flows.

variables.I_esc_rated_min: minimum recommended ESC continuous-current rating, A
variables.k_headroom: safety/headroom factor, dimensionless (typical 1.5-2.0 for weapon ESCs that will see real stalls)

extra.worked_example: Weapon motor I_stall = 30 A, using k_headroom = 1.75 (mid-range, since vertical-spinner weapon motors do stall briefly on every hit): I_esc_rated_min = 1.75 * 30 = 52.5 A -- round up to a commonly-available 60A-rated ESC.

entities.name: Battery C-rating to continuous amps
entities.summary: Converts a LiPo pack's C-rating (a multiple of its own capacity) into an actual continuous-current figure in amps, the number that needs to be compared against total robot current draw.

variables.I_continuous: continuous discharge current the pack is rated for, A

extra.worked_example: A 300 mAh (0.3 Ah) 2S LiPo rated at 60C: I_continuous = 60 * 0.3 = 18 A.

entities.name: Battery energy capacity in watt-hours
entities.summary: Converts a battery's amp-hour capacity and nominal voltage into total stored energy in watt-hours, useful for comparing packs across different cell counts (voltages) on an equal-energy basis.

entities.name: Voltage sag from internal resistance under load
entities.summary: The battery's terminal voltage drops below its nominal/open-circuit voltage in proportion to the current drawn and the pack's internal resistance. Underestimating this leads to overestimating available torque/power right when it's needed most (weapon stall, hard push).

variables.V_loaded: actual terminal voltage under load, V

extra.worked_example: 2S LiPo, V_nominal = 7.4 V, R_internal = 0.020 ohm (20 mOhm, typical small high-C pack). At a modest I_draw = 10 A: V_loaded = 7.4 - 10*0.020 = 7.4 - 0.20 = 7.20 V. At the pack's rated max continuous I_draw = 18 A (from formula-battery-c-rating-to-amps): V_loaded = 7.4 - 18*0.020 = 7.4 - 0.36 = 7.04 V -- a ~5% sag right when the weapon needs full torque.

entities.name: Motor efficiency estimate at an operating point
entities.summary: Ratio of useful mechanical power out to electrical power in, at a specific torque/speed operating point -- NOT a constant, it varies across the motor's speed range and is generally best near (but not exactly at) the peak-power point.

variables.eta: efficiency at this operating point, dimensionless (0-1)
variables.T: torque delivered at this operating point, N*m
variables.omega: angular velocity at this operating point, rad/s
variables.I: current drawn at this operating point, A

extra.worked_example: At the 20,000 rpm (omega = 2094.4 rad/s) operating point: T = 0.03595 N*m (from formula-power-curve-peak-power), V = 11.1 V. Current at that torque: I = T/Kt = 0.03595/0.003472 = 10.36 A. P_out = T*omega = 0.03595*2094.4 = 75.3 W. P_in = V*I = 11.1*10.36 = 115.0 W. eta = 75.3/115.0 = 0.655 -> 65.5% efficient at this operating point.

entities.name: Impact force from momentum change and contact time
entities.summary: The average force during an impact equals the momentum change divided by how long the impact takes -- the key reason very brief, stiff impacts produce enormous peak forces compared to the same momentum change spread over a longer contact time (see formula-compliance-reduces-peak-force).

extra.expression: F_avg = delta_p / delta_t = m_eff * delta_v / delta_t

variables.F_avg: average force during the impact, N
variables.delta_p: momentum change during the impact, kg*m/s
variables.m_eff: effective mass involved (e.g. weapon effective mass at the tip), kg
variables.delta_v: velocity change during the impact, m/s

extra.worked_example: Weapon effective mass m_eff = 0.03174 kg slows from v = 67.0 m/s to about 57.0 m/s tip speed during a hit (delta_v = 10.0 m/s, consistent with the 20,000->17,000 rpm drop used in formula-energy-per-hit-vs-stored), over a contact time delta_t = 0.0015 s (1.5 ms, typical for a hard metal-on-metal impact). delta_p = 0.03174 * 10.0 = 0.3174 kg*m/s. F_avg = 0.3174 / 0.0015 = 211.6 N.

entities.name: Basic stress from force and area
entities.summary: The foundational stress equation, used to check whether an impact force is survivable for a given material and contact-patch size, by comparing the resulting stress to the material's yield strength.

variables.A: cross-sectional or contact area the force acts over, m^2

extra.worked_example: Impact force F = 211.6 N (from formula-impact-force-momentum-time) concentrated over a small contact patch A = 5mm x 5mm = 0.005 * 0.005 = 0.000025 m^2 (25 mm^2). sigma = 211.6 / 0.000025 = 8,464,000 Pa = 8.46 MPa -- comfortably below 6061-T6 aluminum's ~276 MPa yield strength, but could still locally dent a softer plastic armor panel at that same contact area.

entities.name: Beam bending stress in a flat armor panel
entities.summary: Models an armor panel bolted at two edges as a simply-supported beam under a central point impact load, giving the peak bending stress at the panel's surface -- the standard first check for whether a given armor thickness/material will survive a hit without cracking or permanently bending.

extra.expression: M = F * L / 4 ; I_beam = b * t^3 / 12 ; sigma_max = M * c / I_beam , with c = t/2

variables.M: bending moment at the panel's midspan, N*m
variables.F: impact force applied at midspan, N
variables.L: span between the panel's two support/mount points, m
variables.I_beam: second moment of area of the panel's cross-section, m^4
variables.c: distance from the neutral axis to the outer surface (= t/2 for a symmetric panel), m
variables.sigma_max: maximum bending stress at the panel surface, Pa

extra.worked_example: Aluminum armor panel: b = 0.050 m (50mm wide), t = 0.003 m (3mm thick), mounted with L = 0.040 m (40mm) between bolts, hit at midspan with F = 211.6 N. M = 211.6 * 0.040 / 4 = 8.464/4 = 2.116 N*m. I_beam = 0.050 * 0.003^3 / 12 = 0.050 * 0.000000027 / 12 = 0.00000000135/12 = 1.125e-10 m^4. c = 0.0015 m. sigma_max = 2.116 * 0.0015 / 1.125e-10 = 0.003174 / 1.125e-10 = 2.82e7 Pa = 28.2 MPa -- well under 6061-T6 aluminum's ~276 MPa yield strength (safety factor ~9.8x), so this panel survives the hit with margin to spare.

entities.name: Why compliance (a longer stopping time) reduces peak impact force
entities.summary: For the same momentum change, spreading the impact over a longer contact time (via a compliant mount, standoff, or slightly flexible armor) directly and proportionally lowers the peak force -- the physical reason 'a little give' in a mount often survives hits that a rigid one cracks under.

extra.expression: F_peak_compliant = delta_p / delta_t_compliant , where delta_t_compliant > delta_t_rigid

variables.F_peak_compliant: peak force with the more compliant mounting, N
variables.delta_p: momentum change (same regardless of mounting stiffness), kg*m/s
variables.delta_t_compliant: longer contact/deceleration time provided by the compliant mount, s

extra.worked_example: Same delta_p = 0.3174 kg*m/s as formula-impact-force-momentum-time. Rigid mount: delta_t = 0.0015 s gives F_peak = 211.6 N. A compliant standoff (rubber bushing, slight frame flex) doubles the stopping time to delta_t = 0.0030 s: F_peak = 0.3174 / 0.0030 = 105.8 N -- exactly half the peak force, for the same impact.

entities.name: Bolt shear stress estimate
entities.summary: Estimates the shear stress carried by a group of bolts resisting a reaction force (e.g. a weapon-motor mount reacting the impact force), by spreading the force evenly across the bolts' shear cross-sectional area.

variables.F: total force the bolted joint must resist, N
variables.n_bolts: number of bolts sharing the load
variables.A_bolt: cross-sectional (shear) area of one bolt, m^2 (= pi/4 * d^2)

extra.worked_example: A weapon-motor mount uses n_bolts = 2 M3 bolts (d = 0.003 m). A_bolt = pi/4 * 0.003^2 = 0.7854 * 0.000009 = 7.065e-6 m^2. Reaction force F = 211.6 N (from the impact-force example). tau = 211.6 / (2 * 7.065e-6) = 211.6 / 1.413e-5 = 1.497e7 Pa = 15.0 MPa -- far below typical alloy-steel socket-head cap screw shear strength (~350-500 MPa), a safety factor of over 20x on a single hit, which is appropriate given bolts see this load repeatedly (fatigue) rather than just once.

entities.name: Weight budget allocation across subsystems
entities.summary: Splits the robot's total weight limit into subsystem budgets by percentage, the first step of any antweight design before a single part is chosen. Typical splits differ sharply between a metal-weapon spinner and a plastic-antweight build (see the two worked-walkthrough chunks).

variables.weight_component_g: weight budget for one subsystem, g
variables.total_weight_g: total robot weight limit, g (454 g for a 1 lb antweight)
variables.pct_component: percentage of total weight allocated to that subsystem

extra.worked_example: A metal-weapon vertical-spinner budget at total_weight_g = 454 g: weapon 30% -> 454*0.30 = 136.2 g; drive 20% -> 454*0.20 = 90.8 g; armor/frame 30% -> 454*0.30 = 136.2 g; electronics 12% -> 454*0.12 = 54.5 g; fasteners/misc 8% -> 454*0.08 = 36.3 g. Sum = 136.2+90.8+136.2+54.5+36.3 = 454.0 g, exactly on budget.

entities.name: Tipping angle from CG height and track/wheelbase
entities.summary: The lateral (or fore-aft) tilt angle at which a robot's center of gravity passes directly over its wheel contact line and it starts to roll over -- a low, wide robot with a low CG resists tipping far better than a tall, narrow one, which matters both for wedge rammer defense and for the gyro-dance check above.

variables.theta_tip: tipping angle, rad (convert to degrees for intuition)
variables.track_or_wheelbase: distance between the two wheel contact lines being tipped over (track width for side tipping, wheelbase for fore-aft tipping), m
variables.h_cg: height of the center of gravity above the ground, m

extra.worked_example: Low, wide build: track_width = 0.090 m, h_cg = 0.025 m (25mm, low battery/electronics stack). theta_tip = atan((0.090/2)/0.025) = atan(0.045/0.025) = atan(1.8) = 60.9 deg -- very stable, hard to tip. Tall, narrow build for contrast: track_width = 0.060 m, h_cg = 0.040 m (40mm, stacked components). theta_tip = atan((0.060/2)/0.040) = atan(0.03/0.04) = atan(0.75) = 36.9 deg -- noticeably easier to tip over from a side hit or an aggressive turn.

entities.name: Approximate self-righting condition for a rounded-shell design
entities.summary: A simplified rule of thumb for shell/dome-shaped robots (common on shell spinners and some invertible bots): if the robot's center-of-gravity height stays below the radius of its rounded shell, gravity alone tends to roll it back onto its wheels when flipped, rather than leaving it balanced or stuck upside-down.
entities.notes: A rough qualitative rule of thumb, not a rigorous rigid-body stability derivation; real self-righting also depends on shell shape uniformity, weapon drag, and floor friction.

variables.h_cg: height of the center of gravity above the ground when the robot rests normally, m
variables.R_shell: radius of the rounded outer shell profile, m

extra.worked_example: A shell-spinner has a domed shell of radius R_shell = 0.045 m (45mm) and its CG sits at h_cg = 0.030 m (30mm, low battery/motor placement). Since 0.030 < 0.045, the design satisfies the rule of thumb and should tend to self-right if flipped. If h_cg were instead 0.050 m (a top-heavy build), it would fail the check and risk resting stably upside-down.

entities.name: Sheet/panel weight from area, thickness, and material density
entities.summary: Basic mass-from-volume-and-density calculation, used constantly when picking armor or frame stock thickness against the weight budget.

variables.weight: mass of the sheet/panel, g (if density is g/cm^3 and area/thickness are in cm)

extra.worked_example: HDPE (plastic-antweight-legal) panel: area = 100 cm^2 (10cm x 10cm), thickness = 0.6 cm (6mm), density = 0.95 g/cm^3. weight = 100 * 0.6 * 0.95 = 57.0 g. For comparison, the same 100 cm^2 panel in 6061 aluminum (density 2.70 g/cm^3) at a thinner 0.3 cm (3mm): weight = 100 * 0.3 * 2.70 = 81.0 g -- illustrating why plastic-class frames need much greater thickness to compete structurally, but still often land lighter or comparable per panel once thickness is matched to stiffness needs.

entities.name: Bite depth from closing speed, weapon RPM, and tooth count
entities.summary: How far (in material depth) a spinning weapon's tooth advances into an opponent between successive tooth strikes, given how fast the two robots are closing together. Fewer teeth at the same RPM means a LONGER gap between hits, so each hit gets a deeper 'bite' -- the core reason single-tooth vertical spinners are favored for maximum per-hit penetration over multi-tooth designs.

variables.tooth_count: number of teeth/striking points on the weapon
variables.bite_depth: material depth engaged per hit, m
variables.v_closing: closing speed between the two robots at the moment of contact, m/s

extra.worked_example: Weapon at rpm = 20,000, single tooth (tooth_count = 1), closing speed v_closing = 1.5 m/s (combined approach speed of both robots). f_hit = (20000/60) * 1 = 333.3 hits/s. bite_depth = 1.5 / 333.3 = 0.0045 m (4.5 mm) engaged per hit.

entities.name: Hit frequency from RPM and tooth count
entities.summary: How many times per second a spinning weapon's tooth (or teeth) strike, used both for the bite-depth formula above and for estimating cumulative impact loading on the weapon mount and motor over a fight.

variables.tooth_count: number of teeth/striking points on the weapon

extra.worked_example: Same weapon re-designed with 2 teeth instead of 1, same rpm = 20,000: f_hit = (20000/60) * 2 = 666.7 hits/s -- double the single-tooth hit rate. At the same v_closing = 1.5 m/s, bite_depth becomes 1.5/666.7 = 0.00225 m (2.25 mm), HALF the single-tooth bite depth -- the direct trade-off between hit rate and per-hit penetration depth that drives the classic 'single big tooth vs multiple smaller teeth' vertical-spinner design debate.

entities.name: Kv (velocity constant)
entities.summary: A motor's Kv rating describes how many RPM it would spin per volt applied, with no load and no back-EMF losses considered. Higher Kv motors spin faster but produce less torque per amp for a given size/winding.

entities.name: Kt (torque constant)
entities.summary: A motor's Kt rating describes how much torque it produces per amp of current. The physically exact relation to Kv is Kt[N*m/A] = 9.5493/Kv[rpm/V]; a widely-used hobby shorthand, Kt = 8.27/Kv, bakes in an assumed ~87% efficiency and gives a lower number than the exact form. See formula-kt-from-kv.

entities.name: Moment of inertia (MOI)
entities.summary: A measure of how a mass's distribution around a rotation axis resists angular acceleration -- the rotational equivalent of mass. Depends strongly on how far mass sits from the spin axis (radius squared), which is why small changes in weapon radius have an outsized effect on stored energy.

entities.name: Radius of gyration
entities.summary: The distance from the rotation axis at which the weapon's entire mass could be concentrated as a single point and produce the same moment of inertia. Useful as a single number summarizing how spread-out (vs concentrated) a weapon's mass distribution is.

entities.name: Stall current
entities.summary: The current a motor draws when its rotor is fully locked (zero RPM), limited only by winding resistance. This is the highest current the motor and its ESC will ever see, and is the number ESC/wire/connector sizing should be checked against.

entities.name: Stall torque
entities.summary: The maximum torque a motor can produce, occurring at zero RPM when the full stall current flows.

entities.name: No-load speed
entities.summary: The RPM a motor spins at with no mechanical load applied, close to (but slightly above) its real free-spinning speed once bearing drag and air resistance are accounted for.

entities.name: ESC (Electronic Speed Controller)
entities.summary: The electronic module that takes a control signal and battery power and drives a motor (brushed or brushless) at a commanded speed/direction. Antweights use one ESC per drive motor plus a separate ESC for the weapon motor, each sized with current headroom above the motor's stall current.

entities.name: Gear ratio
entities.summary: The reduction between a motor's own shaft speed and its output shaft speed after a gearbox, expressed as motor-turns-per-output-turn (e.g. 20:1 means the output turns once for every 20 motor turns, at 1/20th the RPM but roughly 20x the torque, efficiency losses aside).

entities.name: Bite depth
entities.summary: How far into an opponent's material a spinning weapon's tooth penetrates before the next tooth (or the same tooth on its next revolution) arrives -- governed by closing speed, weapon RPM, and tooth count.

entities.name: Effective (reduced) mass
entities.summary: A way of re-expressing a rotating weapon's inertia as an equivalent straight-line mass at a chosen reference radius (usually the tooth tip), so that ordinary linear collision/impact formulas can be applied directly.

entities.name: Traction-limited (vs torque-limited)
entities.summary: Describes a drivetrain whose real-world acceleration/pushing force is set by how much force the wheels can transmit to the floor (weight x friction coefficient) rather than by how much torque the motors can produce -- the normal condition for lightweight (1 lb class) combat robots.

entities.name: Parallel axis theorem
entities.summary: The rule for computing a part's moment of inertia about an axis other than its own center of mass: add the mass times the square of the offset distance to the part's own center-of-mass MOI. Used to combine a multi-part weapon (disc plus bolted-on tooth, etc.) into one total MOI.

entities.name: Compliance (structural)
entities.summary: Deliberate flexibility or give in a mount, standoff, or panel that extends the time over which an impact decelerates a part, which lowers the peak force for the same momentum change -- a key reason 'slightly soft' mounts often survive hits that fully rigid ones crack under.

entities.name: Center of gravity (CG)
entities.summary: The single point at which a robot's entire weight can be considered to act. Its height above the ground and its position relative to the wheelbase/track strongly influence tipping resistance, wedge performance, and self-righting behavior.

entities.name: Tipping angle
entities.summary: The angle of tilt at which a robot's center of gravity passes directly over its wheel (or shell) contact line and it begins to roll over, set by CG height relative to track width or wheelbase.

entities.name: FingerTech "Silver Spark" 16mm Gearmotor
entities.summary: The default drive gearmotor for 1 lb antweight robots: a Mabuchi FK-050 brushed motor mated to an all-metal 16mm spur gearhead, sold across a ladder of 9 gear ratios from 11.1:1 (fast) to 600:1 (slow/high-torque).
pros: All-metal gearbox is far more durable than plastic-geared alternatives
9 stock ratios cover the whole speed/torque range antweights need
Extra-long 3mm shaft allows direct (live-axle) wheel mounting
Very well documented, huge installed base, easy to source spares
cons: More expensive per unit than generic N20/N30 motors
Bare motor (not brushless) has lower efficiency and shorter brush life than premium brushless drive pods
600:1 and 300:1 ratios are fragile-ish under sustained stall loads
entities.notes: Base Mabuchi FK-050 motor spec (same for every ratio): 11,530 RPM no-load and 1.3A stall current, quoted for the 7.4V (2S LiPo) range typical of antweights; FingerTech states it runs 3V-18.5V. Bare-motor stall torque is ~0.0461 kg-cm; output stall torque at the wheel shaft is approximately bare_stall_torque x ratio x gearbox_efficiency, using ~0.75 efficiency for a 2-3 stage spur gearbox (medium confidence, not officially published). Full ratio ladder: 11.1, 22.2, 33.3, 50, 83.3 (discontinued/low stock), 100, 200, 300, 600:1. Weight by ratio: 11:1 = 28g, 22:1 through 100:1 = 29g, 200:1/300:1 = 31g, 600:1 = 32g. Shaft is 3mm with a flat, 38mm standard length, with a shorter 22mm version available on 22:1/33:1/50:1 for tighter builds. 11mm circular face-mount pattern for standard FingerTech motor mounts.

entities.name: FingerTech Silver Spark 16mm Gearmotor, 11.1:1
entities.summary: The fastest stock Silver Spark ratio, used when a builder wants maximum top speed and dodge/reposition ability rather than pushing torque, typically paired with a larger (~2in) wheel.
pros: Highest stock top speed of the Silver Spark family
Good choice for spinners that just need to aim/dodge, not ram hard
cons: Lowest stock torque of the ladder — can be traction-limited or torque-limited depending on wheel size and weight distribution
entities.notes: rpm_no_load and torque_stall_kgcm here are computed from the shared base-motor spec (11,530 RPM / 0.0461 kg-cm) divided/multiplied by the 11.1:1 ratio with an assumed ~0.75 gearbox efficiency; treat as medium-confidence estimates, not a FingerTech-published per-ratio table (their site shows the ratio table as an image).

entities.name: FingerTech Silver Spark 16mm Gearmotor, 100:1
entities.summary: A mid-high torque Silver Spark ratio popular on control bots and lifters that need strong pushing/lifting force more than raw speed.
pros: High torque headroom, good for pushing/wedge bots and small lifter actuation
Same footprint/price as every other Silver Spark ratio
cons: Slow top speed, not ideal for a bot that needs to dodge quickly
entities.notes: Computed from base motor spec at ~0.75 gearbox efficiency; medium confidence.

entities.name: FingerTech Silver Spark 16mm Gearmotor, 200:1
entities.summary: One of the highest stock-ratio Silver Sparks, used for slow, high-torque applications like weapon lifters, self-righters, or extremely traction-limited pushing bots rather than main drive.
pros: Very high torque for its size/weight
Same base motor reliability as the rest of the line
cons: Far too slow for main drive on a competitive bot
At this ratio the output gear stage becomes the limiting strength factor, not the motor
entities.notes: Computed estimate at ~0.75 efficiency; medium confidence. FingerTech's Gold Spark datasheet explicitly warns that torque above 6.84 kg-cm (95 oz-in) will damage the output gear stage on that line, and a similar mechanical ceiling likely applies to Silver Spark's higher ratios even though it uses an all-metal gearbox.

entities.name: FingerTech "Gold Spark" 16mm Gearmotor
entities.summary: FingerTech's budget-tier 16mm gearmotor: the same Mabuchi FK-050 base motor as the Silver Spark but with a plastic (not all-metal) gear stage, sold in 8 ratios from 20:1 to 360:1. Positioned for hobby/mini-sumo/line-following use and lighter-duty antweight builds rather than front-line competitive drive.
pros: Cheaper than Silver Spark for the same base motor
Fine for plastic antweights and lighter-contact builds
Same 11mm face-mount pattern as Silver Spark for easy swapping
cons: Plastic final gear stage is explicitly rated to fail above 6.84 kg-cm (95 oz-in) output torque
Not recommended as the sole drive on a bot expected to take direct hits or heavy ramming loads
entities.notes: Ratio ladder: 20:1, 35:1, 50:1, 86:1, 115:1, 150:1, 250:1, 360:1. All ratios share the same 28g weight and $14.79 price point per FingerTech's page. Output rpm/torque here computed from the shared base motor (11,530 RPM / 0.0461 kg-cm) at an assumed ~0.65 efficiency (lower than Silver Spark due to the plastic stage) — medium confidence.

entities.name: FingerTech Gold Spark 16mm Gearmotor, 150:1
entities.summary: A higher-torque Gold Spark ratio near the top of its safe operating range before hitting the plastic output gear's 6.84 kg-cm damage threshold.
pros: Cheap way to get real torque for a plastic-ant lifter or pusher
cons: Approaching the gearbox's rated damage threshold under stall; avoid pinning at full stall for long periods
entities.notes: Estimated output figures at ~0.65 efficiency; medium/low confidence on exact torque number.

entities.name: FingerTech "MegaSpark" Brushless 24mm Planetary Gearmotor
entities.summary: A premium 24mm brushless planetary gearmotor sold through the FingerTech ecosystem (via resellers), sized more for beetleweight than antweight but relevant as the high-end brushless benchmark antweight brushless pods are compared against.
pros: All-metal planetary gearbox is far more torque-dense and durable than a spur gearbox
Brushless motor avoids brush wear
cons: Oversized/heavy for a standard 1 lb antweight budget; more common on beetleweights
Requires a reversing brushless ESC, adding cost/weight/complexity vs a plug-and-play brushed motor
entities.notes: Included as context for how the antweight brushless drive-pod trend (Repeat Robotics, etc.) scales up; full spec sheet (kv, ratio options, price) was not available in this research pass — treat weight/price as unknown rather than guessed.

entities.name: Repeat Robotics "Mini Brushed" Mk2 Antweight Gearmotor
entities.summary: Repeat Robotics' antweight brushed planetary gearmotor, positioned as a more durable alternative to spur-gear motors like Silver Spark, using a multi-stage all-metal planetary gearbox for higher torque density and durability.
pros: Planetary gearbox is more durable under shock loading than a single-stage spur gearbox
Popular, well-regarded in the antweight community as a Silver Spark alternative
cons: Costs more than a Silver Spark or generic N20
Exact published RPM/torque/current spec table was not accessible in this research pass
entities.notes: Listed at $25 on the Repeat Robotics shop as "Mini Pro Brushed." Detailed numeric specs (no-load RPM, stall current, torque per ratio) were not extractable from the shop listing page in this pass; treat weight/rpm/torque as domain-knowledge estimates only, not sourced numbers, until verified directly against the product page.

entities.name: Repeat Robotics "Mini" Brushless 1106 Mk4.1 Gearmotor
entities.summary: Repeat Robotics' flagship antweight brushless drive gearmotor: a custom-wound 1106 outrunner brushless motor built directly into a 2-stage, 28.5:1, all-metal 16mm planetary gearbox with a 4mm hardened output shaft, aimed at builders who want more speed and efficiency than brushed Silver Sparks at a similar weight.
pros: Brushless motor = no brush wear, higher efficiency, higher power density than a same-size brushed motor
Metal planetary gearbox handles shock loads better than spur gears
Rated for 2S-4S, so voltage alone can retune top speed without swapping hardware
cons: Requires a reversing brushless ESC (not a simple brushed H-bridge)
Sensorless brushless motors can cog/stutter at very low duty cycle / near-stall, an issue brushed motors don't have
Historically has had periods of being sold out due to demand
entities.notes: The earlier Mk3/Mk4 generation used a 1104-size custom-wound motor (~3500kv); Mk4.1 moved to a 1106 stator (more stator volume/copper) for more torque and power in the same 16mm gearbox footprint. Using a 3500kv assumption and the 28.5:1 gearbox: at 2S (7.4V) no-load motor speed is ~25,900 rpm giving ~909 rpm at the output shaft; at 3S (11.1V) ~1,363 rpm output; at 4S (14.8V) ~1,818 rpm output (all idealized, no-load, medium/low confidence since kv was reported for the earlier 1104 version, not confirmed for 1106).

entities.name: Repeat Robotics "Mini Pro" 1106 Gearmotor
entities.summary: A higher-spec / higher-price variant of Repeat's 1106 brushless antweight drive gearmotor line, sold alongside the standard Mk4.1 for builders wanting extra performance or refinement (e.g. better bearings, tighter tolerances).
pros: Positioned as the premium option in Repeat's antweight brushless lineup
cons: More than double the price of the standard Mini Brushless variant
Detailed spec differences vs the standard Mk4.1 were not confirmed in this pass
entities.notes: Price ($42) confirmed from the Repeat Robotics shop listing; exact technical differentiation from the standard Mini Brushless 1106 was not available in the pages fetched.

entities.name: Repeat Robotics Compact Brushless 1806 Drive Gearmotor
entities.summary: A lightweight brushless planetary gearmotor built around an 1806-size motor, marketed as the lightest brushless beetleweight drive motor on the market; included here as context for scaling brushless drive up from antweight, or for extra-light plastic-antweight-adjacent builds where a lower part count matters more than absolute minimum weight.
pros: Very light for a brushless beetleweight motor
Hardened steel 4mm shaft with dual bearings on the gearbox output
cons: Sized and priced for 3 lb beetleweight, oversized/overpriced for a standard 1 lb antweight budget
entities.notes: Context only — not a direct fit for 1 lb antweight or plastic antweight, but shows the same drive-pod architecture (brushless motor cast directly into a planetary gearbox) scaled up one weight class.

entities.name: Generic N20 Gearmotor, 6V, 100:1
entities.summary: A widely sold 12mm-diameter micro DC gearmotor (compatible with Sanyo NA4S-style gearboxes) used by budget and plastic-antweight builders as a cheap alternative to FingerTech/Repeat/Pololu motors, at the cost of unit-to-unit quality consistency.
pros: Extremely cheap (a few dollars each), widely available from many sellers
Small and light, good for plastic antweights on a tight budget
cons: Quality varies drastically unit to unit and listing to listing (the "quality lottery")
Many units mix plastic gears into otherwise "metal gear" listings
No standardized spec sheet across sellers — published numbers are unreliable
entities.notes: Base N20 motor is commonly quoted at ~15,000 RPM no-load at 6V for the bare motor before gearing; a 100:1 gearbox gives ~150 RPM output, consistent with a 298:1 listing observed selling at 50 RPM (15,000/298 ~= 50). Gearbox torque ratings published by manufacturers cap around 20 kg*mm (2.0 kg-cm) of continuous output torque for most ratios below 380:1, meaning the motor's theoretical stall torque at high ratios exceeds what the gearbox can survive — a mechanical, not electrical, limit. Price and exact weight vary a lot by seller; treat as representative, low-confidence figures.

entities.name: Generic N20 Gearmotor, 6V, 298:1
entities.summary: A slow, high-torque N20 variant near the top of the common ratio ladder, used for lifters, self-righters, or very traction-limited plastic-antweight drives rather than fast main drive.
pros: High torque per dollar
Directly confirmed real-world sale listing (298:1, 50 RPM, 6V) validates the ~15,000 RPM bare-motor assumption
cons: Same quality-lottery risk as all generic N-series motors
Too slow alone for a competitive main-drive ratio
entities.notes: The 50 RPM @ 298:1 @ 6V figure is directly from a specific commercial listing, which is good corroboration for the family's base-motor speed assumption.

entities.name: Generic N20 Gearmotor, 12V, 1000:1
entities.summary: The slowest, highest-torque stock N20 ratio; the 1000:1 (and 380:1) versions get a slightly longer, reinforced gearbox and a higher torque rating than the rest of the line, making them the ones most likely to survive at this extreme reduction.
pros: Reinforced gearbox stage rated to ~25 kg*mm (2.5 kg-cm), higher than the ~20 kg*mm (2.0 kg-cm) rating of lower ratios
Very high torque for actuators/lifters
cons: Far too slow for drive; this ratio belongs on weapon-lift or self-righting mechanisms, not wheels
Gearbox is 3.5mm longer than other ratios, a minor packaging difference
entities.notes: Torque rating sourced from a manufacturer listing noting 25 kg*mm for 1000:1 and 380:1 vs 20 kg*mm for other ratios; RPM computed from the ~15,000 RPM bare-motor assumption.

entities.name: Generic N30 Gearmotor, 6V, 50:1
entities.summary: The larger sibling of the N20, using a bigger-diameter motor can (~30mm class) for more torque and current handling at the cost of extra weight; used in antweights (not usually plastic antweights, where every gram counts more) when N20 torque isn't enough but a 16mm FingerTech-class motor is still preferred to save weight.
pros: More torque and current headroom than N20 for a modest weight increase
Still cheap relative to name-brand combat motors
cons: Same quality-lottery sourcing risk as other generic N-series motors
Larger diameter can be harder to package in a slim 1 lb chassis than a 16mm motor
entities.notes: N30 specs are far less standardized/published than N20; numbers here are rough, low-confidence estimates based on the general pattern that N30 motors run roughly 1.5-2x the torque of an equivalent-ratio N20 at somewhat higher current draw and weight.

entities.name: Generic N10 Gearmotor, 6V, 100:1
entities.summary: The smallest of the common N-series (N10/N20/N30) gearmotor family, used in fairyweight robots and the very lightest plastic antweight builds where every gram matters more than raw torque.
pros: Lightest option in the N-series family
Cheap and small enough for micro-scale plastic antweights
cons: Least torque and current handling of the family
Least standardized specs / hardest to verify quality before buying
entities.notes: Specs are rough low-confidence estimates; N10 is far less documented in English-language combat-robot sources than N20.

entities.name: Pololu Micro Metal Gearmotor HP 6V, 30:1
entities.summary: Pololu's High-Power (HP) tune of its popular micro metal gearmotor line at a fast 30:1 ratio: a 10x12mm all-metal gearbox on a 3mm D-shaft output, favoring speed and current draw over the LP/MP tunes of the same physical motor.
pros: Precision-manufactured, far more consistent unit-to-unit than generic N-series motors
Well documented performance curves from Pololu
Very compact 10x12mm gearbox cross-section
cons: More expensive than generic N20 motors
3mm output shaft is short (9mm) — needs a hub or coupler, not usually long enough for direct antweight wheel mounting like a Silver Spark
entities.notes: HP variant free-run current is ~100mA and stall current ~1.6A at 6V (confirmed). Exact no-load RPM at 30:1 was not independently confirmed this pass; Pololu's published family typically gives high-hundreds to low-thousands RPM at this ratio (medium/low confidence on the exact figure — verify against the specific product's datasheet before final BOM lock).

entities.name: Pololu Micro Metal Gearmotor MP 6V, 30:1
entities.summary: The Medium-Power (MP) tune of Pololu's micro metal gearmotor, splitting the difference between the low-current LP and high-current HP versions of the same physical gearbox and ratio.
pros: Lower current draw than HP for the same ratio, easing ESC/battery sizing
Same precision metal gearbox as HP/LP
cons: Less torque/power than the HP tune at the same ratio
entities.notes: Stall current (0.67A) and free-run current (~70mA) at 6V are confirmed from Pololu's published data; RPM/torque at this specific ratio were not independently confirmed this pass.

entities.name: Pololu Micro Metal Gearmotor LP 6V, 50:1
entities.summary: The Low-Power (LP) tune of Pololu's micro metal gearmotor, drawing the least current of the three power tunes for a given ratio — useful when a builder is current-budget constrained (e.g. a very small ESC or shared receiver battery).
pros: Lowest current draw of the family, easiest on small ESCs
Same durable metal gearbox as MP/HP
cons: Least torque/power of the three tunes — can be traction- and power-limited on a heavier antweight
entities.notes: Stall current (0.36A) and free-run current (~40mA) at 6V confirmed from Pololu data.

entities.name: Pololu Micro Metal Gearmotor HP 6V, 100:1
entities.summary: A commonly chosen ratio/power combination for antweight-scale robots wanting a precision-made alternative to generic N20 motors, balancing speed and torque for typical 1.5-2in wheels.
pros: Good balance of speed and torque for a typical 1.5-2in antweight wheel
Precision metal gearbox, consistent unit to unit
Compact 10x12mm gearbox
cons: Higher stall current draw than MP/LP tunes — size ESC accordingly
Short 9mm output shaft needs a hub/coupler
entities.notes: Stall current confirmed from the HP family spec (1.6A at 6V); exact no-load RPM/torque at 100:1 specifically was not independently re-confirmed this pass — Pololu's own product page datasheet should be checked for the final number before locking a BOM.

entities.name: Pololu Micro Metal Gearmotor, Extended Motor Shaft variant
entities.summary: A version of the micro metal gearmotor line with the motor's rear shaft extended through the back of the case, letting a builder mount an encoder disc, a second small pulley, or a cooling/inertia element on the motor's non-gearbox end without modifying the motor.
pros: Enables encoder feedback or a rear-mounted pulley/sprocket without custom machining
Same gearbox performance as the standard version
cons: Small weight/cost premium over the standard (non-extended) version
Rarely needed on a simple 2WD antweight without closed-loop control
entities.notes: Useful mainly for control-bot builders who want wheel-speed encoders for closed-loop drive, or who need to power a secondary belt/pulley off the back of the motor in a 4WD belt-driven layout.

entities.name: 1104-size Brushless Motor (FPV-derived) for Custom Drive Pods
entities.summary: An 11mm-diameter, 4mm-tall outrunner brushless motor, originally developed for micro FPV drones, repurposed by combat robot builders into custom or off-the-shelf (e.g. Repeat Robotics) 16mm drive gearboxes for antweight main drive.
pros: Very high power-to-weight ratio compared to a brushed motor of similar size
No brushes to wear out
Wide range of kv (winding) options available from FPV motor market
cons: Sensorless variants can cog or stutter at very low speed/duty cycle, hurting fine driving control
Requires a reversing brushless ESC rather than a simple brushed driver
Needs to be built into or bought as part of a gearbox — not a drop-in drive-and-wheel solution by itself
entities.notes: kv commonly seen in this application is in the 3000-6000kv range depending on the specific winding chosen by the seller/builder; Repeat Robotics' early Mk3/Mk4 drive pod used a custom-wound ~3500kv 1104 motor.

entities.name: 1404-size Brushless Motor (FPV-derived) for Custom Drive Pods
entities.summary: A 14mm-diameter, 4mm-tall outrunner brushless motor, larger-stator sibling of the 1104/1106 sizes, used in higher-power antweight or lighter beetleweight custom drive builds where more torque/current handling is wanted from a similarly slim motor.
pros: More stator volume than 1104/1106 for a given height, so more torque/current capability
Same FPV-market kv/winding flexibility
cons: Larger diameter can be harder to fit inside a slim antweight chassis
Same brushless-drive complexity: reversing ESC required, sensorless cogging risk at low speed
entities.notes: Used mostly in custom-built drive pods (3D-printed or machined gearbox housing) rather than sold as a complete antweight-ready gearmotor product; treat as a component a builder pairs with their own gear reduction.

entities.name: Modified Continuous-Rotation 9g Micro Servo (Drive)
entities.summary: A standard 9g hobby micro servo (e.g. SG90-class) with its position-limiting potentiometer removed or bypassed (replaced with a fixed voltage divider) so it spins continuously instead of to a commanded angle, letting the transmitter's stick position set speed and direction directly with zero external electronics.
pros: No separate ESC/driver needed — plugs straight into a receiver channel
Extremely cheap and small, ideal for gram-constrained plastic antweights
Simple to source and modify with widely available tutorials
cons: Low top speed and low torque compared to a dedicated gearmotor + ESC of similar weight
Modification quality varies (pot removal/centering must be done carefully or the "stopped" position drifts)
Internal gearbox (plastic in cheap servos) is not built for combat shock loads
entities.notes: The standard mod: remove the servo's positional potentiometer and replace it with two fixed resistors (dividing voltage to sit at the servo's centered/neutral setpoint), and often trim/cut a mechanical stop tab inside the gearbox so the output gear can rotate freely. A 1ms pulse spins one direction, 2ms the other, ~1.5ms stops it, mirroring standard RC PWM servo signal ranges.

entities.name: Stock Continuous-Rotation Micro Servo (FS90R-class)
entities.summary: A factory-built continuous-rotation micro servo (no user modification needed), functionally equivalent to a hand-modified 9g servo but sold ready to use, popular for beginner plastic antweight and fairyweight drive.
pros: Zero-modification, works out of the box
Same weight/cost/simplicity benefits as the hand-modified version, with more consistent "stopped" centering
cons: Same low speed/torque ceiling as any 9g-servo-based drive
Still uses a small plastic internal gearbox not designed for combat impacts
entities.notes: A good first-build option for absolute beginners or very light plastic antweights where simplicity and low part count outweigh top-end performance.

entities.name: 16mm Planetary Gearbox Module (generic/Repeat-style)
entities.summary: A multi-stage (typically 2-3 stage) all-metal planetary gearbox module in the same 16mm form factor popularized by FingerTech's spur-gear Spark line, used by Repeat Robotics and others to mate to brushed or brushless motors for higher torque density and durability than a comparable spur gearbox.
pros: Higher mechanical efficiency (typically ~80-90%) than a comparable spur gearbox (~65-80%)
Planetary gear meshing distributes load across multiple planet gears, more shock-tolerant than a single spur gear train
More torque-dense for the same envelope size
cons: More expensive and complex to manufacture than a simple spur gearbox
Harder to hand-repair/re-lubricate in the field than an open spur gearbox
entities.notes: Represents the general category of planetary gearboxes used in Repeat Robotics' brushed and brushless antweight drive motors; efficiency figures are typical-range estimates from general gearbox engineering knowledge, not a specific manufacturer's published test data.

entities.name: N-Series (N10/N20/N30) Gearbox: Metal vs Plastic Gear Stages
aliases: N20 metal gear vs plastic gear
entities.summary: A comparison entity describing the inconsistent internal construction of budget N-series gearmotors: many listings advertise "metal gear" but only some internal stages are actually metal, with the rest plastic, and quality varies not just by listing but by individual unit within the same order — the core of the antweight community's "quality lottery" problem with these motors.
pros: When a unit is good, it is very cheap for the torque delivered
All-metal-gear versions do exist and can be nearly as durable as name-brand options at a fraction of the cost
cons: No reliable way to verify actual gear material from a listing photo or description alone
Reported failure modes include stripped final-stage gears, inconsistent KV/no-load speed between "identical" units, and out-of-box dead units
No standardized manufacturer datasheet across the many resellers of what is often the same underlying OEM part
entities.notes: Community-standard mitigation: buy several spares from the start (treat them as a consumable), bench-test every motor before installing it (measure free-run current and no-load RPM, compare across the batch, and reject outliers), and avoid using an untested cheap N-series motor as the sole drive on a bot going into an important match. Name-brand options (FingerTech Silver/Gold Spark, Repeat Robotics, Pololu) cost more specifically because they remove this variance.

entities.name: FingerTech Lite Flite Foam Wheel
entities.summary: FingerTech's neoprene foam wheel, the most widely used antweight wheel: extremely light, shock-absorbing, and surprisingly grippy for a plain foam tire, sold in a wide range of diameters and two widths to fit the Twist/Snap/Lite hub system.
pros: Very light — a major reason it's the default antweight wheel choice
Neoprene foam absorbs shock from arena floor impacts and hazards, protecting the gearbox/shaft
Surprisingly good grip for its weight, especially versus hard plastic wheels
Wide diameter range (25.4-76.2mm / 1.0-3.0in in 6.35mm/0.25in steps) lets builders dial in speed vs torque without changing motors
cons: Less absolute grip than a silicone-coated or compliant rubber tread wheel
Foam compresses/wears over many hard hits, eventually needs replacement
Needs a separate hub (Lite/Snap/Twist) adding a small amount of weight and an assembly step
entities.notes: A 2.00in diameter tire alone weighs about 0.14oz (~4g); smaller/larger diameters scale roughly with tire volume. Widths available: 12.7mm (0.5in, "Thin") and 19.1mm (0.75in, "Wide"). Plastic hubs used with Lite Flites weigh about 3g each, so a full wheel+hub assembly at 1.5-2in is roughly 7-10g depending on width and hub choice.

entities.name: Silicone-Coated / Cast Silicone Tire
entities.summary: A foam or 3D-printed wheel core coated or wrapped in a thin layer of cast silicone rubber (Shore A ~20-50 durometer), a common DIY upgrade path when bare foam or bare plastic doesn't provide enough grip for a control bot or pushing match.
pros: Significant traction improvement over bare foam or bare plastic/TPU
Durometer is tunable by the builder (softer = more grip but faster wear, harder = more durable but less grip)
Can be applied over an existing lightweight foam or printed core, keeping most of the weight savings
cons: Requires casting/mixing 2-part silicone rubber (extra build step, cure time, some skill)
Adds some weight over bare foam
Tackier compounds pick up arena debris faster, sometimes needing cleaning mid-event
entities.notes: Shore A 30-50 durometer silicone/urethane compounds are commonly cited as delivering the best grip on polished wood or acrylic arena floors without being so soft they wear out quickly or gum up with debris.

entities.name: 3D-Printed TPU Wheel
entities.summary: A wheel (tire, or tire+hub as one piece) 3D printed in flexible TPU filament (commonly 85-95A shore hardness), a zero-marginal-cost option extremely popular in plastic antweights since it fits the class's plastic-construction ethos and needs no purchased hub/tire hardware.
pros: Essentially free if you already own a printer and filament
Can be printed as a single piece with the hub/shaft-bore built in, saving assembly and weight of a separate metal hub
Tread pattern, diameter, and width are all fully custom per design
Very impact-resistant, harder to crack than rigid printed wheels
cons: TPU can be harder to print reliably (stringing, needs a direct-drive extruder ideally) than rigid filaments
Grip is generally lower than a soft cast-silicone tire at similar hardness, though still much better than a rigid PLA/PETG wheel
Print layer lines/infill can affect roundness/balance if not printed carefully
entities.notes: Common shore hardness for printable TPU filament is 85A-95A; softer (lower shore) TPUs exist but are harder to print and more prone to tearing on impact.

entities.name: O-Ring Tire Wheel
entities.summary: A lightweight wheel technique where a plain hub (aluminum, printed plastic, or Delrin) has a groove sized to hold a rubber O-ring (or several stacked), which is stretched onto the hub's outer diameter to act as a cheap, easily replaceable, grippy tire.
pros: Very cheap and easy to replace when worn or damaged — just pull off the old o-ring and stretch on a new one
Rubber compound gives solid grip, often better than bare foam
Hub itself can be very light and simple to make or print
cons: O-ring can roll or shift in its groove under high torque/lateral load if the groove isn't sized tightly enough
Less shock absorption than a full foam tire
Buna-N/silicone o-ring compound and durometer choice affects grip and wear, requiring some trial and error
entities.notes: A well-known low-cost DIY approach used across weight classes, including small o-ring sizes on antweight-scale hubs.

entities.name: Banebots T61 Compliant Wheel
entities.summary: A compliant (flexible tread) wheel line from Banebots that conforms to surfaces for extra grip and control, sold in 6 hardness options, 4 diameters, and 4 hub-shaft sizes, primarily sized for beetleweight/hobbyweight but with small diameters usable in heavier antweight or control-bot-focused builds; the smaller Banebots T40 line is aimed more directly at ant/fairy scale.
pros: Compliant rubber tread conforms to the arena floor for better grip and control than a rigid wheel
Wide range of hardness options (10A soft/max-grip up to 60A firm/durable) to tune grip vs longevity
Well-known, widely trusted brand in combat robotics with a long track record
cons: Heavier than a foam or TPU wheel of similar diameter — a real cost on a 1 lb weight budget
Smallest available diameters may still be larger/heavier than what a competitive lightweight antweight wants
entities.notes: T61 compliant hardness options: 10A (yellow, maximum flexibility/grip) and 60A (black, firmer/more durable) were specifically confirmed; the line is stated to offer 6 hardness options total, 4 diameters, and 4 hub shaft sizes. The smaller T40 line is described as better suited to antweight/fairyweight builds.

entities.name: FingerTech Lite Hub
entities.summary: FingerTech's lightest wheel hub, designed to mount common foam wheels onto a 3mm motor shaft with minimal added weight.
pros: Lightest hub option in the FingerTech lineup
Simple, proven, widely used with Lite Flite wheels
cons: Less robust than Snap/Twist hubs under very high shock/torque loads
entities.notes: Approximate weight ~3g each based on general FingerTech plastic-hub weight figures cited for Lite Flite assemblies.

entities.name: FingerTech Snap Hub
entities.summary: An anodized 6061 aluminum hub from FingerTech that holds a foam tire tightly via a custom washer with a recess to prevent the retaining snap ring from coming loose, offering more strength than the plastic Lite Hub at a modest weight cost.
pros: Anodized 6061 aluminum construction is stronger and more durable than plastic hubs
Positive snap-ring retention keeps the tire from working loose over a match
cons: Heavier than the plastic Lite Hub
entities.notes: Exact per-unit weight not confirmed this pass.

entities.name: FingerTech Twist Hub
entities.summary: An anodized 6061 aluminum hub secured to the motor shaft with an 8-32 setscrew, holding the foam tire tightly via a locking washer; sold in Thin (0.50in) and Wide (0.75in) widths for both 3mm and 4mm shafts.
pros: Setscrew retention onto the motor shaft is very secure against slipping under torque
Aluminum build is strong and light
Available for both 3mm and 4mm shafts, and Thin/Wide widths
cons: Heavier than the plastic Lite Hub
Setscrew must be properly torqued/thread-locked or it can back out over repeated hits
entities.notes: Thin (0.50in wide) version confirmed at 5.5g each.

entities.name: GT2 Belt & Pulley Drivetrain Set (antweight scale)
entities.summary: A small GT2 (2mm pitch) timing belt and matching aluminum or 3D-printed pulley set used to link a front and rear wheel on each side of a 4WD antweight, letting two motors drive four wheels instead of needing four separate drive motors.
pros: Gives 4-wheel traction and redundancy (surviving a lifted/high-centered wheel) using only 2 drive motors
GT2 belts are cheap, widely available (from 3D printer supply chains), and don't require the precision of chain
Printed pulleys keep the added weight low
cons: Adds mechanical complexity and a few extra failure points (belt tension, pulley wear, belt skipping teeth under shock)
Extra weight vs a simple 2WD direct-drive layout, competing with armor/weapon weight budget
Belt can be damaged by direct weapon hits if not shielded
entities.notes: A common way to get 4WD traction and pushing power on a 1 lb control bot without the weight and complexity of 4 separate gearmotors and ESCs.

entities.name: Robot Speed from Motor RPM and Wheel Diameter
entities.summary: Converts a drivetrain's output (wheel) RPM and wheel diameter into a theoretical no-load top speed, the first step in sizing any antweight drivetrain.

variables.motor_rpm_no_load: no-load RPM of the bare motor at the chosen nominal voltage
variables.gear_ratio: total gearbox reduction, expressed as N:1 (use N)
variables.v_mph: theoretical no-load top speed in miles per hour (real-world loaded speed is lower)

extra.worked_example: FingerTech Silver Spark at 11.1:1 (motor_rpm_no_load = 11,530 at 7.4V) with a 2.0in wheel: wheel RPM = 11,530 / 11.1 = 1,038.7 RPM. v_mph = 1,038.7 x pi x 2.0 / 1056 = 1,038.7 x 6.283 / 1056 ~= 6.18 mph. This matches commonly reported antweight sprint speeds of roughly 6 mph. Real-world speed under load (current draw sagging the battery voltage, rolling resistance, and wheel slip) typically comes in at ~70-90% of this theoretical number.

entities.name: Required Motor Torque for a Target Acceleration / Pushing Force
entities.summary: Sizes the motor-shaft stall torque needed to accelerate a given robot mass at a target rate (or to sustain a target pushing force), working back through the wheel radius, gear ratio, and gearbox efficiency.

extra.expression: F = m * a;  T_wheel = F * r / n_driven_wheels;  T_motor_stall_required = T_wheel / (gear_ratio * efficiency)

variables.a: target acceleration or deceleration, m/s^2 (e.g. 1-2g for a fast start/ram)
variables.n_driven_wheels: number of powered wheels sharing the load
variables.T_wheel: required torque at the wheel/output shaft, N*m
variables.efficiency: gearbox mechanical efficiency, ~0.65-0.80 for spur gearboxes, ~0.80-0.92 for planetary
variables.T_motor_stall_required: minimum motor-shaft stall torque needed, N*m (convert to kg-cm by dividing N*m by 0.09807)

extra.worked_example: 1 lb robot (m = 0.4536 kg) targeting 2g acceleration (a = 19.6 m/s^2) on two driven wheels of radius 0.019 m (1.5in diameter): F = 0.4536 x 19.6 = 8.89 N. T_wheel per side = 8.89 x 0.019 / 2 = 0.0844 N*m = 0.86 kg-cm. With a 33.3:1 Silver Spark gearbox at ~0.75 efficiency: T_motor_stall_required = 0.86 / (33.3 x 0.75) = 0.0345 kg-cm, comfortably under the Silver Spark's ~0.046 kg-cm bare-motor stall torque, so this ratio has margin to spare for a 2g start. At the fast 11.1:1 ratio, the same math needs 0.86 / (11.1 x 0.75) = 0.103 kg-cm at the motor shaft — more than the bare motor's stall torque can supply, meaning 11.1:1 alone cannot sustain a full 2g acceleration at stall (though brief transient acceleration before the motor reaches that speed is a separate, more forgiving calculation).

entities.name: Traction Limit: Why Torque Beyond Available Grip Is Wasted
entities.summary: Defines the maximum pushing/accelerating force a drivetrain can actually put to the ground, set by wheel-to-floor friction rather than motor torque; any drivetrain torque capacity beyond this ceiling just spins the wheels and wastes battery/heat instead of producing more force.

variables.mu: coefficient of friction between the wheel tread and the arena floor (dimensionless; roughly 0.3-0.5 for bare foam on polycarbonate, 0.5-0.8 for silicone/compliant rubber tread on polycarbonate or wood)
variables.N: normal force pressing the driven wheels into the floor, Newtons (approximately the full robot weight for a 2WD antweight with no significant weight on non-driven casters/skids)
variables.F_max: maximum pushing/traction force before the wheels slip, Newtons

extra.worked_example: 1 lb robot (weight = 0.4536 kg x 9.81 = 4.45 N) on silicone-tread wheels with mu ~= 0.6 on a polycarbonate floor: F_max = 0.6 x 4.45 = 2.67 N. Compare this to the pushing force available at the wheel from formula-required-torque-acceleration-pushing: even the lowest-torque stock Silver Spark ratio (11.1:1, ~0.38 kg-cm output stall torque, ~0.0373 N*m) on a 0.019 m wheel radius over 2 driven wheels can produce up to 2 x 0.0373 / 0.019 = 3.9 N of force at the wheel before the motor itself stalls — already above the 2.67 N traction ceiling. In other words, the wheels slip before the motor runs out of torque, so choosing a slower/higher-torque ratio than 11.1:1 purely to 'push harder' would not actually increase the robot's real-world pushing force; it would only reduce top speed. Common guidance (e.g. from Just 'Cuz Robotics) is to size the gear ratio with roughly 1.5-2x the torque strictly required to reach the traction limit, then optimize the remaining ratio choice for speed and control feel.

entities.name: Stall Current vs ESC Rating and Duty-Cycle Thermal Limits
entities.summary: Explains how to size a drive ESC/driver's continuous and burst current ratings against a motor's stall current, and why sustained full-stall (e.g. pinned against a wall or opponent) is a thermal, time-limited event rather than something a small combat robot motor can hold indefinitely.

extra.expression: I_stall_total = n_motors * I_stall_per_motor;  esc_continuous_rating >= I_cruise_expected;  esc_burst_rating >= I_stall_total (with margin);  t_safe_stall is inversely related to I^2 (I^2*R resistive heating)

variables.I_stall_per_motor: stall current of one drive motor at the operating voltage, Amps
variables.n_motors: number of drive motors on that ESC/battery branch
variables.I_stall_total: worst-case simultaneous stall current draw, Amps
variables.I_cruise_expected: typical current draw while driving normally (well below stall), Amps
variables.esc_burst_rating: ESC/driver's short-burst peak current rating, Amps
variables.t_safe_stall: approximate time a motor can be safely held at stall before winding damage from resistive heating

extra.worked_example: Two FingerTech Silver Sparks, each 1.3A stall at 7.4V: I_stall_total = 2 x 1.3 = 2.6A combined worst case (both wheels pinned simultaneously). Normal cruising current is much lower, roughly 0.2-0.6A per motor. A drive ESC/driver should have a continuous rating comfortably above the cruising current (so it runs cool during normal driving) and a burst rating at or above the 1.3A per-channel stall figure with headroom (e.g. a 2-3A continuous per-channel rating is typical for antweight brushed ESCs). Because these small motors have very little thermal mass, holding full stall (e.g. wedged against an arena wall) for more than roughly 10-20 seconds risks overheating the winding insulation even though the ESC itself may tolerate the current — drivers are taught to 'bump' the throttle in short pulses rather than holding full stall continuously in a pushing match.

entities.name: Selecting a Gear Ratio from a Desired Top Speed
entities.summary: Rearranges the speed formula to solve for the gear ratio needed to hit a target top speed with a given motor and wheel diameter, then checks the result against the ratios actually available off the shelf.

variables.motor_rpm_no_load: no-load RPM of the bare motor at the chosen nominal voltage
variables.gear_ratio: gearbox reduction ratio needed, N:1 (solve for N)

extra.worked_example: Target: 8 mph top speed using a Silver Spark motor (motor_rpm_no_load = 11,530 at 7.4V) and a 2.0in wheel. gear_ratio = 11,530 x pi x 2.0 / (8 x 1056) = 72,444 / 8,448 ~= 8.6:1. Silver Spark's fastest stock ratio is 11.1:1, not 8.6:1, so an exact 8 mph target isn't reachable with this motor/wheel pairing off the shelf. Two fixes: (1) increase wheel diameter to 2.5in and re-check the stock 11.1:1 ratio: wheel RPM = 11,530/11.1 = 1,038.7, v_mph = 1,038.7 x pi x 2.5 / 1056 ~= 7.7 mph, very close to the 8 mph target; or (2) switch to a higher-RPM brushless drive pod (e.g. Repeat Robotics' 1106 gearmotor), which can exceed this speed range easily by running a higher supply voltage (3S/4S) instead of changing wheel size.

entities.name: Plastic Antweight
entities.summary: A 1 lb (454 g) variant of antweight in which the entire robot (except electronics, motors, and fasteners) must be built from approved 3D-printable/thermoplastic materials. Started by Western Allied Robotics to make antweight building cheaper and more accessible, later folded into SPARC as an official weight-class variant. It is the fastest-growing beginner class because a full robot can be printed on a hobby FDM printer for well under $50.
entities.notes: Originated with Western Allied Robotics (WAR) in 2015 as an intentionally weaker-material 1lb class so that new builders could compete without CNC machining or metal fabrication. SPARC later formalized 'Plastic Classes' (section 4.4 of the SPARC Robot Construction Specifications) as a template most North American regional events now copy verbatim or with minor local amendments. It is functionally the same 454 g weight limit as a normal antweight; the only difference is the construction-material restriction. Some clubs also run a lighter plastic fairyweight/150g class, especially in the UK, which is a distinct weight bracket, not the same as the 1lb US plastic ant.

extra.typical_arena: Same antweight arena as the standard 1lb class: a small (roughly 4x4 to 8x8 ft) Lexan/polycarbonate-walled box, run as its own bracket rather than mixed with metal antweights

entities.name: SPARC Plastic Class (Robot Construction Specifications v1.6, §16.3)
entities.summary: The template ruleset most North American plastic-ant events build from. Defines the class's spirit, the exact allowed plastics list (verified verbatim against the current v1.6 PDF, 21 September 2025), the COTS-parts exemption with explicit permitted/not-permitted examples, and a notably strict post-processing ban.
entities.notes: This is the single most copy-pasted plastic-ant ruleset in the US; SCAR, Robot Ruckus and many one-off regional events either quote it directly or diverge from it in a clearly marked 'deviations' section per SPARC's own template instructions (§2). Notably, SPARC's own §16.3.4 explicitly BANS annealing/acetone-smoothing/boiling as illegal 'durability-enhancing' post-processing — a direct, verified contradiction with SCAR's separate Plastic Ant FAQ, which explicitly ALLOWS annealing and acid smoothing. This is real, current org-to-org variation, not a hypothetical: a part legally annealed for a SCAR event would need to be reprinted un-annealed to be legal at a strict-SPARC event, and vice versa is a non-issue since SPARC's list is the stricter one.

extra.organization: SPARC (Standardized Procedures for the Advancement of Robotic Combat)
extra.version: v1.6, 21 September 2025, section 16.3 'Plastic Class' (this section was numbered §4.4 in older v1.4-era copies still quoted around the community; content is materially unchanged)
key_rules: 16.3 spirit (verbatim): 'The spirit of this class is to create an accessible and affordable class that encourages experimentation and rapid iteration by utilizing 3D printing.'
16.3.1.1 (verbatim): 'Frames, weapons and other custom parts may only be made from PLA, PLA+, PET, PETG, ABS, or ASA and must be FDM/FFF 3D printed.'
16.3.1.2 (verbatim): 'Materials that are functionally identical to PLA+ but have a different name for marketing purposes will be considered PLA+ when determining legality. (ex. PLA Pro, Super PLA)'

16.3.1.3/16.3.1.4 (verbatim): 'No other types of plastics or materials are allowed (ie. metal, carbon fiber, UHMW, etc). Composite and blended materials that use legal materials as a base are not permitted. Examples include but are not limited to: Carbon Fiber PLA, Glass Filled ABS, and Flex PLA.'

16.3.2.1 (verbatim, COTS exemption): 'Commercial Off The Shelf parts can be made from any material. This includes components such as motors, electronics, axles, bushings, bearings, fasteners, and adhesives.'

16.3.2.1.1 (verbatim, the actual policing test): 'COTS parts may not be used outside of their typically accepted function.' Permitted example given: 'Using shafts and bearings to allow wheels or a weapon to spin freely, using screws to attach two parts together.' Not-permitted example given: 'Using COTS parts as counterbalances for weapons, as weapon impactors, or as armor.'

16.3.2.1.2/16.3.2.1.3 (verbatim): COTS parts may be modified 'so long as the function of the part is not significantly changed' (e.g. shortening motor shafts, adding flats for set screws), and 'COTS equivalent parts are allowed' — builder-sourced/manufactured gearmotors, custom electronics, prototype components, and non-commercially-available axles all count as COTS-equivalent.
16.3.2.1.4 (verbatim): 'Magnets to enhance traction or downforce are prohibited.'

16.3.3 (wheels/tires, verbatim highlights): tires/traction elements may be COTS rubber, custom cast rubber, rubber coatings, or foam; parts between motor/shaft and tire must be COTS, foam, or printed from allowed materials; non-allowed-material traction elements 'may not be designed such that they provide more armor or structure than a COTS equivalent part.'

16.3.4 (verbatim, post-processing — notably strict): 'Painting or otherwise marking robots is permitted if done solely for aesthetic purposes... Post-processing of materials using techniques that enhance durability is not permitted. Disallowed processes include but are not limited to annealing, acetone soaking, and boiling of parts.'
16.3.5 (verbatim): 'Robots may be disqualified at the Event Organizer's discretion if it is deemed to violate the spirit of the class.'

Standard SPARC weight-bonus table applies on top (§4.1): 1lb/454g base, 1.25x (1.25lb) shuffler bonus, 1.5x (1.5lb) non-traditional-locomotion bonus, 2x (2lb) walker bonus — plastic ants can claim these bonuses exactly like standard-material antweights.

General SPARC safety rules apply on top: 60-second full manual deactivation (§3.4.3), visible weapon locking pin required at power-on (§3.4.6), drive fail-safe typically required even at 1lb (§6.4.1), at-least-two-frequency radio requirement (§6.4.2).
banned: any plastic not on the PLA/PLA+/PET/PETG/ABS/ASA list unless the organizer grants an exception
composite/blended filaments built on a legal base plastic (carbon-fiber PLA, glass-filled ABS, flex PLA, etc.)
COTS parts used as weapon counterbalance, weapon impactor, or armor
post-processing meant to enhance durability: annealing, acetone soaking, boiling of parts
