entities.name: SCAR 2025 Ruleset — Plastic Ant Weight Class
aliases: SoCal Attack Robots plastic ant rules
entities.summary: SoCal Attack Robots' 2025 ruleset section covering Plastic Ant, closely following SPARC's template but adding explicit weight bonuses for shufflers and non-wheeled locomotion and an explicit magnet/UHMW ban.

key_rules: Base weight 1lb / 454g; 1.25lb / 567g shuffler bonus; 1.5lb / 681g non-wheeled-motion bonus.
Structure, armor and weapons restricted to PET, PETG, ABS, ASA, PLA, or PLA+ (organizers may permit more at their discretion).
Motors, electronics, axles, fasteners and adhesives exempt from the plastic-only rule as long as they don't enhance structural integrity, armor, or weapon performance.
Metal, carbon fiber and UHMW explicitly prohibited as structural/armor/weapon material.
Magnets designed to boost traction or downforce are forbidden; foam is allowed for wheels and electronics padding.
Disqualification at event-organizer discretion for violating 'the spirit of the class'.

entities.name: SCAR Plastic Ant FAQ
entities.summary: A supplementary FAQ document SCAR publishes alongside its main ruleset that names specific approved filament brands and explicitly bans several materials (TPU, nylon, composites, epoxy coatings) that are ambiguous under the base ruleset's plain-language material list.
entities.notes:
IMPORTANT ORG-VARIANCE FINDING #1: SCAR is one of the stricter interpreters of the plastic-only rule on MATERIALS — it explicitly bans TPU and nylon by name, materials that are commonly praised in general antweight/beetleweight circles as tough flexible armor. Builders moving a design between events must check the local FAQ, not just the base material list, since 'PETG/PLA/ABS' alone does not settle whether TPU trim or nylon gears are legal.

IMPORTANT ORG-VARIANCE FINDING #2 (verified against both primary sources directly): SCAR's FAQ explicitly ALLOWS 'annealing or smoothing with heat or acid,' while SPARC's current v1.6 Robot Construction Specifications (§16.3.4) explicitly BANS annealing, acetone soaking, and boiling as illegal 'durability-enhancing' post-processing. This is a direct, confirmed contradiction between two real, currently-published plastic-ant rulesets on the exact same question — a concrete case where a part legal at one event is illegal at another with no visual difference at inspection time, entirely dependent on which ruleset the event runs.

key_rules: Chassis/weapon material must be PLA, ABS, or PETG printable under 260°C; named approved brands include FusionFilaments HTPLA+, Duramic PLA+, Overture Super PLA+, and Hatchbox ABS.

COTS wheel parts (e.g. FingerTech, Repeat Robotics, Pololu) are allowed, along with COTS rubber, cast urethane, foam, or rubber coatings and traction additives (silicone/latex) for tires, unless they create entanglement risk.
Metal bearings, axles, shafts, fasteners, COTS motor-mount adapters, and metal servo horns/gears are exempted as long as the weapon is non-functional without its plastic parts.
Post-processing: annealing or smoothing with heat or acid is allowed, thin decorative paint is allowed; material additives are not.
Inspection is primarily visual; datasheets are not required by default, but suspicious builds can be investigated further.
banned: TPU, including custom TPU wheel hubs
'flex' or blended filaments marketed for enhanced properties
epoxy coatings, Bondo, or similar fillers

entities.name: Western Allied Robotics (WAR) Plastic Antweight — Original 2015 Rules
entities.summary: The founding ruleset of the plastic antweight class, introduced by Western Allied Robotics in 2015, restricting the chassis and weapon to PET/PETG/ABS/PLA/PLA+ while exempting motors, electronics, axles, fasteners and adhesives.
entities.notes: This WAR wording is essentially word-for-word what became SPARC section 4.4, making WAR the direct ancestor of nearly every plastic-ant ruleset now in use.

extra.version: 2015 origin ruleset (language subsequently absorbed into SPARC §4.4)
key_rules: 1lb weight limit, same as standard antweight.
Chassis and weapon restricted to PET, PETG, ABS, PLA, PLA+.
Motors, electronics, axles, fasteners, adhesives exempt from the material restriction provided they don't add structural strength, armor, or weapon performance.
Robot competes in a separate plastic-only bracket, never mixed with standard-material antweights.
banned: metal or any non-listed plastic used as chassis/armor/weapon material

entities.name: Robot Ruckus Plastic Ant Construction Rules
entities.summary: Robot Ruckus's plastic ant rules, requiring 3D-printed PLA/PLA+/ABS/PETG construction and following the standard metal-fastener exemption, with an explicit requirement that surface screws be countersunk or shrouded so they cannot act as armor or weapon impactors.

key_rules: Plastic Ant robots must be 3D printed in PLA, PLA+, ABS or PETG.
Non-plastic parts (motors, electronics, axles, fasteners, adhesives) may be any material but cannot enhance structural integrity, armor, or weapon performance.
Metal fasteners are allowed, but where they appear on the outer surface they should be countersunk or shrouded so they cannot act as an impact point or armor plate.
banned: metal, carbon fiber or other non-approved material used structurally, as armor, or as a weapon surface
exposed/proud metal fastener heads used as de facto armor studs

entities.name: Plastic Ant Vertical Spinner
entities.summary: The single most common competitive plastic-ant archetype: a spinning disc or drum on a vertical (side-to-side relative to the arena floor, striking-face-forward) axis, printed from PETG or ABS, driven by a small brushless outrunner. Dominant because a thick printed disc keeps its weapon mass close to the axis and hits with blunt, ring-shaped force rather than requiring a hardened cutting edge.
pros: Printed disc/hub is simple to design and cheap to replace after a broken tooth or crack
Blunt ring impact matches what plastic can survive better than a thin blade
Good self-righting behavior if the disc doubles as a bumper
cons: Printed weapon can crack or delaminate at the bore/keyway under repeated hits
Needs a well-designed containment/guard since a plastic disc can shatter more unpredictably than metal
Kinetic energy per gram is inherently lower than a metal disc of the same size
entities.notes: Because printed plastic is roughly 3-6x less dense and far weaker in tension than hardened steel, plastic-ant vertical spinners spend a disproportionate share of the 454g budget on the disc/hub and its surrounding shroud rather than on drive power.

extra.typical_weapon_motor: Small brushless outrunner, roughly 1811-2205 size, 1900-2800kv, run on 2S
extra.typical_drive: Two micro brushed gearmotors (N20 or 130-size) direct-driving small printed/TPU-tired wheels

entities.name: Plastic Ant Drum Spinner (Undercutter)
entities.summary: A full-width horizontal drum, usually printed in PETG for impact ductility, spun on an axis parallel to the ground and low to the floor to drive under opponents. The drum's wall thickness itself does the damage (blunt/ram) rather than teeth, and the wide printed cylinder is naturally stronger against delamination than a thin bar.
pros: A full cylindrical drum wall resists cracking better than a thin bar because load is spread around the ring
Low profile makes it hard for wedges to get underneath
Printed teeth/paddles on the drum are cheap to reprint after being chipped
cons: Full-width weapon leaves the whole front exposed; a chip anywhere can unbalance the drum
Needs precise balancing since a small amount of unbalanced printed mass vibrates badly at high RPM
entities.notes: Popular open-source design (e.g. the community 'drum spinner combat robot' shared on Printables) demonstrates the class's move away from bar spinners toward drums for exactly this durability reason.

extra.typical_weapon_motor: Brushless outrunner 1811-2204 size, 2600-3000kv on 2S, occasionally geared down slightly for torque
extra.typical_drive: Two micro gearmotors, often mounted to keep the drum as low to the ground as possible

entities.name: Plastic Ant Horizontal (Bar) Spinner
entities.summary: A single spinning bar or blade on a vertical axis (spinning in the horizontal plane, striking outward in a circle), the dominant weapon type in metal antweight but a comparatively weak and fragile choice in plastic because the weapon tip itself must be printed plastic rather than hardened steel.
pros: Can hit from any side without needing to line up a face, useful defensively
Simple single-part weapon geometry is easy to print and swap
cons: A thin printed bar tip is the weakest possible cross-section in the weakest material allowed in the class — it is the archetype most likely to shatter on its own first hit
Raises the robot's center of gravity and exposes a large flat profile for wedges/lifters to exploit
Kinetic energy transfer to the opponent is poor compared to metal because the bar has to be kept thick (hence slower or lighter) to survive its own swing
entities.notes: This is the archetype most changed by the plastic-only rule. In metal antweight, bar spinners with hardened steel or titanium tips are a top-tier weapon; in plastic, the same geometry with a printed tip is fragile and prone to catastrophic self-destruction, which is a large part of why drums and vertical spinners with thick printed hubs dominate the plastic meta instead.

extra.typical_weapon_motor: Brushless outrunner 1400-2000kv on 2S-3S (lower kv than vertical spinners to keep tip speed in a survivable range for the printed blade)
extra.typical_drive: Two micro gearmotors

entities.name: Plastic Ant Beater Bar / Egg-beater
entities.summary: A low, wide horizontal weapon bar mounted close to the floor at the front of the robot that beats upward into an opponent's underside, similar in geometry to a drum spinner but usually a simpler bar rather than a full cylinder, printed thick to survive repeated low-clearance strikes.
pros: Cheaper/simpler to print than a full drum
Low profile discourages opposing wedges
cons: Narrower than a drum so it can miss off-center hits
Bar ends are a stress concentration point that tends to crack first

extra.typical_weapon_motor: Brushless outrunner 2200-2700kv on 2S
extra.typical_drive: Two micro gearmotors, low ground clearance chassis

entities.name: Plastic Ant Wedge / Control Bot
entities.summary: A weaponless or lightly-weaponed robot built around a low front wedge and strong drivetrain, designed to win on driving skill, ring-out and judges' decision rather than weapon damage — often the recommended first build and a strong beginner-friendly counter to fragile plastic spinners.
pros: Nothing to break: no weapon motor, ESC, or fragile printed weapon to crack
Thick printed wedge is one of the best uses of plastic's weight-cheap bulk
Excellent way to learn driving and electronics before adding a weapon
Directly counters the fragile plastic-only spinner archetypes by denying them a clean hit
cons: Cannot win by knockout/damage, relies on ring-outs, pins and judges' decisions
Loses to a well-driven spinner that gets underneath or around the wedge
entities.notes: Almost every 'first plastic ant' guide recommends starting here because the failure mode (a cracked wedge) is a five-minute reprint, unlike a broken weapon motor mount.

extra.typical_weapon_motor: none, or a small servo-driven active wedge/lifter
extra.typical_drive: Two drive motors sized for torque over top speed, direct-drive to grippy TPU-tired wheels

entities.name: Plastic Ant Lifter
entities.summary: A wedge-fronted robot with a servo- or small-motor-actuated arm that scoops and lifts an opponent to expose their underside or throw them, using printed linkages instead of the pneumatics common in bigger lifters.
pros: Can win by control and occasional big flips without needing a fast-spinning weapon
Lift arm doubles as self-righting mechanism
cons: Printed linkage pins/hinges wear and can strip under repeated combat loads
Slower to act than a spinner, needs good positioning

extra.typical_weapon_motor: Micro servo or small geared DC motor with a printed cam/linkage, occasionally a rubber-band-assisted snap lift
extra.typical_drive: Two drive motors on printed wheels

entities.name: N20 Micro Gearmotor (6-12V)
entities.summary: A tiny brushed DC gearmotor in a roughly 12x10x10mm metal gearbox, the most common drive motor in plastic antweights due to its low cost, light weight, and wide range of stock gear ratios.
pros: Very cheap and widely available
Metal gearbox is more durable than plastic-gear toy motors
Many stock gear ratios (from ~30 RPM crawlers to 1000+ RPM speedsters)
cons: Low torque compared to bigger motors, limits ramming power
Output shaft can shear under sudden weapon-strike shock loads if used for anything but drive
entities.notes: Realistic weight range 9-12g depending on gear ratio; price typically $3-5 each bought in bulk.

extra.vendor: various (generic/AliExpress/Amazon; also sold by hobby motor shops)

entities.name: 130-Size Brushed Drive Motor
entities.summary: A classic small brushed can motor (the same family used in cheap toy cars) sometimes paired with a 3D-printed or small stock gearbox for antweight drive; cheaper and more available than purpose-built combat drive motors.
pros: Extremely cheap
High no-load RPM gives room for a wide range of gear ratios
cons: Needs a separate gearbox (adds weight/complexity) since raw RPM is too high for direct drive
Lower quality bearings than purpose-made combat motors

entities.name: Micro Brushless Outrunner, ~2600KV (1811-size class)
entities.summary: A small brushless outrunner motor in the size class commonly used for antweight vertical spinner and drum weapons, run on 2S LiPo for a good balance of RPM and torque within a plastic ant's weight and tip-speed goals.
pros: Good RPM-to-weight ratio for spinning a light printed disc/drum
Widely available from hobby drone/FPV suppliers
cons: Needs a compatible brushless ESC and careful gearing/direct-drive sizing to avoid over-revving a plastic weapon past its burst speed
entities.notes: 2800kv is commonly cited as a 'vertical spinner' sweet spot kv in community guides; 1400kv is more typical for slower horizontal spinners.

extra.vendor: various (e.g. hobby drone-motor brands repurposed for combat)

entities.name: Micro Brushless Outrunner, ~1400KV
entities.summary: A lower-kv small outrunner used for horizontal/bar spinners and drums where more torque and a lower tip speed (kinder to a printed weapon) is preferred over raw RPM.
pros: Lower RPM is easier on a printed weapon's burst strength
More torque for heavier drums
cons: Lower tip speed means less kinetic energy transfer per hit

entities.name: Micro Brushless Weapon ESC (~6A)
entities.summary: A tiny brushless ESC (often an AM32 or BLHeli-based FPV-drone-derived board) used to run the weapon motor in a plastic ant, valued for its very low weight relative to the alternative of a brushed weapon motor and controller.
pros: Extremely light
Programmable spin-up behavior (some support instant full throttle at arm for combat)
cons: Small package can be sensitive to heat if run continuously at max current
Needs correct motor-timing configuration for reliable spin-up under weapon load

entities.name: Micro Combo RX + Dual Brushed ESC Board
entities.summary: An all-in-one micro PCB combining a radio receiver with two small brushed motor drivers, the standard drive-electronics solution in antweights because it saves the weight and wiring of separate RX and ESC boards.
pros: One part instead of three (receiver + two ESCs), saving weight and wiring
Common failsafe-on-signal-loss behavior built in, satisfying rules requiring drive failsafe
cons: If it fails, the whole robot loses both drive and radio at once
Current rating (often 2-4A per channel) can limit motor choice

entities.name: 2S 300mAh LiPo Battery
entities.summary: A small 2-cell lithium polymer pack, the most common power source for plastic ant vertical spinner and drum builds, giving 7.4V nominal for both a brushless weapon motor and brushed drive motors.
pros: Good energy density for the weight
Widely available in the FPV-drone hobby supply chain
cons: Requires a LiPo-safe charger and storage practice
Capacity/runtime trade-off against the 454g total weight budget

entities.name: 1S 300-500mAh LiPo Battery
entities.summary: A single-cell LiPo pack used in budget or control-focused plastic ants running low-voltage brushed drive motors without a brushless weapon.
pros: Lightest common battery option, frees weight budget for armor
Cheapest LiPo option
cons: Only suitable for low-voltage drive motors and small brushed weapon setups, not brushless spinners

entities.name: Printed Hub + TPU Tire Wheel
entities.summary: A 3D-printed rigid hub (PLA+/PETG) with a separately printed TPU tire pressed or glued on, the standard plastic-ant wheel: fully print-and-replace, and legal everywhere since both hub and tire are on the approved plastic list (subject to local TPU rulings).
pros: Essentially free once you own a printer and TPU spool
Easy to redesign tread pattern for grip
Print-and-replace after wear or damage
cons: TPU is explicitly banned by some events (e.g. SCAR); always check local rules before relying on it
Lower grip than purpose-made silicone/foam tires unless tread is well designed

entities.name: COTS Foam/Silicone Antweight Wheel
entities.summary: An off-the-shelf foam or silicone-tired wheel (e.g. FingerTech, Repeat Robotics, Pololu) explicitly allowed as a non-plastic-restricted exemption for wheels/tires under most plastic-ant rulesets, offering better and more consistent grip than a printed tire.
pros: Consistent, well-tested grip
No printing/gluing labor
Explicitly named as legal by SCAR's FAQ regardless of the plastic-only rule
cons: Costs more than a printed wheel
Less customizable diameter/tread than a printed part

entities.name: Small Flanged Ball Bearing (3-4mm bore)
entities.summary: A tiny flanged metal bearing used to support a plastic ant's weapon shaft, explicitly allowed as a metal exemption in every plastic-ant ruleset since bearings are functional hardware, not armor or weapon surface.
pros: Cheap and standardized sizes
Explicitly rules-legal as a metal component in every plastic-ant ruleset reviewed
cons: Needs a properly toleranced printed bore to press-fit without cracking the surrounding plastic

entities.name: Small-Diameter Steel Weapon Shaft
entities.summary: A short length of steel drill rod or precision shaft used to carry a plastic weapon disc/drum, exempt from the plastic-only rule as an 'axle' under SPARC-derived language as long as it does not itself act as an armor surface or weapon edge.
pros: Much stiffer and more wear-resistant than a printed shaft would be
Explicitly allowed as an axle exemption in every ruleset reviewed
cons: Must be fully shrouded by the printed weapon body so it can't be argued to be acting as a metal weapon tip

entities.name: M2/M3 Screws + Heat-Set Threaded Inserts
entities.summary: Small metal machine screws combined with brass heat-set threaded inserts melted into printed holes, the standard plastic-ant fastening method, explicitly allowed everywhere as long as screw heads on outer surfaces are countersunk or shrouded rather than left proud as de facto armor studs.
pros: Reusable threads in soft plastic (printed threads alone strip quickly)
Universally rules-legal metal exemption
cons: Requires a soldering iron or heat-set tool to install inserts
Proud/exposed screw heads on the outer shell can draw a rules objection if not countersunk (per Robot Ruckus wording)

entities.name: Micro Slide/Toggle Power Switch
entities.summary: A small mechanical switch used as the required manual main power disconnect, mounted in a printed slot so it can be actuated without contacting moving parts, satisfying the SPARC-derived 15-second manual-disconnect rule.
pros: Cheap, simple, satisfies safety inspection requirements
cons: Must be positioned so it can be reached without risk from a still-armed weapon

entities.name: PLA+ (Modified PLA)
entities.summary: A modified PLA filament formulation marketed for improved impact resistance over standard PLA while keeping PLA's easy printability, one of the five materials SPARC and SCAR explicitly name as legal for plastic-ant chassis and weapons.
pros: Easiest of the legal plastics to print reliably
Rarely warps, good for small precise parts
Explicitly legal in every plastic-ant ruleset reviewed
cons: Still more brittle than PETG/ABS under sharp impact despite the '+' marketing
Lower heat resistance than PETG/ABS

extra.machinability: Excellent for FDM printing; low warp, prints cool (190-215C typical), poor for post-print machining

entities.name: PETG
entities.summary: A tougher, more impact-ductile filament than PLA, widely considered the best default choice for plastic-ant weapon discs/drums and load-bearing chassis members because it bends and absorbs energy rather than shattering.
pros: Best combination of legal-everywhere status and real-world impact toughness
More heat resistant than PLA (useful near weapon-motor heat)
Ductile failure mode (bends/cracks slowly) instead of shattering
cons: More prone to stringing/oozing than PLA, needs tuned retraction settings
Slightly heavier per volume than PLA/ABS

extra.machinability: Prints slightly hotter than PLA (230-250C), can string more, but layer adhesion is strong

entities.name: ABS
entities.summary: A strong, impact-resistant, comparatively low-density filament, one of the five universally-legal plastic-ant materials; harder to print reliably (needs an enclosure to prevent warping) but rewards the effort with a lighter, tougher part than PLA.
pros: Lowest density of the commonly-used legal plastics, saving weight for the same part size
Very impact resistant when printed well
Acetone-smoothable, which can weld layer lines together for extra strength
cons: Warps badly without an enclosure and a heated bed
Fumes require ventilation
Less beginner-friendly than PLA/PETG

use_cases: chassis shells where weight savings matter
extra.machinability: Needs an enclosed/heated-chamber printer to avoid warping; can be acetone-vapor-smoothed for extra surface strength

entities.name: TPU (Thermoplastic Polyurethane)
entities.summary: A rubber-like flexible printable filament popular in the wider combat-robot community for flexible armor panels and wheel tires because it bends and springs back instead of cracking — but it is NOT on the standard SPARC/SCAR approved-material list and is explicitly banned by name in SCAR's FAQ, making it a key org-to-org variance point in the plastic-ant class.
pros: Excellent energy absorption; deflects and springs back rather than cracking
Great for wheel tires and shock-mounts when the local ruleset allows it
cons: NOT on the base SPARC 4.4.1 list (PET/PETG/ABS/PLA/PLA+ only) unless an organizer grants an explicit exception
Explicitly named as banned by SCAR's Plastic Ant FAQ, including for wheel hubs
entities.notes: Builders should never assume TPU is legal in a plastic-ant event just because it's a 3D-printed plastic — check the specific event's material list or FAQ before designing it in.

extra.machinability: Prints slowly, needs direct-drive extruder, high flexibility makes it hard to feed through bowden setups

entities.name: Nylon (Printed)
entities.summary: A tough, wear-resistant, semi-flexible printable nylon filament that, like TPU, sits outside the base SPARC 4.4.1 approved list and is explicitly banned by name in SCAR's plastic ant FAQ, despite being a popular choice for gears and living-hinge parts in general 3D-printing use.
pros: Very tough and abrasion-resistant in general use
cons: Explicitly banned by SCAR's plastic ant FAQ
Not on the SPARC baseline approved list either
Moisture-sensitive, harder to print reliably than PLA/PETG/ABS

use_cases: gears and wear parts (in general 3D printing, not this class)
extra.machinability: Hygroscopic (absorbs moisture, needs dry storage/drying before printing), prints hot

entities.name: Force Knight — Open-Source 1lb Plastic Antweight
entities.summary: A free, open-source 1lb plastic antweight design by community builder Michael K, published as downloadable STL files on Printables and described as intended for SCAR-legal component kits — a good example of the fully-open designs the plastic ant scene shares.
entities.notes: No purchase price — it's a free STL download; the builder still has to source motors/electronics/battery/fasteners/filament separately.

includes: build documentation on the model page

entities.name: CRNZ Antweight Combat Robot Kit
entities.summary: An open-source printable antweight chassis kit published by CombatRoboticsNZ on Thingiverse, designed to be extensible and modular so builders can swap weapon and drive modules without redesigning the whole robot.

includes: documentation for extending/upgrading the base design

entities.name: Legally Distinct — Open-Source 150g UK Drum Spinner Design
entities.summary: A free printable 150g UK-class antweight drum-spinner design by community builder Blessy (published on Thingiverse and documented on Hackaday.io), explicitly built as an homage/iteration on the established UK drum spinner 'Siren' — a clear, verified illustration of how the plastic scene iterates openly on successful designs.
entities.notes: Weight-classed here as 'fairyweight' per this database's vocabulary because it is a UK 150g class robot, NOT the US 1lb/454g plastic antweight this file is centered on — included because it's a well-documented, frequently cited example of the wider 'plastic ant' design-sharing culture, especially in the UK, where 'antweight' historically refers to the 150g bracket rather than 1lb. Concrete build details (verified via the Hackaday.io project page): drive uses 2x N20 gearmotors (~600rpm class), the drum weapon motor mount is sized for a BE1806 2300kv brushless motor with a 3mm bearing on the opposite side of the drum, and the design runs a 'malenki nano' micro ESC (a BBB Dual ESC was noted as a possible but tighter-fitting swap). The design iterated through weight: V2.1 was reported ~4g over the 150g limit, and V3.1 was revised to cut weight and reportedly finished at ~139g — a real example of the iterate-and-reprint weight-budget process that defines the plastic-ant/printable-ant design culture at any scale.

includes: Printable STL files for a drum-spinner chassis and drum weapon
Hackaday.io build log with component list

entities.name: Siren (UK 150g Antweight / US Fairyweight)
entities.summary: A 150g UK-Antweight/US-Fairyweight drum-spinner combat robot by designer drcameron, published as free STL files on Thingiverse and Cults3D, well-known enough in the printable-antweight scene to have directly inspired the open-source 'Legally Distinct' drum spinner.
entities.notes: Note this is the UK 150g 'Antweight' (equal to the US 'Fairyweight' class), NOT the US 1lb/454g plastic antweight this file is centered on — flagged here specifically because it is the real-world design lineage (Siren -> Legally Distinct) that the wider plastic/printable-ant community points to as an example of open, iterative design-sharing, a practice equally common at the 1lb plastic-ant scale.

achievements: Directly credited as the design inspiration for the widely-built Thingiverse/Hackaday.io 'Legally Distinct' plastic drum spinner
extra.active_years: unknown (design still actively referenced/built as of 2025-2026)
extra.image_hint: A low, wide 150g-class robot with a full-width horizontal drum spinner across the front, printed chassis

entities.name: Blunt Force Over Cutting
entities.summary: The plastic-ant design principle that, since no metal weapon edge is legal, weapons should be designed to transfer kinetic energy through mass and impact area (denting, cracking, flinging) rather than trying to cut or penetrate as a hardened steel blade would.
entities.notes: Printed PETG/ABS/PLA+ simply cannot hold a durable sharp edge the way S7/M2 tool steel can, so plastic ant weapons are built as thick rings, discs, and bars that hit like a hammer rather than a knife.

entities.name: COTS (Commercial Off-The-Shelf)
entities.summary: Parts bought ready-made rather than fabricated by the builder — motors, ESCs, receivers, bearings, and (per most plastic-ant FAQs) wheels/tires are explicitly allowed as COTS even though they aren't plastic, since the rule targets structural/armor/weapon plastic, not every component.

entities.name: Technical Inspection (Plastic-Only Check)
entities.summary: The pre-event safety/legality check where an event official visually inspects a plastic ant for compliance: verifying the chassis/armor/weapon are printed plastic, checking that any metal fasteners are countersunk/shrouded rather than proud, and looking for banned materials like TPU, nylon, or composite reinforcement layered into a printed part.
entities.notes: Per SCAR's FAQ, inspection is primarily visual and datasheets are not required by default, but 'suspicious' builds (e.g. an implausibly stiff or dense-looking part) can trigger further investigation, sometimes including a request to cut into or weigh/measure a suspect part.

entities.name: Sacrificial Armor Panel
entities.summary: A deliberately weaker, easily-detachable printed panel placed over a robot's vulnerable areas so that a hit cracks/pops off the panel (a 5-minute reprint) instead of transmitting damage into the main chassis or electronics bay.

entities.name: Modular Bolt-On Section
entities.summary: A design pattern where the chassis is split into independently printed, bolt-together sections (e.g. separate front wedge, weapon pod, and drive base) so a single damaged section can be reprinted and swapped without remaking the whole robot.

entities.name: Printed-In Flexure
entities.summary: A thin, deliberately flexible section printed as part of a single larger piece (rather than a separate hinge with a pin) that acts as a spring or hinge — used in plastic ants for snap-fit panels, simple lifter linkages, and shock-absorbing mounts without adding a metal hinge part.

entities.name: Wall Count / Perimeters
entities.summary: The number of solid outer print loops (walls) surrounding a part's infill; combat-ready plastic ant parts typically use significantly more walls (5-8+) than a decorative print (2-3) because the solid perimeter, not the infill, carries most of an impact load.

entities.name: Infill Percentage (Combat Printing)
entities.summary: The proportion of a printed part's interior that is filled with a lattice pattern rather than left hollow; competitive plastic ant chassis parts commonly run 40-100% infill with a gyroid or cubic pattern, well above the 15-20% typical of non-structural prints, trading weight for toughness within the 454g budget.

entities.name: Layer Adhesion Anisotropy
entities.summary: The property that FDM-printed plastic is much stronger for forces applied parallel to its print layers than for forces trying to pull layers apart (perpendicular to them); the single most important physical fact plastic ant designers work around, driving choices about print orientation for weapons, wedges and shafts.
entities.notes: '3D printed parts will always have more strength parallel to their layers as opposed to perpendicular' — a design constraint repeatedly emphasized in plastic-ant build guides.

entities.name: Annealing (3D Print Post-Processing)
entities.summary: A post-print heat-treatment process (baking a printed part at a temperature below its melt point, sometimes packed in sand or salt to limit warping) that can meaningfully increase a part's layer strength and heat resistance; explicitly permitted post-processing under SCAR's plastic ant FAQ.

entities.name: Five-Minute Pit Repair
entities.summary: The plastic-ant repair philosophy of designing bolt-on, single-piece printed sub-assemblies so that a cracked wedge, wheel, or weapon can be swapped for a spare printed at home in under five minutes between matches, rather than requiring on-site fabrication or welding as a metal repair might.
entities.notes: The realistic window at a busy event is ten to twenty minutes. That is enough to swap a wheel, replace a weapon, re-solder a wire, change a battery or straighten a wedge. It is not enough to re-print a chassis or rebuild a gearbox. Design for it: modular bolt-on armour, spare weapons already balanced, and pre-made wiring harnesses.

entities.name: Robot Ruckus
entities.summary: A US SPARC-compliant combat robotics event run in conjunction with Maker Faire Orlando, popular with antweight and plastic-antweight builders. Insect weight classes (fairyweight/antweight/beetleweight) run double-elimination, while the larger 12lb/30lb/30lb-super-class divisions use a pools/Swiss fight format instead.

entities.name: SoCal Attack Robots (SCAR)
entities.summary: A Southern California combat robot organization/event series with one of the most detailed published Plastic Ant rulesets and FAQs in the US scene, explicitly naming approved filament brands and banning TPU/nylon.

entities.name: Bot Blast
entities.summary: An annual US insectweight-focused combat robotics event running a modified SPARC ruleset. Its main deviations from stock SPARC are a modified double-elimination format, a ban on autonomous robots, an immediate KO (at official discretion) for any robot with an exposed/damaged LiPo battery, and simplified judging criteria versus full SPARC judging.
entities.notes: The exposed-LiPo-equals-immediate-KO rule is a notable Bot-Blast-specific safety escalation beyond baseline SPARC, directly reflecting how seriously LiPo fire risk is treated in the hobby.

entities.name: National Havoc Robot League (NHRL)
entities.summary: A major US combat robot league best known for its livestreamed 3lb (beetleweight) and 12/30lb events; NHRL itself is not the primary home of the 1lb plastic ant class (its own plastic-material class is Plastic Beetleweight), but many smaller 'NHRL-adjacent' local and remote-competition circuits run 1lb plastic ant undercards using a similar remote-competition/streamed format.
entities.notes: Included here as context for the 'NHRL-adjacent' plastic-ant scene mentioned by many builders: local clubs running plastic ants often borrow NHRL's remote-shipping/streamed-match format even though NHRL's own smallest weight bracket is 3lb, not 1lb.

extra.location: Denver, Colorado, USA (event venue); competitors ship robots in

entities.name: FingerTech Robotics
entities.summary: A Canadian combat-robot parts supplier whose wheels, motors, and hubs are explicitly named as legal COTS options in plastic ant FAQs, making it one of the standard go-to sources for the non-plastic-exempt parts of a plastic ant build.

entities.name: Spinning Weapon Tip Speed
entities.summary: The standard combat-robotics formula for converting a spinning weapon's no-load RPM and diameter into tip speed in feet per second, taken verbatim from SPARC's Robot Construction Specifications (used to set/verify Sportsman-class and open-air tip-speed limits) and used informally by builders in every weight class, plastic ant included, to sanity-check a weapon design before it's built.
entities.notes: Builders should treat the no-load RPM figure as an upper bound only; a printed weapon's SURVIVABLE rpm (the ceiling before the weapon itself fails from centrifugal stress) is usually the true limiting factor in plastic ant, not motor Kv or battery voltage — see the printed-weapon burst-strength discussion in the build-spec chunks.

variables.tip_speed_ft_s: weapon tip/rim speed at the outer edge, in feet per second
variables.no_load_rpm: the weapon's unloaded (free-spinning, no-load) RPM as measured by tachometer or estimated from motor kv * voltage / gear or pulley ratio
variables.diameter_in: the weapon's outer diameter in inches (for a disc/drum, its full diameter; for a bar, the full swept diameter tip-to-tip)

extra.worked_example: A plastic-ant vertical spinner disc with a 3.5in printed diameter, driven by a 2600kv brushless motor on 2S (7.4V) direct-drive (no reduction), has a theoretical no-load RPM of about 2600 * 7.4 = 19,240 RPM. Applying the formula: tip_speed = 19,240 * 3.5 * 0.00436 ≈ 293 ft/s (about 200 mph) at the theoretical no-load ceiling. Real-world loaded RPM is always lower than this no-load figure (ESC/motor sag under load, printed-disc drag), so builders typically see tip speeds in the 120-220 ft/s (~80-150mph) band once the disc is actually spinning under battery sag, which is still enough kinetic energy to crack a printed panel or dent a wedge on a solid hit. For reference, SPARC's own Sportsman-class rule caps NON-toothed slow spinners at 20 ft/s using this exact formula, which shows how enormous the gap is between a 'slow spinner' and a full-power plastic-ant spinner: roughly a 10-15x difference in tip speed.

entities.name: Vertical spinner vs Wedge
entities.summary: The wedge wins the initial engagement but has no way to convert it into a win, while the spinner only needs one clean hit.
pros: Game plan for Vertical spinner: Do not charge head-on into the wedge face. Circle, attack the side or rear, and use the arena wall to deny the wedge a straight approach. Keep the weapon at speed so any contact is a hit.
cons: Game plan for Wedge: Get under and stay under. Drive the spinner into a wall and hold it there, deny it any opening, and bank control points for the decision.
entities.notes:
**Favoured:** Vertical spinner (~60% confidence).

**Why:** The wedge wins the initial engagement but has no way to convert it into a win, while the spinner only needs one clean hit.

**Vertical spinner should:** Do not charge head-on into the wedge face. Circle, attack the side or rear, and use the arena wall to deny the wedge a straight approach. Keep the weapon at speed so any contact is a hit.

**Wedge should:** Get under and stay under. Drive the spinner into a wall and hold it there, deny it any opening, and bank control points for the decision.

**The mistake that loses it:** The spinner drives straight at the wedge face repeatedly, gets ramped every time, and loses on control.

entities.name: Vertical spinner vs Horizontal bar spinner
entities.summary: The horizontal's reach and sweep attack the vertical's exposed weapon and wheels before the vertical can close to its own engagement range.
pros: Game plan for Vertical spinner: Approach at an angle and time the gap between bar passes. Armour the wheels and keep the weapon between you and the bar.
cons: Game plan for Horizontal bar spinner: Keep the bar at full speed and stay at range. Let the vertical come to you; every approach it makes is a chance to hit its weapon or wheels.
entities.notes:
**Favoured:** Horizontal bar spinner (~60% confidence).

**Why:** The horizontal's reach and sweep attack the vertical's exposed weapon and wheels before the vertical can close to its own engagement range.

**Vertical spinner should:** Approach at an angle and time the gap between bar passes. Armour the wheels and keep the weapon between you and the bar.

**Horizontal bar spinner should:** Keep the bar at full speed and stay at range. Let the vertical come to you; every approach it makes is a chance to hit its weapon or wheels.

**The mistake that loses it:** The vertical closes head-on at full speed and loses its weapon or a wheel to the first bar strike.

entities.name: Vertical spinner vs Undercutter
entities.summary: The undercutter strikes below the vertical spinner's weapon arc, hitting wheels and ground clearance where the vertical cannot defend.
pros: Game plan for Vertical spinner: Attack from directly in front where the disc can meet the bar, or rush before the undercutter reaches speed. Protect the wheels.
cons: Game plan for Undercutter: Stay low, keep the bar spinning and let the vertical approach. Target the wheels and the front wedge mounts.
entities.notes:
**Favoured:** Undercutter (~60% confidence).

**Why:** The undercutter strikes below the vertical spinner's weapon arc, hitting wheels and ground clearance where the vertical cannot defend.

**Vertical spinner should:** Attack from directly in front where the disc can meet the bar, or rush before the undercutter reaches speed. Protect the wheels.

**Undercutter should:** Stay low, keep the bar spinning and let the vertical approach. Target the wheels and the front wedge mounts.

**The mistake that loses it:** The vertical tries to circle and gives the undercutter a clean side profile full of wheels.

entities.name: Vertical spinner vs Drum spinner
entities.summary: Both hit upward, but the drum's larger diameter and lower mounting give it better bite, so it usually lands first in a head-on exchange.
pros: Game plan for Vertical spinner: Avoid the head-on exchange. Attack from the side where the drum's advantage disappears.
cons: Game plan for Drum spinner: Take the head-on engagement. Your bite advantage means you win the exchange more often than not.
entities.notes:
**Favoured:** Drum spinner (~55% confidence).

**Why:** Both hit upward, but the drum's larger diameter and lower mounting give it better bite, so it usually lands first in a head-on exchange.

**Vertical spinner should:** Avoid the head-on exchange. Attack from the side where the drum's advantage disappears.

**Drum spinner should:** Take the head-on engagement. Your bite advantage means you win the exchange more often than not.

**The mistake that loses it:** Trading head-on with a weapon that has better bite than yours.

entities.name: Vertical spinner vs Control bot
entities.summary: The control bot has no answer to accumulating damage, and at 1 lb a few clean upward hits end the match.
pros: Game plan for Vertical spinner: Stay at weapon speed and take the hits that present themselves. Do not get pushed into a wall and pinned.
cons: Game plan for Control bot: Pin immediately and never let the weapon spin up. Push to the wall, hold, and win on control.
entities.notes:
**Favoured:** Vertical spinner (~70% confidence).

**Why:** The control bot has no answer to accumulating damage, and at 1 lb a few clean upward hits end the match.

**Vertical spinner should:** Stay at weapon speed and take the hits that present themselves. Do not get pushed into a wall and pinned.

**Control bot should:** Pin immediately and never let the weapon spin up. Push to the wall, hold, and win on control.

**The mistake that loses it:** The control bot lets the spinner disengage and re-spin repeatedly.

entities.name: Vertical spinner vs Grabber
entities.summary: If the grabber closes on the spinner the match is effectively over, but surviving the approach against a live weapon is genuinely hard.
pros: Game plan for Vertical spinner: Never let the grabber close. Keep moving, keep the weapon up, and punish every failed grab attempt.
cons: Game plan for Grabber: Approach from an angle with jaws low. Absorb one hit if you must, then clamp and carry to the wall or the pit.
entities.notes:
**Favoured:** Grabber (~55% confidence).

**Why:** If the grabber closes on the spinner the match is effectively over, but surviving the approach against a live weapon is genuinely hard.

**Vertical spinner should:** Never let the grabber close. Keep moving, keep the weapon up, and punish every failed grab attempt.

**Grabber should:** Approach from an angle with jaws low. Absorb one hit if you must, then clamp and carry to the wall or the pit.

**The mistake that loses it:** The grabber approaches head-on with jaws open and loses a jaw to the weapon.

entities.name: Vertical spinner vs Flipper
entities.summary: The flipper attacks from underneath, which is the one direction a vertical spinner cannot defend, and a flip against a non-invertible spinner ends it.
pros: Game plan for Vertical spinner: Be invertible. Keep the weapon low and forward so the flipper cannot get its arm under.
cons: Game plan for Flipper: Get under and fire. Against a non-invertible spinner one good flip is the whole match.
entities.notes:
**Favoured:** Flipper (~55% confidence).

**Why:** The flipper attacks from underneath, which is the one direction a vertical spinner cannot defend, and a flip against a non-invertible spinner ends it.

**Vertical spinner should:** Be invertible. Keep the weapon low and forward so the flipper cannot get its arm under.

**Flipper should:** Get under and fire. Against a non-invertible spinner one good flip is the whole match.

**The mistake that loses it:** A spinner that cannot self-right meeting a flipper that can get under it.

entities.name: Vertical spinner vs Hammer
entities.summary: The spinner accumulates energy over seconds; the hammer only has its swing arc. The energy difference is decisive at 1 lb.
pros: Game plan for Vertical spinner: Stay at speed and engage normally. The hammer must be almost touching you to be a threat.
cons: Game plan for Hammer: Close the distance behind a wedge and strike the top. Your only path is landing on thin top armour while the weapon cannot reach.
entities.notes:
**Favoured:** Vertical spinner (~75% confidence).

**Why:** The spinner accumulates energy over seconds; the hammer only has its swing arc. The energy difference is decisive at 1 lb.

**Vertical spinner should:** Stay at speed and engage normally. The hammer must be almost touching you to be a threat.

**Hammer should:** Close the distance behind a wedge and strike the top. Your only path is landing on thin top armour while the weapon cannot reach.

**The mistake that loses it:** The hammer trades in the open and loses its arm to the disc.

entities.name: Vertical spinner vs Thwackbot
entities.summary: The thwackbot cannot attack and manoeuvre at once; the spinner simply engages while it is spinning up.
pros: Game plan for Vertical spinner: Attack while it is rotating to build tail speed — it cannot steer during that.
cons: Game plan for Thwackbot: Use the tail to keep the spinner at distance and look for a wall pin. Do not trade.
entities.notes:
**Favoured:** Vertical spinner (~75% confidence).

**Why:** The thwackbot cannot attack and manoeuvre at once; the spinner simply engages while it is spinning up.

**Vertical spinner should:** Attack while it is rotating to build tail speed — it cannot steer during that.

**Thwackbot should:** Use the tail to keep the spinner at distance and look for a wall pin. Do not trade.

**The mistake that loses it:** The thwackbot spins up in the open and gets hit mid-rotation.

entities.name: Vertical spinner vs Rammer
entities.summary: A 454 g ram carries very little energy, and the rammer must close to contact range where the weapon lives.
pros: Game plan for Vertical spinner: Hold your ground with the weapon up. Any contact is on your terms.
cons: Game plan for Rammer: Attack the rear or sides only, and try to push out or pin. Never approach the weapon face.
entities.notes:
**Favoured:** Vertical spinner (~80% confidence).

**Why:** A 454 g ram carries very little energy, and the rammer must close to contact range where the weapon lives.

**Vertical spinner should:** Hold your ground with the weapon up. Any contact is on your terms.

**Rammer should:** Attack the rear or sides only, and try to push out or pin. Never approach the weapon face.

**The mistake that loses it:** The rammer charges the weapon face and destroys itself.

entities.name: Wedge vs Horizontal bar spinner
entities.summary: The bar sweeps harmlessly over a wedge that touches the floor, while the wedge lifts the spinner and removes its traction.
pros: Game plan for Wedge: Drive straight in. Your edge goes under the sweep. Once under, push to the wall and hold.
cons: Game plan for Horizontal bar spinner: Stay at range and attack the wedge's sides and wheels. Never let it get square to you.
entities.notes:
**Favoured:** Wedge (~70% confidence).

**Why:** The bar sweeps harmlessly over a wedge that touches the floor, while the wedge lifts the spinner and removes its traction.

**Wedge should:** Drive straight in. Your edge goes under the sweep. Once under, push to the wall and hold.

**Horizontal bar spinner should:** Stay at range and attack the wedge's sides and wheels. Never let it get square to you.

**The mistake that loses it:** The horizontal lets the wedge approach head-on and gets ramped.

entities.name: Wedge vs Shell spinner
entities.summary: A shell spinner's weapon is its outer edge, which a good wedge slides beneath; once lifted, a shell has no recovery.
pros: Game plan for Wedge: Approach square and low, get under the shell's edge, and lift. A lifted shell spinner loses all its ground contact.
cons: Game plan for Shell spinner: Keep the shell at full speed and stay away from the wedge's front. Attack the wedge's rear and wheels.
entities.notes:
**Favoured:** Wedge (~65% confidence).

**Why:** A shell spinner's weapon is its outer edge, which a good wedge slides beneath; once lifted, a shell has no recovery.

**Wedge should:** Approach square and low, get under the shell's edge, and lift. A lifted shell spinner loses all its ground contact.

**Shell spinner should:** Keep the shell at full speed and stay away from the wedge's front. Attack the wedge's rear and wheels.

**The mistake that loses it:** The shell spinner engages the wedge face-on and gets ramped while its energy does nothing.

entities.name: Wedge vs Undercutter
entities.summary: The undercutter's whole purpose is beating wedges — it strikes below the wedge's leading edge, where the wedge offers no protection.
pros: Game plan for Wedge: Rush before the bar reaches speed. If it is already up, disengage and force it to chase you, spending its energy.
cons: Game plan for Undercutter: Keep the bar low and spinning. Let the wedge come to you; its edge is exactly what you are aiming at.
entities.notes:
**Favoured:** Undercutter (~70% confidence).

**Why:** The undercutter's whole purpose is beating wedges — it strikes below the wedge's leading edge, where the wedge offers no protection.

**Wedge should:** Rush before the bar reaches speed. If it is already up, disengage and force it to chase you, spending its energy.

**Undercutter should:** Keep the bar low and spinning. Let the wedge come to you; its edge is exactly what you are aiming at.

**The mistake that loses it:** The wedge treats the undercutter like an ordinary horizontal and drives straight in.

entities.name: Wedge vs Drum spinner
entities.summary: The drum's low mounting and large diameter let it engage a wedge's edge rather than riding over it.
pros: Game plan for Wedge: Attack the drum's sides. Try to get under from an angle where the drum body cannot scoop you.
cons: Game plan for Drum spinner: Meet the wedge head-on. Your geometry beats its geometry.
entities.notes:
**Favoured:** Drum spinner (~60% confidence).

**Why:** The drum's low mounting and large diameter let it engage a wedge's edge rather than riding over it.

**Wedge should:** Attack the drum's sides. Try to get under from an angle where the drum body cannot scoop you.

**Drum spinner should:** Meet the wedge head-on. Your geometry beats its geometry.

**The mistake that loses it:** The wedge assumes its edge will win and drives straight into the drum.

entities.name: Wedge vs Control bot
entities.summary: Two control robots meeting is decided almost entirely by ground clearance, edge quality and driving.
pros: Game plan for Wedge: Win the edge. A flatter, thinner, floor-contacting edge beats a thicker one regardless of power.
cons: Game plan for Control bot: Out-drive rather than out-wedge. Use the walls, attack from angles, and avoid a straight edge-to-edge contest.
entities.notes:
**Favoured:** Wedge (~55% confidence).

**Why:** Two control robots meeting is decided almost entirely by ground clearance, edge quality and driving.

**Wedge should:** Win the edge. A flatter, thinner, floor-contacting edge beats a thicker one regardless of power.

**Control bot should:** Out-drive rather than out-wedge. Use the walls, attack from angles, and avoid a straight edge-to-edge contest.

**The mistake that loses it:** Meeting edge-to-edge with the worse edge and pushing anyway.

entities.name: Wedge vs Hammer
entities.summary: A hammer has to be nearly touching to strike; a wedge that gets under removes its footing before the arm comes down.
pros: Game plan for Wedge: Get under and keep pushing. A hammer being carried cannot aim.
cons: Game plan for Hammer: Strike as the wedge commits, then reverse out. Never let it settle underneath you.
entities.notes:
**Favoured:** Wedge (~70% confidence).

**Why:** A hammer has to be nearly touching to strike; a wedge that gets under removes its footing before the arm comes down.

**Wedge should:** Get under and keep pushing. A hammer being carried cannot aim.

**Hammer should:** Strike as the wedge commits, then reverse out. Never let it settle underneath you.

**The mistake that loses it:** The hammer stands still to aim and gets wedged.

entities.name: Horizontal bar spinner vs Shell spinner
entities.summary: Two horizontal weapons meeting is largely a coin-flip decided by which has more energy and better tooth geometry; the bar usually has higher tip speed.
pros: Game plan for Horizontal bar spinner: Engage at full speed and accept the exchange. Your tip speed advantage decides it.
cons: Game plan for Shell spinner: Use the shell's mass and omnidirectional coverage to survive the exchange, then close.
entities.notes:
**Favoured:** Horizontal bar spinner (~55% confidence).

**Why:** Two horizontal weapons meeting is largely a coin-flip decided by which has more energy and better tooth geometry; the bar usually has higher tip speed.

**Horizontal bar spinner should:** Engage at full speed and accept the exchange. Your tip speed advantage decides it.

**Shell spinner should:** Use the shell's mass and omnidirectional coverage to survive the exchange, then close.

**The mistake that loses it:** Engaging at partial weapon speed.

entities.name: Horizontal bar spinner vs Drum spinner
entities.summary: The horizontal's reach lets it strike the drum's supports and wheels before the drum closes to its own range.
pros: Game plan for Horizontal bar spinner: Stay at range, target the drum's shaft supports and wheels.
cons: Game plan for Drum spinner: Close fast and get under. Inside the bar's arc you win; outside it you lose.
entities.notes:
**Favoured:** Horizontal bar spinner (~55% confidence).

**Why:** The horizontal's reach lets it strike the drum's supports and wheels before the drum closes to its own range.

**Horizontal bar spinner should:** Stay at range, target the drum's shaft supports and wheels.

**Drum spinner should:** Close fast and get under. Inside the bar's arc you win; outside it you lose.

**The mistake that loses it:** The drum spends time at mid-range where only the bar can reach.

entities.name: Horizontal bar spinner vs Forkbot
entities.summary: Hinged forks float on the floor and slide under the bar's sweep, which passes over them harmlessly.
pros: Game plan for Horizontal bar spinner: Attack the forkbot's rear and sides. Never present your front to its forks.
cons: Game plan for Forkbot: Drive straight in. The bar cannot reach your forks and you can reach its underside.
entities.notes:
**Favoured:** Forkbot (~70% confidence).

**Why:** Hinged forks float on the floor and slide under the bar's sweep, which passes over them harmlessly.

**Horizontal bar spinner should:** Attack the forkbot's rear and sides. Never present your front to its forks.

**Forkbot should:** Drive straight in. The bar cannot reach your forks and you can reach its underside.

**The mistake that loses it:** The horizontal lets a forkbot approach from the front.

entities.name: Drum spinner vs Control bot
entities.summary: A drum's bite means it engages a control bot reliably, and repeated upward hits break wheels and armour.
pros: Game plan for Drum spinner: Engage normally; your bite means you rarely miss.
cons: Game plan for Control bot: Pin before the drum reaches speed, and keep it against the wall.
entities.notes:
**Favoured:** Drum spinner (~70% confidence).

**Why:** A drum's bite means it engages a control bot reliably, and repeated upward hits break wheels and armour.

**Drum spinner should:** Engage normally; your bite means you rarely miss.

**Control bot should:** Pin before the drum reaches speed, and keep it against the wall.

**The mistake that loses it:** The control bot gives the drum space to re-engage repeatedly.

entities.name: Drum spinner vs Undercutter
entities.summary: The drum's low front can engage the undercutter's bar and supports, and its bite works even against a low target.
pros: Game plan for Drum spinner: Meet it low and let the drum scoop under the bar.
cons: Game plan for Undercutter: Stay at range and target the drum's wheels rather than its front.
entities.notes:
**Favoured:** Drum spinner (~55% confidence).

**Why:** The drum's low front can engage the undercutter's bar and supports, and its bite works even against a low target.

**Drum spinner should:** Meet it low and let the drum scoop under the bar.

**Undercutter should:** Stay at range and target the drum's wheels rather than its front.

**The mistake that loses it:** The undercutter trades head-on with a weapon designed to engage low.

entities.name: Flipper vs Horizontal bar spinner
entities.summary: The flipper needs to close and get under, and the bar's reach punishes the approach.
pros: Game plan for Flipper: Time the approach between bar passes and get under in one committed move.
cons: Game plan for Horizontal bar spinner: Stay at range and hit the flipper arm and wheels during its approach.
entities.notes:
**Favoured:** Horizontal bar spinner (~60% confidence).

**Why:** The flipper needs to close and get under, and the bar's reach punishes the approach.

**Flipper should:** Time the approach between bar passes and get under in one committed move.

**Horizontal bar spinner should:** Stay at range and hit the flipper arm and wheels during its approach.

**The mistake that loses it:** The flipper approaches slowly and loses its arm.

entities.name: Flipper vs Control bot
entities.summary: A control bot with no weapon has nothing to deter the flipper's approach, and a flip removes its only asset — ground contact.
pros: Game plan for Flipper: Get under and fire. Repeat until the opponent is out or counted out.
cons: Game plan for Control bot: Stay square and low, deny the arm any gap, and push the flipper into the wall.
entities.notes:
**Favoured:** Flipper (~65% confidence).

**Why:** A control bot with no weapon has nothing to deter the flipper's approach, and a flip removes its only asset — ground contact.

**Flipper should:** Get under and fire. Repeat until the opponent is out or counted out.

**Control bot should:** Stay square and low, deny the arm any gap, and push the flipper into the wall.

**The mistake that loses it:** The control bot lets the flipper get a corner underneath.

entities.name: Flipper vs Invertible brick
entities.summary: Flipping an invertible robot achieves nothing — it drives away the same either way up.
pros: Game plan for Flipper: Use the flipper for pushouts rather than flips. Aim to put the opponent over the wall or into the pit.
cons: Game plan for Invertible brick: Ignore the flips entirely and play your normal control game.
entities.notes:
**Favoured:** Invertible brick (~60% confidence).

**Why:** Flipping an invertible robot achieves nothing — it drives away the same either way up.

**Flipper should:** Use the flipper for pushouts rather than flips. Aim to put the opponent over the wall or into the pit.

**Invertible brick should:** Ignore the flips entirely and play your normal control game.

**The mistake that loses it:** The flipper keeps flipping an opponent that does not care and banks no points for it.

entities.name: Grabber vs Horizontal bar spinner
entities.summary: Once clamped, a horizontal spinner's weapon cannot reach the grabber at all, and its energy becomes useless.
pros: Game plan for Grabber: Approach from an angle, absorb one hit, clamp and carry.
cons: Game plan for Horizontal bar spinner: Never let the grabber close. Keep moving and keep the bar between you and the jaws.
entities.notes:
**Favoured:** Grabber (~60% confidence).

**Why:** Once clamped, a horizontal spinner's weapon cannot reach the grabber at all, and its energy becomes useless.

**Grabber should:** Approach from an angle, absorb one hit, clamp and carry.

**Horizontal bar spinner should:** Never let the grabber close. Keep moving and keep the bar between you and the jaws.

**The mistake that loses it:** The spinner stops moving to line up a hit and gets grabbed.

entities.name: Grabber vs Wedge
entities.summary: A wedge gets under the grabber before the jaws can close, and a lifted grabber cannot grip anything.
pros: Game plan for Grabber: Grab from the side or rear where the wedge's edge does not point at you.
cons: Game plan for Wedge: Drive straight at the jaws. Your edge gets under before they close.
entities.notes:
**Favoured:** Wedge (~60% confidence).

**Why:** A wedge gets under the grabber before the jaws can close, and a lifted grabber cannot grip anything.

**Grabber should:** Grab from the side or rear where the wedge's edge does not point at you.

**Wedge should:** Drive straight at the jaws. Your edge gets under before they close.

**The mistake that loses it:** The grabber meets a wedge head-on with jaws open.

entities.name: Hammer vs Control bot
entities.summary: Against an opponent with no weapon, the hammer can close safely and work on the top armour at leisure.
pros: Game plan for Hammer: Close behind your wedge, then strike repeatedly at one spot on the top armour.
cons: Game plan for Control bot: Stay mobile and push. Never let the hammer settle on top of you.
entities.notes:
**Favoured:** Hammer (~60% confidence).

**Why:** Against an opponent with no weapon, the hammer can close safely and work on the top armour at leisure.

**Hammer should:** Close behind your wedge, then strike repeatedly at one spot on the top armour.

**Control bot should:** Stay mobile and push. Never let the hammer settle on top of you.

**The mistake that loses it:** The control bot lets the hammer sit on it and take free swings.

entities.name: Thwackbot vs Control bot
entities.summary: The thwackbot's tail outranges a weaponless pushing robot and can damage wheels.
pros: Game plan for Thwackbot: Use the tail to keep distance and target wheels. Do not let it close.
cons: Game plan for Control bot: Close inside the tail's arc where it cannot hit you, then push.
entities.notes:
**Favoured:** Thwackbot (~55% confidence).

**Why:** The thwackbot's tail outranges a weaponless pushing robot and can damage wheels.

**Thwackbot should:** Use the tail to keep distance and target wheels. Do not let it close.

**Control bot should:** Close inside the tail's arc where it cannot hit you, then push.

**The mistake that loses it:** The control bot stays at exactly tail range.

entities.name: Multibot vs Vertical spinner
entities.summary: Each half of a multibot is small and fragile, and a spinner only needs to destroy one at a time.
pros: Game plan for Multibot: Split the opponents and destroy them sequentially. Never let both engage at once.
cons: Game plan for Vertical spinner: Pincer from two sides at once so the weapon can only face one robot.
entities.notes:
**Favoured:** Vertical spinner (~60% confidence).

**Why:** Each half of a multibot is small and fragile, and a spinner only needs to destroy one at a time.

**Multibot should:** Split the opponents and destroy them sequentially. Never let both engage at once.

**Vertical spinner should:** Pincer from two sides at once so the weapon can only face one robot.

**The mistake that loses it:** The multibot attacks one at a time and gets picked off.

entities.name: Multibot vs Wedge
entities.summary: A single wedge can only face one direction; two robots attacking from opposite sides defeat that.
pros: Game plan for Multibot: Attack from both sides simultaneously. One holds the front, the other takes the rear.
cons: Game plan for Wedge: Isolate one robot against a wall and immobilise it before the other arrives.
entities.notes:
**Favoured:** Multibot (~60% confidence).

**Why:** A single wedge can only face one direction; two robots attacking from opposite sides defeat that.

**Multibot should:** Attack from both sides simultaneously. One holds the front, the other takes the rear.

**Wedge should:** Isolate one robot against a wall and immobilise it before the other arrives.

**The mistake that loses it:** The multibot's two robots attack together from the same side.

entities.name: Armour bot vs Vertical spinner
entities.summary: A spinner's energy has to go somewhere, and against heavy compliant armour a large share goes back into the spinner.
pros: Game plan for Armour bot: Present your thickest, most compliant face and let the spinner hurt itself. Survive to the decision.
cons: Game plan for Vertical spinner: Do not attack the armour. Target wheels and any exposed structure, and win on control instead.
entities.notes:
**Favoured:** Armour bot (~55% confidence).

**Why:** A spinner's energy has to go somewhere, and against heavy compliant armour a large share goes back into the spinner.

**Armour bot should:** Present your thickest, most compliant face and let the spinner hurt itself. Survive to the decision.

**Vertical spinner should:** Do not attack the armour. Target wheels and any exposed structure, and win on control instead.

**The mistake that loses it:** The spinner repeatedly hits the strongest part of the armour bot and breaks its own weapon.

entities.name: Wedge + spinner hybrid vs Wedge
entities.summary: The hybrid matches the wedge's ground game with its own wedgelets, then adds damage the wedge cannot answer.
pros: Game plan for Wedge + spinner hybrid: Win the edge with your wedgelets, then apply the weapon. You have both tools.
cons: Game plan for Wedge: Attack from the rear or side, away from the wedgelets, and try to pin.
entities.notes:
**Favoured:** Wedge + spinner hybrid (~70% confidence).

**Why:** The hybrid matches the wedge's ground game with its own wedgelets, then adds damage the wedge cannot answer.

**Wedge + spinner hybrid should:** Win the edge with your wedgelets, then apply the weapon. You have both tools.

**Wedge should:** Attack from the rear or side, away from the wedgelets, and try to pin.

**The mistake that loses it:** The wedge engages the hybrid's front, loses the edge contest and then takes weapon hits.

entities.name: Wedge + spinner hybrid vs Undercutter
entities.summary: The hybrid's advantage is its wedgelets, and the undercutter attacks below exactly that line.
pros: Game plan for Wedge + spinner hybrid: Rush before the bar is up, or force it to chase you and drain its energy.
cons: Game plan for Undercutter: Target the wedgelets and wheels, which sit in your strike zone.
entities.notes:
**Favoured:** Undercutter (~55% confidence).

**Why:** The hybrid's advantage is its wedgelets, and the undercutter attacks below exactly that line.

**Wedge + spinner hybrid should:** Rush before the bar is up, or force it to chase you and drain its energy.

**Undercutter should:** Target the wedgelets and wheels, which sit in your strike zone.

**The mistake that loses it:** The hybrid assumes its wedgelets protect it and drives straight in.

entities.name: Melty brain vs Wedge
entities.summary: The melty presents a spinning face from every direction, so the wedge has no safe approach angle.
pros: Game plan for Melty brain: Keep spinning and translate into the wedge's side.
cons: Game plan for Wedge: Rush it during translation, when it is slow and predictable.
entities.notes:
**Favoured:** Melty brain (~55% confidence).

**Why:** The melty presents a spinning face from every direction, so the wedge has no safe approach angle.

**Melty brain should:** Keep spinning and translate into the wedge's side.

**Wedge should:** Rush it during translation, when it is slow and predictable.

**The mistake that loses it:** The melty stops spinning to reposition and gets wedged.

entities.name: Beater bar vs Control bot
entities.summary: Even a modest beater bar accumulates damage that a weaponless robot cannot answer.
pros: Game plan for Beater bar: Engage often. Your weapon is weak but the opponent has none.
cons: Game plan for Control bot: Pin early and keep the bar against a wall where it cannot spin freely.
entities.notes:
**Favoured:** Beater bar (~60% confidence).

**Why:** Even a modest beater bar accumulates damage that a weaponless robot cannot answer.

**Beater bar should:** Engage often. Your weapon is weak but the opponent has none.

**Control bot should:** Pin early and keep the bar against a wall where it cannot spin freely.

**The mistake that loses it:** The control bot trades space for time and lets the bar keep hitting.

entities.name: Beater bar vs Vertical spinner
entities.summary: Same damage vector, far more energy on the vertical spinner's side.
pros: Game plan for Beater bar: Avoid the head-on exchange entirely; play for control and pushouts.
cons: Game plan for Vertical spinner: Take the head-on exchange — you win it on energy.
entities.notes:
**Favoured:** Vertical spinner (~70% confidence).

**Why:** Same damage vector, far more energy on the vertical spinner's side.

**Beater bar should:** Avoid the head-on exchange entirely; play for control and pushouts.

**Vertical spinner should:** Take the head-on exchange — you win it on energy.

**The mistake that loses it:** The beater bar trades directly with a much higher-energy weapon.

entities.name: Shell spinner vs Control bot
entities.summary: There is no safe angle to push a shell spinner from, and its energy is enormous.
pros: Game plan for Shell spinner: Stay at speed. Any contact from any direction is a hit.
cons: Game plan for Control bot: Attack only when the shell is spinning down, and aim for a pushout.
entities.notes:
**Favoured:** Shell spinner (~70% confidence).

**Why:** There is no safe angle to push a shell spinner from, and its energy is enormous.

**Shell spinner should:** Stay at speed. Any contact from any direction is a hit.

**Control bot should:** Attack only when the shell is spinning down, and aim for a pushout.

**The mistake that loses it:** The control bot tries to push a shell spinner at full speed.

entities.name: Lifter vs Vertical spinner
entities.summary: The lifter must get under to work, and the approach exposes its arm to the weapon.
pros: Game plan for Lifter: Protect the arm. Get under from an angle and lift before the weapon engages.
cons: Game plan for Vertical spinner: Keep the weapon facing the lifter's front and punish the approach.
entities.notes:
**Favoured:** Vertical spinner (~60% confidence).

**Why:** The lifter must get under to work, and the approach exposes its arm to the weapon.

**Lifter should:** Protect the arm. Get under from an angle and lift before the weapon engages.

**Vertical spinner should:** Keep the weapon facing the lifter's front and punish the approach.

**The mistake that loses it:** The lifter approaches with its arm raised and loses it.

entities.name: Lifter vs Horizontal bar spinner
entities.summary: A lifter with a wedge-quality edge gets under the sweep, then carries the spinner where it likes.
pros: Game plan for Lifter: Get under, lift, and carry to the wall. A lifted spinner has no traction.
cons: Game plan for Horizontal bar spinner: Stay at range and target the lifter's arm and wheels.
entities.notes:
**Favoured:** Lifter (~60% confidence).

**Why:** A lifter with a wedge-quality edge gets under the sweep, then carries the spinner where it likes.

**Lifter should:** Get under, lift, and carry to the wall. A lifted spinner has no traction.

**Horizontal bar spinner should:** Stay at range and target the lifter's arm and wheels.

**The mistake that loses it:** The horizontal lets the lifter approach square-on.

entities.name: Rammer vs Control bot
entities.summary: Two weaponless robots — the one with better traction, edge and driving wins.
pros: Game plan for Rammer: Commit to pushouts and use momentum on the approach.
cons: Game plan for Control bot: Win the edge and out-drive. You do not need to out-muscle.
entities.notes:
**Favoured:** Control bot (~55% confidence).

**Why:** Two weaponless robots — the one with better traction, edge and driving wins.

**Rammer should:** Commit to pushouts and use momentum on the approach.

**Control bot should:** Win the edge and out-drive. You do not need to out-muscle.

**The mistake that loses it:** Relying on momentum against a robot that simply wedges you.

entities.name: Judging Criteria
entities.summary: When a match goes the distance, judges score it — usually on damage, aggression and control.
entities.notes: Most rulesets weight damage most heavily, then aggression, then control, though the exact split varies by organisation. Practical consequences: a robot that lands two clean hits and then hides often beats one that pushed for three minutes without damaging anything; conversely a control robot that pins, carries and dominates position can beat a spinner that missed all match. Know your event's published split before you plan a strategy around it.

entities.name: Driving Practice
entities.summary: Deliberate practice at driving, which decides more antweight matches than design does.
entities.notes: The highest-value drills: driving a figure-eight without touching walls; driving the same course inverted; driving with one side disabled (unplug a motor); approaching a stationary target from an angle rather than head-on; and practising the first three seconds of a match over and over, because box rushes decide a surprising share of outcomes. Twenty minutes a week beats any component upgrade you can buy.

entities.name: Scouting
entities.summary: Watching your bracket before you fight it, and adapting your configuration.
entities.notes: At a one-day antweight event you can usually watch every opponent before you meet them. Note their weapon spin-up time, whether they are invertible, which side their weakest armour is on, and whether they drive well. A configuration swap — different wedge, different wheels, weapon removed for a control match — is legal at most events between matches and is often worth more than any in-match adjustment.

entities.name: Configuration Swap
entities.summary: Changing the robot between matches to counter a specific opponent.
entities.notes: Common antweight swaps: fitting a taller wedge against an undercutter, switching to grippier wheels for a pushing match, removing a weapon to add armour against a much stronger spinner, or swapping a two-tooth disc for a one-tooth to increase bite against thick armour. Confirm the event allows it and that every configuration passes weigh-in.

entities.name: Weigh-In
entities.summary: The check that your robot is inside the class weight limit.
entities.notes: Antweight is 454 g. Weigh on your own scale before you travel and again at the event, because event scales are the ones that count and they disagree with yours. Build to about 445 g so you have margin for threadlocker, tape, and the bolt you add in the pits. Being overweight at check-in is one of the commonest ways to lose a match without fighting.

entities.name: 1104 brushless motor (weapon)
entities.summary: Tiny 11mm-diameter, 4mm-tall stator motor from the FPV whoop/toothpick world, used as an ultra-light vertical spinner or micro-drum motor on plastic antweights and fairyweights.
pros: Extremely light (under 10 g), leaves more of a 1 lb budget for armor/drive
Cheap and disposable, easy to keep spares
cons: Very small stator volume caps torque and stall current headroom
Fragile bearings/shaft under weapon shock loading, not designed for impacts
entities.notes: 1104-size motors are pulled straight from tiny whoop drones. In combat use they almost always run a small direct-drive vertical disc or paddle weapon under ~40g on a plastic antweight, at 2S. Confidence on the exact KV/weight is medium since this is a generic size class rather than one branded part; values are representative of typical 1104 whoop motors (4500-6000kv range).

entities.name: 1106 brushless motor (weapon)
entities.summary: 11mm x 6mm stator motor, one step up from 1104 in stator height/torque, used for slightly heavier plastic-ant vertical spinners and paddle weapons.
pros: Noticeably more torque than 1104 for only ~2g extra weight
Still cheap, widely available as whoop replacement motors
cons: Still a whoop-grade bearing/shaft; not shock-rated for weapon impacts
Small mounting screws (M2) strip easily
entities.notes: Representative specs for the 1106 class; treat exact numbers as a typical range, not a single branded product.

entities.name: 1204 brushless motor (weapon)
entities.summary: 12mm-diameter, 4mm-tall stator motor, a common toothpick-drone motor repurposed as a plastic-ant or fairyweight vertical spinner/beater motor.
pros: Good torque-to-weight step up from 11xx sizes
M2 mount, easy to print an adapter plate
cons: Still limited peak current before demagnetizing the small magnets

entities.name: 1306 brushless motor (weapon)
entities.summary: 13mm x 6mm stator motor originally built for FPV micro racing quads (2-3 inch props); a very common plastic-ant and light 1 lb weapon motor because of its wide KV range and cheap availability.
pros: Huge range of KV options on the market (2200-4000kv) from racing-drone suppliers
9x9mm M2 mount pattern is easy to adapt with a printed plate
Good torque for its 15-19g weight, popular for small vertical discs
cons: 3mm-class magnets can demagnetize if driven well past rated current during a hard stall
1.5mm shaft is thin for anything beyond a small disc or paddle

entities.name: 1404 brushless motor (weapon)
entities.summary: 14mm x 4mm stator motor, a step above 1306 in diameter (more torque, similar height); used on heavier plastic ants and light 1 lb spinners.
pros: Wider stator than 1306 gives more low-end torque at similar KV
Still under 25 g
cons: Less common than 1306/1408 so fewer KV choices in stock

entities.name: 1408 brushless motor (weapon)
entities.summary: 14mm x 8mm stator motor, one of the most popular 'toothpick' drone sizes; a very common choice for 1 lb antweight vertical spinners, small drums, and light bars where a 1806 is too heavy.
pros: Tall stator (8mm) gives real torque for its size, good spin-up
12x12mm M2 mount pattern common and easy to adapt
Cheap, sold in bulk by every FPV motor vendor as 2.5in toothpick motors
cons: Bearings are still drone-spec, not shock-rated for hard weapon impacts
Bell can loosen/separate under repeated impact loading if not threadlocked

entities.name: 1806 brushless motor (weapon)
entities.summary: 18mm x 6mm stator motor from the older 200-250 class mini-quad era; a long-running staple antweight weapon motor thanks to its 3mm shaft and 16x16mm M3 mount that make it easy to bolt straight to a hub or pulley.
pros: 3mm shaft is much stiffer than 1.5mm 13xx/14xx shafts, tolerates direct-drive hubs better
16x16mm M3 mount matches many printed and metal mount patterns
Wide KV selection (1400-2700kv) still sold new
cons: Heavier than 13xx/14xx for builders on a tight plastic-ant budget
Still uses drone-grade sleeve/ball bearings, not a combat-rated shaft

entities.name: 2004 brushless motor (weapon)
