entities.summary: 20mm x 4mm cinewhoop-derived stator, a lighter-weight alternative in the 20xx bracket for antweight builders who want a bit more diameter/torque than 1806 without the weight of a 2205+.
pros: Wide stator diameter gives good torque despite short 4mm height
Common and cheap (cinewhoop production run)
cons: Thin 1.5mm shaft is the weak point versus 1806/2205's 3-4mm shafts

entities.name: 2205 brushless motor (weapon)
entities.summary: 22mm x 5mm stator, one of the definitive FPV racing-motor sizes and a very common 1 lb antweight vertical-disc/bar weapon motor because of its balance of torque, RPM range, and cheap availability.
pros: 4mm shaft is stiff enough for small direct-drive discs
16x16mm M3 bolt pattern is a de-facto antweight standard
Huge range of KV from 1300-2700 available from racing-drone brands
cons: At the top of the antweight weight budget once you add a bell/prop-nut hub
Needs a good ESC with real current headroom (30A+ burst) for hard weapon stalls

entities.name: 2206 brushless motor (weapon)
entities.summary: 22mm x 6mm stator, a taller/torquier sibling of the 2205, popular in freestyle-quad builds and equally popular as an antweight bar or disc spinner motor.
pros: Taller stator than 2205 gives noticeably more torque at similar KV
Good tip-speed headroom at 4S for 3-4in discs and bars
cons: A few extra grams versus 2205; matters on a tight 1 lb build

entities.name: 2207 brushless motor (weapon)
entities.summary: 22mm x 7mm stator, one of the most common freestyle/racing FPV motor sizes and a direct antweight favorite; Repeat Robotics' antweight hubmotor is built on this stator size for plug-and-play direct-drive weapons.
pros: Best stator-volume-to-weight ratio in the 22xx family, strong low-RPM torque
5mm shaft handles direct-drive hub loads well
Base stator size used by purpose-built combat hubmotors (e.g. Repeat 2207)
cons: Near the top of what a 1 lb build can spend on motor weight alone if also running a full-size hub

entities.name: 2306 brushless motor (weapon)
entities.summary: 23mm x 6mm stator, the long-time standard 5-inch mini-quad motor size; used in antweights as a slightly larger-diameter alternative to the 22xx family for bar and drum spinners needing more torque.
pros: Larger diameter than 22xx gives a bit more stall torque for the same weight class
19x19mm and 16x16mm mount options both exist on most 2306 shells
cons: Slightly heavier than a 2205/2207 for a similar power band

entities.name: 2504 brushless motor (weapon)
entities.summary: 25mm x 4mm stator; a lighter member of the 25xx family used where extra diameter (torque) is wanted without jumping fully into 28xx weight, common on heavier 1 lb bar/drum builds pushing into light-beetle territory.
pros: Wide stator gives strong low-speed torque, good for belt-reduced drums
5mm shaft suits belt pulleys well
cons: Heavy for a strict 1 lb budget; usually only fits builds that skimp elsewhere

entities.name: 2508 brushless motor (weapon)
entities.summary: 25mm x 8mm stator, a tall/high-torque long-range and heavy-lift drone motor; in combat it is a low-KV, high-torque option for belt-reduced 1 lb drums and bars that need bite more than raw tip speed.
pros: Very strong stall torque for its class, low KV keeps bite high even geared 1:1
Popular, well-supported size from long-range FPV so parts are cheap
cons: 75g+ is a big bite out of a 454g total robot weight; almost always needs the rest of the bot built light

entities.name: 2806 brushless motor (weapon)
entities.summary: 28mm x 6mm stator, entry point of the 28xx family; used on heavy 1 lb builds and as a light-beetleweight crossover weapon motor, usually belt-driven to keep tip speed in range at low KV.
pros: Big stator diameter gives strong torque even at moderate weight for a 28xx
Good belt-drive drum/bar motor
cons: At 68g+ this is a beetleweight-style motor squeezed into a 1 lb build; leaves little weight for armor

entities.name: 2812 brushless motor (weapon)
entities.summary: 28mm x 12mm stator, a very tall/torquey size from the heavy-lift/cinelifter drone world; occasionally used on the heaviest 1 lb builds or light beetles as a high-torque belt-driven weapon motor.
pros: Exceptional stall torque and thermal mass for sustained weapon use
Low KV keeps bite very high
cons: Too heavy for almost any legal 1 lb build; realistically a light-beetleweight part

entities.name: 2814 brushless motor (weapon)
entities.summary: 28mm x 14mm stator, the classic heavy-lift/heavy-ant-beetle-crossover size; the Cobra 2814 in particular is a well-known belt-drive weapon motor used across heavy 1 lb and light beetleweight spinners.
pros: Huge stator volume gives serious torque and thermal headroom for belt-driven drums/discs
Cobra 2814 1850kv specifically documented as a belt-drive combat weapon motor choice
cons: Well over 1 lb (454g) motor-only weight budget on its own in some windings; realistically a beetleweight part used at the antweight/beetle crossover on the lightest windings

entities.name: Repeat Robotics 2822 Weapon Motor
entities.summary: Purpose-built antweight weapon outrunner on a 28mm-diameter, 22mm-length can, sold specifically for direct-drive antweight spinners rather than repurposed from a drone; widely regarded as one of the most durable off-the-shelf antweight weapon motors.
pros: Designed from the start for weapon shock loads, not adapted from a camera-drone motor
Low-ish KV (1100kv seen in the product line) suits direct drive at 4S without gearing down
Screw-retained bell rather than relying only on a C-clip, addressing the classic bell-separation failure
cons: Costs more than a generic same-size drone motor
Weight/price not independently confirmed for every winding in this listing
entities.notes: Multiple KV windings are sold under the Repeat 2822 name (e.g. 1100kv variants seen in resale listings). Exact weight and price were not confirmed in this pass; do not treat the numbers above as complete -- only KV, can size, and general design intent are confirmed.

entities.name: Repeat Robotics 2207 Battle Ready Hubmotor
entities.summary: A 2207-stator combat hubmotor sold as a complete direct-drive weapon solution for antweights: the weapon hub/disc bolts straight to the motor bell, eliminating a separate shaft-and-bearing weapon assembly.
pros: Simplifies a vertical-disc weapon to 'bolt disc to bell' with no separate weapon shaft/bearings needed
Purpose-hardened bell/bearing set for weapon shock versus a stock drone 2207
cons: Locks you into the hub's specific weapon-mounting interface
KV/weight/price not confirmed in this research pass

entities.name: Repeat Robotics Scalar Antweight Weapon Motor (2305)
entities.summary: A 23mm-stator-class purpose-built antweight weapon motor with an oversized ~28.2mm outer bell for extra rotor mass/flywheel effect relative to its stator size.
entities.notes: Outer bell diameter (~28.2mm) is larger than the 23mm stator class, i.e. the bell itself adds rotating mass/inertia beyond a standard drone-motor bell of that stator size -- useful context when estimating total weapon-side MOI, since the motor bell is part of the flywheel, not just the blade. KV/weight/price not confirmed in this pass.

entities.name: RDY-5022 Antweight Hubmotor
entities.summary: Just 'Cuz Robotics antweight direct-drive hubmotor, offered in 1100kv and 1700kv windings, sized for antweight vertical spinners at typical 3-4S antweight voltages.
entities.notes: Also offered in a 1100kv winding for builders wanting more torque/less top speed at the same voltage. Weight, dimensions and price not confirmed in this pass.

entities.name: RDY-5536 Beetleweight Hubmotor
entities.summary: Just 'Cuz Robotics beetleweight-class direct-drive hubmotor, offered in 900kv and 1200kv windings; relevant to antweights mainly as the upper end of the size ladder / heavy-ant crossover reference point.

entities.name: JCR-4935 Horizontal Spinner Motor
entities.summary: Just 'Cuz Robotics 1000kv motor specifically marketed for horizontal spinners (bars/blades spun about a vertical-ish or horizontal axis with high aerodynamic drag), where a lower KV is used to keep current sane against drag.
entities.notes: 1000kv is deliberately low for the size class because horizontal bars/blades have much higher aerodynamic drag than a thin vertical disc, so a lower target RPM keeps continuous current and heat manageable.

entities.name: BadAss 23-series 2315 Weapon Motor
entities.summary: A 23mm-diameter, 15mm-length belt-drive weapon motor at 1480kv, cited as a common antweight/heavy-ant belt-drive option that trades some direct-drive simplicity for a taller, torquier stator than typical 23xx drone motors.

entities.name: Turbo 2830 Weapon Motor
entities.summary: A 28mm-diameter, 30mm-length belt-drive weapon motor at 1300kv; one of the largest commonly cited motors used at the antweight/beetleweight belt-drive crossover for high-torque drums and bars.

entities.name: Required motor KV from target tip speed and battery voltage
entities.summary: Back-solves the motor KV (or KV x gear-ratio) needed to hit a target tip speed on a given battery voltage, the single most common weapon-motor sizing question in the hobby.

extra.expression: RPM_target = v_mph * 336.14 / D_in   |   KV_needed = (RPM_target * ratio) / V_pack

variables.RPM_target: weapon RPM needed to hit that tip speed
variables.ratio: reduction ratio, weapon-pulley-teeth / motor-pulley-teeth (1.0 for direct drive)
variables.V_pack: fully-charged pack voltage, e.g. 12.6V for 3S, 16.8V for 4S
variables.KV_needed: motor KV to select, in RPM per volt

extra.worked_example: Target: 250 mph tip speed on a 4 in disc, direct drive, 3S (12.6V full charge). RPM_target = 250 * 336.14 / 4 = 21,009 RPM. KV_needed = 21009 * 1.0 / 12.6 = 1667 kv. For an 8 in bar at the same 250 mph target, RPM_target halves to ~10,500 RPM, so KV_needed also halves to ~833 kv -- illustrating why bigger weapons want lower KV for the same tip speed.

entities.name: Rotational kinetic energy stored in a spinning weapon
entities.summary: Computes the joules of kinetic energy stored in a weapon flywheel from its moment of inertia and angular velocity -- the number that actually predicts damage potential, not RPM alone.

extra.expression: KE_J = 0.5 * I_kgm2 * omega_rads^2   where omega_rads = RPM * pi / 30

variables.I_kgm2: weapon moment of inertia about its spin axis, kg*m^2

extra.worked_example: A 150 g (0.15 kg) solid steel disc, 4 in (0.0508 m radius), approximated as a uniform disc: I = 0.5 * m * r^2 = 0.5 * 0.15 * 0.0508^2 = 0.0001935 kg*m^2. At 21,000 RPM: omega = 21000 * pi / 30 = 2199 rad/s. KE = 0.5 * 0.0001935 * 2199^2 = 0.5 * 0.0001935 * 4,835,600 approx 468 J. Typical antweight vertical-disc spinners store roughly 100-500 J at full speed, so this is a fairly strong hit for the class.

entities.name: Weapon spin-up time estimate from torque and MOI
entities.summary: Estimates the time to bring a weapon from rest to full speed given the weapon's moment of inertia and the motor's average available accelerating torque over that speed range -- the calculation that explains why an underpowered motor loses matches before the fight even starts.

extra.expression: t_s (approx) = (I_kgm2 * omega_final_rads) / tau_avg_Nm   where tau_avg is roughly half of stall torque for a fixed-voltage DC/BLDC speed-torque line

variables.I_kgm2: weapon-side moment of inertia (blade/disc + bell + hub, reflected through any gear ratio)
variables.tau_avg_Nm: average accelerating torque during spin-up, Nm (approx 0.5 x stall torque for a motor driven at constant voltage with a linear torque-speed curve)

extra.worked_example: Same 0.0001935 kg*m^2 disc targeting 2199 rad/s (21,000 RPM), driven direct-drive by a 2207 at 1950kv with an assumed 30A stall current: Kt = 8.27/1950 = 0.00424 Nm/A, so stall torque tau_stall = 0.00424*30 = 0.127 Nm, and average torque during spin-up approx 0.5*0.127 = 0.0636 Nm. t = (0.0001935 * 2199) / 0.0636 = 0.4255 / 0.0636 approx 6.7 s. A 6-7 second spin-up is dangerously slow in a 3-minute antweight match -- this is exactly why builders either shrink the weapon MOI, raise motor torque (bigger stator / lower KV / more cells), or accept a slower-spinning but faster-spooling weapon.

entities.name: Weapon motor peak and steady electrical power draw
entities.summary: Estimates electrical power draw during weapon spin-up (near stall) versus steady-state windmilling, used to size battery C-rating and ESC current headroom.

extra.expression: P_elec_W = V_applied * I_draw   |   P_mech_W = tau_Nm * omega_rads   |   P_copper_loss_W = I_draw^2 * R_ohm

variables.P_elec_W: electrical power drawn from the battery, watts
variables.V_applied: voltage applied to the motor (approx pack voltage minus ESC/wiring drop), volts
variables.P_mech_W: mechanical power delivered to the weapon shaft, watts
variables.omega_rads: angular velocity at that instant, rad/s
variables.P_copper_loss_W: power lost to heat in the windings, watts

extra.worked_example: 2207 weapon motor, 1950kv, R=0.06 ohm, near stall on a 4S pack (14.8V nominal) pulling 30A: P_elec = 14.8 * 30 = 444 W peak electrical draw. Copper loss at that same 30A: P_copper = 30^2 * 0.06 = 54 W dissipated as heat in the stator -- a meaningful fraction of the 444 W, which is why repeated hard stalls (weapon hitting the floor/wall/opponent and stopping) heat the stator far faster than free-spinning. Once at full RPM with only bearing/aero drag to overcome, steady electrical draw for the same motor is typically only 5-20 W, which is why spin-up, not cruising, is what drains an antweight pack fastest.

entities.name: RPM to angular velocity (rad/s) conversion
entities.summary: Simple unit conversion used throughout weapon-motor sizing math to move between RPM (what motor/ESC specs use) and rad/s (what physics formulas for torque, power and kinetic energy need).

entities.name: KV (motor velocity constant)
entities.summary: The unloaded RPM a brushless motor spins per volt applied, in RPM/V. Determines top speed for a given voltage, but says nothing about torque or power by itself -- a motor's stator size and winding resistance matter just as much.
entities.notes: KV is fixed by the motor's winding turns/wire gauge, not by voltage or load. Doubling voltage roughly doubles no-load RPM for the same KV motor; changing KV via rewinding changes the RPM-per-volt but trades off torque per amp inversely (lower KV windings of the same stator generally deliver more torque per amp, higher KV windings more RPM per amp).

entities.name: Stator volume (diameter x height)
entities.summary: The product of a brushless motor's stator diameter and stator height/stack length, encoded directly in FPV motor names (e.g. '2207' = 22mm diameter x 7mm height). Stator volume is the single best predictor of how much torque and continuous power a motor can produce, because it sets how much copper and iron can be packed in to carry current and hold magnetic flux without saturating.
entities.notes: Diameter mostly buys torque (longer moment arm for the magnetic force acting at the rotor's radius); height mostly buys sustained power/RPM headroom (more copper per phase, more heat capacity, less current needed for the same torque). Two motors with the same stator volume but different diameter/height splits behave differently: a wide-short stator (e.g. 2504) favors low-RPM torque, a narrow-tall stator (e.g. 1408) favors higher RPM at less bulk. For weapons, bigger stator volume at a given KV always means more available stall torque and more thermal mass to survive hard stalls.

entities.name: Back-EMF (counter-electromotive force)
entities.summary: The voltage a spinning motor generates that opposes the applied drive voltage, proportional to RPM and inversely proportional to KV (Back-EMF volts = RPM / KV). As a weapon motor spins up, rising back-EMF is what makes available current -- and therefore torque -- fall off as speed increases, producing the classic linear torque-speed line.
entities.notes: At stall (RPM=0) back-EMF is zero, so the only thing limiting current is winding resistance -- this is why stall current is so high and why stalls generate the most heat. At no-load top speed, back-EMF has risen until it nearly equals the applied voltage, current drops toward zero, and torque drops toward zero too.

entities.name: Outrunner vs inrunner
entities.summary: Outrunner motors spin the outer magnet-lined bell/can around a fixed inner stator (the common FPV/drone layout); inrunner motors spin a small magnet rotor inside a fixed outer stator can. Outrunners dominate weapon-motor use because their larger effective rotor radius gives more torque per amp and the bell itself doubles as a flywheel/weapon-mounting surface.
entities.notes: Inrunners (common in RC car/boat brushless motors) spin at much higher RPM for a given KV-equivalent and need external gearing to be useful as low-speed, high-torque weapon drives; they are rarely chosen for antweight weapons because outrunner FPV motors are cheaper, lighter, and already torque-biased.

entities.name: Demagnetization (weapon motor failure)
entities.summary: Permanent partial loss of magnetic strength in a motor's rotor magnets, caused by driving current far beyond the motor's rated stall current (common during a hard weapon-vs-weapon or weapon-vs-wall impact stall) or by sustained overheating past the magnet's Curie-adjacent temperature limit. A demagnetized motor permanently loses torque and top KV-equivalent speed even after the fault current stops.
entities.notes: Small FPV-derived weapon motors are especially vulnerable because their magnets are thin and cheap; a single violent stall against a wedge or wall, or a jammed weapon, can push instantaneous current to several times rated stall current for a few milliseconds -- enough to demagnetize without ever tripping a slower-reacting ESC current limit.

entities.name: Fairyweight (150g)
entities.summary: The smallest weight class in common use, capped at 150 grams (about 0.33 lb). In the US/SPARC world it is called Fairyweight; confusingly, this exact 150g limit is what British builders call 'Antweight', which is far lighter than the US 1lb antweight. It is a popular entry point because parts are cheap and damage is minimal.
entities.notes: Robots must also fit within a 150mm x 150mm footprint under UK/AWS rules, with no overhang at any height. Non-rotary/non-rolling locomotion (walkers, shufflers) gets a bonus up to 225g under UK rules (see plastic-antweight and walker-bonus term entries).

extra.typical_arena: Small tabletop or club-scale arena (roughly 4-8 ft across), often polycarbonate-walled, shared with antweight-class fights

entities.name: Antweight (1 lb)
entities.summary: The classic North American entry class, capped at 1 lb (454 g). It is the most-run class at US and Canadian events (SPARC, RoboGames, Motorama, Robot Ruckus, Bot Blast) and is roughly three times heavier than the UK 'Antweight' (150 g), a naming collision that trips up new builders reading rules from the wrong region.
entities.notes: Because it is 3x the mass of the UK fairyweight/antweight, US 1lb antweights typically run larger motors, bigger batteries, and heavier armor than their UK 150g counterparts even though both are called 'antweight'.

extra.typical_arena: Small combat box, roughly 8x8 ft to 12x12 ft, polycarbonate walls, often shared with beetleweight

entities.name: Beetleweight (3 lb)
entities.summary: A 3 lb (1.36 kg) class, the second most popular class in the US after antweight, and one of NHRL's three official divisions. It allows meaningfully more powerful weapons and drivetrains than antweight while still being affordable and easy to transport.

extra.typical_arena: Mid-size combat box, roughly 12x12 ft to 24x24 ft polycarbonate arena

entities.name: Plastic Beetleweight
entities.summary: The 3 lb equivalent of plastic antweight: robots must be built almost entirely from approved 3D-printable plastics rather than metal. Less common than plastic antweight but growing at the same regional US events that run plastic-only brackets.
entities.notes: Uses the same allowed-material list as plastic antweight (PLA, PLA+, ABS, PETG, ASA, PET; no TPU, nylon, or fiber-filled composites).

entities.name: Hobbyweight (12 lb)
entities.summary: A 12 lb (5.44 kg) middle-tier class, one of NHRL's three flagship divisions and a common SPARC class. It's a step up in cost and danger from beetleweight, generally viewed as an intermediate builder's class.

entities.name: Featherweight (30 lb)
entities.summary: A 30 lb (13.6 kg) class, NHRL's largest flagship division and a long-standing SPARC/RoboGames class. Featherweight fights are visibly more destructive than smaller classes and require more serious safety gear and containment.

entities.name: Lightweight (60 lb)
entities.summary: A 60 lb (27.2 kg) class run mainly by SPARC and RoboGames. It sits between the popular small hobby classes and the TV-scale heavyweights, requiring real machine-shop fabrication and industrial-grade components.

entities.name: Middleweight (120 lb)
entities.summary: A 120 lb (54.4 kg) class run by SPARC and RoboGames, sitting just below the TV-scale heavyweight class. Robots at this size need hydraulic/pneumatic or large brushless weapon systems and significant safety infrastructure.

entities.name: Heavyweight (220-250 lb)
entities.summary: The top-tier 'TV weight' class. BattleBots' modern single division caps at 250 lb (113 kg) ready-to-fight, while SPARC's traditional heavyweight class is 220 lb (100 kg); RoboGames also runs a 250 lb class plus a heavier walking-bonus tier. These robots require professional-grade fabrication, hydraulics/large brushless weapons, and are only run at events with heavy-duty arenas.
entities.notes: Exact heavyweight cap differs by organization: BattleBots = 250 lb (500 lb if a qualifying walker), classic SPARC heavyweight = 220 lb, RoboGames runs both a 250 lb class and a 500 lb walking-bonus tier. Always check the specific event's rulebook rather than assuming one universal 'heavyweight' number.

extra.typical_arena: Reinforced steel/polycarbonate arena (e.g. BattleBox), often with hazards (pulverizer, screws)

entities.name: SPARC (Standardized Procedures for the Advancement of Robotic Combat)
entities.summary: SPARC is the dominant unified US/international rule set for hobby-scale combat robotics. A single 'SPARC-legal' build is accepted at essentially every SPARC-compliant event worldwide, covering weight classes from fairyweight (150g) up to heavyweight (220 lb), plastic-class material rules, weight bonuses for walkers/shufflers, multibot/clusterbot rules, and standardized safety requirements.

extra.organization: SPARC (community-maintained standard, not a single company)
extra.version: maintained on a rolling basis at sparc.tools (this research references the v1.2-derived rules and later community revisions)
key_rules: Weight classes: Fairyweight 150g, Antweight 1lb, Beetleweight 3lb, Mantisweight 6lb, Hobbyweight 12lb, Dogeweight 15lb, Featherweight 30lb, Lightweight 60lb, Middleweight 120lb, Heavyweight 220lb
Walkers (no rolling/cam-based ground contact) get a 100% weight bonus (double normal class weight)
Shufflers/non-wheeled-but-not-full-walkers may get up to a 50% weight bonus depending on locomotion type
Plastic-class variants (Plastic Antweight, Plastic Beetleweight) restrict construction to approved 3D-printable plastics only
Multibot/clusterbot teams share the class weight limit, with extra allowance if all members are walkers

entities.name: NHRL Open Rules (National Havoc Robot League)
entities.summary: NHRL runs the largest recurring US combat robotics series (Franklin, MA) across exactly three weight classes: 3lb (beetleweight), 12lb (hobbyweight), and 30lb (featherweight). It uses a qualifying-then-bracket tournament format, mandatory weapon locks and radio failsafe testing, and pays cash prizes, which distinguishes it from most hobbyist-only events.

key_rules: Three weight classes only: 3lb, 12lb, 30lb, weighed at or below the max at the start of each fight
Non-Traditional Locomotion bonus: +1.5lb (3lb class), +6lb (12lb class), +15lb (30lb class) — a 50% bonus
True Walker bonus: +3lb (3lb class), +12lb (12lb class), +30lb (30lb class) — a 100% bonus, doubling the class weight
Every robot needs a weapon lock preventing spinning weapons from moving outside the cage, and a tool-free external power-off
All robots must pass a radio failsafe test before competing
3-minute matches; win by tap-out, knockout, or judges' decision if time expires
Two-stage tournament: Qualifying rounds then a single-elimination Bracket; top 50% by NHRL ranking are seeded
banned: entanglement devices, defined as any component designed to entangle in the rotational or moving parts of the opponent
liquids expelled from the bot, except liquid used purely as a fuel source or liquid that becomes gaseous shortly after leaving the bot / before hitting the opponent
tethered projectiles designed in a way likely to entangle the opponent
domain knowledge: general SPARC-aligned bans on explosives and EMP/RF-jamming also apply

entities.name: RoboGames Combat Robot Rules
entities.summary: RoboGames (formerly ROBOlympics) is a large annual US multi-discipline robotics expo whose combat division runs six standard weight classes (150g through 250lb) plus parallel walking-bonus classes at 100% extra weight and separate 1lb/3lb autonomous divisions. It has one of the most detailed public banned-weapon and judging-scoring rulesets of any hobby organization.

key_rules: Regular classes: 150g, 1lb, 3lb, 60lb, 120lb, 250lb
Walking-bonus classes (100% weight bonus over regular class): 300g, 2lb, 6lb, 120lb, 240lb, 500lb
Separate 1lb and 3lb autonomous-robot divisions
Manual main power disconnect must be operable within 15 seconds without endangering the operator; full deactivation within 60 seconds
Weapon lock must be a clearly visible, high-visibility (neon orange or similar) physical locking device, in place during power-on
Radio must use digitally coded, mated transmitter/receiver pairs with a fail-safe; toy-grade and AM-band systems are banned
Judging: 3-judge panel, each judge scores Aggression (max 5 points) and Damage (max 6 points) = 11 points per judge, 33 total
Pinning capped at 15 seconds before the pinned robot must be released
banned: heat weapons except specially approved flamethrowers

entities.name: BattleBots Design & Safety Rules
entities.summary: BattleBots is the flagship US televised combat robotics league, running one professional heavyweight division at 250 lb ready-to-fight (up to 500 lb for a qualifying articulated-leg walker). Lifting/flipping weapons must pass a functional test lifting 250 lb to 12 inches before being allowed to compete, and every robot goes through a rigorous in-person tech and safety inspection ('the box') before being cleared to fight.
entities.notes: Judging point split (5 Damage / 3 Aggression / 3 Control on an 11-point scale) reflects the Judges' Guide used in recent seasons (Rev. 2021.0/2022.0); BattleBots has revised its judging system across seasons (e.g. the 2026 Pro League merges Aggression and Engagement), so builders/analysts should check the current-season Judges' Guide PDF rather than assume this split is permanent.

extra.version: Design Rules Rev. 2020.0 baseline (later seasons carry incremental updates)
key_rules: Single standard weight class: 250.0 lb maximum ready-to-fight
Walking-bonus allowance: up to 500.0 lb if the robot walks via articulated legs and meets additional design criteria
Any lifting or grappling weapon must demonstrate it can lift 250 lb to a height of 12 inches during inspection
Full in-person technical/safety inspection ('the box') required before every event
3-judge panel scores on an 11-point scale when a match goes the distance without a KO: 5 points for Damage, 3 points for Aggression, 3 points for Control (recent-season point split)
Damage is scored on relative non-cosmetic damage dealt, including systems that stop working correctly by match end, and can include self-inflicted damage
Aggression is scored on frequency, severity, boldness, and intent of attacks the robot deliberately initiates
Control is scored on how well and how long a robot controls the fight: pushing, lifting, pinning the opponent, or using the arena against them
Ahead of the BattleBots Pro League (2026), the judging system was revised to combine Aggression with 'Engagement' into a single 5-point scored category
banned: domain knowledge: standard combat-robotics banned list applies (entanglement, liquids, uncontained fire without approval, explosives, EMP/jamming, unlicensed high-power lasers)

entities.name: Antweight World Series Rules (UK)
entities.summary: The Antweight World Series (AWS) is the primary UK/European antweight ruleset, run in association with Bristol Bot Builders. It defines UK-scale classes far lighter than their US namesakes (Antweight 150g roller / 225g non-roller, Fleaweight 75g/113g, Nanoweight 25g/38g), a detailed banned-weapons list, and specific electrical/radio/battery safety rules distinct from US SPARC practice.

extra.organization: Antweight World Series / Bristol Bot Builders
key_rules: Antweight: 150g for rollers, 225g for non-rollers (50% non-roller bonus)
Fleaweight: 75g roller / 113g non-roller
Nanoweight: 25g roller / 38g non-roller
Clusterbot roller allowance formula: Roller weight = Roller Limit - (2/3 x Total non-roller weight)
Allowed radio frequencies: 27MHz, 40MHz, 418MHz, 433-434MHz, 868MHz, and 2.45GHz
Battery max 24V, and batteries must not contain liquid acid or free electrolyte
Weapons must be remotely deactivable; pressurized systems capped at 100 psi (7 bar); detachable weapon parts must be tethered (max 3 ft / 914mm)
Matches run 3 minutes max; 10-second immobility countdown ends a fight; pinning capped at 20 seconds; touching the pit floor is an automatic loss

entities.name: Fighting Robots Association (FRA) Build Rules
entities.summary: The Fighting Robots Association publishes build rules used across a number of UK and continental European combat events, complementing the AWS antweight-specific ruleset with guidance that spans a wider range of weight classes and general safety practice for European events.
entities.notes: Full rule text was found only as a PDF (2024 FRA build rules) via a French mirror (makerfight.fr); detailed clauses were not individually verified in this pass — treat specifics as low confidence pending a direct read of the PDF.

key_rules: General European build/safety rules referenced by multiple UK/EU events
Complements AWS for weight classes above antweight

entities.name: RoboWars Australia Weight Classes & Rules
entities.summary: The Australian combat robotics scene (RoboWars Australia) follows essentially the same SPARC-style weight ladder used in the US and Canada, not the lighter UK/AWS scale: Antweight is 1 lb (454 g), matching US antweight rather than the UK's 150 g class. Australia's ladder additionally runs a Super Heavyweight class at 340 lb (154 kg), one tier above the common 220 lb heavyweight, plus a separate off-arena 'UltiBot' outdoor-terrain division.
entities.notes: This corrects an earlier, less reliable search snippet that had conflated Australian antweight with the UK's 150g standard; a direct read of the RoboWars Australia wiki confirms Australia actually uses the heavier 1lb/454g US-style antweight class.

key_rules: Weight ladder: Antweight 1lb/454g, Beetleweight 3lb/1.36kg, Mantisweight 6lb/2.72kg, Hobbyweight 12lb/5.44kg, Featherweight 30lb/13.6kg, Lightweight 60lb/27.21kg, Middleweight 120lb/54.43kg, Heavyweight 220lb/99.79kg, Super Heavyweight 340lb/154.22kg
100% weight bonus for non-wheeled (walking) robots at most weight classes
Reduced 35% non-wheeled weight bonus specifically at the 340lb Super Heavyweight tier
Separate 'UltiBot' division for outdoor-terrain combat robots: 30kg for a mobile entrant, 25kg for a fixed/stationary entrant
Rules framework is explicitly based on the SPARC ruleset rather than a wholly separate Australian standard
banned: domain knowledge: follows standard SPARC-aligned banned weapon list (entanglement, liquids, explosives, EMP/jamming, uncontained flame)

entities.name: RoboGames
entities.summary: The largest general-purpose robotics competition and expo in the US, featuring a large combat robotics division alongside other robot sports. Combat weight classes run from 150g fairyweight through 250lb heavyweight, plus walking-bonus and autonomous divisions.

extra.location: San Mateo/San Francisco Bay Area, California, USA (historic venue; has moved between events)

entities.name: BattleBots (TV Series & Live Events)
entities.summary: The best-known televised combat robotics competition, running a single professional 250lb heavyweight division (up to 500lb for qualifying walkers) with a dedicated fighting arena (the BattleBox) and celebrity/expert judging panels.

extra.location: Various US studio/arena venues (historically Long Beach and Las Vegas)

entities.name: Motorama
entities.summary: One of the longest-running US combat robotics events, historically held in Pennsylvania and now associated with Doswell, Virginia. Runs SPARC-aligned weight classes with a strong antweight/beetleweight/plastic-antweight community presence, and is a well-known season-opener on the US hobby calendar.
entities.notes: Exact current-year class list and venue should be confirmed against the event's own page each season; this entry reflects general/historical pattern rather than a single verified current-year program.

entities.name: Antweight World Series Championship (UK)
entities.summary: The championship event of the UK Antweight World Series circuit, the top competitive target for UK-scale 150g antweight, fleaweight, and nanoweight builders, run under the AWS ruleset via Bristol Bot Builders.

extra.organization: Antweight World Series / Bristol Bot Builders
extra.cadence: Annual championship, feeding from a season of qualifying events

entities.name: Walker/Non-Wheeled Weight Bonus
entities.summary: A weight allowance given to robots that move without continuous rolling or cam-driven contact with the floor, since true walking mechanisms are heavier and less efficient than wheels for a given weight. Typical bonus is +100% (double weight) for a full walker and roughly +50% for shufflers/other non-wheeled-but-not-strict-walker locomotion.
entities.notes: SPARC: 100% bonus for true walkers, up to 50% for shufflers. NHRL: True Walker = +100% (e.g. 3lb class robot may weigh 6lb); Non-Traditional Locomotion = +50% (e.g. 3lb class robot may weigh 4.5lb). RoboGames: walking-bonus classes are exactly double the regular class weight (150g->300g, 1lb->2lb, 3lb->6lb, 120lb->240lb, 250lb->500lb). AWS (UK): non-roller antweight bonus is 50% (150g->225g).

entities.name: Multibot / Clusterbot
entities.summary: A single competition entry made of two or more physically separate robots controlled together as one 'weapon system,' sharing the weight limit of their class. Rules typically require all sub-units to be destroyed/immobilized for the team to lose, and extra weight allowance can apply if all sub-units are walkers.
entities.notes: Example from SPARC-style rules: a 12lb class multibot made of one walker/one shuffler is allowed 18lb total; a 12lb multibot made of two full walkers is allowed 24lb total. AWS (UK) clusterbots mixing roller and non-roller units use the formula: Roller allowance = Roller class limit - (2/3 x total non-roller weight), which prevents teams from gaming the non-roller bonus by loading most of the mass into non-rolling parts.

entities.name: Tap-Out
entities.summary: A rule allowing a robot's driver to voluntarily concede a match (usually by a verbal call or a pit-crew signal to the referee) to stop the fight before further damage or danger occurs. Common across NHRL, SPARC-style events, and AWS.

entities.name: Knockout (KO) / Immobility Count
entities.summary: A robot that shows no controlled, purposeful movement for a set count (commonly 10 seconds) is ruled 'out' and the match ends in the opponent's favor, similar to a boxing knockout. AWS/UK rules use a 10-second countdown; many US events use similar counts, sometimes referee-judged rather than a strict clock.

entities.name: Pit / Arena Hazard
entities.summary: A hole, drop, or automated hazard (spikes, hammers, saws) built into some arenas that can end a match instantly if a robot falls in or is forced into it — commonly touching the bottom of a pit is an automatic loss under UK/AWS-style rules. Larger UK 'house robot'-style arenas historically had multiple hazards; most hobby-class US arenas are simpler flat boxes without hazards.

entities.name: Weapon Lock
entities.summary: A required, highly visible physical device (often neon orange) that mechanically prevents a weapon (spinner, lifter, hammer) from moving while the robot is powered but outside the arena — during pit setup, transport, and pre-match staging. Inspectors check that it is fitted before power-on and removed only once the robot is placed in the arena.

entities.name: Radio Fail-Safe
entities.summary: A required behavior of the receiver/ESC system: if the transmitter signal is lost (turned off, out of range, or interfered with), all motion (drive and weapon) must stop automatically rather than continue at the last commanded value. Nearly universal requirement (SPARC, NHRL, RoboGames, AWS) and is actively tested by inspectors turning off the transmitter during check-in.

entities.name: Removable Link / Master Power Switch
entities.summary: A tool-free, externally accessible way to fully disconnect the main battery from the rest of the robot. Many rulesets require both a switch (for routine on/off) and, for larger classes, a physically removable link/jumper as a secondary, more certain isolation method that a marshal or the builder can pull in an emergency without needing the switch to still be functional.
entities.notes: RoboGames requires the disconnect to be operable within 15 seconds without endangering the operator, with full deactivation achievable within 60 seconds. AWS requires it be operable without tools. This is one of the first things a tech inspector checks.

entities.name: Plastic-Class Material Restriction
entities.summary: The defining rule of plastic antweight/plastic beetleweight: the entire structure must be built from an approved list of 3D-printable/injection-moldable plastics, excluding electronics, motors, fasteners, and bearings. This keeps cost and damage low, which is why plastic antweight is recommended as a first build.
entities.notes: Approved under SPARC: PLA, PLA+, ABS, PETG, ASA, PET. Banned: TPU, nylon, and any fiber-reinforced/composite filament (carbon-fiber or fiberglass loaded).

entities.name: Pinning Time Limit
entities.summary: A rule capping how long one robot may hold or corner an opponent without active combat, to prevent stalling wins. Typical limits: 15-20 seconds before the referee orders separation or the pin counts against the pinning robot; cornering an opponent against the wall is generally treated the same as a physical pin.
entities.notes: AWS (UK): 20 seconds. RoboGames: 15 seconds.

entities.name: Tethered Detachable Weapon Rule
entities.summary: A safety rule requiring that any weapon part designed to detach in combat (e.g. a thrown hammer head or a shattering disc meant to break away) remain physically tethered to the main robot body, with a maximum tether length, to prevent uncontrolled projectiles reaching the crowd or arena walls.
entities.notes: AWS (UK) caps detachable-weapon tethers at 3 feet (914mm) and caps pressurized weapon systems at 100 psi (7 bar).

entities.name: Judges' Decision
entities.summary: When a match runs its full time without a knockout or tap-out, a panel of judges (commonly 3) decides the winner using weighted criteria, most often a mix of damage dealt, aggression/control shown, and (in some rulesets) strategy. RoboGames formalizes this as Aggression (max 5 pts) + Damage (max 6 pts) per judge, for 33 total points across a 3-judge panel.
entities.notes: Damage severity is often bucketed (e.g. trivial/cosmetic/minor/significant/major/massive) rather than scored as a raw number, then translated into judge points. Exact weighting varies significantly by organization; BattleBots' precise public point breakdown was not confirmed in this research pass (confidence: low for BattleBots specifically).

entities.name: LiPo Battery Safety Handling
entities.summary: A set of near-universal pit-safety practices for lithium-polymer batteries used in combat robots: charge only in a fireproof LiPo bag or vented metal/ammo box, never leave a charging battery unattended, inspect for swelling/puncture damage before every use, and store/transport in fire-resistant bags. Several major events (e.g. RoboGames 2017) have had LiPo fires in the pits, which is why fireproof bags are now commonly mandatory rather than optional.
entities.notes: Arenas/venues are commonly required to be ventilated for roughly one full air exchange every 60 seconds, and pit areas should have a clear evacuation path in case of a battery fire.

chunks.title: Choosing an archetype for your first antweight
chunks.body_md:
The archetype you pick determines what you spend your 454 g on, what you need to be able to build, and which opponents you will struggle against. For a first robot, the honest ranking is:

**Build a control bot or wedge first if** you have never driven a combat robot. Driving is the skill that decides more antweight matches than design does, and a control bot lets you practise it without a weapon that can destroy your own robot. You will also finish every match, which is how you learn what actually breaks.

**Build a beater bar or small vertical spinner if** you want a weapon and have a printer or basic tools. The beater bar is the cheapest real weapon: bar stock, a hub, a brushless motor. You get to learn spin-up management, bite and gyro handling on a robot that survives its own mistakes.

**Build a drum if** you are on your second or third robot and can machine or print accurately. Drums have the best bite of any spinner and hit upward, which is the damage vector a 1 lb robot cannot resist.

**Avoid on a first build:** shell spinners, melty brains, grabbers, crushers and flippers. Each has a specific hard problem — a large bearing race, custom firmware, a reliable grab, enormous force, a latch that survives impact — that is not a good place to learn.

A note on the meta: almost every top competitive antweight now looks like a vertical spinner with hinged wedgelets either side of the weapon. That combination exists because a bare spinner loses the ground game to a wedge and a bare wedge cannot generate damage. If you are optimising for winning rather than learning, that is the configuration to converge on.

chunks.title: The three spinner families and what separates them
chunks.body_md:
Every spinning weapon falls into one of three families defined by the axis it turns about, and the axis decides nearly everything else.

**Vertical spinners** (discs, bars, drums, beater bars, eggbeaters) turn about a horizontal axis across the robot. Their damage vector is upward. This is the strongest vector at antweight because a 454 g robot has so little mass that a modest hit lifts it clear of the floor, and a robot in the air is not driving, not defending and not scoring. Their weakness is engagement: the weapon has to reach the opponent, and a good wedge prevents that.

**Horizontal spinners** (bars, discs, shells) turn about a vertical axis. Their damage vector is sideways, and their reach is enormous — the weapon sweeps a circle far larger than the robot. They are devastating against wheels and against other spinners' weapons. Their weakness is that a wedge simply passes underneath the sweep, and every hit throws them backwards as hard as it throws the opponent.

**Undercutters** are horizontal spinners mounted low enough to strike below an opponent's armour line. They exist specifically to beat the wedges that beat ordinary horizontals. The cost is precision: the weapon runs millimetres off the floor and must stay there after being hit.

The practical consequence is a rock-paper-scissors that is not quite balanced. Vertical spinners beat wedges and control bots. Wedges beat horizontal spinners. Horizontal spinners and undercutters beat vertical spinners by attacking the weapon and the wheels. Because the wedge is cheap and reliable, the meta settles on vertical spinners that carry wedges — which is why undercutters are the interesting counter-play.

chunks.title: Why bite decides whether your spinner actually works
chunks.body_md:
Two robots can store identical energy and produce completely different results, because energy only matters if the weapon engages. That is bite.

When two robots close at speed v and a weapon has t teeth turning at N rpm, teeth arrive at a rate of N/60 * t per second. The deepest a tooth can possibly reach is the distance the robots close between arrivals:

    bite_depth = v / (N/60 * t)

Put real numbers in. A 20,000 rpm weapon with two teeth, closing at 1.5 m/s, presents 667 teeth per second and can bite 2.25 mm. The same weapon with six teeth bites 0.75 mm — likely less than the opponent's armour thickness, so it skates off and converts its energy into noise and sparks.

This is counter-intuitive and it explains a lot of antweight design:

- **Fewer teeth hit harder.** Most competitive discs run one or two effective teeth.
- **Slower can hit harder.** Dropping weapon rpm increases bite. Past a point, spinning faster makes you less effective.
- **Closing speed is part of your weapon.** Driving into the opponent increases bite. Sitting still and waiting reduces it to zero.
- **Drums bite best.** A drum's large diameter and low mounting mean the drum body itself wedges under the opponent, forcing engagement rather than hoping for it.

Bite is also why the opponent's wedge is such an effective defence: a wedge presents a ramp that the tooth glances off, and raises the contact point away from the bite-favourable geometry.

chunks.title: Gyroscopic effects and how to live with them
chunks.body_md:
A spinning weapon is a gyroscope, and it will fight you every time you turn.

The physics is simple. A weapon of inertia I spinning at angular velocity omega_w, in a robot turning at omega_t, produces a precession torque:

    torque = I * omega_w * omega_t

acting about the axis perpendicular to both. For a vertical spinner that torque tries to roll the robot — it lifts one wheel. Lift a wheel, and the robot loses traction on that side, turns further, precesses harder, and lands. Repeat, and the robot appears to walk sideways across the arena. That is gyro dance.

Worked example: a 120 g, 90 mm disc has I = 1.2e-4 kg·m². At 20,000 rpm (2094 rad/s), turning at 180 deg/s (3.14 rad/s), precession torque is about 0.8 N·m. For a 454 g robot that is enough to unload a wheel comfortably.

What to do about it:

- **Turn gently.** Precession scales linearly with turn rate. Smooth, wide turns cost almost nothing; snap turns cost you the wheel.
- **Lower the weapon's inertia**, or accept lower rpm. Both reduce the effect proportionally.
- **Widen the wheelbase and lower the centre of gravity.** This does not reduce the torque, but it raises the torque needed to actually lift a wheel.
- **Use it.** A vertical spinner's precession can be used deliberately to hop the robot back onto its wheels, and experienced drivers steer partly with it.

Horizontal spinners precess too, but the torque tries to pitch the robot nose-up or nose-down rather than roll it, which is usually less disruptive — though it does change your ground clearance mid-turn, which matters a great deal for an undercutter.

chunks.title: The case for building a control bot
chunks.body_md:
New builders almost always want a spinner, and almost always would learn more from a control bot. The argument:

**Most antweight matches are lost, not won.** At 1 lb the commonest outcomes are a loose bolt, a dead battery, a thrown wheel, a weapon that would not spin up, and a robot that failed inspection. A control bot has fewer things that can do any of that.

**Driving is the dominant skill at this level and you cannot practise it with a broken robot.** A control bot finishes every match, which means every match is practice. A fragile spinner gets ninety seconds of experience and then goes back in the pit.

**The weight budget is generous.** With no weapon, no weapon ESC and no weapon battery load, you have something like 75% of your mass for drive and armour. That buys a drivetrain that out-pushes everything in its bracket and armour that survives what does hit you.

**Spinners beat themselves against good armour.** A significant fraction of a spinner's energy goes back into the spinner. A hard, compliant, well-braced target is a genuine counter to a fragile high-energy opponent.

The honest counter-argument: control bots must win on judges' decisions, which are not guaranteed, and a control bot that cannot generate damage will lose to a competent vertical spinner that also carries a wedge. That is real. But as a first or second robot, the learning rate is much higher, and the drivetrain and armour knowledge carries directly into whatever you build next.

chunks.title: What makes a wedge actually work
chunks.body_md:
A wedge is conceptually the simplest robot in combat robotics and one of the easiest to build badly. Four things decide whether it works, roughly in order of importance.

**1. The leading edge must touch the floor.** Not nearly touch. A wedge that rides two millimetres high is not a wedge; it is a ramp the opponent drives onto. Hinged forks or wedgelets solve this by floating independently of the chassis and following the floor.

**2. The edge must be thin and hard.** A thick edge presents a step for the opponent to climb rather than a ramp to be lifted by. Thin means the opponent's edge cannot get under yours. Hard means it stays thin after contact — a soft edge curls upward on its first hit and then you are the one being wedged.

**3. The edge must be backed.** A thin edge with nothing behind it folds. The usual construction is a hardened or spring-steel leading strip supported immediately behind by the chassis or by a thicker plate, so the tip cannot deflect upward.

**4. The angle should be shallow.** A shallow wedge lifts progressively and keeps the opponent's weight forward of your own axle. A steep wedge acts like a wall — it stops the opponent instead of lifting them, and it gives their weapon a flat face to hit.

Beyond the wedge itself: traction decides what happens once you are under. Pushing force is limited by friction, not by torque — a robot with more torque than its tyres can transmit simply spins its wheels. Soft, grippy tyres and weight over the driven wheels matter more than gear ratio.

chunks.title: How the archetypes match up
chunks.body_md:
A compact summary of who beats whom at antweight, and why. Treat these as tendencies, not laws — driving overturns most of them.

| Attacker | Beats | Loses to | Why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Vertical spinner | Wedges, control bots, rammers, hammers | Horizontals, undercutters, grabbers | Upward damage is unanswerable; but its own weapon and wheels are exposed to horizontal sweeps |
| Drum | Wedges, control bots, undercutters | Horizontals, grabbers | Best bite of any spinner — it wedges under and then hits upward |
| Horizontal bar | Vertical spinners, drums, hammers | Wedges, forkbots, rammers | Huge reach and attacks weapons and wheels; passes harmlessly over a good wedge |
| Undercutter | Wedges, forkbots, vertical spinners | Drums, grabbers | Strikes below the wedge line, so the wedge no longer protects |
| Wedge / forkbot | Horizontals, shells, hammers, rammers | Verticals, drums, undercutters | Removes traction from anything whose weapon cannot reach below its edge |
| Grabber | Every spinner, once clamped | Wedges, control bots | Neutralises a weapon completely; but must survive the approach |
| Hammer | Control bots, invertible bricks | All spinners | Concentrated point damage, but far less total energy than a spinner |
| Thwackbot | Control bots, wedges | All spinners, grabbers | Free weapon, but cannot attack and manoeuvre simultaneously |
| Flipper (spring) | Vertical spinners, wedges, control bots | Horizontals, invertible bricks | Attacks spinners from underneath where they cannot respond; useless against an invertible opponent |

The important structural fact: the wedge beats the horizontal, the vertical beats the wedge, and the horizontal beats the vertical. Because the wedge is cheap and can be bolted onto anything, the stable solution is a vertical spinner carrying wedgelets — which is exactly what the top of the class looks like. The genuine counter-play to that meta is the undercutter, which is why it persists despite being difficult to build.

chunks.title: Weight budgets by archetype
chunks.body_md:
A 1 lb antweight is 454 g. Where those grams go is the single most consequential set of decisions in the design, and the split is largely determined by archetype.

| Archetype | Weapon | Drive | Armour + chassis | Electronics | Battery |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Vertical disc spinner | 32% | 20% | 24% | 12% | 8% |
| Drum spinner | 34% | 19% | 23% | 12% | 8% |
| Vertical bar spinner | 34% | 19% | 23% | 12% | 8% |
| Beater bar | 28% | 21% | 25% | 13% | 9% |
| Shell spinner | 38% | 18% | 22% | 11% | 8% |
| Wedge / control bot | 0% | 34% | 40% | 14% | 8% |
| Forkbot | 5% | 33% | 37% | 13% | 8% |
| Lifter | 18% | 26% | 30% | 15% | 8% |
| Spring flipper | 22% | 24% | 29% | 14% | 8% |
| Grabber | 22% | 26% | 27% | 15% | 7% |
| Hammer | 26% | 23% | 28% | 14% | 7% |
| Thwackbot | 12% | 32% | 34% | 14% | 6% |

In grams against 454 g, a 32% weapon share is 145 g and a 20% drive share is 91 g.

Three observations that catch people out:

**Electronics is nearly fixed.** A receiver, ESCs, wiring and connectors come to something like 50-65 g regardless of archetype. You cannot economise your way out of it, so it is effectively a fixed tax on the budget.

**Battery is smaller than people expect.** A 450 mAh 3S pack is around 35-40 g. Antweight matches are short; capacity is rarely the constraint, sag is.

**Leave 3-5% slack.** Robots always come in heavier than the model says — fasteners, wire, glue, threadlocker and the bits you add in the pits. Budgeting to exactly 454 g means failing inspection.

chunks.title: How each archetype actually fails
chunks.body_md:
Archetypes do not fail randomly; each has a characteristic way it dies. Knowing yours tells you what to carry spares for.

**Vertical spinners** lose the weapon bell off the motor. Stock drone motors retain the bell with a C-clip that was never designed for combat shock loads. They also bend weapon shafts, and a bent shaft means an unbalanced weapon, which destroys bearings within a match.

**Bar spinners** bend the bar. A bent bar is an unbalanced bar, and the vibration will shake fasteners loose across the whole robot. Carry a spare bar, not a spare bolt.

**Drums** fail at the hub-to-shaft interface. Set screws back out under vibration and the drum starts slipping on the shaft, which looks like a weapon that spins up slowly and then stops biting.

**Horizontal spinners** destroy themselves on the arena wall. They also suffer the worst of the self-inflicted-recoil problem — every hit throws them into something.

**Wedges and forkbots** bend their edges. A curled edge turns a wedge into a ramp, and the robot silently stops working without anything visibly breaking. Check the edge against a flat surface between matches.

**Lifters and flippers** fail at the pivot or the latch. The arm is a lever that transmits every impact straight into its mounting, and latches that hold spring force are precision parts being hit repeatedly.

**Grabbers** fail by not grabbing. The mechanism usually survives; the approach does not.

**Thwackbots and control bots** mostly fail electrically — brownouts on impact, connectors shaking loose, a receiver that resets. With no weapon to break, the failure moves into the wiring.

**Everything** loses bolts. Thread locker on every fastener, and a torque check between every match, is the highest-value maintenance in the sport.

chunks.title: How the archetype picture changes in plastic ant
chunks.body_md:
The plastic antweight class changes the relative value of the archetypes, because the weapon can no longer be made of metal.

**Damage becomes blunt force.** A printed tooth cannot cut. What a plastic weapon does is deliver impulse — it knocks the opponent around, breaks printed parts by shock, and occasionally cracks a chassis. The archetypes that rely on cutting or piercing (saws, crushers) become almost pointless. The ones that rely on delivering impulse upward (vertical spinners, drums, beater bars) still work.

**Compliance beats hardness.** In metal ant you armour with titanium or UHMW. In plastic ant, TPU armour is the strong choice, because a flexible panel spreads the impact over time and returns energy rather than fracturing. Rigid PLA armour cracks; an 85A-95A TPU panel bounces.

**Spinners hurt themselves more.** A printed weapon taking a hard impact fails at the layer lines. Weapons become consumables, which is fine — that is the point of the class — but it shifts the design toward cheap, fast-to-reprint weapons rather than precious ones.

**Control archetypes gain value.** Because damage is harder to achieve, more matches go to decisions and to ring-outs. A well-driven plastic wedge or control bot is proportionally stronger than its metal-ant equivalent.

**Horizontal spinners get worse.** Their recoil problem is unchanged, but their ability to convert that recoil into opponent damage is reduced. Vertical spinners and drums dominate the class more completely than they do in metal ant.

One rules caveat worth knowing: organisations disagree about post-processing. SPARC's plastic class explicitly bans annealing, acetone smoothing and boiling as durability-enhancing treatments, while some other events permit them. A weapon that is legal at one event can be illegal at another, so check before you print.

chunks.title: The novelty archetypes and whether they are worth it
chunks.body_md:
Some archetypes exist more for the challenge than for the win rate. An honest assessment of each at 1 lb:

**Melty brain** — genuinely clever and genuinely hard. You need an accelerometer, custom firmware, and a tolerance for a robot that translates slowly and loses all its energy whenever it manoeuvres. Worth building if the software is the point. Not worth building to win.

**Walkers** — the weight bonus is real and large, commonly up to double the class limit for a true walker. The catch is that qualifying is strictly judged and the mechanism consumes much of the bonus it earns. Confirm your event's exact bonus and qualification criteria before designing around it.

**Shufflers** — a partial bonus for a simpler mechanism, but some rulesets classify shufflers as wheeled and award nothing. Check first; the entire value proposition depends on it.

**Multibots** — splitting 454 g gives you numbers and positioning at the cost of each robot being individually fragile. Rules differ sharply on whether both robots must be immobilised to lose. Read the specific ruleset.

**Crushers** — scale badly downward. The force needed to pierce armour demands gearing that makes the mechanism slow and heavy, and a 1 lb robot lacks the traction to hold an opponent still while it works.

**Saws** — spectacular and ineffective. Combat armour resists cutting, and the weight spent on an arm plus a blade motor buys less damage than the same grams in a disc.

**Tracked robots** — look ideal for pushing, disappoint in practice. A thrown track is an instant loss and antweight-scale tensioners are hard to make robust.

None of these are bad projects. They are bad *first* projects, and several are bad competitive choices. Build them because you want to solve their specific problem, not because you expect them to win a bracket.

chunks.title: What drivetrain each archetype needs
chunks.body_md:
The archetype sets the drivetrain requirement, and getting this wrong wastes more weight than any other single decision.

**Spinners need enough drive, not maximum drive.** A spinner wins by landing hits, which needs controllable positioning rather than raw pushing force. Two brushed 16 mm gearmotors at a moderate ratio, giving roughly 2-4 m/s, is the standard. Spending more weight on drive takes it from the weapon, which is where a spinner's value is.

**Control bots and wedges need traction above all.** Pushing force is limited by friction, not torque: max push = coefficient of friction × weight on driven wheels. For a 454 g robot with grippy tyres that is only around 4-5 N. Once you have enough torque to reach that limit, more gearing achieves nothing — the wheels just slip. So the priorities are soft tyres, weight over the driven wheels, and four-wheel drive to put all 454 g to work.

**Lifters, flippers and grabbers need torque and control.** They must hold position while the mechanism works, which means low-speed controllability matters more than top speed. Higher gear ratios, and a drivetrain that does not stall when pushed.

**Thwackbots need rotational acceleration.** Their weapon energy comes from how fast the drivetrain can spin the whole robot, so they want high torque and high-grip tyres at a wide track.

**Melty brains need matched, predictable motors.** The translation algorithm assumes both sides respond identically. Mismatched motors make the robot curve.

A general antweight rule: wheel diameter sets your speed for a given rpm, and it is usually easier to change speed by changing wheels than by changing gearboxes. A 500 rpm output on a 32 mm wheel gives about 0.84 m/s; the same motor on a 50 mm wheel gives 1.3 m/s with proportionally less torque at the contact patch.

chunks.title: Self-righting: invertibility versus a mechanism
chunks.body_md:
Every antweight will end up on its back. There are three answers, and at 1 lb only two are sensible.

**Be invertible.** Build the robot so being upside down does not matter: wheels that protrude above and below the chassis, a weapon that works in both orientations, and an invert switch on the transmitter that reverses steering. This costs essentially nothing in weight and is the default choice at antweight. The main design constraints are that the wheels must stick out both ways — which exposes them to undercutters — and the weapon arc must clear in both orientations.

**Use the weapon.** A vertical spinner or a drum can be used to flip the robot back over by firing the weapon against the floor and letting the reaction torque roll the robot. This is free — the mechanism already exists — but it is unreliable on a smooth floor and needs the weapon to be undamaged, which is exactly what it may not be when you are upside down.

**Carry a srimech.** A dedicated arm, ram or lever whose only job is righting. At 1 lb this typically costs 8-15% of the weight budget for a function that invertibility provides for free. It is justified mainly when the archetype cannot be invertible — a wedge with a fixed low edge, a lifter with an arm that only works one way up.

The practical recommendation for antweight: design for invertibility from the start. It is much harder to retrofit than to plan for, and it removes an entire category of match-ending failure. If your archetype genuinely cannot be invertible, budget the srimech weight honestly rather than hoping the weapon will do it.

chunks.title: How the antweight meta got to where it is
chunks.body_md:
The current antweight meta is the product of a few technology shifts, and understanding them explains why robots look the way they do.

**Cheap brushless motors changed weapons.** The FPV drone market made small, powerful outrunners — 1104 through 2814 — available for a few dollars. Before that, antweight weapons were limited by what a brushed motor could deliver. Afterwards, a 1 lb robot could store a few hundred joules, which is enough to end matches. The whole class became more damaging.

**Cheap 3D printing changed iteration.** When a chassis is an afternoon's print rather than a week's machining, builders iterate faster and take more design risk. It also created the plastic antweight class outright, which is now many builders' entry point.

**Integrated ESC/receiver boards changed reliability.** A single board carrying a receiver, two drive ESCs and a weapon ESC removed most of the wiring that used to shake loose on impact, and cut electronics weight substantially. That freed grams for weapon and armour.

**AM32 and modern ESC firmware changed drive.** Proper low-rpm control, braking and reversing made brushless drive practical at antweight, where previously brushed gearmotors were the only sane option.

The design consequence of all this: weapons got strong enough that pure control bots stopped being reliably competitive, while wedges stayed cheap enough that pure spinners stopped being reliably competitive either. The equilibrium is the hybrid — a vertical spinner or drum with hinged wedgelets — which wins the ground game and then applies damage.

Where it goes next is contested. The undercutter is the principled counter to a meta built on wedges, and better brushless drive makes the precision it requires more achievable. Whether it displaces the hybrid depends largely on whether builders can solve its ground-clearance fragility.

chunks.title: Archetype-specific safety
chunks.body_md:
Different archetypes present different hazards, and the safety requirements follow the archetype.

**Spinners** store the most energy and are the most dangerous. A competitive 1 lb spinner can hold a few hundred joules — enough to break bone or destroy an eye. The rules that exist because of spinners:

- A **weapon lock** — a physical device that prevents the weapon rotating — must be fitted whenever the robot is powered outside the arena, and removed only inside it.
- A **removable link or accessible power switch** so the robot can be made safe without tools.
- A tested **failsafe** that stops the weapon if the radio signal is lost. This is the single most-checked item at tech inspection.

**Flippers, springs and pressure systems** are dangerous when stored energy is released unexpectedly. A cocked spring is a loaded weapon. Never work on a cocked mechanism; discharge it first. Pressurised systems attract additional scrutiny and are restricted or banned at some events.

**Thwackbots and melty brains** are unusual in that the whole robot is moving unpredictably. They are hard for a referee to make safe and hard for a driver to stop precisely.

**Control bots and wedges** are the safest archetype to build and test, which is another argument for building one first.

Universal rules regardless of archetype: never spin a weapon outside a proper enclosure, treat the robot as live whenever the battery is connected, and set the failsafe before the first time you power up — not the night before the event.

chunks.title: Battery Chemistry Choices for Antweights: LiPo, LiHV, Li-ion, LiFePO4, NiMH
chunks.body_md:
LiPo (lithium polymer) is the default power source for essentially every competitive 1 lb antweight built since the mid-2000s, and for good reason: it offers the best combination of energy density (roughly 150-200+ Wh/kg), discharge rate, and pouch-format packaging flexibility of any chemistry available in small sizes. A standard LiPo cell is charged to 4.20V and discharged to about 3.0-3.3V under load, giving a 3.7V nominal per cell used for all voltage-tier math (2S = 7.4V, 3S = 11.1V, 4S = 14.8V).

**LiHV (high-voltage LiPo)** is a chemistry variant, not just a different label — the cell construction is tuned to tolerate a higher full-charge voltage, typically 4.35V/cell (some cells go to 4.40V) instead of 4.20V. Nominal voltage for LiHV is usually quoted as 3.8V/cell rather than 3.7V. The real gain is modest but real: at the same physical cell, LiHV stores roughly 5-10% more energy than standard LiPo, and since it runs at a higher voltage across the whole discharge curve, motors and ESCs see more usable voltage right up until the pack is nearly empty — a genuine antweight advantage for spinner tip speed and drive punch late in a match. The tradeoffs: an LiHV pack must be charged on a charger or profile that explicitly supports the 4.35V/cell ceiling (charging it on a standard LiPo profile just leaves capacity on the table; overcharging a standard cell to LiHV voltages is dangerous), and LiHV cells generally show somewhat shorter cycle life at aggressive charge/discharge rates than standard LiPo.

**Li-ion (18650/21700 cylindrical, e.g. Molicel)** offers even higher energy density and much better cycle life than LiPo pouch cells, and is the backbone of e-bikes, power tools, and larger combat weight classes' main packs. It is essentially absent from competitive 1 lb antweight main-battery use, though, because a single round cell is too heavy relative to its usable current for the weight budget, and the rigid cylindrical format doesn't pack efficiently into a flat antweight chassis. It shows up in antweight discussions mostly as context or in bench/test setups, not in the ring.

**LiFePO4 (LiFe)** cells run a lower nominal voltage (3.3V/cell) and lower energy density than LiPo, but have a much flatter discharge curve, far higher abuse tolerance, and a dramatically lower fire risk. Antweight builders occasionally use a small 2S LiFe pack (6.6V nominal) as an *isolated receiver/electronics* power source specifically because it won't sag or brown out the way the shared main LiPo can under weapon load — not as a main weapon/drive battery.

**NiMH** was the default antweight chemistry before affordable LiPo took over, typically a 6-cell 7.2V stick pack. It is essentially obsolete today: roughly 1/3 the energy density of LiPo by weight and unable to sustain modern brushless weapon current without severe sag. It survives only in legacy kit documentation and exhibition/vintage classes.

chunks.title: Choosing 2S vs 3S vs 4S for an Antweight
chunks.body_md:
Cell count sets the pack's nominal voltage: 2S = 7.4V, 3S = 11.1V, 4S = 14.8V (add roughly 0.1V/cell for LiHV packs at the same series count). For a fixed weapon motor, more cells means proportionally more no-load RPM (RPM ~= KV * Voltage), so builders pick cell count and motor KV together, not independently.

**2S (7.4V)** is the traditional antweight baseline, especially for control bots, wedges, and lower-KV weapon setups. It asks the least of the pack (lowest voltage means lower current for a given power level is *not* automatically true — power = V*I, so a 2S system needs *more* current than a 3S system for the same weapon power) and is the lightest option cell-for-cell, but a 2S pack has to work harder (more amps) to deliver the same wattage as a higher cell count, which increases both voltage sag and wiring/connector demands.

**3S (11.1V)** is the most common sweet spot for antweight spinners today. Popular weapon motors in the 2000-2600KV range paired with 3S land in a practical tip-speed/torque range for a 1 lb disc or drum, and 3S packs in the 300-550mAh range keep total weight reasonable. As one antweight motor example puts it, a 2400KV motor on 3S yields roughly 25,000+ RPM no-load — already fast enough that most builders don't need to go to 4S with that motor.

**4S (14.8V)** shows up on plastic antweights and metal antweights chasing higher tip speed with lower-KV motors (roughly 1000-1800KV) to avoid overspeeding a given weapon geometry, or on drivetrains wanting more headroom before voltage sag becomes limiting. The tradeoff is weight and risk: a 4S pack of a given capacity weighs more than an equivalent-Wh 3S or 2S pack (an extra series cell is roughly a flat 20-30% weight adder over 3S for the same mAh rating), and pairing a high-KV motor with 4S without checking the math is a documented way to overspeed and burn out a weapon motor — one antweight builder specifically warned that a 2600KV motor on 4S would not survive, while the 1250KV version of the same motor was fine.

**Rule of thumb weight penalty per cell:** going from 2S to 3S at the same mAh rating typically adds 30-50% pack weight; 3S to 4S adds a further 20-30%. Because weight is the antweight's tightest constraint, most builders choose the *lowest* cell count that lets their chosen weapon motor reach the RPM/tip-speed they want, rather than defaulting to 4S for headroom.

chunks.title: Real Antweight Pack Sizes and Brands: What Builders Actually Buy
chunks.body_md:
Antweight LiPo/LiHV packs cluster tightly around a handful of capacity/cell-count combinations because they have to fit inside a 1 lb chassis alongside a receiver, ESCs, and a weapon system, while still delivering multi-minute runtime.

**180-300mAh 2S** is the smallest practical antweight size, common on the lightest control bots and early builds. Example: the Tattu 300mAh 2S 45C (7.4V nominal, ~23g, 48.6x18.8x13.9mm, JST-SYP) — a widely stocked pack that crosses over directly from micro FPV. The Palm Beach Bots Palm Power 2S 300mAh 65C is a combat-market-specific equivalent with a JST connector and separate balance lead.

**300-450mAh 3S** is the most common antweight spinner size. The CNHL MiniStar 3S 450mAh 70C (11.1V, XT30) and its LiHV sibling, the CNHL LiHV MiniStar 3S 450mAh 70C (11.4V nominal, same 70C/XT30), are directly comparable real products that illustrate the LiHV capacity gain in the same physical pack. Palm Beach Bots' Palm Power 3S 450mAh 45C (XT30) sells for $14.99 as of recent listings — a useful real price anchor for this size class.

**350-550mAh 4S** is used for higher-voltage plastic antweight and metal antweight builds; the GNB LiHV 4S 350mAh 70C (15.2V nominal, XT30) is a real example sized for this niche.

**Brand landscape:** Tattu and Gens Ace are sister brands from the same manufacturer (Grepow group) and their packs of matching spec are usually near-identical. CNHL (China Hobby Line) is a major supplier of small-format packs, including combat-labeled MiniStar and LiHV MiniStar lines. GNB (Gaoneng) is notable for actively marketing LiHV packs directly to the antweight community, not just FPV. Lumenier and RDQ Series (RaceDayQuads' house brand) are FPV-first lines that get cross-shopped into antweight builds because their micro-pack sizes overlap almost exactly with antweight needs, though specific SKU weights/prices for combat use are less consistently documented than the combat-market-specific brands. FingerTech Robotics' Galaxy line and Palm Beach Bots' Palm Power line are combat-market-specific options sold directly by long-standing antweight vendors, bundled with kits like the Viper V3.

Across all of these, weight for a given capacity/cell-count/C-rating combination is fairly consistent regardless of brand — a 3S 450mAh pack lands in the 30-40g range whichever manufacturer makes it — so the deciding factors in practice are connector type (JST for the smallest/oldest builds, XT30 once current climbs), C-rating credibility, and price/availability rather than dramatic weight differences between brands.

chunks.title: C Rating: What the Number Means and Why It Lies
chunks.body_md:
A pack's C rating is a multiplier on its capacity: **Max current (A) = Capacity (Ah) x C rating.** A 450mAh (0.45Ah) pack rated 70C is claiming 0.45 x 70 = 31.5A continuous, and many packs also print a separate, higher "burst" C rating (often 1.5-2x the continuous number) for short spikes.

The uncomfortable truth is that printed C ratings on budget and mid-tier packs are marketing numbers, not lab-tested guarantees, and they have been for as long as small LiPo packs have existed. Manufacturers competing on a spec sheet have every incentive to print an impressive number, and there is no independent, universally enforced test standard behind most of them. Reputable brands (name-brand Tattu, CNHL's better lines, GNB) are generally closer to honest than unbranded eBay packs, but even they should be treated with a healthy discount, especially for continuous (not burst) draw.

**A realistic antweight rule of thumb:** for planning purposes, trust roughly 40-60% of a pack's printed continuous C rating from a mainstream combat/FPV brand, and treat the printed burst rating as, at best, a one-to-two-second spike capability rather than something the pack can repeat every few seconds for a full match. So a "70C continuous" 450mAh pack should be planned around as if it were really good for something like 13-19A of sustained current, not 31.5A.

**How to compute what you actually need:** estimate combined continuous drive+weapon current (see formula-power-budget-drive-weapon) and multiply by a comfortable safety margin (1.5-2x) to get your target *continuous* current requirement; separately estimate your worst-case simultaneous spike (weapon spin-up plus a hard driving input) for your target *burst* requirement. Pick a pack whose *discounted* continuous rating clears the continuous target and whose burst rating clears the spike target — not a pack whose printed continuous number merely looks bigger than your estimated draw.

In practice, for a typical antweight combined draw in the 10-20A continuous / 25-35A brief-spike range, almost any name-brand 3S pack rated 45C or higher in the 300-550mAh range clears this bar even after the realistic discount — which is why C-rating shopping matters less in antweight than pack *capacity*, weight, and voltage sag behavior (internal resistance) do. Chasing an ever-higher printed C rating on an already-adequate pack mostly buys marketing, not match performance.

chunks.title: Voltage Sag: The Real Limiter in a 1 lb Bot
chunks.body_md:
More antweight matches are lost to voltage sag than to an outright battery failure. Sag is the momentary drop in a pack's output voltage that happens the instant current draw spikes, caused by the pack's internal resistance (R_internal): **V_sag = I_draw x R_internal**. Every real battery has some internal resistance; it is never zero. A brand-new small antweight LiPo cell might have on the order of 0.015-0.04 ohm per cell, but that number climbs steadily as the pack ages, as it takes repeated hard cycles, as it gets cold, and especially after any physical damage (even damage too small to see) from a hit in a previous match.

Why does this matter more in a 1 lb bot than in bigger classes? Because antweight packs are necessarily tiny — a 300-550mAh pack simply has less parallel cell area than a beetleweight or featherweight pack, so its *internal resistance per amp of current requested* is proportionally higher. At the same time, a 1 lb bot's weapon motor spin-up and its drive motors under a hard push both draw current from the *same small pack simultaneously*, so the current spike a tiny antweight pack has to absorb is large relative to its own capacity.

The consequence is a **brownout**: system voltage sags below the minimum operating voltage of the receiver, ESC, or weapon controller for a fraction of a second, which is enough to reset the receiver, cause the ESC to cut out, or make the weapon controller glitch — exactly the moment a bot appears to "die" mid-match even though the battery still reads a healthy voltage once the load is removed.
