This is why some builders isolate receiver power onto its own small, low-sag pack (a dedicated 2S LiPo or LiFe RX pack) rather than sharing the main weapon/drive battery's rail for the receiver.

**Sizing to avoid sag** comes down to three levers: (1) choose a pack with genuinely low internal resistance for its size — larger mAh at the same physical footprint tends to help since more parallel cell material shares the current; (2) retire packs once they show age (a pack that sagged fine as new but now visibly dips further under the same load has risen internal resistance and should be rotated out of weapon-heavy duty); (3) don't run a pack right at the edge of its *discounted* C rating (see the c-rating chunk) — headroom above your estimated draw directly buys headroom against sag. A pack that is "big enough" on paper capacity but chosen at the rock-bottom of its usable C rating will still sag hard, because sag is driven by resistance and instantaneous current, not by whether the pack has enough total energy left for the match.

chunks.title: Building a Power Budget: Current Draw, Match Drain, and Target Capacity
chunks.body_md:
A useful power budget for an antweight starts by estimating current draw separately for drive and weapon, then combining them.

**Drive current:** a typical small antweight brushed gearmotor pulls roughly 1-3A under normal driving load, spiking to 5-8A when stalled against a wall or an opponent's push. With two drive motors, typical combined drive draw is therefore about 2-6A, with brief stall spikes to 10-16A if both motors stall at once (rare, but worth padding for).

**Weapon current:** highly dependent on motor and weapon geometry, but a common antweight brushless outrunner running a disc or drum draws roughly 3-10A once spun up and cutting normally, with sharp, brief spikes well above that at initial spin-up or when the weapon bites into an opponent and briefly bogs down.

**Combined typical draw:** for a moderately aggressive antweight spinner+drive combo, a combined *typical* draw around 8-15A is a reasonable planning number, with instantaneous spikes into the 20-30A range during simultaneous weapon spin-up and hard driving.

**What a 3-minute match actually drains:** using the match-runtime formula in reverse, a combined average draw of ~10A over a 3-minute (180 second = 3 minute) match works out to 10A x (3/60) hours = 0.5Ah = 500mAh consumed — notably more than the *nominal* capacity of a 300-450mAh pack. This is not a contradiction: real matches are not fought at full weapon+drive draw for the entire 3 minutes (there are pauses, positioning, and lulls), so actual average draw over the whole match is usually well under the peak combined figure. But it does explain why builders don't simply match pack mAh to "current draw x 3 minutes" using worst-case numbers — that would demand an unrealistically large, heavy pack.

**Target capacity in practice:** the widely repeated antweight rule of thumb is to estimate your realistic average-draw energy need for the match (using nominal, not worst-case, average current) and then round the *capacity* up 25-50% over that bare-minimum number for margin — covering pack aging, an extra practice run before a battery swap, and the fact that voltage (not just remaining mAh) needs to stay high enough to avoid sag late in the pack's discharge curve. In concrete terms, this is exactly why 300-550mAh packs (rather than the bare ~200mAh a pure energy calculation might suggest for a single 3-minute match) dominate the antweight market: the extra capacity is buying sag margin and multi-run flexibility, not just runtime.

chunks.title: Charging Practice: Balance Charging, Rates, Storage Voltage, and Chargers
chunks.body_md:
**Balance charging is mandatory, not optional**, for any multi-cell LiPo/LiHV pack. A balance charger monitors each cell individually through the balance lead and tops each one off in step, preventing any single cell from being overcharged while others lag behind — the single biggest safeguard against the cell-imbalance failures that lead to puffing, capacity loss, or fire. Never charge a multi-cell pack through the main leads only.

**Charge rate:** the safe default is 1C (a 450mAh pack charges at 0.45A) for best pack longevity, though most modern packs and chargers support faster charging (2-5C on some packs) when time is tight, at some cost to long-term cycle life. Always charge to the chemistry-correct cutoff: 4.20V/cell for standard LiPo, 4.35V/cell for LiHV — charging an LiHV pack on a standard LiPo setting leaves capacity unused, while charging a standard LiPo pack to LiHV voltage is a real overcharge/fire risk.

**Storage voltage:** for any pack that won't be used within the next few days, discharge or charge it to roughly 3.8V/cell (an acceptable range is about 3.7-3.85V/cell). This keeps the cell chemistry in its most stable state for long-term storage, unlike leaving a pack fully charged (accelerates degradation) or fully depleted (risk of over-discharge damage) between events.

**Chargers combat builders commonly use:** ISDT's compact chargers (e.g. the ISDT 608AC, an 8A/200W AC/DC unit supporting LiPo/LiHV/Li-ion/LiFe/NiMH from 1-6S with an XT60 port) are popular for their small size and multi-chemistry support — useful given how many different chemistries show up across an antweight builder's battery drawer. HOTA's D6 Pro is well regarded for balance accuracy and a high 1.6A/cell balance current, which matters on the very small capacities antweight packs use (a weak balance current struggles to actually balance a 300mAh pack in reasonable time). SkyRC's T1000 and similar units combine charge and discharge functions in one box, letting a builder both charge match packs and discharge them to storage voltage after an event without a separate tool.

**Parallel charging safety:** charging multiple packs simultaneously through a parallel charging board is common for efficiency, but every pack in the parallel group must be the same cell count, a very similar state of charge, and in good health — a damaged or significantly more depleted pack in the group can pull a dangerous surge of current from its healthier neighbors the moment the group is connected, before the charger even starts. Never parallel-charge a pack you have not individually voltage-checked, and never mix cell counts or chemistries in one parallel group.

chunks.title: Parallel Charging: Why It's Convenient and How It Goes Wrong
chunks.body_md:
Antweight builders frequently own many small packs — several 300-550mAh cells for the main bot plus spares — and charging them one at a time on a single-channel charger is slow, so parallel charging boards (a small PCB with multiple balance/main connectors wired in parallel, feeding one charger channel) are a common convenience. Used correctly, parallel charging is safe and is exactly how many combat pit areas charge banks of small packs quickly between rounds.

The failure mode is specific and avoidable: when packs at meaningfully different voltages are connected together in parallel, current flows *between the packs themselves* the instant they're connected — before the charger has done anything — as the higher-voltage pack tries to equalize with the lower-voltage one. If one pack in the group is significantly more depleted, damaged, or has higher internal resistance than the others, this equalization current can be large and, in a worst case, generate enough localized heat to damage or ignite the weaker pack. This is why every credible parallel-charging guide insists on three checks before connecting packs together: (1) all packs must be the same cell count and chemistry, (2) all packs should be within about 0.1-0.2V of each other per cell before connecting, and (3) every pack must be visually and electrically healthy (no puffing, no damaged leads, no cells reading suspiciously low).

For antweight builders specifically, this matters because match-day packs often come back from a bout at very different states of charge — one pack might have fought a short match and returned at 70% capacity, another might have gone the full 3 minutes and returned near-empty. Tossing both into the same parallel board without checking voltage first is a common and preventable mistake. The safe habit is to check each pack's resting voltage individually (a simple LiPo checker or the balance port on a multimeter) before adding it to a parallel group, and to keep visibly damaged or hard-hit packs (see the mounting/impact-damage chunk) out of any parallel group entirely, charging them alone and watching them the whole time, or retiring them outright.

chunks.title: LiPo Fire Risk, Puffed Packs, and Packs Damaged by a Hit
chunks.body_md:
LiPo and LiHV cells store a lot of chemical energy in a very thin, mechanically fragile pouch, and that combination is the source of essentially all LiPo fire incidents: puncture, crush damage, severe overcharge, or an internal short from age/manufacturing defect can trigger thermal runaway, a self-sustaining exothermic reaction that releases the cell's stored energy rapidly as heat and, often, fire. One widely repeated comparison in RC and combat robotics safety writeups is that the energy density of a LiPo pack is in the same rough order of magnitude as TNT per unit mass — not because LiPo burns like an explosive, but because the amount of stored energy per gram is genuinely large and should be respected. Most LiPo fires happen during charging (which is why an unattended charging pack is the single most common cause) or immediately after physical damage.

**Puffed packs** — visibly swollen pouches — are the most common warning sign a builder will see directly. Swelling means gas has built up inside the pouch from internal chemical breakdown, which happens from overcharging, over-discharging, age, or damage. A puffed pack should never be charged, discharged normally, or "one more match" risked on it: treat it as compromised and retire it immediately. Do not attempt a charger's "recovery" or "trickle" mode on a puffed pack.

**A hit that damages the battery bay is one of the most serious failure modes in antweight combat specifically**, because the whole point of the class is deliberately smashing small, densely packed robots into each other. A hard hit that crushes, dents, or punctures the battery — even if the pack still reads a normal voltage afterward and the robot still drives — can have compromised the internal cell structure invisibly, creating a short that may not manifest as heat or smoke until minutes later, often while the bot is sitting in a pit box or a carry case. **The standard safe practice is: after any hit that reaches the battery compartment, physically remove and inspect the pack before doing anything else with the robot** — do not just check that it still powers on. If the pack shows any deformation, a punctured pouch, an exposed foil layer, unusual heat, or a chemical smell, isolate it immediately in a fireproof/LiPo-safe bag or a metal container away from other batteries, vehicles, and flammable material, and let it fully off-gas or cool in a safe outdoor location before disposal. Never put a suspect pack back in your pit box, bag, or car.

**Event and venue rules** at most organized combat events require charging to happen only in a designated charging area, often with a LiPo-safe bag or ammo-can-style container required under each charger, and require damaged packs to be reported and isolated rather than quietly discarded — check the specific event's rules packet, since requirements vary by organization and venue (some venues require this due to fire-marshal/insurance rules, not just robotics-club preference).

chunks.title: Storage, Disposal, and Shipping/Flying with LiPos
chunks.body_md:
**Long-term storage:** any pack not going to be used within the next few days should be brought to storage voltage, roughly 3.8V/cell (acceptable range about 3.7-3.85V/cell). This is the voltage at which the cell's internal chemistry sits in its most stable, lowest-stress state. Store packs in a LiPo-safe bag or a fireproof container, away from direct sunlight, extreme heat, or anything flammable, and check on packs stored for a long time periodically (over months, voltage will slowly drift and should be topped back up if it falls too low).

**Disposal:** a pack at true end of life (persistently puffed, damaged, or no longer holding a usable charge) should be fully discharged before disposal — many hobby shops and some municipal hazardous-waste programs accept LiPo packs for proper recycling/disposal; check local rules rather than simply throwing a pack in household trash, since a damaged cell can still short and ignite in a garbage truck or landfill. A genuinely swollen or physically damaged pack should not be "one more cycle"-tested to use up its capacity before disposal — isolate and dispose of it as-is rather than experimenting with a compromised cell.

**Shipping LiPos** by mail or courier is regulated (LiPo/lithium batteries are classified as hazardous material for transport in most jurisdictions) — small antweight-size packs are usually well under the watt-hour thresholds that trigger the strictest hazmat shipping rules, but sellers and shippers still generally require packs to be shipped at a partial state of charge (often at or near storage voltage) and properly packaged (terminals covered/isolated, cushioned, sometimes in a dedicated LiPo-safe shipping bag) to limit short-circuit and fire risk in transit.

**Flying with LiPos (air travel to an event):** airlines and aviation regulators (in the US, TSA/FAA rules) generally require spare lithium batteries — which most competitors' antweight packs are, since they travel disconnected from the robot — to go in **carry-on baggage only, never checked luggage**, specifically because a battery fire in the cargo hold is far harder to detect and fight than one in the cabin. Batteries typically must have terminals protected from short-circuiting (tape over exposed connector pins, or individual plastic bags/battery cases) and are usually subject to a per-battery watt-hour limit for carry-on without special airline approval (commonly cited around 100 Wh per battery for unrestricted carry-on, with a smaller number of higher-capacity batteries allowed with airline permission above that) — small antweight packs are so far under this threshold (a few Wh each, see formula-pack-energy-wh) that the practical requirement for most antweight travelers is simply: pack them in carry-on, in a LiPo-safe bag, with terminals covered, and be ready to show them if asked at security.

chunks.title: Mounting the Battery in a 1 lb Bot: CG, Protection, and Why a Puncture Ends Your Day
chunks.body_md:
Battery placement in an antweight is a compromise between three goals that often pull in different directions: keeping the pack near the robot's center of gravity (CG) for predictable handling, keeping it away from the weapon and likely impact zones, and keeping it accessible enough to swap or inspect between matches.

**CG placement:** because the battery is one of the densest single components in a 1 lb robot, its position has an outsized effect on the bot's balance and how it drives, especially for wedge and lifter-style bots where weight distribution affects how well the wedge gets under an opponent. Most builders place the pack as close to the geometric/horizontal center of the chassis as the internal layout allows, and centered left-right, so it doesn't bias the bot's handling to one side or make it tip more easily toward one end.

**Protecting the pack from the weapon and impacts** is arguably more important than CG optimization, because a punctured or crushed pack is not a performance problem, it is a fire and match-ending safety problem (see the fire-risk chunk). The battery should be positioned as far as practically possible from the weapon's own moving parts and from the sides/faces of the robot most likely to take a direct hit (typically the front, where wedges and weapon strikes concentrate). Many antweight designs route the battery low and central, shielded on the vulnerable sides by the drivetrain, gearboxes, or a AR500/polycarbonate structural wall, effectively using the robot's own structure as an armor layer between the outside world and the pack.

**Mounting method — velcro vs. foam vs. a printed cradle:** hook-and-loop (velcro) strap or dual-lock tape is the simplest and most common method, letting a builder pull the pack for charging/inspection between matches without tools, but it provides essentially no cushioning against shock, so it's often paired with a thin foam pad underneath and around the pack to absorb vibration and blunt impact energy. A closed-cell foam wrap (sometimes called a "battery sock" in FPV/drone contexts, adapted for combat use) adds crush protection on top of vibration damping. A 3D-printed cradle sized precisely to the pack gives the most positive, repeatable location and the best resistance to the pack shifting under impact, at the cost of being sized for one specific pack footprint — swap to a different-size battery later and the cradle needs to be reprinted. Many competitive antweights combine methods: a printed or machined pocket that constrains the pack's position, with a layer of foam between the pack and the pocket walls, and a velcro or dual-lock strap holding it down against the pocket floor so it can't launch out under a hard hit.

**Why a punctured pack ends your day:** a pouch cell has no rigid outer casing, so a puncture directly exposes the layered foil/electrolyte structure to a short circuit and to air, either of which can trigger thermal runaway rapidly, sometimes within seconds. Unlike a mechanical failure elsewhere on the robot, there is no safe way to "finish the match" or even calmly walk the robot back to the pit once the battery bay has been breached — the correct response is to stop, isolate power, and get the pack to a safe, monitored, fireproof location immediately, which is why battery protection is treated as a safety requirement, not just a performance nice-to-have, in antweight design.

chunks.title: LiHV in Practice: Real Gain vs. Standard LiPo
chunks.body_md:
LiHV's pitch to antweight builders is straightforward: the same physical pack, the same weight, but charged to a higher per-cell ceiling (4.35V vs 4.20V) for more stored energy. Because energy scales with voltage, and LiHV runs at a higher voltage across essentially its entire discharge curve (not just at the very top), the real-world gain shows up both as slightly more total watt-hours and as *more usable voltage later in the discharge*, which is the part antweight builders actually feel: a weapon or drivetrain running on a partly-depleted LiHV pack sees a meaningfully higher voltage than the same drivetrain on an equally-depleted standard LiPo pack, translating to less RPM droop and less sag-driven brownout risk as the match goes on.

Using the two CNHL MiniStar 3S 450mAh packs as a direct real-world comparison: the standard-LiPo version is rated 11.1V nominal (3.7V/cell) while the LiHV version of the same 450mAh/70C/XT30 spec is rated 11.4V nominal (3.8V/cell). Computed with the pack-energy formula, that is roughly 5.0 Wh for the standard pack versus roughly 5.13 Wh for the LiHV pack at the same nominal-voltage basis — about a 2.7% nominal-energy gain — and the gap widens further when comparing full-charge voltage (12.6V standard vs 13.05V LiHV) and the practical "still has real voltage on the clock at match end" behavior LiHV is prized for, since 4.35V/cell packs simply start and stay higher throughout discharge than 4.20V/cell packs of otherwise identical construction.

**The tradeoffs are real but manageable:** an LiHV pack absolutely requires a charger or charge profile that supports the 4.35V/cell ceiling — charging it on a plain "LiPo" setting on an older or budget charger will stop at 4.20V/cell and simply waste the extra capacity the pack was built for, while attempting to push a *standard* LiPo cell to 4.35V/cell on an LiHV setting is a genuine overcharge and fire risk, so builders need to know which chemistry each of their packs actually is and label packs clearly if they run a mixed drawer of both. LiHV cells also generally show somewhat reduced cycle life compared to standard LiPo when both are cycled hard at similar C-rates, meaning an LiHV pack used aggressively across many matches may need replacing somewhat sooner — an acceptable trade for most antweight builders given how cheap small packs are and how much competitive value the extra voltage-under-load provides during a match.

For antweight builders deciding between an otherwise-identical standard and LiHV pack at similar price, the LiHV version is almost always the better choice given the modest but real gain and the low cost of chemistry-appropriate charging (most current chargers from ISDT, HOTA, and SkyRC already support LiHV profiles natively) — the main caveat is simply confirming the charger and charge profile match the chemistry before the first charge.

chunks.title: Connectors and Wiring for Antweight Battery Systems
chunks.body_md:
Connector choice on an antweight battery system is a direct current-handling decision, not just a matter of what the pack ships with. **JST-PH (2.0mm pitch)** connectors are standard on the smallest 1S-2S micro packs and are used essentially everywhere as the balance-lead connector regardless of pack size, but they are only rated for a few amps continuous — fine as a main-power connector on the very smallest, lowest-draw antweight builds, but a real bottleneck (and a source of resistive heating that worsens voltage sag) once combined drive+weapon draw climbs into double-digit amps. **XT30** is the common step-up connector, rated for roughly 15-30A depending on source and wire gauge, and is what most of the combat-market-specific and combat-crossover packs in the 300-550mAh antweight range (CNHL MiniStar, GNB LiHV 4S) ship with as standard. Larger XT60/XT90 connectors exist but are oversized and unnecessarily heavy for realistic antweight current levels; they belong in beetleweight and up.

Wire gauge matters as much as the connector: a pack's connector rating is only as good as the wire feeding it, and the thin factory leads on some micro packs (commonly 20-26AWG on the smallest packs) can become the actual current bottleneck and heat source even when the connector itself is rated higher. Builders running a demanding weapon setup sometimes re-terminate a pack's factory JST lead to XT30 and upgrade to a slightly heavier gauge wire in the same operation, both to raise the safe current ceiling and to reduce the resistive voltage drop (and associated heat) in the wiring itself — effectively reducing the system's total internal-resistance-like losses on top of whatever the cells themselves contribute, which directly helps with voltage sag under weapon spin-up.

A secondary but important wiring practice is keeping the battery's main power leads short and direct to the ESCs/power distribution point; every extra centimeter of thin wire between pack and load adds resistance and therefore adds to voltage drop under load, compounding the sag problem discussed elsewhere in this file. In a chassis as small as an antweight's, this is rarely a big factor in absolute terms, but it costs nothing to route the main power leads as short and direct as the layout allows rather than coiling excess length inside the electronics bay.

chunks.title: Worked Example: Sizing a Battery for a New Antweight Spinner
chunks.body_md:
Putting the formulas in this file together for a concrete antweight build: a 1 lb horizontal spinner with two small brushed drive motors and a 3S-rated brushless weapon motor around 2200KV.

**Step 1 — estimate current draw.** Drive: two brushed motors at roughly 2A typical each under normal driving = 4A combined, with stall spikes to perhaps 12-16A if both jam simultaneously (formula-power-budget-drive-weapon). Weapon: the 2200KV motor on 3S (11.1V nominal) draws roughly 6-9A once spun up and cutting normally, with brief spikes above 15A at spin-up or on a hard hit to an opponent. Combined typical draw: roughly 10-13A; combined worst-case brief spike: roughly 25-30A.

**Step 2 — set continuous and burst current targets.** Applying a 1.5-2x safety margin to the 10-13A typical figure gives a target continuous rating of roughly 20-25A; the worst-case spike figure of ~30A sets the burst target.

**Step 3 — pick a candidate pack and discount its C rating.** A CNHL MiniStar 3S 450mAh 70C pack claims (0.45Ah x 70) = 31.5A continuous on paper (formula-continuous-current-c-rating). Applying the realistic 40-60% discount for planning gives roughly 13-19A of *trustworthy* continuous capability — this falls a bit short of the 20-25A target computed in Step 2, suggesting either stepping up to a higher-rated pack (a genuine 100C-class pack from a reputable brand) or a larger-capacity pack at the same C rating (a 550mAh pack at 70C nominally claims 38.5A, discounting to roughly 15-23A) to close the gap with more margin.

**Step 4 — check runtime.** Using the 450mAh pack at 80% usable capacity (360mAh) against the ~10-13A typical combined draw: Runtime = (360/11500) x 60 ≈ 1.9 minutes at continuous full-typical-load — noticeably short of a 3-minute match if the bot ran flat-out the whole time, but real matches include lulls, positioning, and pauses that bring *average* draw well below the "flat-out typical" figure used here, which is exactly why this worked example, like the real product landscape, points toward sizing up: a 550mAh (or a pair of 450mAh packs to swap between preliminary rounds) gives meaningfully more margin on both the current-rating shortfall from Step 3 and the runtime tightness from Step 4, for a a few extra grams of pack weight — a trade almost every antweight builder makes deliberately rather than by accident.

**Step 5 — sanity-check voltage sag.** Even a healthy 3S pack with 0.03 ohm/cell (0.09 ohm total) hit with a 25A worst-case spike sags roughly 2.25V (formula-voltage-sag-estimate), from 11.1V down to about 8.85V for that instant — comfortably above most 3S-rated ESC/receiver brownout thresholds when the pack is fresh, but a real warning that an aged or previously-hit pack with double that internal resistance would sag to a genuinely risky ~6.6V under the same spike, reinforcing why pack age and impact history matter as much as the printed spec sheet.

chunks.title: Designing a 1 lb vertical spinner from scratch: a numeric walkthrough
chunks.body_md:
This walkthrough sizes a full metal-weapon vertical spinner for a 454 g (1 lb) antweight, using the formulas on this page end to end.

**1. Set targets.** Aim for a hard-hitting but achievable tip speed around 150 mph (67 m/s) and a spin-up time under ~1.5 s.

**2. Size the weapon.** Pick a compound weapon: a 60 g solid disc (radius 28 mm) plus a 10 g bolt-on steel tooth at 30 mm radius, tooth tip reaching out to 32 mm. Using `formula-moi-solid-disc` and `formula-parallel-axis-theorem`: I_disc = 0.5*0.060*0.028^2 = 2.35e-5 kg*m^2; tooth adds 0.010*0.030^2 = 9.0e-6 kg*m^2. **I_total = 3.25e-5 kg*m^2.**

**3. Pick the operating speed.** Target v_tip = 67 m/s at r_tip = 0.032 m gives omega = v/r = 2094 rad/s = 20,000 rpm (`formula-tip-speed` rearranged). Stored energy (`formula-rotational-ke`): KE = 0.5 * 3.25e-5 * 2094.4^2 = **71.3 J** -- a genuinely hard-hitting 1 lb spinner.

**4. Pick the motor.** A small brushless weapon motor at Kv = 2750 rpm/V on 3S (11.1 V) gives no-load rpm = 30,525 (`formula-no-load-rpm`), comfortably above the 20,000 rpm target so the motor isn't being asked to run at its very top end. Using the exact Kt relation (`formula-kt-from-kv`): Kt = 9.5493/2750 = 0.003472 N*m/A. With a 30 A stall current: T_stall = 0.1042 N*m.

**5. Check spin-up time.** Average torque across the 0-20,000 rpm range works out to about 0.0701 N*m (`formula-spin-up-time`), giving t_spinup = I*omega/T_avg = 3.25e-5*2094.4/0.0701 = **0.97 s** -- meets the under-1.5s target.

**6. Check the gyro-dance risk.** At full weapon speed, the tipping-moment threshold for a 90 mm track / 454 g chassis is 0.2004 N*m (`formula-tipping-moment-threshold`), and the max safe in-place turn rate before the precession torque exceeds that is about 2.94 rad/s (~169 deg/s) (`formula-max-safe-turn-rate-gyro`) -- driving software/driver technique should respect that limit, or turn in wider arcs.

**7. Weight budget.** Weapon system (motor+disc+ESC) 30% = 136 g; drive 20% = 91 g; armor/frame 30% = 136 g; electronics 12% = 55 g; fasteners 8% = 36 g (`formula-weight-budget-allocation`), summing to 454 g.

**8. Battery check.** A 300 mAh 2S/3S 60C pack gives 18-60A continuous depending on cell count/rating (`formula-battery-c-rating-to-amps`) -- plenty above the weapon's ~10 A cruise current and enough headroom for the 30 A stall.

**Final spec:** 3.25e-5 kg*m^2 compound disc weapon, 20,000 rpm / 67 m/s tip speed, 71.3 J stored, ~1.0 s spin-up, 2750 Kv / 30 A-stall brushless weapon motor on 3S, 60A-rated weapon ESC, 90 mm track width chassis for gyro stability, within a 454 g total budget.

chunks.title: Designing a 1 lb plastic-antweight vertical spinner: a numeric walkthrough
chunks.body_md:
Plastic-antweight rulesets generally restrict most structural/weapon material to non-metal (motors, fasteners, bearings, and small hardened inserts are usually still allowed in metal, but frame, armor and the bulk of the weapon typically must be plastic). This changes the weight-math story significantly compared to the metal-weapon walkthrough above.

**1. Weapon in plastic.** A nylon disc (density ~1.15 g/cm^3) at the same 30 mm radius / 6 mm thick geometry as a metal example has volume = pi*r^2*t = pi*0.030^2*0.006 = 1.70e-5 m^3 = 16.96 cm^3, giving mass = 16.96*1.15 = **19.5 g** -- versus 133 g if the identical shape were cut from steel (16.96*7.85). Using `formula-moi-solid-disc`: I = 0.5*0.0195*0.030^2 = **8.775e-6 kg*m^2**, roughly a quarter of the metal build's compound-weapon MOI.

**2. Pick a realistic plastic-weapon tip speed.** Plastic teeth/edges are far more failure-prone at high tip speed than hardened steel, so plastic-class spinners are usually run slower: target ~80 ft/s (24.4 m/s) rather than 150+ mph. omega = v/r = 24.4/0.030 = 813 rad/s = **7,767 rpm**.

**3. Stored energy.** KE = 0.5*8.775e-6*813.3^2 = 0.5*8.775e-6*661,457 = **2.9 J** -- an order of magnitude below the metal build's 71 J. This is normal and expected: plastic-antweight spinners are built for board-clearing and harassment rather than devastating single hits; wedges and control tactics carry more relative weight in this class.

**4. Drivetrain is unaffected by the material rule** (motors, wheels, gearboxes are usually still metal/off-the-shelf), so the same drivetrain numbers as the metal build apply: 11,000 rpm base motor, 20:1 gearbox, 32 mm wheel -> 0.92 m/s top speed (`formula-top-speed-drivetrain`).

**5. Weight budget shifts toward armor/frame.** Because plastic structure needs much greater thickness for the same stiffness (see `formula-sheet-weight-per-area`: a 6mm HDPE panel weighs 57 g vs 81 g for a thinner 3mm aluminum panel of the same area, but the HDPE panel needed 2x the thickness just to compete structurally), a realistic plastic-ant budget is: weapon 15% = 68 g; drive 20% = 91 g; armor/frame 40% = 182 g; electronics 15% = 68 g; fasteners 10% = 45 g -- notice armor/frame roughly doubles its percentage share versus the metal build's 30%.

**Final spec:** ~20 g nylon disc weapon, ~7,800 rpm / 24.4 m/s tip speed, ~2.9 J stored, same drivetrain as a metal build, but with 40% of weight (182 g) committed to armor/frame instead of 30%.

chunks.title: Sanity-check numbers every antweight should hit
chunks.body_md:
A quick set of realistic target ranges to check any new 1 lb design against, before committing to parts.

| Metric | Typical metal-weapon spinner | Typical plastic-antweight | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Weapon tip speed | 100-200+ ft/s (30-60+ m/s) | 60-100 ft/s (18-30 m/s) | Higher isn't always better once structural survival is the limit |
| Stored weapon KE | 20-80 J (some builds 100 J+) | 2-10 J | Use `formula-rotational-ke`; energy scales with the SQUARE of speed, so doubling rpm quadruples KE |
| Drivetrain top speed | 0.6-1.5 m/s (2-5 ft/s) | 0.6-1.5 m/s | Faster control bots can push 2+ m/s but trade off pushing torque and precision |
| Weapon spin-up time | 0.5-3 s (direct/lightly-geared) | 0.5-2 s | Large slow high-inertia drums can run 5-10 s+, a real tactical liability |
| Run time on a 300 mAh pack | ~2-6 minutes depending on average current draw | ~3-8 minutes (lower average current) | A typical fight runs 2-3 minutes, so margin matters more than max theoretical runtime |
| Weight budget: weapon system | 25-40% of total weight | 10-20% of total weight | Metal weapons carry proportionally more weight for their energy payoff |
| Weight budget: armor/frame | 20-30% | 35-45% | Plastic structure needs more mass for equivalent stiffness |

**Worked run-time sanity check:** a 300 mAh (0.3 Ah) pack under an average combined draw of 8 A (mixing idle weapon-maintain current with occasional drive current) gives runtime = Capacity_Ah / I_avg = 0.3/8 = 0.0375 h = **2.25 minutes** -- right in the expected range for a spinner-class build, underscoring why battery capacity vs average current draw needs an explicit check rather than an assumption.

Use these ranges as a first filter: if your design's tip speed, KE, or spin-up time falls far outside these bands, re-check your MOI, Kt/Kv, and gear-ratio math before assuming the design itself is simply "better" or "worse" than the norm.

chunks.title: The five most common numeric mistakes in antweight design
chunks.body_md:
**1. Confusing the exact Kt = 9.5493/Kv with the hobby shorthand Kt = 8.27/Kv.** The hobby shorthand already assumes ~87% efficiency baked in (8.27/9.5493 = 0.866). Using the exact form and THEN separately derating for efficiency is correct; using the hobby shorthand and derating AGAIN double-counts losses and can understate real available torque by ~25% or more, leading to over-gearing or oversized motors that were never actually needed. See `formula-kt-from-kv`.

**2. Assuming all available motor torque converts into acceleration or pushing force.** For a 454 g robot, wheel-to-floor traction is almost always the real limit, not motor torque. In the worked drivetrain example on this page, the drivetrain could theoretically deliver 20.0 N of driving force, but the traction limit (`formula-traction-limited-force`) was only 3.56 N -- meaning the wheels would spin long before the motor ran out of torque. Builders who chase higher-torque motors or lower gear ratios to "push harder" without also improving wheel grip are solving the wrong problem.

**3. Treating total stored kinetic energy as the energy delivered in one hit.** A weapon rarely gives up all its stored KE in a single strike; it slows down by only however much the impact actually resisted it, keeping the rest of its spin for the next hit. In the worked example, only about 19.8 J of a 71.3 J stored total was delivered in one hit (`formula-energy-per-hit-vs-stored`) -- using the full stored KE number to size structure or predict single-hit damage overstates the real per-hit force.

**4. Ignoring gyroscopic precession torque when picking turn rate for a vertical spinner.** Precession torque scales directly with weapon MOI, weapon speed, AND commanded turn rate (`formula-gyroscopic-precession-torque`); a chassis that seems perfectly stable standing still or driving straight can start to rock or tip the instant the driver spins it in place at full weapon speed. The worked example shows a case where the precession torque (0.204 N*m) barely exceeds the chassis's own tipping threshold (0.200 N*m) -- a small change in turn rate is the difference between stable and "gyro dance."

**5. Sizing the ESC and motor from no-load rpm and stall current alone, without checking spin-up time or battery voltage sag under load.** A motor's real available torque at the actual operating point is much lower than its stall torque, and battery voltage sags under load (`formula-voltage-sag`) right when full stall current is being demanded (weapon impacts, drivetrain stalls). Skipping this check leads to slower-than-expected spin-up, ESC brownouts under load, and weapon motors that seem "weaker than the spec sheet" mid-fight -- when the real cause is under-provisioned battery C-rating or ESC current headroom (`formula-esc-current-headroom`).

chunks.title: Moment of inertia shapes and building a compound weapon's total MOI
chunks.body_md:
Moment of inertia (MOI, symbol I, units kg*m^2) is the rotational equivalent of mass: it measures how hard it is to angularly accelerate a spinning object, and it depends heavily on how far the mass sits from the spin axis (radius SQUARED, not just radius). Nearly every weapon-sizing calculation on this page starts from getting I right.

**Standard shapes** (see the individual formula entities for each): a solid disc/cylinder about its own axis (I = 0.5*m*r^2), an annulus/washer with a bore (I = 0.5*m*(r_outer^2+r_inner^2)), a thin ring or thin-walled cylinder where all mass sits at one radius (I = m*r^2), a slender rod about its own center as in a horizontal bar spinner (I = (1/12)*m*L^2), the same rod about one end as in a hammer or axe arm (I = (1/3)*m*L^2), and a small point mass at a radius as in a counterweight or bolt-on tooth (I = m*r^2).

**Real weapons are almost never a single pure shape.** A typical single-tooth vertical-spinner disc is really a solid disc PLUS a bolted-on hardened tooth sticking out further than the disc's own radius. The **parallel axis theorem** is what lets you combine these correctly: each part's own moment of inertia about its own center of mass, plus that part's mass times the square of its distance from the ACTUAL rotation axis, summed over every part.

**Worked compound example:** a 60 g solid disc (radius 28 mm, I_disc = 0.5*0.060*0.028^2 = 2.35e-5 kg*m^2, already centered on the rotation axis) plus a 10 g bolt-on tooth, small enough that its own MOI about its own center is negligible, mounted 30 mm from center: tooth contribution = 0 + 0.010*0.030^2 = 9.0e-6 kg*m^2. **I_total = 2.35e-5 + 9.0e-6 = 3.25e-5 kg*m^2.**

A useful intuition check: since I scales with r^2, a tooth mounted twice as far out contributes four times as much MOI for the same mass -- which is exactly why single, far-flung teeth are so effective at maximizing stored energy per gram of added weapon mass, at the cost of needing a longer spin-up time for that same reason (more MOI per gram means more torque-seconds needed to reach the same rpm).

chunks.title: Kt from Kv: the exact relation vs the hobby shorthand, and why the difference matters
chunks.body_md:
Every brushed or brushless DC motor has two closely related constants: Kv (rpm produced per volt of back-EMF, at no load) and Kt (torque produced per amp of current). They describe the SAME underlying physical motor constant, just in different units, and are related by a fixed physical law -- but the combat-robotics hobby commonly uses a shortcut formula that is NOT the same thing.

**The exact, physically derived relation** is: **Kt [N*m/A] = 60 / (2*pi*Kv[rpm/V]) = 9.5493 / Kv**. This comes directly from the definitions of Kv and Kt in consistent SI units and holds for an ideal motor regardless of size, winding, or efficiency.

**The hobby shorthand** commonly seen in RC and combat robotics circles is **Kt = 8.27 / Kv**. This is NOT a different physical law -- it is the exact relation with an assumed real-world mechanical/electrical efficiency of roughly 87% already multiplied in (8.27/9.5493 = 0.866). It's a convenient "expected real output torque" estimate for a typical small hobby motor, but it silently bundles in a loss assumption that may not match your actual motor.

**Why this matters:** if you use the exact 9.5493/Kv form to compute Kt, then SEPARATELY apply your own efficiency estimate downstream (e.g. in `formula-motor-efficiency-estimate`), your math is internally consistent. But if you use the hobby's 8.27/Kv shorthand AND THEN also apply a separate efficiency derating on top of it, you are double-counting losses -- understating real available torque by roughly 13-25%+ depending on the second derating applied. This directly skews spin-up time predictions (`formula-spin-up-time`) and stall-torque estimates (`formula-stall-torque`) toward being overly pessimistic (or, if done backwards, overly optimistic).

**Worked comparison** for a Kv = 2750 rpm/V motor: Kt_exact = 9.5493/2750 = 0.003472 N*m/A. Kt_hobby = 8.27/2750 = 0.003007 N*m/A -- 86.6% of the exact value. Every other worked example on this page uses the exact 9.5493/Kv form for Kt, and applies efficiency as a separate, explicit factor where relevant, so the two effects can always be told apart.

chunks.title: Gyroscopic effects on a spinner-weapon chassis, and predicting 'gyro dance'
chunks.body_md:
A spinning weapon carries angular momentum along its own spin axis. When the chassis carrying that weapon is itself rotated (yawed) by the drivetrain -- turning in place, or even just cornering hard -- that angular momentum reacts via gyroscopic precession, producing a torque about a THIRD axis, perpendicular to both the weapon spin axis and the turn axis. In a vertical spinner (weapon axis roughly horizontal, side to side), turning the chassis produces a precession torque that tries to pitch the front or back of the robot up -- the visible "gyro dance" or "gyro wobble" many builders describe.

**The core relation** is `formula-gyroscopic-precession-torque`: tau_precession = I * omega_weapon * omega_turn. Precession torque scales directly (linearly) with all three of weapon inertia, weapon speed, AND how fast the driver yaws the chassis -- meaning a robot that feels perfectly planted driving straight, or even turning gently, can suddenly start rocking the instant the driver spins hard in place at full weapon RPM.

**Comparing against the chassis's own resistance to tipping** (`formula-tipping-moment-threshold`, M_tip = W * track_width/2) tells you whether a given turn rate is actually going to destabilize the robot. In the worked example (I = 3.25e-5 kg*m^2, weapon at 20,000 rpm, 454 g chassis with a 90 mm track), a fairly modest 3 rad/s (~0.5 rev/s) in-place turn rate produces 0.204 N*m of precession torque against a 0.200 N*m tipping threshold -- meaning this specific robot is right at its tipping edge at that turn rate and weapon speed.

**Predicting the safe limit directly** (`formula-max-safe-turn-rate-gyro`): rearranging for the maximum safe turn rate gives omega_turn_max = M_tip/(I*omega_weapon) = 2.94 rad/s (~169 deg/s) for this example -- a concrete number a driver or an autonomous turn-rate limiter can be tuned against.

**Practical mitigations** informed by these formulas: widen the track/wheelbase (raises M_tip), lower the CG (raises the tipping angle per `formula-cg-tipping-angle`, giving more margin at the same M_tip), reduce weapon MOI or top speed if turning agility matters more than raw hitting power, or simply train the driver to turn in wide arcs rather than spinning in place whenever the weapon is at speed.

chunks.title: Drivetrain sizing: why traction, not torque, usually sets the limit for a 1 lb bot
chunks.body_md:
Drivetrain sizing for an antweight starts with `formula-top-speed-drivetrain`: v_top = (rpm_motor/gear_ratio/60) * pi * D_wheel. A base motor at 11,000 rpm through a 20:1 gearbox and a 32 mm wheel gives an output shaft speed of 550 rpm and a top speed of 0.92 m/s -- solidly in the typical antweight range of 0.6-1.5 m/s.

**The trap most new builders fall into is stopping there and assuming more gear reduction (or a beefier motor) automatically means more real-world pushing power.** `formula-acceleration-from-torque` shows the drivetrain COULD deliver a driving force of 20.0 N from a small motor (10 mN*m stall torque) through a 20:1 gearbox at 80% efficiency -- but `formula-traction-limited-force` shows the wheels can only actually transmit about 3.56 N to the floor before slipping, using a realistic mu = 0.8 and the robot's own 4.453 N weight. Since 20.0 N (available) far exceeds 3.56 N (transmittable), this drivetrain is firmly **traction-limited**, not torque-limited (`formula-wheel-slip-threshold`) -- real achievable acceleration is 3.56/0.454 = 7.85 m/s^2, set entirely by wheel grip and robot weight, with huge spare motor torque doing nothing useful.

**This has a direct, practical design consequence:** for a 454 g robot, spending weight or money on a lower gear ratio or a higher-torque motor rarely improves pushing power once you're already past the point where torque exceeds what the wheels can grip -- which happens at a surprisingly low torque for such a light robot. Better wheel material (higher mu), more weight over the drive wheels, or a wider contact patch improve pushing power far more reliably than more gear reduction.

**Climbing an opponent's wedge** (`formula-torque-to-climb-wedge`) requires checking BOTH conditions separately: the torque needed at the wheel to overcome gravity up the slope (usually easily available), and the traction needed to actually grip the (possibly slippery, now-tilted) wedge surface, which caps out entirely at theta_max = atan(mu) regardless of how much torque is on tap -- at mu = 0.8, that's about 38.7 degrees, a hard physical ceiling no amount of extra motor torque can push past.

**Power draw stays modest at cruise and only climbs near the traction limit** (`formula-power-at-speed`): P = F*v gives just 0.205 W cruising against rolling resistance, versus 3.28 W pushing at the full traction-limited force while still moving at top speed -- useful bounds when sizing drive ESCs and battery current budget.

chunks.title: Battery and ESC sizing: C-rating, voltage sag, and current headroom
chunks.body_md:
Sizing the electrical system starts from the battery. `formula-battery-c-rating-to-amps` converts a pack's label rating into a real continuous-current number: a common 300 mAh (0.3 Ah) 2S pack rated 60C gives I_continuous = 60*0.3 = 18 A. `formula-battery-wh-capacity` gives its total stored energy on an equal footing across cell counts: Wh = V*Ah = 7.4*0.3 = 2.22 Wh for that same 2S pack.

**Voltage sag is the detail most commonly skipped.** `formula-voltage-sag`: V_loaded = V_nominal - I_draw*R_internal. With a typical small high-C pack's R_internal = 0.020 ohm, drawing a modest 10 A sags the 7.4 V pack to 7.20 V, and drawing the full rated 18 A sags it to 7.04 V -- a ~5% voltage drop exactly when the weapon or drivetrain needs full torque most (during a stall or hard impact). Since motor torque and power both scale with applied voltage, ignoring sag means overestimating real available torque right when it matters.

**ESC sizing should headroom well above stall current, not cruise current** (`formula-esc-current-headroom`): a weapon motor with a 30 A stall current should sit behind an ESC rated at least 1.5-2x that (52.5-60 A), since weapon motors stall briefly on every real hit -- an ESC sized only to the motor's typical cruise draw will brown out or cook itself the first time the weapon connects solidly.

**Efficiency is not a fixed number** (`formula-motor-efficiency-estimate`): eta = P_out/P_in = (T*omega)/(V*I) varies across the motor's speed range. In the worked weapon-motor example, efficiency at the 20,000 rpm operating point came out to 65.5% -- useful for estimating how much of the battery's Wh capacity actually turns into weapon KE and run time, rather than assuming a fixed number pulled from a datasheet's single peak-efficiency point.

**Putting it together for run time:** with an average combined current draw of 8 A (mixing idle weapon-maintain current with occasional drive current) and the 0.3 Ah pack above, runtime = Capacity_Ah/I_avg = 0.3/8 = 0.0375 h = 2.25 minutes -- worth checking explicitly against the typical 2-3 minute fight length, since it's easy to assume a battery's mAh number is "plenty" without doing this division.

chunks.title: Structural math for impact survival: force, stress, bending, and why compliance helps
chunks.body_md:
Impact survival math starts from the impulse-momentum relation, `formula-impact-force-momentum-time`: F_avg = delta_p/delta_t = m_eff*delta_v/delta_t. A weapon's effective mass (0.03174 kg, from `formula-effective-mass-at-tooth`) losing 10 m/s of tip speed over a brief 1.5 ms contact produces an average force around 212 N -- a genuinely large force from a genuinely small, light part, entirely because the contact time is so short.

**That force then has to be checked against real materials and geometry.** `formula-stress-force-area` (sigma = F/A) shows the same 212 N spread over a small 25 mm^2 contact patch produces about 8.5 MPa of stress -- fine against aluminum's ~276 MPa yield strength, but potentially enough to locally dent a softer plastic panel at that same tiny contact area. For an actual armor panel bolted at two edges, `formula-beam-bending-armor-panel` models it as a simply-supported beam under a midspan point load: a 3mm-thick, 50mm-wide aluminum panel spanning 40mm between mounts under that same 212 N hit sees about 28.2 MPa peak bending stress -- roughly a 9.8x safety margin against yield, comfortably surviving the hit.

**Why compliance (a little "give") helps** (`formula-compliance-reduces-peak-force`): for the SAME momentum change, doubling the contact/stopping time exactly halves the peak force (F = delta_p/delta_t). A rigid mount stopping the same impact in 1.5 ms sees 212 N; a compliant standoff or slightly flexible frame stretching that to 3.0 ms sees only about 106 N -- half the peak force, for physically the same hit. This is why armor and weapon mounts that allow a small amount of flex often outlast perfectly rigid ones: they're not absorbing less energy, they're absorbing the SAME energy over more time, which is what peak force (and therefore cracking/yielding) actually cares about.

**Fasteners get checked the same way** (`formula-bolt-shear-estimate`): two M3 bolts sharing that 212 N reaction force see about 15.0 MPa of shear stress each, versus a typical alloy-steel bolt's 350-500 MPa shear strength -- over 20x margin on a single hit, though real mounts should still account for fatigue from repeated hits across a fight, not just a single worst-case load.

chunks.title: Weight budgeting and center-of-gravity math for a 1 lb chassis
chunks.body_md:
Every antweight design starts with splitting the 454 g total weight limit into subsystem budgets (`formula-weight-budget-allocation`): weight_component = total_weight * pct/100. A metal-weapon vertical spinner typically runs weapon 30% / drive 20% / armor 30% / electronics 12% / fasteners 8%, while a plastic-antweight build shifts hard toward armor/frame (weapon 15% / drive 20% / armor 40% / electronics 15% / fasteners 10%) because non-metal structure needs more mass for the same stiffness.

**Center of gravity (CG) height, relative to track width or wheelbase, sets tipping resistance** (`formula-cg-tipping-angle`): theta_tip = atan((track_or_wheelbase/2)/h_cg). A low, wide chassis (90mm track, 25mm CG height) resists tipping to nearly 61 degrees of tilt; a tall, narrow one (60mm track, 40mm CG height) tips at just under 37 degrees -- a huge practical difference in how easily a side hit, a hard turn, or an opponent's wedge can flip the robot over. This same math underlies both wedge defense (a low-CG robot is harder to flip up and over a wedge) and the gyro-dance tipping-moment check elsewhere on this page (a wider/lower robot has a higher tipping-moment threshold for the same reason).

**Self-righting shapes** (`formula-self-righting-shell-condition`) use a simplified rule of thumb for domed/shell designs: keeping the CG height below the shell's own radius (h_cg < R_shell) tends to make gravity roll the robot back onto its wheels if flipped, rather than leaving it resting stably upside-down. This is a rough qualitative check, not a rigorous stability proof -- real self-righting also depends on shell uniformity, weapon drag during the roll, and floor friction.

**Sheet/panel weight** (`formula-sheet-weight-per-area`, weight = area*thickness*density) is the workhorse calculation for checking any armor or frame stock choice against the weight budget before cutting it: a 100 cm^2 panel in 6mm HDPE (density 0.95 g/cm^3) weighs 57 g, while the same area in 3mm aluminum (density 2.70 g/cm^3) weighs 81 g despite being half the thickness -- illustrating why plastic needs roughly double the thickness to be structurally competitive, but can still sometimes land at a comparable or lower weight once thickness is matched to the actual stiffness requirement rather than compared at equal thickness.

chunks.title: Bite depth and tooth count: the hit-frequency trade-off
chunks.body_md:
"Bite" refers to how deep a spinning weapon's tooth digs into an opponent's material before the next tooth strike arrives -- and it depends on three things: how fast the two robots are closing together, how fast the weapon spins, and how many teeth it has.

**The core relation** (`formula-bite-depth`): hit frequency f_hit = (rpm/60)*tooth_count, and bite_depth = v_closing/f_hit. At 20,000 rpm with a single tooth and a 1.5 m/s closing speed, f_hit = 333.3 hits/s and bite_depth = 1.5/333.3 = 4.5 mm engaged per hit.

**Adding a second tooth at the same RPM doubles the hit frequency and HALVES the bite depth** (`formula-hit-frequency`): the same weapon with 2 teeth at the same 20,000 rpm gives f_hit = 666.7 hits/s and bite_depth = 1.5/666.7 = 2.25 mm -- half the per-hit penetration, for twice the hit rate.

**This is the physical reason single-tooth designs dominate hard-hitting vertical spinners:** for a given weapon RPM and closing speed, fewer teeth means a longer gap between successive strikes, which means more material gets engaged (and more damage delivered) per individual hit -- at the cost of a lower overall hit rate and, if the tooth is mounted further out to add MOI, a longer spin-up time (see `formula-parallel-axis-theorem`). Multi-tooth designs trade this away for a higher, steadier hit rate and (often) a smoother-spinning, easier-to-balance weapon, which suits control-oriented or lower-power builds where sheer per-hit penetration matters less than reliable, frequent contact.

**Practical use:** given an opponent's known or estimated armor thickness, this formula can be run in reverse to check whether a given tooth-count/RPM combination will actually penetrate on a single pass, or whether the design needs either a slower/single-tooth weapon for deeper bite, or simply relies on cumulative multi-hit damage instead.

chunks.title: The 1 lb Antweight Drive Motor Landscape
chunks.body_md:
Antweight combat robots (1 lb / 454 g total weight) have a narrow but well-developed set of drive motor choices, almost all built around small brushed or brushless motors in the 12-16mm size range. The dominant, most trusted choice remains **FingerTech's Silver Spark**: a Mabuchi FK-050 brushed motor behind an all-metal 16mm spur gearbox, sold in nine stock ratios from a fast 11.1:1 to a crawling 600:1, all at the same ~29g weight and ~$19 price. Its budget sibling, the **Gold Spark**, uses the same base motor but a plastic final gear stage, trading some durability for a lower price (~$14.79) — fine for lighter-duty plastic antweights, riskier as the sole drive on a bot expected to take direct hits.

A newer and increasingly popular tier is **Repeat Robotics'** lineup: brushed and brushless planetary gearmotors that swap the Spark line's simple spur gearbox for a multi-stage all-metal planetary gearbox, which is generally more shock-tolerant and torque-dense for its size. Repeat's brushless "Mini" 1106 gearmotor (evolved through Mk3, Mk4, and Mk4.1 revisions) packages a custom-wound outrunner brushless motor directly into a 28.5:1 planetary gearbox with a hardened 4mm shaft, letting builders trade a simple brushed H-bridge for a reversing brushless ESC in exchange for higher efficiency and higher top speed at the same weight.

At the budget end of the market sit the generic **N-series gearmotors** (N10/N20/N30, 10-30mm motor cans) sold by dozens of overlapping AliExpress/Amazon/Banggood listings, often for a few dollars each in a huge range of ratios (30:1 up to 1000:1). These are the cheapest way to get a drive motor and are extremely popular in plastic antweights, but they carry a well-known "quality lottery" risk: two motors from the same listing, or even the same order, can have different windings, different gear materials (mixed metal/plastic despite "metal gear" branding), and different failure rates. **Pololu's micro metal gearmotors** (HP/MP/LP power tunes, many ratio options) sit between these tiers: a precision-manufactured 10x12mm metal gearbox with well-documented, consistent specs, at a price above generic N-series but usually below FingerTech/Repeat.

Finally, **modified or stock continuous-rotation 9g servos** offer the simplest possible drive for plastic antweights: no ESC required, direct receiver connection, at the cost of speed and torque. Choosing among these options is mostly a question of budget, desired reliability, and how much of the 454g weight budget is left after the weapon, battery, and armor.

chunks.title: FingerTech Silver Spark and Gold Spark: The Ratio Ladder Explained
chunks.body_md:
Both FingerTech Spark motors share the exact same base motor: a Mabuchi FK-050 brushed can rated for roughly 11,530 RPM no-load and 1.3A stall current at the 7.4V (2S LiPo) voltage most antweights run on, though FingerTech states it will run anywhere from 3V to 18.5V. What differs between Silver and Gold Spark — and between the ratios within each line — is entirely in the gearbox.

**Silver Spark** uses an all-metal spur gearhead across nine stock ratios: 11.1, 22.2, 33.3, 50, 83.3 (discontinued), 100, 200, 300, and 600:1. Weight climbs gently with ratio (28g at 11:1 up to 32g at 600:1) because the gearbox needs progressively more/larger gear stages to reach the higher reductions, but the motor and price stay constant across the whole family. The output shaft is a 3mm-diameter flatted shaft, standard length 38mm, with a shorter 22mm option on the 22:1/33:1/50:1 ratios for tighter builds — long enough that a wheel can be mounted directly onto it (a live-axle setup) without an intermediate shaft or bearing block, though FingerTech does offer an optional bearing block for extra support on the far side of the wheel.

**Gold Spark** uses the identical base motor but a gearbox with a plastic final gear stage, across a slightly different eight-ratio ladder: 20, 35, 50, 86, 115, 150, 250, and 360:1, all at a constant 28g and roughly 25% lower price than Silver Spark. FingerTech explicitly documents a mechanical ceiling on Gold Spark: output torque above 6.84 kg-cm (95 oz-in) will damage the plastic output gear stage, which caps how much of the higher-ratio end of the ladder (250:1, 360:1) can actually be exploited before self-destructing under stall.

Because no-load RPM and stall current are properties of the shared base motor, output RPM at any given ratio is simply 11,530 divided by that ratio, and output stall torque is (very roughly) the bare-motor stall torque (~0.046 kg-cm) multiplied by the ratio and by gearbox efficiency (~0.75 for Silver Spark's metal spur stages, somewhat lower for Gold Spark's plastic stage). This lets a builder pick a ratio directly from a target speed or torque without needing FingerTech's full published table for every combination. In practice, 22.2:1 through 50:1 covers most competitive antweight main-drive builds — fast enough to dodge and reposition, with enough torque margin over the traction limit to push confidently — while 100:1 and above are reserved for weapon lifters, self-righters, or bots that specifically prioritize crawling torque over speed.

chunks.title: Repeat Robotics: Brushed and Brushless Planetary Drive for Antweights
chunks.body_md:
Repeat Robotics built its antweight product line around one core idea: replace the simple spur gearbox found in motors like FingerTech's Spark line with a multi-stage, all-metal **planetary** gearbox, which generally handles shock loading and delivers torque more efficiently than a spur train of the same size. Their catalog spans both brushed and brushless motor options in the same 16mm-class form factor antweight builders are used to.

On the brushed side, the **Mini Brushed Mk2** (sold as the "Mini Pro Brushed" for around $25) offers a straightforward drop-in alternative to a Silver Spark, with the planetary gearbox as its main differentiator, at a modest price premium over FingerTech's spur-geared option.

On the brushless side, Repeat pioneered selling off-the-shelf 16mm brushless gearmotors specifically for combat robots — before this, brushless drive meant a builder sourcing a bare FPV-style outrunner motor and building or 3D-printing a custom gearbox around it. The **Mini Brushless** line went through several revisions: early Mk3/Mk4 versions used a custom-wound ~3500kv 1104-size motor; the current **Mk4.1** upgrades to a larger-stator 1106-size motor for more torque and power capability in the same envelope, paired with a 28.5:1 two-stage all-metal planetary gearbox and a hardened 4mm output shaft, weighing about 24g complete. Because it's brushless, it needs a reversing brushless ESC rather than a simple brushed H-bridge — Repeat sells a matching ESC designed specifically for their motors — but in exchange gets higher efficiency, no brush wear, and a rated 2S-4S voltage range that lets a builder retune top speed just by changing battery cell count rather than swapping hardware. A higher-spec "Mini Pro 1106" variant is also sold at roughly double the price for builders wanting the premium tier.

Repeat's catalog also includes larger motors like the Compact Brushless 1806 (marketed as the lightest brushless beetleweight drive motor on the market), useful context for how this same drive-pod architecture scales up a weight class, though it's oversized for a standard 1 lb budget. The general trade-off across Repeat's line versus FingerTech's Spark motors is: more durability and (for brushless) more speed/efficiency, at a real cost premium and, for brushless specifically, added ESC complexity and the sensorless-cogging caveats that come with any FPV-derived brushless motor run at very low speed.

chunks.title: N10/N20/N30 Gearmotors and the Quality-Lottery Problem
chunks.body_md:
The N-series family — N10 (smallest, ~10mm), N20 (most common, 12mm), and N30 (largest, ~30mm) micro gearmotors — is the budget backbone of plastic antweight and hobby-grade drivetrains. These motors are sold by dozens of overlapping resellers on AliExpress, Amazon, and similar marketplaces, almost always originating from the same small set of OEM factories, in an enormous range of stock gear ratios: 20:1, 30:1, 50:1, 75:1, 100:1, 150:1, 210:1, 250:1, 298:1, 380:1, and 1000:1 are all commonly available, alongside 3V/6V/12V motor voltage options.

The base N20 motor (before gearing) runs at roughly 15,000 RPM no-load at 6V — this is corroborated by real product listings, e.g. a 298:1 N20 gearmotor advertised and sold specifically as running 50 RPM at 6V (15,000 / 298 ≈ 50, a clean match). Gearbox length is constant across most ratios (~9mm) except 1000:1 (and sometimes 380:1), which get a 3.5mm-longer, reinforced housing rated for roughly 25 kg·mm (2.5 kg-cm) of continuous output torque versus ~20 kg·mm (2.0 kg-cm) for the standard ratios — a purely mechanical strength limit on the gear teeth, independent of how much torque the motor could theoretically produce electrically at that ratio.

The real problem with this whole family isn't the published spec sheet — it's that the spec sheet often doesn't reflect what actually arrives. Listings frequently advertise "metal gear" motors that turn out to have only some gear stages in metal and the rest in plastic, and even within a single order, individual units can vary in winding quality, no-load speed, stall current, and outright dead-on-arrival rate. This inconsistency is widely known in the antweight community as the "quality lottery." It doesn't make N-series motors unusable — plenty of successful plastic antweights run on them — but it does change how a builder should treat them: buy spares from the start and treat them as a semi-consumable part, bench-test every single unit before final installation (measuring free-run current and no-load RPM and rejecting any outlier compared to its batch-mates), and avoid depending on an untested cheap motor as the sole drive for an important match. Builders who want to skip this risk entirely pay the premium for FingerTech, Repeat Robotics, or Pololu motors instead, all of which publish (and generally meet) a consistent, verifiable spec.

chunks.title: Pololu Micro Metal Gearmotors: HP, MP, LP and Extended-Shaft Variants
chunks.body_md:
Pololu's micro metal gearmotor line sits in a useful middle ground between the quality-lottery risk of generic N-series motors and the higher price of FingerTech/Repeat combat-specific products: a precision-manufactured, well-documented 10x12mm all-metal gearbox on a 3mm D-shaped output shaft (9mm long), sold in a wide range of gear ratios and, distinctively, in three separate power tunes of the same base motor.

The three tunes — **LP** (Low Power), **MP** (Medium Power), and **HP** (High Power) — use the same physical gearbox and shaft but different motor winding/brush choices, trading current draw for speed and torque at any given ratio. At 6V, LP draws a stall current of about 0.36A (free-run ~40mA), MP about 0.67A (free-run ~70mA), and HP about 1.6A (free-run ~100mA). All three use shorter-life precious-metal brushes at 6V, which are lower-friction and preferred for these lower-current applications; Pololu also sells higher-voltage (12V) versions of some ratios with carbon brushes better suited to sustained higher-current use. For antweight drive, HP is the tune most builders reach for when they want the most power in the smallest package, while LP or MP make sense when a design is current-budget constrained, for example sharing a small ESC or battery branch with other electronics.

A useful variant is the **extended motor shaft** option, which brings the motor's rear shaft out through the back of the case in addition to the normal gearbox output shaft. This lets a builder mount a wheel-speed encoder disc, a second small pulley, or another accessory on the back of the motor without any machining — handy for a control-bot build that wants closed-loop wheel-speed feedback, or a 4WD layout that needs to drive an extra belt/pulley off the same motor.

The main trade-off versus FingerTech's Spark line is shaft length and mounting convention: Pololu's 9mm output shaft is too short for FingerTech's typical direct-wheel-mount (live-axle) approach and needs a hub or coupler, and Pololu doesn't publish a combat-specific mounting pattern the way FingerTech does. In exchange, a builder gets Pololu's much larger and more precisely documented range of ratios and power tunes, plus the reliability of a company whose entire business is measuring and publishing exactly this kind of spec — a meaningful advantage over generic N-series sourcing for a builder who wants predictable performance without over-paying for a combat-specific brand name.

chunks.title: Brushless Drive for Antweights: 1104/1106/1404 Motors, Pods, and Low-Speed Cogging
chunks.body_md:
Brushless drive on antweights has grown mainly out of the FPV micro-drone motor market. Motors labeled by a four-digit size code — **1104**, **1106**, **1404**, and similar — describe their stator dimensions (the first two digits are diameter in mm, the last two are stack height/length in mm): an '1104' is roughly 11mm in diameter and 4mm tall, an '1106' is the same 11mm diameter but a taller 6mm stack (more copper/stator volume, meaning more achievable torque and current handling at similar RPM), and a '1404' steps up to a 14mm diameter for still more capability in a similarly slim package. These motors are sold at a range of kv (RPM per volt) windings, and combat builders — or companies like Repeat Robotics who now sell them pre-integrated — pick a kv and pair it with a small gear reduction (commonly a 2-3 stage planetary gearbox in the 16-24mm class) to land in a useful antweight speed/torque range.

The major practical difference from brushed drive is that brushless motors require a **reversing brushless ESC** rather than a simple brushed H-bridge, and most of these motors are **sensorless** — they infer rotor position from back-EMF rather than dedicated Hall-effect sensors. Back-EMF is proportional to rotor speed, so at very low RPM (exactly the speed range a combat robot spends a lot of time in — creeping, jockeying for position, or making a fine positioning move) the signal an ESC needs to commutate smoothly gets weak and noisy. This shows up as **cogging**: jerky, notchy, sometimes stalling rotation right around zero speed, instead of the smooth linear response a brushed motor gives down to a full stop. **Sensored** brushless motors (with embedded Hall sensors) avoid this because the ESC always has a clean absolute rotor-position signal regardless of speed, but sensored micro combat motors are rarer and typically cost more; the more common combat-robotics fix is a gear reduction high enough that the motor itself is still spinning at a meaningfully high electrical RPM even when the wheel is barely turning, combined with an ESC/firmware tuned specifically for low-speed sensorless combat driving (as opposed to a generic multirotor ESC optimized for one direction and a fast spin-up) — which is exactly what purpose-built combat brushless ESCs like Repeat Robotics' reversing ESC are designed to handle.

The upside that keeps builders choosing brushless despite this complexity is power density and efficiency: no brushes to wear out, generally more torque and speed available per gram of motor than an equivalent brushed can, and (since kv and voltage set speed directly) the ability to retune top speed just by changing battery cell count (2S/3S/4S) rather than swapping hardware, useful for quickly adapting a drivetrain between a slower control-bot setup and a faster spinner-chassis setup.

chunks.title: Servo-Based Drive for Plastic Antweights
chunks.body_md:
Plastic antweights, built and raced on tight budgets and gram counts, have long used the cheapest, simplest drive mechanism available in the RC hobby world: the **9g micro servo**, modified (or purchased pre-modified) for continuous rotation. A normal hobby servo takes a PWM pulse (typically 1-2ms) and moves its output shaft to a corresponding angle, using an internal potentiometer to sense and hold position via a small feedback control loop. Removing that positional feedback — physically pulling the potentiometer and replacing it with two fixed resistors set to the servo's centered voltage, and usually clipping a mechanical stop tab inside the gearbox — breaks the position-holding behavior and turns the same PWM signal into a direct speed-and-direction command instead: a 1ms pulse spins one direction, 2ms spins the other, and roughly 1.5ms (the old 'centered' position) stops the motor. The result behaves almost exactly like a small ESC-driven gearmotor from the transmitter's point of view, but needs zero separate ESC or motor driver hardware — the servo plugs straight into a receiver channel.

Builders who don't want to do the modification themselves can buy factory continuous-rotation servos (commonly referred to by part numbers like FS90R) that ship ready to use, with more consistent centering than a hand-modified unit, at a small price premium over a basic positional 9g servo.

The appeal for plastic antweights is straightforward: at roughly 9g each, two servos plus a receiver is often the lightest and cheapest complete drive system available, with no ESC weight or cost, no separate motor-driver wiring, and a huge amount of freely available documentation and tutorials for the modification. The trade-offs are real, though. Servo gearboxes are built from a stack of small plastic gears sized for holding a load still, not for absorbing repeated combat impacts, and the motor inside is sized for positioning torque rather than continuous drive torque — so top speed and pushing power both fall well short of what a dedicated gearmotor-plus-ESC combination of similar weight can deliver. In practice, servo drive suits beginner builds, very light or defensive plastic antweights that don't need to win pushing matches, and builds where simplicity of wiring and zero extra electronics genuinely outweighs raw performance. Builders chasing a competitive edge in the plastic antweight class typically graduate to N-series or Pololu gearmotors with a small ESC once they're ready to trade some of that simplicity for speed and torque.

chunks.title: Wheels and Tires: Foam, Silicone, TPU, O-Rings, and Banebots
chunks.body_md:
Wheel choice on an antweight is a direct trade between weight, grip, shock absorption, and cost, and the options span a wide range of approaches.

**FingerTech Lite Flite foam wheels** are the default choice for most standard-material antweights: light neoprene foam tires available in diameters from 25.4mm to 76.2mm (1.0-3.0in) in 6.35mm (0.25in) steps, in two widths (12.7mm/0.5in and 19.1mm/0.75in), mounted via FingerTech's Lite, Snap, or Twist hub system. A 2.0in tire alone weighs only about 4g, and the foam's compliance absorbs shock from arena hazards and hard impacts that would otherwise transmit straight into the gearbox and shaft. Grip is described as "surprisingly good" for how light the material is, but it's still a step below purpose-built rubber compounds.

**Silicone-coated or cast-silicone tires** address that grip gap directly: a thin layer of 2-part silicone rubber, typically in the Shore A 30-50 durometer range, cast or brushed onto a foam or printed core. Softer compounds in that range grip best on polished wood or acrylic/polycarbonate arena floors, at the cost of faster wear and more debris pickup; it's a common DIY upgrade for control bots that need to win pushing matches rather than just drive around.

**3D-printed TPU wheels**, printed in flexible filament typically rated 85-95A Shore hardness, are the natural fit for plastic antweights: essentially free once a printer and filament are on hand, printable as a single piece with the hub bore built in (eliminating a separate hub's weight), and highly impact-resistant. Grip sits above rigid PLA/PETG wheels but below a soft cast-silicone tire at similar hardness.

**O-ring tires** are a cheap, DIY-friendly technique across weight classes: a plain hub (aluminum, printed, or Delrin) machined or printed with a groove sized for a rubber O-ring, stretched on as the tread. They're inexpensive to replace when worn, give solid rubber-compound grip, and let the hub itself stay very light — the main risk is the O-ring rolling in its groove under high torque if the groove isn't sized tightly enough.

**Banebots** wheels represent the name-brand compliant-tread option: the T61 line offers 6 hardness options (from a very soft, maximum-grip 10A yellow rubber up to a firmer, more durable 60A black rubber), 4 diameters, and 4 hub shaft sizes, while the smaller T40 line is aimed more specifically at ant/fairy-scale builds. Banebots wheels are heavier than foam or TPU for a given diameter — a real cost against a 1 lb weight budget — but their compliant tread conforms to the floor for grip and control that's hard to match with a rigid or foam alternative, which is why they show up more often on control-bot and pushing-focused designs than on speed- or weight-optimized spinners.

Across all of these, the general rule holds: softer/more compliant tread gives more grip but wears faster and adds weight/debris-pickup; harder/lighter tread (foam, rigid TPU) saves weight and lasts longer but gives up some pushing power to wheel slip on a smooth arena floor.

chunks.title: Drivetrain Topologies: 2WD, 4WD, Belt/Chain/Gear, Dead vs Live Axle
chunks.body_md:
The overwhelming majority of 1 lb antweights use **2WD direct (live-axle) drive**: two drive gearmotors, one per side, each with a wheel mounted straight onto its output shaft. This is the simplest, lightest, and most repairable layout — no belts, chains, or extra shafts to fail — and it's exactly what FingerTech's extra-long Silver Spark shaft is designed around. Its main limitation is that all of the robot's weight rides on two contact points (plus perhaps a rear skid or caster), so if one wheel is lifted off the ground (climbing over an opponent's wedge lip, or after a weapon hit), the robot can lose most of its drive traction at once.

**4WD** layouts address that by putting a powered wheel at each corner, giving redundancy (the robot still has drive even with one wheel airborne) and more overall traction for pushing matches, at the cost of extra weight and complexity. On a 1 lb budget, running four full motors is often too heavy, so 4WD antweights frequently use a **belt-driven** approach instead: one motor per side, with a small GT2 timing belt and pulley set (common because GT2 hardware is cheap and widely available from the 3D-printer supply chain) linking the front and rear wheel on that side so they spin together. This gets 4-wheel traction from only 2 motors, at the cost of belt tension/wear as an extra maintenance and failure point, and the belt run needs to be shielded from direct weapon hits. **Chain** drive is a heavier, more robust alternative to belts seen more often on larger weight classes, and **gear-driven** linkages (a small gear train connecting front and rear wheel shafts) are a third option that trades some efficiency for eliminating belt tension entirely.

A separate design axis is **dead axle vs live axle** mounting. In a live-axle setup (the antweight default), the wheel is mounted directly to the motor's output shaft, and that shaft is what takes the wheel's structural and impact loads. In a **dead axle** setup, the wheel spins freely on a fixed, non-rotating shaft (supported by its own bearings), and is driven separately — typically by a sprocket, pulley, or gear fixed to the wheel and linked back to the motor by a chain, belt, or gear train. This isolates the motor's own output shaft from direct impact loads (useful in wedge or lifter bots where a wheel might take a hard hit) and lets multiple wheels share a single structural axle, but adds parts, weight, and assembly complexity that most 1 lb antweights can't easily afford — dead axles show up far more often on beetleweight and larger designs.

Finally, **ground clearance and wheel guards** matter more on an antweight than the raw drivetrain numbers might suggest: exposed wheels are one of the most common ways to lose a match, since a stray hit from an opposing weapon (or even the arena floor's hazards) can destroy a wheel or knock a robot immobile in seconds.
