Competitive builds usually keep wheels tucked fully inside the body's footprint (inboard, not protruding past the armor line) and add minimal ground clearance — just enough to clear floor screws, seams, and hazards, no more — since every extra millimeter of clearance is extra exposed wheel and extra leverage for an opponent's wedge to get underneath.

chunks.title: Worked Example: Robot Speed from Motor RPM and Wheel Diameter
chunks.body_md:
The most basic drivetrain calculation a builder needs is converting a motor's rated speed into a robot's actual top speed on the floor. The relationship is: wheel RPM equals motor no-load RPM divided by the total gear ratio, and linear speed equals wheel RPM times the wheel's rolling circumference.

In a convenient mixed-units form: **v(mph) = (motor_rpm / gear_ratio) x pi x wheel_diameter(in) / 1056**. The constant 1056 converts inches-per-minute into miles-per-hour (there are 63,360 inches in a mile and 60 minutes in an hour, so 63,360/60 = 1,056).

**Worked example:** Take a FingerTech Silver Spark at its fastest stock ratio, 11.1:1, with a base motor no-load speed of 11,530 RPM (at 7.4V, the common 2S LiPo antweight voltage), paired with a 2.0in diameter wheel.

1. Wheel RPM = 11,530 / 11.1 = 1,038.7 RPM
2. v(mph) = 1,038.7 x 3.1416 x 2.0 / 1056
3. v(mph) = 1,038.7 x 6.283 / 1056 = 6,527 / 1056 ≈ 6.18 mph

This lines up well with commonly cited real-world antweight sprint speeds of roughly 6 mph across a short arena run. It's worth being clear about what this number is and isn't: it's a **theoretical no-load** top speed, calculated as if the motor were spinning completely unloaded at its rated voltage forever. In practice, actual top speed on the floor comes in lower — typically 70-90% of this figure — because of three effects this simple formula ignores: (1) **voltage sag**, since a small LiPo's internal resistance and the motor's own current draw pull the actual voltage at the motor below the pack's rated nominal voltage under load; (2) **rolling and gearbox friction losses**, which this formula doesn't subtract at all (it assumes 100% efficiency); and (3) the fact that a wheel does still need a small amount of torque even at 'cruising' speed to overcome friction, meaning the motor never quite reaches the true zero-load RPM the datasheet lists. Builders typically treat the no-load formula as a solid *upper bound* / rough comparison tool for choosing between ratios or wheel sizes, then confirm the real number with an actual timed run once the robot is built.

chunks.title: Worked Example: Sizing Motor Torque for a Target Acceleration
chunks.body_md:
Once a target top speed sets the gear ratio in the ballpark, the next question is whether that ratio can actually deliver the acceleration or pushing force the robot needs — this is a torque-sizing problem, not a speed problem.

Start from Newton's second law, F = m x a, to find the total force the robot needs at the ground. Convert that to a torque requirement at the wheel by multiplying by wheel radius and dividing across however many wheels share the load: **T_wheel = F x r / n_driven_wheels**. Finally, work back through the gearbox to the motor shaft itself: **T_motor_required = T_wheel / (gear_ratio x efficiency)**, using roughly 0.65-0.80 efficiency for a typical spur gearbox (like Silver Spark) or 0.80-0.92 for a planetary gearbox (like Repeat Robotics' motors).

**Worked example:** Take a standard 1 lb robot, m = 0.4536 kg, targeting an aggressive 2g acceleration (a = 19.6 m/s²) — a reasonable target for a bot that wants to close distance quickly or absorb a ram — on two driven wheels of 1.5in diameter (radius r = 0.019 m).

1. F = m x a = 0.4536 x 19.6 = 8.89 N
2. T_wheel (per side) = F x r / n = 8.89 x 0.019 / 2 = 0.0844 N·m ≈ 0.86 kg-cm
3. At a 33.3:1 gear ratio with ~0.75 gearbox efficiency: T_motor_required = 0.86 / (33.3 x 0.75) ≈ 0.0345 kg-cm

Compare that 0.0345 kg-cm requirement to the Silver Spark's bare-motor stall torque of roughly 0.046 kg-cm: there's real margin, meaning 33.3:1 comfortably supports a 2g start. Repeat the same math at the fastest stock ratio, 11.1:1: T_motor_required = 0.86 / (11.1 x 0.75) ≈ 0.103 kg-cm — more than double the bare motor's stall torque, meaning 11.1:1 alone cannot sustain a full 2g acceleration all the way from a dead stop under stall conditions (it can still accelerate, just not at that aggressive a rate, and the motor will spend less time near stall as RPM builds).

The practical takeaway: faster (lower) gear ratios trade away low-speed acceleration/pushing headroom for top speed, and slower (higher) ratios do the reverse. A builder picks the ratio that keeps enough torque margin for the robot's actual job (a control bot needs more low-end torque margin than a spinner that mostly just needs to reposition) — but as the next formula shows, that torque margin only matters up to the point where the wheels can actually put it to the ground.

chunks.title: Worked Example: The Traction Limit and Why Extra Torque Gets Wasted
chunks.body_md:
No matter how much torque a drivetrain can theoretically produce, it can only push as hard as the wheels' grip on the floor allows before they simply spin in place. That ceiling is the **traction limit**: F_max = μ x N, where μ is the coefficient of friction between the wheel tread and the arena floor, and N is the normal force (weight) pressing the driven wheels down.

**Worked example:** A 1 lb robot weighs 0.4536 kg x 9.81 m/s² = 4.45 N. Fit it with silicone-tread wheels giving a friction coefficient around μ = 0.6 against a typical polycarbonate arena floor (foam alone would be lower, roughly 0.3-0.5; a soft compliant tread can push toward 0.7-0.8). F_max = 0.6 x 4.45 = 2.67 N — that's the absolute maximum forward force this robot can generate on this floor, no matter what drivetrain sits behind the wheels.

Now compare that to what the drivetrain itself can supply. Take the lowest-torque stock Silver Spark ratio, 11.1:1, with an estimated output stall torque around 0.38 kg-cm (≈0.0373 N·m) per motor, on the same 1.5in-diameter (0.019m radius) wheels, split across 2 driven wheels: the wheels together can theoretically deliver up to F = 2 x T / r = 2 x 0.0373 / 0.019 ≈ 3.9 N of force before the *motors* stall out. That's already above the 2.67 N traction ceiling — meaning this robot's wheels will slip and spin before its motors ever reach their torque limit, even at the fastest, lowest-torque ratio in the whole Silver Spark lineup.

This is the core reason "just gear it down more for more pushing power" is often a wasted move on a well-traction-matched antweight: once a drivetrain's available torque already exceeds the traction limit, adding more torque (by choosing a higher, slower gear ratio) doesn't increase real-world pushing force at all — the extra torque just goes into wheel slip, heat, and battery drain, while the robot gets slower and less maneuverable for no pushing benefit. The useful design target, as commonly recommended in the antweight community, is to size the drivetrain with roughly 1.5-2x the torque strictly required to reach the traction limit (giving margin for wear, voltage sag, and imperfect weight distribution) and then spend any additional gear-ratio choice on speed and control feel rather than further torque, since torque beyond that point is traction-limited, not motor-limited.

chunks.title: Worked Example: Stall Current, ESC Ratings, and Duty-Cycle Heating
chunks.body_md:
Every drive motor draws its highest current right at stall (zero RPM, full voltage applied) — this is the number an ESC, wiring, connectors, and battery all need to be sized to survive, at least briefly, even though the robot won't spend most of a match sitting at true stall.

**Worked example:** A 2WD antweight running two FingerTech Silver Sparks, each rated 1.3A stall current at 7.4V. Worst case, both motors stall simultaneously (e.g. the robot is pinned against a wall while still commanding full throttle): I_stall_total = 2 x 1.3A = 2.6A combined. Normal cruising current while driving freely is much lower, typically in the 0.2-0.6A-per-motor range, since a motor only draws current in proportion to the torque it's actually producing, not its theoretical maximum.

Sizing rule of thumb: an ESC or motor driver's **continuous current rating** should sit comfortably above the expected cruising current (so it runs cool through normal driving), while its **burst/peak current rating** needs to clear the full per-channel stall current with some safety margin — for a 1.3A-stall motor, a driver rated for 2-3A continuous per channel is typically adequate, which is why most small antweight brushed ESCs (FingerTech's own boards among them) are specified in that range.

The part that trips up new builders is the **duty-cycle / thermal** side of this, separate from the ESC's rating entirely: these tiny motors have very little thermal mass, so even a stall current well within the ESC's rated capability can still cook the motor's own windings if held for too long, because resistive (I²R) heating in the coil accumulates faster than the small motor can shed it. As a rough guide, holding a Silver Spark-class motor at full stall for more than about 10-20 seconds starts to risk winding insulation damage, even though the ESC itself may show no signs of distress. This is why experienced drivers are taught to **"bump" the throttle** — short pulses of full stall rather than holding it — during a pushing match or when momentarily jammed against an obstacle, treating the stall current rating as a brief-duration limit rather than something the motor can sustain indefinitely.

chunks.title: Worked Example: Reverse-Solving Gear Ratio from a Target Top Speed
chunks.body_md:
When a builder starts from a target top speed instead of a specific motor, the speed formula can be rearranged to solve directly for the gear ratio needed: **gear_ratio = motor_rpm_no_load x pi x wheel_diameter(in) / (target_mph x 1056)**.

**Worked example:** Suppose the goal is an 8 mph top speed, using a FingerTech Silver Spark (motor_rpm_no_load = 11,530 at 7.4V) and a 2.0in wheel.

gear_ratio = 11,530 x 3.1416 x 2.0 / (8 x 1056) = 72,444 / 8,448 ≈ **8.6:1**

But Silver Spark's fastest stock ratio is 11.1:1, not 8.6:1 — there's no off-the-shelf ratio fast enough to hit exactly 8 mph with this motor and this wheel size. This is a completely normal outcome of the reverse calculation, and it points to two practical fixes:

1. **Increase the wheel diameter** and re-check the fastest available stock ratio. At 11.1:1 with a larger 2.5in wheel: wheel RPM = 11,530 / 11.1 = 1,038.7, so v(mph) = 1,038.7 x 3.1416 x 2.5 / 1056 ≈ **7.7 mph** — very close to the 8 mph target, achieved with a completely off-the-shelf Silver Spark by simply choosing a bigger wheel instead of hunting for a nonexistent ratio.
2. **Switch to a higher-RPM drivetrain entirely**, most commonly a brushless drive pod. Because a brushless motor's speed is set by kv x voltage rather than a fixed brush-motor RPM, a brushless antweight gearmotor can be tuned well past this target simply by running a higher-cell-count battery (3S or 4S instead of 2S), without touching the gearbox or wheel at all.

The general lesson from reverse-solving gear ratio this way is that **wheel diameter and gear ratio are interchangeable knobs for hitting a speed target** — a builder isn't locked into whatever stock ratios a motor happens to ship in, because changing wheel size (within the traction and torque limits from the other formulas) shifts the achievable speed just as effectively as changing the gearbox. The final choice usually comes down to whichever knob has the least negative side effect on the rest of the build: a bigger wheel raises ground clearance and can increase rotational inertia (slower spin-up/braking) and often adds weight, while a different gear ratio may not exist as a stock part, and a different motor altogether means a bigger BOM and design change.

chunks.title: Recommended Drivetrain: Competitive 1 lb Antweight Spinner
chunks.body_md:
A competitive antweight spinner spends most of its weight budget on the weapon system (motor, bar/disc, containment) and armor, so the drivetrain's job is to be light, reliable, and "just fast/agile enough" to line up hits and dodge — not to win pushing matches. Recommended baseline:

- **Topology:** 2WD direct (live-axle) drive. A spinner rarely needs 4WD's extra traction, and every gram saved on the drivetrain can go into the weapon or armor instead.
- **Motors:** A pair of FingerTech Silver Spark gearmotors in the 22.2:1-33.3:1 range are the proven default — enough torque margin over the traction limit for confident repositioning, with a reasonable top speed (roughly 4-6 mph depending on wheel size) for closing distance and dodging counter-attacks. Builders chasing extra speed and efficiency at similar weight increasingly use a Repeat Robotics brushless "Mini" 1106 drive pod instead, which can be tuned faster on 3S while staying in the same weight class as a Silver Spark pair.
- **Wheels:** 1.25-1.5in FingerTech Lite Flite foam wheels, prioritizing shock absorption (protecting the drivetrain from the vibration and impacts of being near an active spinning weapon and from opposing hits) over maximum grip — a spinner's own gyroscopic effects and hit-and-retreat playstyle rely less on sustained high-friction pushing than a control bot does.
- **Ground clearance and wheel guards:** Keep wheels tucked fully inside the body's outer footprint, ideally behind a hardened skirt or armor lip, since exposed wheels are one of the most common ways a spinner robot gets killed — a single solid hit to an unguarded wheel can end the match instantly.
- **Battery/voltage:** 2S LiPo (7.4V) is the standard baseline; 3S is worth considering specifically to unlock a brushless drive pod's higher speed range, but adds weight that must be budgeted against the (typically much heavier) weapon system.

The overarching principle for a spinner's drivetrain is: size it to comfortably clear the traction limit with margin (per the traction-limit formula) at a ratio that gives useful positioning speed, then stop — any drivetrain weight or complexity beyond that is weight the weapon system could have used instead.

chunks.title: Recommended Drivetrain: 1 lb Antweight Control Bot
chunks.body_md:
A control bot (wedge, rammer, or full-body pusher) lives or dies by its ability to win sustained pushing exchanges, hold a heading under load, and stay mobile after taking a hit — so its drivetrain deserves a noticeably larger share of the weight budget than a spinner's. Recommended baseline:

- **Topology:** 4WD is genuinely worth its weight cost here, more so than on any other antweight archetype, because losing traction on even one corner during a pushing match can mean losing the match outright. The common, weight-efficient way to get there on a 1 lb budget is 2 motors per side linked front-to-rear with a small GT2 belt and pulley set, rather than 4 full independent motors. A well-executed 2WD layout with excellent traction and a low center of gravity is still a completely viable, simpler alternative for builders prioritizing reliability over maximum pushing power.
- **Motors:** FingerTech Silver Spark at 50:1-100:1, or a Repeat Robotics planetary-gearbox brushed/brushless motor at a comparable ratio, favoring the higher-torque end of the practical range compared to a spinner's build — a control bot wants torque margin well above the traction limit so it's never the motor, only the tires, holding back a push.
- **Wheels:** This is the one drivetrain decision worth spending real weight budget on: compliant, higher-grip options like silicone-coated foam or Banebots-style compliant tread genuinely change match outcomes for a control bot, unlike a spinner where wheel choice matters less. Accept the extra weight of a grippier tire here in exchange for meaningfully more pushing force per the traction-limit formula.
- **Ground clearance:** Slightly more forgiving than a spinner's — a control bot often wants a wedge or forward scoop close to the floor, so ground clearance should be set by that geometry first, with wheels and their guards built around it rather than the reverse.
- **Battery/voltage:** 2S (7.4V) remains standard; 3S is less commonly needed here than for a spinner chasing top speed, since a control bot's advantage comes from torque and traction, not raw speed.

The key sizing check for a control bot, more than any other archetype, is running the traction-limit formula against the actual tire compound chosen (not foam's default lower coefficient) and making sure the drivetrain's torque comfortably clears that number with room to spare — an underpowered control bot that can be shoved backward once its wheels break traction has effectively lost its entire strategic purpose.

chunks.title: Recommended Drivetrain: Plastic Antweight
chunks.body_md:
Plastic antweight classes (popularized as an entry-level, low-cost, low-damage-rate scale, generally run at the same 1 lb / 454g total weight as a standard antweight but requiring the robot's structure to be built primarily from plastic rather than metal) put a premium on low cost and simple, printable/hand-buildable parts over absolute competitive performance. Note that the plastic-only requirement almost always targets the robot's *structure/armor*, not its internal drive components — metal-geared motors are still legal even in a strict plastic build, but budget-minded builders in this class often gravitate toward the cheapest available motors anyway, which happen to be the same N-series and servo options with the internal-quality caveats already noted. Recommended baseline:

- **Motors:** For a first build or a very tight budget, a pair of modified (or factory) continuous-rotation 9g servos is the simplest possible complete drive system — no ESC needed, direct receiver connection, and matches the class's low-cost ethos exactly. For a step up in speed and torque while staying cheap, a pair of N20 gearmotors (100:1-150:1 at 6V is a reasonable starting ratio range) is the most common upgrade path — but given the well-documented quality-lottery risk in this motor family, buy at least one or two spares per side and bench-test every unit (checking free-run current and no-load RPM) before final installation, rather than trusting an untested motor straight out of the bag for an event.
- **Wheels:** 3D-printed TPU wheels are close to a perfect match for this class: essentially free, fully custom to the chassis design, printable with the hub built in to save an extra part and its weight, and tough enough to survive typical plastic-antweight-level impacts. A simple o-ring tire on a printed hub is a good lightweight alternative when a builder wants more grip than bare TPU without the complexity of casting silicone.
- **Topology:** 2WD live-axle drive, kept as simple as possible — this class rewards a build that's quick and cheap to repair between matches over one with maximum drivetrain sophistication, and a straightforward direct-drive 2WD layout is the easiest to fix with commonly available parts (a spare N20 or servo, a printed wheel) between rounds.
- **Ground clearance/guards:** Since armor is plastic and generally thinner/lighter than a metal-armored standard antweight, keeping wheels tucked inboard behind whatever armor the design does carry matters just as much here, if not more, since plastic armor may not stop as much as metal would if an opponent gets under an exposed wheel.

Overall, the plastic antweight drivetrain recommendation prioritizes **cost, simplicity, and repairability** over raw performance metrics — the class exists specifically to lower the barrier to entry, and a drivetrain built around cheap, easily replaceable parts (spare N20s, printed wheels) serves that goal better than chasing the same Silver-Spark-and-Banebots spec sheet a competitive metal antweight would use.

chunks.title: What Defines the Plastic Antweight Class
chunks.body_md:
Plastic antweight (also called "plastic ant," "PLA ant," or "3D printed antweight") is a 1 lb / 454 g combat robot class where the weight limit is identical to a normal antweight, but the **construction material is restricted**: the chassis, armor and weapon(s) must be built only from a short list of 3D-printable plastics. Under the SPARC Robot Construction Specifications (v1.4, section 4.4), which most North American events either quote directly or lightly modify, the allowed list is **PET, PETG, ABS, PLA, or PLA+**, with SCAR's ruleset also explicitly naming **ASA**. No other plastic or material is legal for structural/armor/weapon use unless an event organizer grants an exception 'that meets the spirit of the rules.'

Crucially, the rule targets *structure, armor, and weapons* — not every part of the robot. A wide range of non-plastic components are explicitly carved out as exempt: **motors, electronics, axles, fasteners, and adhesives can be any material**, as long as they are not used 'in such a way to enhance the structural integrity, armor the robot, or enhance any weapon' (SPARC 4.4.2, echoed nearly verbatim by SCAR and Robot Ruckus). In practice this means a plastic ant's motors, its steel weapon shaft, its bearings, and its screws can all be metal — only the printed shell, weapon disc/drum body, and any load-bearing armor panels must be plastic.

Most events also require that the plastic be **3D printed specifically**, not just any plastic sheet or rod stock cut or machined into shape. This closes an obvious loophole: a CNC-milled or laser-cut solid polycarbonate/UHMW part would be far stronger than an FDM-printed part of the same material and geometry, defeating the class's purpose of keeping material strength low. The RobotCombatWiki entry on the class states this plainly: 'many if not most events will require plastic parts to be *only* 3D printed' specifically to prevent this kind of milled-part loophole.

The class runs as its own bracket — plastic ants never fight standard-material antweights in the same pool — because the material restriction is understood to make plastic ants meaningfully weaker/more fragile fighters than a metal antweight of the same weight, not merely a cosmetic build constraint.

chunks.title: Exactly What Metal Is Allowed — Wording Across Organizations
chunks.body_md:
Every plastic-ant ruleset carves out a near-identical exemption list, but it's worth reading the exact wording since enforcement details differ.

**SPARC 4.4.2** (the most widely copied phrasing): *"Non-plastic parts such as motors, electronics, axles, fasteners and adhesives can be any material, but cannot be used in such a way to enhance the structural integrity, armor the robot, or enhance any weapon."* This is a *functional* test, not a parts-list test — the question inspectors ask is whether a given metal part is doing double duty as armor or a weapon surface, not simply whether it's metal.

**SCAR's Plastic Ant FAQ** gets more concrete, explicitly naming: metal bearings, axles, shafts and fasteners; COTS motor-mount adapters; and even metal servo horns/gears, *provided the weapon is non-functional without its plastic parts* (i.e., the metal gear alone couldn't act as the striking surface). SCAR also explicitly allows COTS wheel/tire components from vendors like FingerTech, Repeat Robotics, or Pololu — including their rubber, cast urethane, or foam tire materials — since wheels/tires are treated as outside the structural/armor/weapon restriction entirely.

**Robot Ruckus** adds a specific enforcement detail not spelled out elsewhere: where metal fasteners appear on the *outer surface* of the robot, 'they should be countersunk or shrouded' — i.e., a proud screw head sticking up from the shell could be argued to function as tiny armor or a weapon-like protrusion, so it must be recessed or hidden under a plastic cap.

**Practical exemption checklist most events agree on:**
- Drive motors, weapon motors — any material (always metal in practice)
- ESCs, receivers, wiring, connectors, switches — any material
- Weapon shaft/axle — metal is normal and expected
- Bearings — metal is normal and expected
- Screws/fasteners/threaded inserts — metal allowed, but countersink/shroud outer-surface heads
- Adhesives (super glue, epoxy used *as glue*, not as an armor coating) — any material
- Battery — any material (never printed anyway)

What's *not* on this list — and therefore must be plastic — is anything that is itself a structural panel, an armor plate, or the actual striking face/body of a weapon.

chunks.title: Banned Materials and How Bans Are Written
chunks.body_md:
The core ban across every ruleset reviewed is simple: **any material used for chassis, armor, or weapon that is not on the approved plastics list.** SPARC 4.4.1 spells this out with explicit examples — *"No other types of plastics or materials allowed (ie. metal, carbon fiber, UHMW, etc)."* SCAR's base ruleset repeats this trio (metal, carbon fiber, UHMW) verbatim.

SCAR's supplementary Plastic Ant FAQ goes further and names several materials that are technically 3D-printed plastics but are still banned because they sit outside the PLA/PETG/ABS/PET/ASA family or are seen as violating the class's spirit:
- **TPU** (including custom TPU wheel hubs) — banned by name, despite being popular for flexible armor in the wider (metal-legal) antweight/beetleweight community.
- **Nylon** — banned by name, despite being a tough, useful engineering filament in general 3D printing.
- **'Flex' or blended filaments** marketed for enhanced properties — banned as a category, to close the loophole of using an exotic blend that isn't literally named TPU or nylon but behaves the same way.
- **Composite filaments** (carbon-fiber-filled or glass-filled plastics) — banned, consistent with the base ruleset's carbon-fiber ban.
- **Epoxy coatings, Bondo, or similar fillers** — banned as post-processing 'armor' additions.
- **Rubber shock-mount armor ('wubs')** and **multi-layer tape armor** — banned as improvised armor techniques borrowed from full-metal antweight practice that would circumvent the plastic-only spirit.

**Magnets** are separately and universally banned when used to enhance traction or downforce (SPARC 4.4.2, SCAR ruleset) — this is a general antweight-class magnet rule, not specific to plastic ants, but it applies here too.

**Post-processing carve-outs**: SCAR's FAQ explicitly *allows* annealing/heat-or-acid smoothing of a printed part, and thin decorative paint, distinguishing legitimate finishing techniques from material additives that change the part's mechanical properties or add foreign armor material.

The overall pattern: base rulesets ban by naming forbidden *material categories* (metal, carbon fiber, UHMW); FAQs and event-specific clarifications then ban by naming specific *filaments and techniques* that technically dodge the base wording but violate its intent. Builders bringing a design to a new event should always check for a supplementary FAQ, not just the headline ruleset.

chunks.title: Org-to-Org Variation in the Plastic Ant Rules
chunks.body_md:
Although nearly every plastic-ant ruleset in North America descends from the same source (Western Allied Robotics' 2015 original, absorbed into SPARC's template), real differences exist once you compare specific events:

| Organization | Base material list | TPU? | Nylon? | Notable extra rule |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **SPARC (template)** | PET, PETG, ABS, PLA, PLA+ | Not listed (organizer discretion) | Not listed | Organizer can approve additional plastics 'meeting the spirit' |
| **SCAR** | PET, PETG, ABS, ASA, PLA, PLA+ | Explicitly **banned** by FAQ | Explicitly **banned** by FAQ | Names approved filament brands (FusionFilaments HTPLA+, Duramic PLA+, Overture Super PLA+, Hatchbox ABS) |
| **Robot Ruckus** | PLA, PLA+, ABS, PETG | Not explicitly addressed | Not explicitly addressed | Requires countersunk/shrouded surface screws |
| **Western Allied Robotics (origin)** | PET, PETG, ABS, PLA, PLA+ | Not explicitly addressed | Not explicitly addressed | Founding 2015 ruleset; separate bracket from metal ants |
| **Bot Blast** | Modified SPARC rules | Follows SPARC baseline | Follows SPARC baseline | Runs plastic ant as part of a broader insectweight program |
| **UK plastic ant / 150g scene** | Broadly similar plastic-only philosophy | Varies by club | Varies by club | Often applied to the UK's 150g 'antweight' bracket, a *different* weight than the US 1lb class — naming overlap causes confusion |

**The single most important variance to know**: whether TPU and nylon count as legal 'plastic.' SCAR bans both by name. Other events that only quote the bare SPARC 4.4.1 list (which doesn't mention TPU or nylon at all) leave it ambiguous — technically neither is on the approved list either, so a strict reading bans them everywhere unless an organizer explicitly grants an exception. Builders should never assume a design that used TPU tires or a nylon gear at one event will pass technical inspection at another; always check the specific event's FAQ or ask the organizer directly, exactly as SPARC 4.4.3 itself recommends: *'Contact the event organizer ahead of time if you are not sure your robot meets the above definition.'*

Online/remote plastic-ant competitions (where robots are shipped to a central venue and matches are run and streamed by event staff, a format popularized by NHRL for larger classes) generally adopt whichever local ruleset the hosting club already runs rather than inventing new material rules, so the same org-to-org variation applies to them too.

chunks.title: The UK Plastic Ant Scene and the 150g Naming Trap
chunks.body_md:
The UK combat robotics scene uses different weight-class names than the US, and this creates a real point of confusion for anyone researching "plastic antweight" online. In the UK, the term **"antweight" traditionally refers to the 150g class**, not the 1 lb / 454 g class that US builders mean when they say "antweight" or "plastic ant." The US 1lb bracket has a rough UK-terminology equivalent, but the *plastic* movement is active at both scales in the UK: there are 150g plastic/printable antweights as well as heavier printable classes, and community-shared designs freely cross weight brackets in spirit even though they aren't the same competition category.

A good concrete example is **Legally Distinct**, a free, open-source 150g UK antweight drum-spinner design shared on Thingiverse by community builder Blessy, explicitly described as "heavily inspired by" an established UK antweight called **Siren**. This shows the same open, iterative design culture found in the US 1lb plastic ant scene — successful designs get openly documented, and other builders print, remix, and re-share variants — just operating at the UK's 150g weight bracket rather than the US 1lb bracket most SPARC-derived rulesets target.

**Practical implication for researchers and builders**: when reading a UK build log, forum post, or Thingiverse description, always check the stated gram weight rather than assuming "antweight" means 454g. A UK 150g printable drum spinner and a US 1lb / 454g SPARC-legal plastic ant are built to different weight budgets, different arena sizes, and sometimes different club-specific material rules, even though both fall under the broad 'plastic ant' / '3D-printed insect-class robot' umbrella this file otherwise treats as one class.

That said, the underlying design lessons transfer well across the naming gap: both scenes favor thick printed drum/disc weapons over thin cutting bars, both rely on PETG/PLA+/ABS as the workhorse filaments, and both treat a cracked printed part as a five-minute reprint rather than a season-ending failure.

chunks.title: Springs, Rubber Bands, Magnets and Ballast Legality
chunks.body_md:
**Magnets**: Universally banned when used 'to enhance traction or downforce' (SPARC 4.4.2, SCAR ruleset). This is a general antweight-class rule that also applies to plastic ants — the concern is that magnetic downforce would let a light robot behave like a much heavier one against a steel arena floor, which most 1lb-class arenas do use. Small magnets used for non-traction purposes (e.g., holding an access panel shut) are generally not the target of this rule, but builders should confirm with the organizer if in doubt.

**Springs**: SPARC's general springs-and-flywheels section (13.1) explicitly *exempts* robots in the 12lb class or smaller — which includes every plastic ant — from its stricter large-spring loading/remote-actuation requirements, as long as 'safe operation and good engineering' are followed. This means a plastic ant can use a small pre-loaded spring (e.g., in a snap-action flipper or lifter) without needing the remote-arming mechanism required of larger robots' big weapon springs. The spring itself, if it's a coil or leaf spring, is metal and falls under the same 'non-plastic mechanical part' logic as a bearing or shaft — it's not armor or the primary weapon surface, so it's allowed.

**Rubber bands**: Not specifically addressed in any plastic-ant ruleset reviewed, but by the same logic as springs, a rubber band used as a small mechanical actuator (e.g., snapping a lifter arm closed) is a functional non-plastic part, not armor or a weapon surface, and would be treated as legal under the standard exemption language. Builders relying on this for a weapon mechanism should still get organizer sign-off given the general 'contact us if borderline' guidance every ruleset repeats.

**Ballast**: Not explicitly named as banned or allowed in the plastic-only material lists, but ballast is understood by the community to fall under the same test as everything else — if it's simply dense material added to bring the robot up to the full 454g weight limit and it isn't functioning as armor, it's legal regardless of material (a small chunk of steel ballast, screwed into an internal cavity and not exposed as a surface, does not 'enhance structural integrity, armor the robot, or enhance any weapon'). Many plastic ant builders instead use printed ballast (a solid, high-infill printed plug) simply because it's zero-cost and trivially plastic-legal, avoiding the question entirely.

chunks.title: How Tech Inspection Verifies 'Plastic Only'
chunks.body_md:
Plastic ant technical inspection is, by design, lighter-weight than the pressure-vessel-certificate-checking inspection larger weight classes face for pneumatics/hydraulics — but it still has to answer one specific question with confidence: *is the structural/armor/weapon material actually one of the approved plastics, and is it actually 3D printed rather than machined?*

**Visual inspection is the default and primary method.** SCAR's Plastic Ant FAQ states plainly that 'datasheets are not required' for a normal build — an inspector looks at the surface finish (visible layer lines are a good sign it's genuinely printed rather than milled/cast), checks that fasteners are countersunk or shrouded, and looks for obviously non-plastic materials like exposed sheet metal, carbon fiber weave, or a suspiciously glossy/dense coating that might indicate an epoxy or resin reinforcement layer.

**Suspicious builds get closer scrutiny.** If a part looks implausibly rigid, dense, or smooth for its stated material (for example, a 'PETG' panel that doesn't flex at all when pressed, or a part that feels far heavier than its printed volume should), inspectors can investigate further — this might mean asking the builder directly what filament and settings were used, requesting to see other parts printed from the same spool, or in rare cases asking to cut into or otherwise verify a part before allowing the robot to compete.

**Countersinking/shrouding is checked physically**, not just declared: Robot Ruckus's specific wording (screws 'should be countersunk or shrouded') implies an inspector will run a finger or eye over the outer shell looking for proud screw heads that could act as tiny armor studs or catch points.

**Annealed/acid-smoothed parts are pre-approved as a category** (per SCAR's FAQ) so builders don't need to disclose post-processing that doesn't add foreign material — the rule targets *material additives*, coatings like Bondo/epoxy, and reinforcement layers, not heat or solvent treatments of the plastic itself.

**No destructive testing is standard.** Because plastic ant inspection relies on visual/tactile checks and builder honesty backed by the threat of disqualification 'at the Event Organizer's discretion' for violating 'the spirit of the class' (SPARC 4.4.3), the system depends heavily on community trust and the fact that most violations (like a hidden carbon insert) would be visible on close inspection or would show up as an implausible durability advantage in the actual matches, which draws scrutiny from competitors and organizers alike.

chunks.title: Why the Plastic Antweight Class Exists
chunks.body_md:
Plastic antweight exists to solve a specific on-ramp problem in combat robotics: a standard 1lb antweight built to be competitive against titanium/hardened-steel-weaponed opponents typically requires a machine shop, CNC access, or at minimum a mill/lathe and metalworking skill most newcomers don't have. Western Allied Robotics introduced the plastic-only class in 2015 specifically to remove that barrier, and SPARC's official language captures the intent directly: *'to have an easy entry point for new builders and to encourage creative designs by limiting materials to plastics that are easy to work with, commonly used in 3D printers and don't have strength characteristics common in the standard classes.'*

**Accessibility**: A consumer FDM 3D printer costs a fraction of a benchtop mill, needs no specialized safety training, and can be run by a student or hobbyist in a bedroom. Anyone who can draw a shape in free CAD software (Onshape, Fusion 360's free tier, FreeCAD) can go from design to printed part with zero machining skill.

**Cost**: PLA/PETG/ABS filament runs roughly $18-30/kg, and a complete plastic ant chassis rarely uses more than 150-250g of filament — call it $3-8 of raw material for the entire structural half of the robot. Compare that to CNC-machined 7075 aluminum or Delrin stock plus tooling wear for a metal antweight chassis of similar complexity, which easily runs into tens of dollars in material alone before accounting for machine time.

**Damage economics**: This is the biggest practical driver of the class's popularity. When a metal antweight loses a fight to a hardened-steel spinner, repair can mean sourcing and re-machining a replacement part, which might take days and real money. When a plastic ant loses a wedge tip or cracks a weapon disc, the fix is re-slicing the same STL file and printing a replacement overnight for a few cents of filament — the whole philosophy of 'print-and-replace' repairability that pervades the class.

**Why it's the best entry point**: combining low cost, low skill floor, fast iteration (a design change is a CAD edit and a few hours of print time, not a re-machining job), and a large base of freely shared open-source designs (Printables, Thingiverse) means a complete beginner can go from zero to a competing, reasonably durable robot faster and cheaper in plastic ant than in almost any other combat robotics class.

**How the meta differs from metal ants**: because the weapon and armor are made from a weaker, lower-density material, plastic ants cannot rely on the metal-ant playbook of thin hardened cutting edges and high-density armor plates. Instead the class has developed its own meta around thick blunt weapons, generous wall counts, and control/wedge bots that win by denying the opponent's fragile spinner a clean hit — a genuinely different skillset and design philosophy from machining a titanium blade, not just a cheaper version of the same game.

chunks.title: The Plastic Ant Meta: Which Archetypes Dominate and Why
chunks.body_md:
The plastic-only material restriction reshapes which weapon archetypes actually work, producing a meta that looks noticeably different from standard metal antweight.

**Vertical spinners dominate** because a thick printed disc keeps weapon mass close to the rotation axis and strikes with a wide, blunt ring rather than a thin edge — exactly the loading a printed part survives best. A vertical spinner disc is also relatively simple to reprint after damage since it's usually one or two printed parts plus a metal hub/shaft.

**Drum spinners are the second pillar of the meta**, and for similar reasons: a full-width cylindrical drum distributes impact load around its circumference rather than concentrating it at a single tip, so it resists cracking better than a bar of the same weapon weight. Low ground clearance also makes drums hard for opposing wedges to get underneath.

**Horizontal (bar) spinners are comparatively weak in this class** — see the dedicated discussion elsewhere in this file — because the thin tip cross-section that makes a metal bar spinner devastating is also the single most fragile geometry available in the weakest material the rules allow.

**Wedge/control bots punch above their weight class** as both a beginner-friendly first build and a genuine competitive counter-strategy: since fragile plastic weapons are the norm, a robot that simply denies clean hits (via a low, thick, cheap-to-reprint wedge) and wins on driving/ring-outs/judges' decisions is a legitimate way to win matches without ever risking an expensive weapon failure.

**Beater bars and lifters** round out the field as intermediate options — beater bars borrow drum-spinner durability logic in a simpler/cheaper package, while lifters trade weapon speed for control-style scoring opportunities (flips, exposure of an opponent's underside) using printed linkages and small servos instead of pneumatics.

**Why this matters for a new builder**: the single most transferable lesson from the plastic ant meta is that *weapon geometry has to match the material's failure mode*. Printed plastic fails by cracking/delaminating along layer lines under sharp, concentrated, or perpendicular-to-layer loads — so winning weapon designs are the ones that spread load (discs, drums, thick wedges) rather than concentrate it (thin blades, sharp teeth), which is the opposite intuition a builder coming from metal antweight or general engineering might start with.

chunks.title: Why Horizontal Spinners Behave Differently in Plastic
chunks.body_md:
In standard metal antweight, a horizontal (bar) spinner with a hardened tool-steel or titanium tip is one of the most feared weapons in the class: a thin, hard edge concentrates enormous force into a tiny contact area, which is exactly what lets it punch through an opponent's aluminum or polycarbonate armor. In plastic antweight, the exact same geometry becomes one of the *weakest* weapon choices, for reasons rooted directly in how FDM-printed plastic fails.

**The tip has to be plastic.** The rules require the weapon's striking surface to be one of the approved printable plastics — no hardened steel edge is legal. A thin cross-section is the worst possible shape for a printed part because it has the least material spread across the load path and the fewest print layers bonded together resisting a perpendicular impact.

**Layer-line anisotropy compounds the problem.** FDM parts are always weaker across their layer lines than along them ('3D printed parts will always have more strength parallel to their layers as opposed to perpendicular,' as community build guides consistently note). A thin spinning bar takes repeated shock loading at exactly the orientation most likely to peel layers apart at the tip, so bar spinners in this class are disproportionately prone to snapping their own tip off on an early hit — sometimes on the very first swing against a solid target.

**The physics also work against it.** Kinetic energy in a spinning weapon scales with mass and the square of tip speed (KE = 1/2 I omega^2). Because printed plastics are roughly 3-6x less dense than steel, matching a metal bar's stored energy within the same weight budget means either much higher RPM (which raises tip stress and burst risk further) or a physically much larger/thicker bar (which then behaves more like a drum, undercutting the whole point of a thin cutting bar).

**Profile and stability costs.** A bar spinner also typically sits higher and presents a larger flat vertical profile than a low drum or vertical disc, which raises the robot's center of gravity and gives control bots and wedges an easier target to get under or flip.

**Net effect on the meta**: builders who bring a metal-ant bar-spinner mindset into plastic ant consistently find it underperforms drums and vertical spinners, which spread the same kinetic energy across a wider, lower-stress contact area (a disc rim or drum wall) instead of concentrating it at one thin tip — turning 'cutting' into 'blunt ramming,' which is what plastic can actually survive doing to someone else.

chunks.title: TPU Armor and Flexible Structures — Popular, But Check the Rules
chunks.body_md:
A frequently repeated piece of combat-robotics wisdom is that flexible TPU armor 'beats' rigid armor in small weight classes: a rigid PLA/ABS panel absorbs an impact by cracking or shattering, transmitting shock into whatever it's bolted to, while a TPU panel *deflects* under the same impact and springs back to shape, spreading the load over time instead of failing catastrophically. This is genuinely true as material science, and it's why TPU shows up widely in the *general* (metal-legal) antweight and beetleweight scene as flexible skirts, shock-mounted panels, and wheel tires.

**But plastic antweight is where this advice needs a hard caveat.** TPU is not on the SPARC 4.4.1 baseline approved-materials list (PET, PETG, ABS, PLA, PLA+) at all, and SCAR's Plastic Ant FAQ goes further and explicitly *bans TPU by name*, including for custom wheel hubs — one of the few uses that might otherwise seem like an obvious carve-out under the wheels/tires exemption. This makes TPU a genuine org-to-org trap: a builder who read general combat-robotics forum advice praising TPU armor, without separately checking their specific plastic-ant event's material list, can show up with a rules-illegal robot.

**What plastic ant builders do instead, within the approved list:**
- **PETG over PLA/PLA+** for anything expected to take a direct hit, since PETG's more ductile failure mode (bending/cracking slowly) approximates some of TPU's shock-spreading benefit without leaving the approved material family.
- **Print-in-place flexures** — thin, deliberately flexible sections of an otherwise rigid PETG/ABS part, designed as living hinges or shock-absorbing tabs — get some of TPU's benefit from a rules-legal material by using geometry (thin walls) rather than a different filament chemistry to create flex.
- **Where TPU IS explicitly permitted** (some events leave it un-addressed and treat organizer-approved 'additional plastics meeting the spirit of the rules' as covering it, or grant a specific written exception), builders do use it for wheel tires and armor skirts, getting the full flex benefit — but this should never be assumed without confirmation.

**Bottom line**: TPU's flex-beats-rigid advantage is real physics, but its *legality* is the single most variable rule across plastic-ant events reviewed for this file. Always check the specific event's ruleset and FAQ, not general combat-robotics community wisdom, before designing TPU into a competition build.

chunks.title: Designing a Weapon That Must Be Plastic: Blunt Force Over Cutting
chunks.body_md:
Every plastic-ant weapon designer faces the same core constraint: no metal weapon teeth, no hardened cutting edge, no dense tungsten or steel mass concentrated at the tip. The entire striking body of the weapon has to be one of the approved printable plastics. This has pushed the class toward a distinct design doctrine: **blunt force over cutting.**

**Printed drums** are the clearest expression of this doctrine — rather than a thin blade, the weapon is a full cylindrical wall, often 15-25mm thick in PETG, sometimes with small printed paddles or teeth around its circumference. The wall thickness itself (not a sharpened edge) delivers the hit, more like being struck by a rolling pin than cut by a knife. Damage to an opponent comes from blunt impact transferring kinetic energy into denting their armor or knocking them off-balance/into the arena wall, not from penetration.

**Printed discs** for vertical spinners follow the same logic at a smaller scale: a thick disc (often reinforced with a metal hub insert bonded or press-fit into the printed body) with a rounded or lightly toothed rim outperforms a disc with sharp printed teeth, because printed teeth are exactly the thin, stress-concentrated geometry most likely to snap off on first contact.

**What actually does damage without metal teeth**: mass times velocity squared delivered over a wide contact patch. A heavy, slow-spinning printed drum that reliably survives its own hits and knocks an opponent around consistently outperforms a fast, light printed blade that shatters on its first real impact. Community guides repeatedly emphasize over-building the weapon's wall thickness and using more print perimeters/walls than seems necessary, accepting the weight cost, because a weapon that survives to keep hitting is worth more than a lighter one that self-destructs in the first exchange.

**Practical design rules that have emerged**:
- Keep the weapon's outer profile as a smooth curve or wide flat face rather than a pointed tooth wherever possible.
- Orient the print so that the load path runs *along* layer lines, not across them, at the weapon's highest-stress point (often means printing a disc/drum flat rather than on its edge).
- Use a metal shaft/hub insert (explicitly rules-legal as an axle exemption) so the plastic body isn't also trying to survive the torsional load of driving the weapon, only the impact load of hitting something.
- Print weapons in PETG or well-annealed ABS over plain PLA/PLA+ wherever the weapon is expected to take real hits, since both have more ductile (bend-before-break) failure behavior.

chunks.title: Typical Weapon RPM and Tip Speeds Achievable in Plastic
chunks.body_md:
Tip speed — the linear speed of a spinning weapon's outermost point — is the standard way combat robotics talks about weapon power, and it's calculated with the formula SPARC itself uses for its speed-limited classes: **Tip Speed (ft/s) = RPM x diameter (inches) x 0.00436.**

**Typical plastic ant weapon motor/RPM combinations**: small brushless outrunners in the 1811-2205 size class are the norm, run on 2S (7.4V) LiPo. A common vertical-spinner setup pairs a roughly 2600-2800kv outrunner direct-driving (no gearing) a 2-2.5-inch printed disc, giving a free-spin RPM in the 15,000-20,000 RPM range before load, settling lower under real combat load and with the added rotational inertia of the printed disc. Plugging a conservative 12,000 RPM combat-load estimate and a 2.5-inch diameter into the tip-speed formula gives roughly 12,000 x 2.5 x 0.00436 ≈ **131 ft/s** — a meaningful but not extreme tip speed compared to what a similarly-sized metal antweight spinner could sustain.

**Why plastic ants tend to run lower kv/tip speed than metal ants of the same size**: the practical ceiling is set by the printed disc/drum's burst strength, not the motor's capability. Community guidance repeatedly notes that 1400kv motors suit slower horizontal/drum weapons (prioritizing torque and lower stress on the weapon body) while around 2800kv suits lighter vertical spinner discs — both meaningfully lower than the highest-kv motors used in metal-ant record-chasing builds, because a printed weapon spun to the RPM a metal disc could survive would simply fly apart.

**SPARC's formal tip-speed limits** only bind in specific contexts: the 'Sportsman' class caps ordinary spinning weapons at 20 ft/s (with a higher allowance for saw-like weapons meeting a tooth-pitch test), and open-air combat classes cap slow spinners at the same 20 ft/s. Standard enclosed-arena plastic ant classes are not usually tip-speed-limited by the ruleset itself — the practical limit instead comes from the printed material's own failure point, which for a well-designed thick PETG disc or drum tends to land somewhere in the 80-150 ft/s range in community experience, well below what a hardened steel antweight weapon could achieve (some metal antweight spinners exceed 300-400 ft/s), and this gap is treated as a low-confidence estimate based on community reporting rather than a single authoritative source.

*Note: RPM/tip-speed figures are community-sourced estimates, not from a single authoritative measurement; treat as approximate.*

chunks.title: How Matches Are Actually Won: Plastic Ant vs Metal Ant
chunks.body_md:
The path to victory in plastic antweight diverges from standard metal antweight in ways that follow directly from the material restriction.

**In metal antweight**, a well-made hardened-steel spinner or a properly heat-treated blade can end a match in a single clean hit — knockouts and 'kill shots' that disable an opponent's drive or crack their armor open are a realistic, even expected, path to a first-round win for a well-executed weapon build. Damage output per hit is high, and matches often turn on whether a weapon connects cleanly even once.

**In plastic antweight, single-hit knockouts are rarer.** A printed weapon delivers meaningfully less kinetic energy per hit than a metal one of the same weight (lower material density, lower survivable tip speed), and the weapon itself is also more likely to be the first casualty of a hard exchange. This shifts plastic ant matches toward a **war-of-attrition and control-based** win condition more often than metal ant: robots that survive longer, keep functioning after cosmetic damage, and control ring position tend to win on **judges' decision** (aggression, damage, control, strategy scoring) rather than by knockout.

**Control and wedge bots are disproportionately successful** in this environment precisely because they don't depend on a fragile printed weapon surviving the match at all — a robot with nothing to break out-attritions a robot whose weapon might crack on hit one. This is a meaningfully different risk calculus than in metal antweight, where a strong weapon is close to mandatory to be competitive at a top level.

**Damage that does matter**: cracking an opponent's drivetrain access panel, breaking a wheel or wheel hub (printed wheels are as vulnerable as any other printed part), and denting/deforming a chassis enough to jam internal components are the plastic-ant equivalents of the 'kill shots' metal ants chase, rather than clean armor penetration.

**Practical strategic takeaway**: a new builder optimizing for plastic ant win rate should weight 'weapon survives 3 full matches without needing a reprint' above 'weapon deals maximum single-hit damage,' since reliability compounds across a tournament bracket in a way raw power doesn't when the underlying material is the failure-prone part of the system.

chunks.title: Build Spec: Competitive Plastic Ant Vertical Spinner (Full BOM)
chunks.body_md:
A representative, rules-legal competitive plastic ant vertical spinner build, with a full bill of materials summing safely under the 454g limit. Figures are realistic community-typical values; treat exact grams as approximate (confidence: medium) since actual weight varies by printer/settings/hardware batch.

| Part | Material/Spec | Weight (g) |
|---|---|---|
| Chassis/frame (printed, PETG, 5-6 walls, 40% gyroid infill) | PETG | 130 |
| Top shell / weapon guard (printed) | PETG or PLA+ | 90 |
| Vertical spinner disc + hub body (printed) | PETG | 55 |
| Weapon shaft (steel, ~4mm dia, ~35mm long) | steel (exempt) | 5 |
| Flanged bearings x2 (weapon shaft support) | steel/bronze (exempt) | 3 |
| Weapon motor: brushless outrunner ~2600kv | metal/magnet (exempt) | 27 |
| Weapon ESC (micro brushless, ~6A) | electronics (exempt) | 4 |
| Drive motors x2 (N20 micro gearmotor, ~1000 RPM) | metal gearbox (exempt) | 18 |
| Combo RX + dual brushed ESC board | electronics (exempt) | 6 |
| Battery: 2S 300mAh LiPo | LiPo (exempt) | 21 |
| Wheels x2 (printed hub + TPU or COTS foam tire) | printed/COTS (check TPU legality) | 20 |
| Fasteners: M2/M3 screws + heat-set inserts (~20 pcs) | steel/brass (exempt) | 14 |
| Wiring, connectors, switch, foam padding | mixed (exempt) | 12 |
| Paint / decorative finish | paint (permitted) | 5 |
| **Total** | | **~410 g** |

This leaves roughly **44g of headroom** under the 454g limit, typically used to thicken the weapon guard, add a printed skid plate underneath, or carry a small amount of printed ballast for weight distribution.

**Weight budget as percentages**: weapon system (disc+shaft+bearings+motor+ESC = 94g) ≈ **23%**, drive system (motors+wheels+combo board = 44g) ≈ **11%**, armor/structure (chassis+shell = 220g) ≈ **54%**, electronics (battery+wiring = 33g) ≈ **8%**, fasteners ≈ **3%**. The armor/structure share is dramatically higher than a typical metal antweight's, which is the single biggest structural difference the plastic-only rule creates in how weight gets allocated.

**Rules-legality notes**: the disc, shell and chassis are all printed PETG/PLA+ (approved list); the shaft, bearings, motor, ESC, fasteners, wiring and battery are all covered by the standard motors/electronics/axles/fasteners/adhesives exemption; wheel tire material should be confirmed against the specific event's TPU policy before finalizing.

chunks.title: Build Spec: Plastic Ant Control/Wedge Bot (Full BOM)
chunks.body_md:
A representative plastic ant control/wedge build — no fragile spinning weapon, built to win on driving, ring control, and durability. Figures are realistic community-typical values (confidence: medium).

| Part | Material/Spec | Weight (g) |
|---|---|---|
| Chassis + integrated front wedge (printed, thick front face 4-6mm) | PETG | 180 |
| Top shell/armor | PETG or PLA+ | 70 |
| Drive motors x2 (higher-torque micro gearmotor) | metal gearbox (exempt) | 24 |
| Small active-wedge/lifter servo (optional) | electronics/metal gears (exempt) | 15 |
| Combo RX + dual brushed ESC board | electronics (exempt) | 6 |
| Battery: 2S 400mAh LiPo (bigger pack, no weapon to power) | LiPo (exempt) | 26 |
| Wheels x2 (printed hub + grippy foam/TPU tire) | printed/COTS | 18 |
| Fasteners: M2/M3 screws + inserts | steel/brass (exempt) | 14 |
| Wiring, switch, connectors | mixed (exempt) | 8 |
| Printed ballast plug (high-infill, fills remaining budget for pushing power) | PETG/PLA+ | 90 |
| **Total** | | **~451 g** |

**Design rationale**: a control bot deliberately spends almost nothing on 'weapon' (just an optional small active-wedge servo) and instead maximizes armor thickness and low-CG ballast to win pushing matches and resist being flipped. The printed ballast plug is a simple, cheap, 100%-legal way to use the full weight budget when there's no weapon consuming it — solid PETG at high infill is denser and cheaper than any COTS metal ballast option would be to source, and it's trivially plastic-legal since it's just more of the same approved material.

**Weight budget as percentages**: armor/structure (chassis+wedge+shell = 250g) ≈ **55%**, drive (motors+wheels+combo board = 48g) ≈ **11%**, weapon/active-wedge servo (15g) ≈ **3%**, electronics (battery+wiring = 34g) ≈ **8%**, fasteners ≈ **3%**, ballast (90g) ≈ **20%**.

**Why this archetype is recommended as a first build**: every failure mode here (a cracked wedge, a worn wheel, a stripped screw hole) is a five-minute reprint or hardware-store fix, unlike a broken weapon motor mount or a snapped weapon shaft, which are common failure points on a first spinner build and are considerably more frustrating and costly to diagnose and fix mid-tournament.

chunks.title: Build Spec: Absolute-Cheapest First Plastic Ant
chunks.body_md:
For a builder trying to spend as little as possible on a first legal, functional plastic ant (excluding a transmitter/charger they may already own, or plan to reuse across future robots), a minimal control-style build looks roughly like this. Prices are rough 2020s-hobby-market estimates and will vary by region/vendor/sales (confidence: low).

| Part | Approx. cost (USD) | Weight (g) |
|---|---|---|
| Filament (PLA, own printer) for a simple wedge chassis, ~150g of material | $2-3 | 150 |
| Drive motors x2 (N20 micro gearmotor, generic) | $6-8 | 20 |
| Combo RX + dual brushed ESC board (budget option) | $15-20 | 5 |
| Battery: 1S 300-500mAh LiPo | $5-7 | 12 |
| Wheels x2 (printed hub + O-ring or scrap-rubber tire) | ~$1-2 (mostly free with scrap) | 12 |
| Fasteners (from a hardware bin / cheap multi-pack) | $2 | 10 |
| Wiring, switch, connector (from a cheap electronics assortment kit) | $3 | 6 |
| **Incremental robot cost (excl. transmitter/charger)** | **≈ $35-42** | **≈ 215 g** |

**One-time reusable costs not counted above** (a builder typically already owns these or buys them once for many future robots): a basic FlySky-compatible or similar hobby transmitter (~$35-45) and a LiPo-safe charger (~$20-30).

**Note the large weight headroom**: this minimal build uses only about 215g of the 454g budget. Because filament is so cheap relative to the total build cost, the single best 'free' upgrade for a first-time builder is to simply print the chassis with **more walls and higher infill** than the bare minimum — using the full weight budget costs perhaps an extra $1-2 of filament but meaningfully increases durability, since the marginal cost of plastic mass is far lower than the marginal cost of any other component in this class. A cheapest-build budget should therefore prioritize spending the saved money on better electronics reliability (a name-brand combo board over the cheapest option) rather than on unnecessary weapon parts, and spend the 'free' leftover weight budget on structural thickness rather than leaving it unused.

**No weapon in this build** — it is deliberately a bare-minimum control/wedge robot, both because it's the cheapest path to a functional, rules-legal, competition-ready first robot and because it avoids the weapon motor/ESC/shaft/bearing costs (which together typically add $35-50+ to a first build) entirely.

chunks.title: Print Material Choice Per Part
chunks.body_md:
Not every part of a plastic ant should be printed in the same filament; matching material properties to each part's job is a core competitive skill in this class.

**PLA / PLA+ — chassis shells, low-stress structural parts, prototypes.** PLA is the easiest of the approved materials to print reliably (low warp, no enclosure needed, prints cool at 190-215C) and is fine for parts that see moderate load but aren't the primary impact-absorbing structure — electronics trays, standoffs, brackets, and early prototype iterations where print speed and reliability matter more than ultimate toughness. PLA+ specifically markets improved impact resistance over plain PLA while keeping PLA's easy-print behavior, making it a reasonable default for a first build's chassis.

**PETG — weapon discs/drums, load-bearing chassis rails, anything expected to take a direct hit.** PETG's more ductile failure mode (it bends and cracks slowly rather than shattering) makes it the community's most-recommended choice for any part that will actually absorb combat impact, at the cost of slightly trickier print tuning (more prone to stringing, needs dialed-in retraction settings) and marginally higher density (1.27 g/cm3 vs PLA's 1.24 g/cm3).

**ABS — weight-critical parts, acetone-smoothed weapons.** ABS is the lowest-density of the commonly used approved plastics (1.04 g/cm3) and can be acetone-vapor-smoothed, which welds surface layer lines together for extra strength at the outer surface — a real advantage for a weapon disc's outer rim. The tradeoff is that ABS needs an enclosed, heated-chamber printer to avoid warping, making it a more advanced-builder's material choice than PLA or PETG.

**TPU — flexible armor/tires, WHERE LOCALLY LEGAL ONLY.** TPU is not on the SPARC baseline list and is explicitly banned by SCAR's FAQ; never design it into a competition part without confirming the specific event's rules first (see the dedicated TPU/org-variance discussion elsewhere in this file).

**Nylon — generally avoid for competition use.** Nylon's toughness makes it tempting for gears/wear parts, but it sits outside the base approved list and is explicitly banned by SCAR by name; its moisture sensitivity also makes it one of the harder approved-adjacent materials to print reliably even where it might be allowed.

**Practical per-part guide**: chassis body → PLA+ or PETG; weapon disc/drum → PETG (or well-annealed ABS for advanced builders); wheel hub → PLA+ or PETG (any of the rigid approved plastics work); armor shell over electronics → PETG for its ductility; brackets/standoffs → PLA is fine, they rarely take direct impact.

chunks.title: Print Settings That Survive Combat
chunks.body_md:
Slicer settings for a decorative print and a combat-ready plastic ant part are worlds apart. The following settings reflect community-standard practice for parts expected to take real impact (chassis, weapon bodies, wedges); brackets and non-structural parts can use lighter settings to save print time and weight.

**Wall count (perimeters): 5-8+, up from a typical decorative 2-3.** Since the solid outer walls carry most of an impact load (far more than the infill lattice inside), combat parts intentionally run many more perimeters than a normal print. Some builders go further and print small/critical parts at essentially 100% infill by using enough walls that no internal infill pattern is needed at all.

**Infill: 40-100%, gyroid or cubic pattern, up from a typical 15-20%.** Gyroid infill in particular is popular in the community for combat parts because it provides fairly even strength in multiple directions, which matters when a weapon disc or wedge can be hit from an unpredictable angle. The weight cost is accepted deliberately, since (as covered in the build-spec chunks) armor/structure legitimately consumes the majority of a plastic ant's weight budget.

**Layer height: 0.15-0.2mm is typical**, balancing print time against slightly better layer bonding than a faster 0.28-0.3mm layer height would give (thinner layers generally bond a bit better, improving the class's biggest weak point: interlayer strength).

**Print orientation is the single highest-leverage decision.** Because printed plastic is much stronger along its layer lines than across them, parts should be oriented so the primary expected impact load runs *parallel* to the layers wherever geometry allows — for example, printing a weapon disc flat (layers stacked along the spin axis) rather than on its edge, so a radial impact loads the print in-plane rather than trying to peel layers apart.

**Nozzle temperature and print speed**: run at the filament manufacturer's recommended temperature (often slightly hot-end of the suggested range for PETG/ABS specifically) to maximize interlayer adhesion, even at the cost of slightly worse surface finish or more stringing — strength matters more than cosmetics for a fighting robot.

**Post-processing (where the local ruleset allows it)**: annealing (baking below the plastic's melt point, sometimes packed in sand to control warping) can meaningfully improve a part's layer strength and heat resistance after printing, and is explicitly permitted post-processing under at least one major event's FAQ (SCAR). Acetone vapor smoothing on ABS parts can similarly weld outer layers together for extra surface toughness.

chunks.title: Design Patterns: Sacrificial Panels, Modular Sections, Flexures, 5-Minute Pit Repairs
chunks.body_md:
The plastic ant class has developed a recognizable set of design patterns around one central goal: make damage cheap and fast to fix, since the material itself is the class's core weakness.

**Sacrificial armor panels.** Rather than building one thick, monolithic shell, many designs place deliberately weaker, easily-detachable printed panels over the most exposed or vulnerable areas (electronics bay covers, corners most likely to take a hit). A hit cracks or pops off the sacrificial panel — which is designed to be reprinted in well under an hour — while the main chassis underneath stays intact. This trades a small amount of redundant weight for a much shorter repair time than a crack propagating into a load-bearing main-chassis part would cause.

**Modular bolt-on sections.** Splitting the robot into independently printed, bolted-together modules (a separate front wedge/weapon pod, a separate drive base, a separate top shell) means a single damaged module can be swapped for a spare without remaking the whole robot. Competitive builders commonly print two or three spares of the most failure-prone module (usually the weapon pod or wedge tip) before an event specifically so a pit repair is a bolt-swap, not a print-and-wait.

**Printed-in flexures (living hinges).** Instead of a separate metal hinge and pin, a thin flexible section printed as part of a single larger piece can act as a spring or hinge — used for snap-fit access panels, simple lifter linkages, or shock-absorbing tabs, staying entirely within the approved-plastic material list (unlike reaching for TPU) by using geometry rather than filament chemistry to create flex.

**The five-minute pit repair philosophy.** The defining repairability advantage of plastic ant over metal antweight is that most damage is fixed by re-slicing an existing STL and printing a replacement, not by re-machining a part from raw stock. Competitive pit strategy reflects this directly: bringing a laptop with the robot's CAD/slicer files and a portable 3D printer to the event (increasingly common at plastic-ant-focused events) lets a builder print a replacement wedge or wheel between matches rather than being eliminated by damage that would end a metal antweight's tournament run outright.

**Practical takeaway for new builders**: design for disassembly and reprintability from the very first CAD sketch, not as an afterthought — split your chassis at natural stress-concentration points (so a crack there just separates a module rather than propagating through the whole robot), and always keep spare printed copies of your most failure-prone single part ready before you arrive at an event.

chunks.title: Where the Plastic Ant Community Shares Designs
chunks.body_md:
Plastic antweight has one of the most open, actively-shared design cultures in combat robotics, which is itself part of why the class is such a strong entry point — a beginner rarely has to design a robot completely from scratch.

**Printables** (printables.com, Prusa's model-sharing platform) hosts several named open-source plastic ant designs, including **Force Knight**, a free 1lb plastic antweight by community designer Michael K described as intended for SCAR-legal component kits, and a community-shared 3D-printed drum spinner design demonstrating the drum-spinner-as-durability-choice pattern discussed throughout this file.

**Thingiverse** hosts additional well-known open designs, including the **CRNZ Antweight Combat Robot Kit** by CombatRoboticsNZ — an explicitly modular, extensible printable chassis meant to be a base other builders customize and upgrade rather than a fixed one-off design — and, on the UK 150g side of the naming divide, **Legally Distinct**, a drum spinner by community designer Blessy openly credited as inspired by the established UK antweight Siren.

**Cults3D** also lists purchasable/downloadable plastic ant model files (e.g., a specifically-tagged 'Plastic 1lb Antweight Vertical Spinner' design), functioning similarly to Printables/Thingiverse but with more paid listings mixed among free ones.

**Onshape and other cloud CAD tools** are widely used for public, shareable combat-robot CAD documents in the broader combat robotics community (a pattern well established in metal antweight/beetleweight circles), letting other builders view, fork, and remix a design's actual parametric CAD rather than just a fixed STL — though specific named public plastic-ant Onshape documents were not independently confirmed in the sources reviewed for this file (confidence: low on Onshape specifically, though the practice is well-established in the wider community).

**Discord servers** run by regional combat robotics clubs and larger events (SCAR, Robot Ruckus, and similar organizations typically maintain one) are the community's primary place for real-time build questions, rules clarifications ('is X material legal at your event'), and informal design-sharing outside the more formal model-repository sites — a pattern consistent with how modern hobbyist engineering communities generally organize online, though this file was not able to confirm specific named plastic-ant Discord servers independently (confidence: low on specific server names).

**RobotCombatWiki** (robotcombatwiki.com) serves as the community's reference wiki, with a dedicated 'Plastic Antweights' page summarizing the class's rules and history, plus a general '3D Printing' page covering combat-specific printing advice that applies directly to this class.

**Practical entry point for a new builder**: starting from an existing open-source design (Force Knight, CRNZ's kit, or a Cults3D vertical spinner) and modifying it, rather than designing a first chassis from a blank CAD canvas, is both common and explicitly encouraged by how these designs are shared and licensed.

chunks.title: Weapon and Drive Motor Selection for Plastic Ants
chunks.body_md:
Motor selection in plastic ant follows the same electronics landscape as standard antweight (motors are exempt from the plastic-only rule), but the *sizing philosophy* differs because the weapon it drives has a lower burst strength ceiling.

**Drive motors**: small brushed gearmotors dominate, most commonly the N20-size micro metal gearmotor family (roughly 10g each, available in gear ratios from crawler-slow to sprint-fast) or a 130-size can motor paired with a small gearbox. A control/wedge bot generally wants a lower, torquier gear ratio to maximize pushing power; a spinner-focused build can run a faster ratio since it relies on its weapon rather than raw ramming force to win exchanges.

**Weapon motors**: small brushless outrunners in the 1811-2205 size class, run on 2S, are the standard choice. Kv selection is the key design lever: roughly **2600-2800kv suits light vertical spinner discs**, prioritizing RPM within the printed disc's survivable range, while **1400kv suits heavier drums/horizontal weapons**, prioritizing torque to spin up a heavier printed weapon body without stalling, at a lower top RPM that's kinder to the weapon's burst strength.

**ESC pairing**: drive motors typically run off a combo RX+dual-brushed-ESC board (saving weight over separate receiver and ESC units), while the weapon motor needs its own small brushless ESC (roughly 4-6g, 6A-class is usually sufficient for these small outrunners) since a brushed combo board can't drive a brushless motor.

**Why plastic ants don't chase the highest-kv motors available**: unlike metal antweight, where a builder can push a hardened steel disc to very high RPM because the disc can survive it, a plastic ant's practical RPM ceiling is set by the printed weapon's burst strength, not the motor or ESC's capability. Overdriving a light printed disc past its survivable RPM is a common beginner mistake that results in the weapon flying apart (sometimes literally, as shrapnel) on its very first spin-up test, well before the robot ever reaches a match. Community practice is to start conservative on kv/voltage and incrementally test spin-up rather than assuming the motor's rated RPM is a safe operating target for the printed weapon attached to it.

chunks.title: Why driving beats design at antweight
chunks.body_md:
The single most common mistake a new antweight builder makes is believing the robot decides the match. At 1 lb it mostly does not. Here is why.

**The robots are close in capability.** Antweight is a mature class with well-known parts. Most competitive robots in a bracket have similar motors, similar batteries and similar energy. The spread in driver skill is far wider than the spread in robot quality.

**Engagement is a driving problem.** Bite depends on closing speed. Getting under depends on approach angle. Avoiding a horizontal's sweep depends on timing. Every one of those is the driver, not the robot.

**Matches are decided in the first five seconds.** The box rush — charging before the opponent's weapon is up — wins an enormous share of antweight matches, and both executing it and defending it are pure driving.

**Damaged robots still drive.** A robot that has lost its weapon can still win on control if the driver knows how. A robot with a dead side can still be driven in circles well enough to survive to a decision. Both require practice you can only get by driving.

What to actually practise, in order of value:

1. **The first three seconds.** Set up, count down, and execute your opening. Do it fifty times.
2. **Driving inverted.** Flip the robot over and drive the same course. Use your transmitter's invert switch so the controls make sense.
3. **Angled approaches.** Never drive straight at anything. Practise arriving at 30-45 degrees, which is where bite and wedge geometry both favour you.
4. **One side dead.** Unplug a drive motor and learn to steer on one side. You will need this.
5. **Wall work.** Pinning, carrying and pushing out all use the arena. Learn where the walls help you.

A cheap robot with a practised driver beats an expensive robot with an unpractised one, reliably, at this weight class.

chunks.title: The box rush: executing it and defending it
chunks.body_md:
The box rush is charging the opponent the instant the match starts, before their weapon reaches speed. It is the highest-value opening in antweight because spinners are helpless during spin-up and spin-up takes seconds.

**Executing one.** You need a robot that is dangerous immediately — a wedge, a control bot, or a spinner with a very short spin-up. Line up square to the opponent, commit fully on the count, and aim to arrive under them before their weapon is useful. Against a spinner, getting under it during spin-up often wins the match outright: you pin it, it never spins up, and you bank three minutes of control.

**Defending one.** Several layers, use as many as apply:

- **Spin up before the count** if your event's rules allow it. Many do. This removes the entire vulnerability.
- **Start at an angle,** not square on. A rushing opponent has to change direction to reach you, and changing direction costs them speed.
- **Reverse off the line.** Backing away buys a second of spin-up and forces the rusher to cross the arena again.
- **Build a safe front.** If your robot's front face is safe to be hit at any weapon speed — thick armour, wedgelets, nothing fragile exposed — a box rush costs you position rather than the match.
- **Shorten your spin-up.** This is a design fix: less weapon inertia, more motor torque, higher cell count. A weapon that is up in one second cannot be box-rushed meaningfully.
