chunks.title: BattleBots: The TV-Scale Heavyweight Standard
chunks.body_md:
BattleBots is the most visible combat robotics competition to the general public, run as a televised series with a single professional-tier weight class: 250 lb (113 kg) ready-to-fight, with an allowance up to 500 lb for a robot that qualifies as a true walker using articulated legs and meets additional design criteria BattleBots specifies. This mirrors the same 100%-bonus-for-true-walkers pattern used across essentially every other ruleset in the sport, just at a far larger absolute mass than hobby classes.

One distinctive BattleBots requirement is a functional test for lifting/grappling weapons: any robot entering with a lifter, flipper, or grappling weapon must demonstrate, as part of pre-event inspection, that the weapon can actually lift 250 lb to a height of 12 inches. This is a meaningful bar — it means a flipper can't just look impressive on paper or in CAD, it has to prove it can flip a full-weight opponent in a live functional test before being cleared to compete, which keeps underpowered 'flippers' from entering the arena only to fail on air.

Every robot goes through BattleBots' full in-person technical and safety inspection, commonly referred to as 'the box,' before being cleared to fight — a far more rigorous process than most hobby-scale events can afford to run, reflecting both the higher stakes (250 lb robots at full power are genuinely dangerous) and BattleBots' larger operating budget and professional crew.

When a match runs the full duration without a knockout, BattleBots' published Judges' Guide (recent seasons) uses an 11-point scale per judge across a 3-judge panel: 5 points for Damage, 3 points for Aggression, and 3 points for Control. Damage is scored on the relative amount of non-cosmetic damage dealt to each robot — including self-inflicted damage and any system that stops working correctly by the end of the match, whether or not it looks visually dramatic. Aggression is scored on the frequency, severity, boldness, and intent of attacks a robot deliberately initiates against its opponent, rewarding a robot that presses the fight rather than one that merely survives. Control is scored on how well and how long a robot dictates the terms of the fight — pushing the opponent around, lifting it, pinning it, or using arena hazards/walls against it. This point split is not permanent: ahead of the BattleBots Pro League in 2026, the judging system was revised to merge Aggression with a new 'Engagement' concept into a single 5-point scored category, so competitors and analysts should always check the current season's official Judges' Guide rather than assume any one year's exact split carries forward. What has stayed constant across seasons is the baseline mechanical requirement: 250 lb standard weight, 500 lb walker allowance, and the mandatory 250 lb-to-12-inch lift test for any lifting/grappling weapon system.

chunks.title: Antweight World Series (AWS): The UK's Antweight-Scale Standard
chunks.body_md:
The Antweight World Series (AWS), administered in association with Bristol Bot Builders, is the primary UK/European ruleset for antweight-scale combat robotics, and it is built around a materially different, much lighter class ladder than the US SPARC standard: Antweight at 150 g (roller) / 225 g (non-roller), Fleaweight at 75 g / 113 g, and Nanoweight at 25 g / 38 g. There is no US equivalent to Fleaweight or Nanoweight at all — the US ladder's lightest class (1 lb antweight, or SPARC's own separately-named Fairyweight at 150 g) doesn't go nearly as small.

AWS's radio rules reflect the UK scene's longer history with analog and early digital RC systems: it explicitly permits 27 MHz, 40 MHz, 418 MHz, 433-434 MHz, 868 MHz, and 2.45 GHz, a wider allowed-frequency list than most modern 2.4GHz-only US rulesets, likely preserving compatibility with older UK-legal surface radio-control gear still in circulation at hobbyist level. Battery rules cap voltage at 24V and explicitly prohibit any battery containing liquid acid or free electrolyte (ruling out traditional wet-cell chemistries entirely, though this is largely moot in an era of LiPo/LiFe dominance).

Weapon safety rules under AWS are detailed: weapons must be remotely deactivable, any pressurized system (CO2, pneumatics) is capped at 100 psi (7 bar), and any detachable weapon component must remain tethered to the robot with a maximum tether length of 3 feet (914 mm) to prevent it becoming an uncontrolled projectile. The banned-weapons list closely tracks what other rulesets prohibit but is phrased slightly differently: glue or sticky-pad weapons, fluid-based weapons, string/entanglement weapons, flame-based weapons, using electricity itself as a weapon (e.g. deliberately shocking an opponent), explosive weapons, rotating weapons judged prone to shattering (a specific concern given how small and fast antweight-scale spinners can spin), and magnetic/inductive systems intended to interfere with an opponent.

Match structure: 3-minute maximum matches, a 10-second immobility countdown that ends a fight if one robot shows no controlled movement, a 20-second cap on pinning before release is required, and an automatic loss for any robot that touches the bottom of an arena pit. Clusterbots that mix roller and non-roller sub-units use an explicit formula — Roller weight allowance = Roller class limit − (2/3 × total non-roller weight) — to fairly balance the roller/non-roller weight bonus across a multi-unit entry rather than letting teams stack cheap non-roller mass to inflate their effective roller allowance.

chunks.title: Banned Weapons and Materials: What Every Major Org Agrees On
chunks.body_md:
Despite differences in wording, weight classes, and judging systems, the major combat robotics rulesets (SPARC, NHRL, RoboGames, BattleBots, AWS/UK) converge on nearly the same core list of banned weapons and materials, because the underlying safety reasoning is identical everywhere: nothing that endangers spectators/officials beyond the arena barrier, nothing that permanently contaminates the arena surface for the next match, and nothing that makes damage impossible for judges/audiences to verify.

**Liquids and fluids**: banned almost everywhere, though NHRL's wording shows the two narrow exceptions most rulesets implicitly share: liquid expelled from the robot is banned generally, but liquid used purely as a fuel source is allowed, and liquid that turns gaseous shortly after leaving the robot (or before hitting the opponent) is also allowed — i.e. the ban targets a lasting liquid mess or a liquid weapon effect, not incidental fuel or something that evaporates before it can contaminate anything. AWS specifically calls out both 'fluid-based weapons' and separately bans batteries containing liquid acid or electrolyte.

**Untethered and over-speed projectiles**: NHRL puts a hard number on this where many rulesets only say 'no projectiles' — any projectile weapon is capped at 150 mph, and even a tethered projectile must not be designed in a way likely to become entangled with the opponent (blurring into the separate entanglement ban). NHRL defines entanglement itself precisely as any component 'designed to be entangled in the rotational or moving parts of the opponent,' a definition broad enough to cover string, tape, nets, or a deliberately snagging weapon geometry.

**Fire and flame**: banned by default everywhere, though a few large, heavily-supervised events (RoboGames, historically some BattleBots-adjacent exhibitions) allow specially pre-approved, licensed flamethrower weapons under strict extra safety conditions — this is very much the exception, not the rule, and never available at the antweight/beetleweight club level.

**Entanglement**: nets, string, tape, or any device meant to tangle an opponent's weapon or drivetrain is banned nearly everywhere (SPARC, RoboGames, AWS) because it can permanently disable a robot in a way that isn't 'damage' judges can score, and can be dangerous to retrieve after a match. A notable named exception: Germany's RoboGames-adjacent scene has historically permitted entanglement in a separate, clearly-labeled 'net-fighting' side bracket rather than mainstream weight-class combat.

**RF jamming / EMP / electrical weapons**: banned everywhere, since deliberately interfering with an opponent's radio control (rather than beating it in a fair fight) also risks jamming other robots' or the arena's own radio-linked safety systems — an inherently unacceptable risk at any event running multiple simultaneous transmitters.

**Untethered projectiles**: banned nearly universally (RoboGames explicitly, AWS via its tethered-weapon rule, SPARC generally) because anything that can leave the robot uncontrolled is an immediate spectator-safety hazard; where a detachable weapon component is allowed at all, it must remain tethered (AWS: 3 ft / 914 mm max).

**Explosives and hazardous materials**: universally banned, including flammable solids, and most rulesets also prohibit powders, sand, ball bearings, foams, and liquefied gases specifically because of arena-surface contamination risk (explicit in RoboGames' rules) rather than direct combat danger alone.

**Materials at the plastic-class level**: this is a narrower, class-specific restriction rather than a safety ban — plastic antweight/beetleweight forbid TPU, nylon, and fiber-reinforced composite filaments, not because they're dangerous, but to preserve the class's low-cost, low-damage design intent.

A builder moving between organizations should still read each event's current rulebook in full, since specific wording, exceptions (like Germany's net-fighting bracket), and edge cases (what counts as an 'approved' flamethrower, or exactly which magnetic effects are banned) do vary, but the underlying philosophy — no liquids, no uncontrolled fire, no entanglement, no jamming, no loose projectiles, no explosives — is close to universal across every major hobby ruleset in this research.

chunks.title: Core Safety Systems: Power Switches, Weapon Locks, and Radio Fail-Safes
chunks.body_md:
Three safety systems appear on essentially every rulebook's inspection checklist regardless of weight class or organization, because they address the three most common ways a combat robot can hurt someone outside the arena: an accidentally-live robot, an accidentally-spinning weapon during handling, and a robot that keeps moving after its driver loses control.

**Main power disconnect / removable link**: every ruleset requires a way to fully cut power to the robot's motors and weapon that doesn't require tools and can be operated quickly by the builder or a marshal. RoboGames is explicit about timing: the disconnect must be operable within 15 seconds without endangering the operator, and full deactivation of the robot must be achievable within 60 seconds. AWS (UK) simply requires it be 'externally accessible' and operable 'without tools.' Larger classes often add a secondary, more certain isolation method — a physically removable link or jumper that a marshal can pull even if a switch has failed or is hard to reach — on top of the primary switch, precisely because a bigger, more dangerous robot deserves more than one way to guarantee it goes dead.

**Weapon lock**: any robot with a weapon capable of moving under its own power (a spinning disc/drum, a lifting arm, a hammer) must have a physical lock fitted whenever it is powered on outside the arena — during transport, pit setup, and staging before a match. RoboGames requires this lock to be a clearly visible, high-visibility color (neon orange or similar) specifically so an inspector or bystander can tell at a glance whether a weapon is safed or live; NHRL requires a lock that prevents a spinning weapon from moving 'outside of the cage,' i.e. it must contain the weapon even if it somehow spins up unexpectedly. Locks are fitted before power-on and removed only once the robot is placed in the arena and the match is about to begin.

**Radio fail-safe**: the receiver/ESC system must be programmed so that losing the transmitter signal (turned off, out of range, battery dies, interference) causes all motion — drive and weapon alike — to stop immediately, rather than continuing at whatever the last received command was (which could mean a weapon left spinning at full speed or a drivetrain left driving into a wall or an official). This is tested directly at inspection: an inspector or the driver deliberately powers off or unplugs the transmitter while the robot is live, and watches to confirm the robot goes fully inert. NHRL calls this out as a mandatory pass/fail test every robot must clear before competing; AWS requires the same behavior ('robot shall cease all motion when the controlling transmitter is switched off') as a hard rule.

Together these three systems form the backbone of virtually every technical inspection checklist in the sport: an inspector will check for a functioning, accessible power disconnect, a properly colored and fitted weapon lock, and a passing fail-safe test, typically in that order, before moving on to weight, dimensions, and weapon-specific checks.

chunks.title: LiPo Battery Handling, Charging, and Arena Requirements
chunks.body_md:
Lithium-polymer (LiPo) batteries are the dominant power source across nearly every combat robot weight class, from plastic antweight up through TV-scale heavyweights, because of their excellent power-to-weight ratio — but that same energy density makes them the single most common fire-safety concern at any event, and pit safety rules around LiPo handling are taken very seriously after real incidents, including LiPo fires in the pit area at RoboGames 2017 that led directly to fireproof battery bags becoming mandatory rather than optional at many events afterward.

The near-universal practices that show up across event safety documents are: charge only inside a fireproof LiPo charging bag or a vented metal/ammo-can-style box, never inside a plastic tote, cardboard box, or bare on a table; never leave a battery charging unattended, even briefly — an unattended charging LiPo is treated as a serious pit-safety violation that can get a competitor removed from the event; inspect every battery before use for physical damage (punctures, cuts to the outer wrap, bent or corroded connectors) and especially for swelling/puffing, which indicates internal damage and means the cell should be retired immediately rather than risked in a fight; and never allow a battery to be crushed, punctured, or have its leads crossed/shorted, since any of these can trigger thermal runaway — the battery catching fire or venting violently.

Beyond individual battery handling, arena and venue-level requirements exist specifically because of LiPo risk: venues are commonly expected to be ventilated for roughly one full air exchange every 60 seconds, and any area where LiPo batteries are present (pits, charging stations, staging areas) should have a clear, obstruction-free evacuation route to open air, since a LiPo fire can produce toxic smoke quickly. AWS's rules add an antweight-specific voltage cap of 24V, and require that batteries not contain liquid acid or free electrolyte — ruling out old-style wet-cell chemistries entirely, though this is now largely a non-issue given LiPo and LiFe's dominance at every scale from fairyweight up.

For an antweight or plastic-antweight builder specifically, the practical rules of thumb that follow directly from event safety requirements are: buy a small fireproof LiPo bag (they are inexpensive and reusable across a builder's entire career), always charge in that bag on a non-flammable surface away from anything combustible, never charge overnight or walk away mid-charge, retire any cell that develops even mild puffing rather than trying to "get one more fight" out of it, and store spare batteries at storage voltage (roughly 3.8V/cell) rather than full charge when not competing soon, since long-term storage at full charge accelerates degradation and swelling risk.

chunks.title: Match Length, Win Conditions, and Judging Criteria
chunks.body_md:
Match structure is one of the more standardized parts of combat robotics rules across organizations: nearly every event, from UK antweight club nights to NHRL and BattleBots, runs 3-minute matches as the default duration, with the winner decided by one of a small set of standard outcomes rather than a running score kept throughout the fight.

**Win conditions, in rough order of how often they end a match**:
1. **Knockout (KO) / immobility**: a robot that shows no controlled, purposeful movement for a set count (commonly 10 seconds, as under AWS) is ruled out. Some rulesets apply this as a strict referee-operated countdown clock; others leave it to referee judgment of what counts as 'controlled movement' (e.g. a weapon still spinning uselessly on a robot that can no longer drive may or may not count as 'movement' depending on the event).
2. **Tap-out**: a driver can voluntarily concede to stop a match early, most often used when a robot is clearly beaten and continuing risks unnecessary damage or a safety issue (a stuck weapon, smoke, exposed wiring).
3. **Pit fall / arena hazard**: at venues with a pit or built-in hazard, touching the bottom of the pit is treated as an automatic loss under UK/AWS-style rules; most US hobby-class arenas are flat boxes without hazards, so this mainly applies to specific event designs.
4. **Judges' decision**: if the full match time elapses with both robots still mobile and neither has tapped out, a panel (commonly 3 judges) decides the winner. RoboGames formalizes this most explicitly: each judge scores Aggression (0-5 points) and Damage (0-6 points) independently, for 11 points per judge and 33 total across the panel. Damage is typically bucketed into severity tiers (trivial, cosmetic, minor, significant, major, massive) before being converted into points, and aggression specifically credits 'translational movement toward the opponent' rather than just activity in place. Other organizations (BattleBots, NHRL) also judge on a mix of damage, aggression, and control, but publish less granular public point breakdowns than RoboGames.

**Pinning and cornering limits**: to prevent a robot from winning simply by holding an opponent against a wall or under itself without actively fighting, most rulesets cap how long a pin can be held — 15 seconds under RoboGames, 20 seconds under AWS — after which the pinning robot must back off enough to give the opponent a real chance to escape or continue fighting; cornering an opponent against the arena wall is generally treated the same as a physical pin for this purpose.

**Between-match logistics**: some organizations also specify minimum time between a team's matches (RoboGames references a 40-minute minimum gap) to give builders enough time for repairs, battery swaps, and re-inspection before their next fight — a detail that matters a lot for a plastic antweight builder who may need to reprint or hot-glue a cracked chassis between rounds.

chunks.title: What a Technical/Safety Inspector Actually Checks
chunks.body_md:
Every combat robot, from a $30 plastic antweight to a $50,000 BattleBots heavyweight, passes through a technical and safety inspection before it is allowed to compete, and while the depth of inspection scales enormously with weight class, the checklist items are drawn from the same underlying list everywhere. For an antweight or plastic-antweight builder showing up to their first event, a realistic run-through of what an inspector checks looks roughly like this, in a typical order:

1. **Weigh-in**: the robot, fully assembled and ready to fight (batteries installed, all fasteners tight, nothing missing), is placed on a scale and must be at or under the class limit (e.g. 454 g for US antweight, 150 g for UK antweight/fairyweight, or the appropriate walker-bonus weight if claiming that allowance). Many inspectors also re-verify weight after any mid-event repair.
2. **Dimension/footprint check**: some rulesets (notably AWS/UK) also require the robot fit within a defined footprint (150mm x 150mm square for UK antweight-scale classes) with no overhang at any height, checked with a simple frame or template.
3. **Power disconnect check**: the inspector locates and tests the main power switch or removable link, confirming it is externally accessible, operable without tools, and actually cuts all power when used.
4. **Weapon lock check**: for any robot with an active weapon, the inspector confirms a proper high-visibility lock is fitted and prevents the weapon from moving while power is on, and that it's easy for pit staff to see at a glance whether the robot is 'safe' or 'live.'
5. **Radio fail-safe test**: the inspector or driver arms the robot, then deliberately turns off or unplugs the transmitter while watching the robot; a pass means all motion (drive and weapon) stops immediately, and repeats may be requested to rule out a fluke.
6. **Battery/wiring check**: batteries are inspected for physical damage, swelling, or exposed wiring; connectors are checked for secure fit and correct polarity; any battery pack that looks damaged or that exceeds the class's voltage cap (e.g. AWS's 24V limit) is rejected outright.
7. **Banned materials/weapons check**: the inspector visually confirms no banned weapon types are present (entanglement devices, liquid reservoirs, explosive/flame elements, RF-jamming hardware) and, for plastic-class entries, may spot-check that structural parts are visibly plastic and not a banned filament like TPU, nylon, or a carbon-fiber composite passed off as standard PLA/ABS.
8. **Sharp edge / pinch point check**: at even the smallest scale, inspectors look for exposed sharp edges, unshielded gears, or pinch points that could injure a handler during ordinary pit handling, independent of the robot's in-arena weapon.
9. **Sign-off**: once everything passes, the robot is tagged/logged as cleared to fight, sometimes with a sticker or wristband system tying the robot to its driver and confirmed weight class.

For a plastic antweight in particular, inspection is usually fast (often under two minutes) precisely because the class's material and weight limits are tight, weapon energy is low, and there's little to check beyond the basics above — one more reason it remains the easiest class to show up to an event with for the first time and get through check-in without surprises.

chunks.title: European and Other International Ruleset Variants
chunks.body_md:
Outside the US (SPARC/NHRL/RoboGames/BattleBots) and UK (AWS) rulesets, several other regional variants exist, generally built on the same underlying safety philosophy but with local adjustments for weight classes, allowed weapon types, or historical quirks.

**Fighting Robots Association (FRA)**, based in the UK, publishes its own build rules that are referenced across a number of UK and continental European events, generally complementing AWS's antweight-specific rules with guidance for a broader span of weight classes. FRA-affiliated documentation also circulates through European hobbyist mirrors (for example, a French robot-combat community site hosting an FRA build-rules PDF), reflecting how UK-style rules have propagated into continental European club scenes that don't have their own from-scratch rulebook.

**Germany** has historically taken a notably different approach to one specific banned-weapon category: rather than banning entanglement weapons outright the way SPARC, RoboGames, and AWS do, German events (associated with RoboGames-adjacent competition) have permitted entanglement devices (nets, tangling weapons) in a separate, clearly labeled 'net-fighting' side bracket kept apart from mainstream weight-class combat. This is the most commonly cited example of a national/regional ruleset carving out an explicit exception to an otherwise near-universal ban, rather than simply having laxer rules across the board.

**Australia**, via the RoboWars Australia community, is a useful counter-example to the assumption that 'international rules always mean lighter weight classes': it explicitly follows the SPARC ruleset and the same heavier US-style ladder rather than the UK/AWS scale — Australian Antweight is 1 lb (454 g), the same as US antweight, not the UK's 150 g class. Australia's ladder mirrors SPARC almost exactly (Antweight 1lb, Beetleweight 3lb, Mantisweight 6lb, Hobbyweight 12lb, Featherweight 30lb, Lightweight 60lb, Middleweight 120lb, Heavyweight 220lb) but adds one class the mainstream US ladder doesn't commonly run: a 340 lb (154 kg) Super Heavyweight tier above heavyweight. Non-wheeled robots get the standard 100% weight bonus at most classes, but that bonus shrinks to 35% specifically at the 340 lb Super Heavyweight level — presumably because a fully doubled 680 lb walking robot at that scale would be both impractical and disproportionately dangerous relative to the rest of the ladder. Australia also runs a distinct 'UltiBot' division for outdoor-terrain combat robots (30 kg for a mobile entrant, 25 kg for a fixed/stationary entrant), which has no equivalent in indoor-arena US/UK rules at all.

The overall pattern across international variants is consistency in the safety fundamentals (power disconnects, weapon locks, radio fail-safes, bans on liquids/explosives/jamming) with the most visible differences showing up in weight-class numbers and structure: the UK/AWS runs a much lighter, antweight-scale-and-below ladder (150 g down to 25 g) with a 50% non-roller bonus, while the US (SPARC/NHRL/RoboGames) and Australia (RoboWars) share a heavier ladder starting at 1 lb with a 100% walker bonus, and Australia extends that ladder one tier further with a 340 lb Super Heavyweight class at a reduced 35% bonus. Germany's net-fighting exception (permitting entanglement in a dedicated side bracket rather than mainstream classes) is the clearest example of a deliberate weapon-rule carve-out rather than a structural weight-class difference. A builder planning to compete internationally, or sourcing rules information from a non-domestic source, should treat both the weight-class numbers and the walker-bonus percentage as likely points of divergence, and should never assume a class name (especially 'Antweight') transfers its exact weight across borders without checking the specific ruleset.

chunks.title: Motorama, Robot Ruckus, and Bot Blast: The US Regional Event Circuit
chunks.body_md:
Beyond the handful of large, well-documented US organizations (NHRL, RoboGames, BattleBots), a wider circuit of regional, independently-run, SPARC-compliant events forms the backbone of where most antweight and plastic-antweight builders actually get their fight experience. Three names that come up repeatedly in the US hobby scene are Motorama, Robot Ruckus, and Bot Blast.

**Motorama** is one of the longest-running events on the US calendar, historically associated with Pennsylvania and more recently held in the Doswell, Virginia area, and is often treated as an early-season fixture that many builders use to debut a new antweight or plastic-antweight design before the rest of the year's events. Like most regional US events, it runs SPARC-compliant weight classes rather than maintaining its own separate rulebook, which is precisely the point of SPARC's existence: a robot built to spec for Motorama should need no changes to also compete at Robot Ruckus, Bot Blast, or a RoboGames combat bracket.

**Robot Ruckus** is a confirmed annual SPARC-compliant event co-located with Maker Faire Orlando at the Central Florida Fairgrounds (4603 W Colonial Dr, Orlando, FL). It splits its tournament format by class size: the insect classes (fairyweight, antweight, plastic-antweight, beetleweight) run double-elimination brackets, while the larger 12lb, 30lb, and 30lb-super-class divisions use a pools/Swiss-style fight format instead, reflecting how many more matches a small, cheap-to-repair antweight can realistically fight in a single day compared to a larger, slower-to-repair robot.

**Bot Blast** is a confirmed annual insectweight-focused event running a modified version of SPARC rather than stock SPARC. Its documented deviations are: a modified double-elimination format, a ban on autonomous robots (unlike RoboGames, which runs a dedicated autonomous division), an immediate knockout — at the presiding official's discretion — for any robot found with an exposed or damaged LiPo battery during a match (a notable safety escalation beyond baseline SPARC, reflecting how seriously the hobby treats LiPo fire risk), and simplified judging criteria relative to full SPARC judging guidelines. Bot Blast explicitly discourages 'rules-lawyering' loopholes that give an unsportsmanlike advantage, a philosophy stated directly in its published rules.

Both events, along with Motorama, illustrate why SPARC's existence matters in practice: a plastic antweight or antweight built once to SPARC spec can travel between Motorama, Robot Ruckus, and Bot Blast (and on to RoboGames or a regional NHRL-adjacent event) with at most minor, clearly-documented local adjustments (like Bot Blast's exposed-LiPo rule) rather than a full rebuild for each event's own from-scratch rulebook.
